events.title: Wayfair sales jump 10% as furniture retailer says it's winning share of sluggish market
events.summary: Wayfair said its sales jumped 10% in the third quarter as the retailer posted its strongest quarter since the pandemic. The company also reported double-digit revenue growth in the U.S. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC the growth is largely due to the company continuing to take market share in what's been a sluggish housing market. Wayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continues to win over customers and take market share. The company said it saw double-digit revenue growth in the U.S., reaching about $3 billion, an 11.4% increase from the year prior. Still, international net revenue for the quarter decreased 2.3% year over year to $380 million. Wayfair's stock jumped about 10% on Wednesday. The report comes as the housing market remains sluggish. But the furniture and home goods retailer has reported consistent growth over the past year. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair's momentum is building as it takes market share. "We see the overall consumer in the U.S. in this category, we think it's roughly flattish, and so that's our [market] share momentum continuing to build," Gulliver said. She added that shopper loyalty, the opening of new stores, the company's luxury furniture business and an emphasis on value has allowed Wayfair to win more consumers. Customers are also continuing to spend, whether at the company's value prices or on the luxury side, she added. "We've been highly promotional for the last few years, and the promotional activity this year is actually very consistent with last year," she said. "It maintains this sort of momentum on promotional activity this year." Here's how the company performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 93 cents adjusted vs. 79 cents expected Revenue: $3.42 billion vs. $3.38 billion expected For the period ended Sept. 30, Wayfair reported net income of $62 million, or 45 cents per share, compared with a loss of $99 million, or 76 cents per share, the year prior. Total revenue grew 9.7% year over year, reaching $3.42 billion. The company said its active customers grew 4.7% year over year, reaching 22.2 million. It also saw a 12.2% increase in orders delivered during the quarter to about 11 million. As the company looks ahead to the holiday season and the fourth quarter, Gulliver said it's maintaining promotional activity similar to last year. She added that Wayfair is confident that its range of prices and products will appeal to a broad base of consumers. "We've seen that growth play out," Gulliver said. "We've seen that flow through to EBITDA, ultimately to net income positive this quarter, which is really another key piece in the story and the momentum here, so we feel very good about the quarter of the performance."

events.title: ‘Out for blood’: Investigations overshadow dealmaking in newly divided Washington
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump is known to occasionally seek collaboration with — even offer praise to — his opponents. Newly ascendant Democrats, however, aren’t in much of a dealmaking mood. As Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate next year, they are already plotting out ways to investigate the president, his administration, and its allies. Democrats’ ravenous appetite for investigations — and the White House’s hostility towards them — raises serious questions about whether the two parties will be able to work together to any extent, even as administration officials begin floating opportunities for bipartisan cooperation. “They’re going to be out for blood,” one Trump administration official told Semafor. Democrats have spent Trump’s second term on the sidelines, trying to learn from the aftermath of the first Trump administration. Even before voters delivered Republicans a generational rebuke, leaders had been methodically mapping out a multi-pronged oversight approach. Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Semafor his committee will be “laser focused on four major lanes” — the Trump family, immigration, corporations, and convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. “We’ve been laying the groundwork,” said Garcia, who released a statement after the midterms advising Republicans to “lawyer up.” He predicted that every Democratic committee chair would get in on the action: “There’s more than enough corruption to go around.” Prior to the election, returning and incoming House Democrats had expressed “an incredible amount of interest” in joining the Oversight panel, Garcia said. Now, leaders in both chambers believe voters have given them free rein to take their efforts to the next level. “Americans are calling for accountability, not accomodation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday. “Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire.” The administration is already warning them to back off. “As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,′ White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Semafor. Its resistance is no surprise to Democrats, who had already begun strategizing how to circumvent Trump by probing the private sector instead. Government officials can invoke executive privilege to avoid providing documents, as they have in the Kennedy Center case ; corporate leaders cannot. “We are cognizant of lessons learned from Trump 1.0 of how much they use the courts to string out the process,” said Dan Goshorn, Senate Finance Committee Democrats’ chief investigation counsel, said. “So from our perspective, private companies have more of a reputational risk and are going to be more willing to cooperate,” Goshorn added. “We’re going to go wherever the information is.” a modicum of legislative optimism After the bruising results, Trump on Tuesday suggested he’s open to collaborating with Democrats on legislation, telling The New York Times that “we’ll probably work something out.” Some administration officials predicted Trump and Democrats could find common ground on changing immigration enforcement and addressing pharmaceutical costs — though one Trump adviser expressed skepticism at the idea of an immigration deal, pointing to exit polls showing that the issue remained one of the few Republican strengths. That adviser suggested the president and Democrats could also work together on AI — particularly rules around data centers — and other cost-of-living issues. Specific bipartisan ideas could include enacting manufacturing and clean energy tax credits or reauthorizing federal transportation programs. Trump “at his core does like dealmaking,” one person close to the White House told Semafor. But it’s unclear how long that goodwill can last amid a torrent of congressional oversight. Trump’s aides are bracing for impact, with the administration official predicting Democrats would try to tear down Trump’s new ballroom. “There’s going to be a lot more war than peace,” a former Trump administration official said. “The Democrats feel they have a mandate to torture the administration with subpoenas and lawfare.” Spending legislation will pose an early first test. Government funding is slated to lapse next month, which Garcia said Democrats will use to finalize their plans for next year. “It’s going to be very hard for Democrats to look at what happened [Tuesday] and … pass a clean continuing resolution that locks in Medicaid cuts and SNAP cuts and ICE funding and Pentagon funding after you’ve just seen the biggest mandate in the history of midterm elections against the Republican agenda,” Groundwork Collaborative’s Alex Jacquez told Semafor. Working with Democrats would also inevitably expose Trump to criticism from his own party. The person close to the White House warned a bipartisan immigration deal could “damage the GOP even further.” big oversight plans The Trump family’s “enormous amount of grift” is “at the top of [Democrats’] list,” Garcia said, now that lawmakers in both chambers will be able to schedule hearings and issue subpoenas. He pointed to the money the Trumps have made from cryptocurrency; the Russian oligarch who helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding; and Trump Jr. and Jared Kushner’s business ventures. Lawmakers also plan to scrutinize “pay-to-play and profitmaking” at the Department of Homeland Security, including by former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. And they’ll go after “corporate corruption, particularly anyone that’s worked with the Trumps to rip off the American people,” as well as the Epstein investigation. “Republicans have done little to nothing to advance it,” Garcia said of that probe. The House Judiciary Committee is bracing to tackle other corruption issues, like pardons. Other panels will delve deeper into the Trump administration’s economic policies, with many Democrats already warning that a failure to prioritize the cost of living alongside corruption could fail to attract new voters come 2028. Other bicameral priorities include the Trump administration’s oversight of the housing sector; its handling of tariff exemptions and refunds ; and its forays into Venezuela and Iran, particularly when it comes to the latter’s impact on gas prices. Schumer on Wednesday promised that Democrats would wield their power of the purse to “end the war.” Democrats have indicated little interest in impeaching Trump, but his Cabinet could be another matter. Schumer declined to say Wednesday whether the election results gave Democrats a “mandate” to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a politically divisive move. events.title: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
events.summary: CVS Health announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028, separating its pharmacy business from its insurer, Aetna, and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark. Analysts say that after a roughly two-year turnaround the company's retail pharmacy business and other units may be strong enough to stand on their own. CVS in 2024 considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable. The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark. The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own. “Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC. But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate. “For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.” CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer. Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule. "What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength." While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%. CVS's retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC. CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits. Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers. That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses. In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark. The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements.

events.title: These races matter if you care about money, Musk, and the AI boom as Democrats rack up shocking wins
events.summary: Michael Gonzalez/Getty; Brandon Bell/Getty; BI The midterms were, in part, a referendum on AI and Big Tech backlash. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk bet big on the Texas Senate race. His candidate lost. Democrats also won a key race in Ohio, and retook control of the Senate. The 2026 midterms took place on Tuesday, and results are still rolling in. Democrats won control of the House and Senate. They scored a stunning victory in Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat in a race that saw SpaceX CEO Elon Musk donate over $150 million to Republican candidate Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Beyond control of Congress, Tuesday's election will illustrate the extent of Silicon Valley's political power and the breadth of the AI backlash. In addition to the candidates, there are big ballot questions looming, none more so than the California wealth tax fight. Here are some of the key results, and what we're still watching for. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Texas Senate What happened: Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has flipped a Texas Senate seat, per The Associated Press. Talarico's defeat of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is a stunning development that some Republicans feared ever since Paxton emerged from a bitter primary and subsequent runoff. Sen. John Cornyn warned that if Paxton beat him, his fellow Republicans would need to spend gigantic sums of money to hold the seat. Enter Elon Musk. The world's richest man has been frequently trashing Talarico on X. More importantly, Musk has donated at least $158 million that has been routed to a pro-Paxton super PAC. The victory means Democrats are now within striking distance of flipping the Senate, a thought that was considered unlikely just months ago. Ohio Senate Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, walks past President Donald Trump Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images What happened: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown is returning to Congress. Per the AP, Brown has prevailed over Sen. Jon Husted, a former lieutenant governor, who was trying to hang on to former Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat. Brown, a former three-term senator, criticized Husted for his previous support for data center development. Husted has said the issue should be left to communities and no longer supports offering tax incentives for new data center construction. Earlier this summer, Senate Republicans' campaign arm warned AI labs that if Husted goes down "and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one." Pennsylvania 1st District What happened: Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie has defeated five-term Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, per the Associated Press. Harvie focused his first ad of the general election on his call for a data center moratorium. He also blasted Fitzpatrick over the Republican's previous support for a massive Amazon data center in Falls Township, which is in Bucks County. In 2024, Trump narrowly lost the district, but Fitzpatrick still easily won reelection by nearly 13 points. Michigan Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed Jeff Kowalsky/ AFP via Getty Images Michigan Senate What happened: Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, has defeated Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican, per the Associated Press. No race compares to the drama of the Michigan Senate race. On Sunday, Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed after a bitter primary, reversed herself and issued a last-minute endorsement of Rogers. Beyond the headlines, the race offers some interesting policy contrasts. Echoing Sen. Bernie Sanders (and Trump), El-Sayed has called for the government to take equity stakes in AI companies. El-Sayed also wants to force tech giants like Microsoft to divest from AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Rogers, the Republican hopeful, has called for a pause on data center development in the state. Michigan has not elected a Republican senator since 1994. Wisconsin 3rd District What happened: Democrat Rebecca Cooke, a former political consultant who went on to wait tables, has defeated incumbent two-term Wisconsin Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, per the Associated Press. Cooke has echoed Sen. Bernie Sanders' call for a federal moratorium on data center development. Cooke has also hammered Van Orden over data centers. In response, Van Orden has accused Cooke of working too closely with tech groups. Ohio 9th District What happened: Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur has won reelection in her bid against former Ohio state Rep. Derek Merrin, a Republican, per the Associated Press. Kaptur, a 22-term Ohio Democrat, represents a northwestern Ohio district that stretches from the Indiana border to just west of Cleveland. Kaptur has criticized Merrin for voting in favor of tax incentives for data center development. Merrin has said Kaptur is "lying" about his record, but as part of a sweeping 2017 budget law, Ohio lawmakers voted to extend the deadline for certain data centers to qualify for tax incentives. Kaptur is one of 22 Democrats in this year's midterms who represented districts where Trump won. The president took her district by roughly 11 points in 2024, per The Downballot estimates. Kaptur won by under 2,400 votes that year. Michigan 7th District What happened: Democratic candidate William Lawrence defeated Rep. Tom Barrett of Michigan, a Republican, per the Associated Press. Lawrence, a cofounder of the progressive climate-focused organization Sunrise Movement, sought to tie Barrett to a proposed $1 billion hyperscale data center near Mason, Michigan. Barrett previously said said that local officials should be able to make decisions about data centers, contrasting his views with Lawrence's support of a data center moratorium. Two competing proposals would effectively nullify the proposed tax. The sides: The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West labor union proposed the tax. Rep. events.title: Democrats take Congress in a blue wave. Here's what it means for your money
events.summary: Democrats’ blue wave gives the party control of both chambers of Congress, with rising costs a top voter concern. The new majority could pursue changes involving health insurance, taxes, student loans, housing and Social Security, among other pocketbook issues. President Donald Trump’s veto power limits what Democrats can enact alone, and any changes will take time. With Democrats flipping control of Congress in the midterm election , the shift in power on Capitol Hill could reshape household budgets — from student loan bills and health insurance premiums to housing costs and taxes. Experts say results show that rising costs were top of mind for voters. "I see this election as a repudiation of the anti-affordability agenda from the Trump administration," said Daniel Bunn, president and CEO of the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization. "Whether that's the conflict in the Middle East or the tariffs, just top to bottom, it's clear to me that was a real concern of the electorate," he said. Midterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in an emailed statement that the Trump administration has delivered "tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families." Officials "will continue to put hardworking American's first with or without support from Democrats," he wrote. Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, which could make it easier for the party to advance legislation. They can also use hearings and investigations to press federal agencies and companies to answer for policies and practices that impact consumers, and exert leverage over confirmation of President Donald Trump's nominees. But turning campaign promises into changes people feel in their finances won't be easy. Trump can veto bills a Democrat-controlled Congress passes, limiting how much of their agenda could become law. Based on projections, Democrats will lack the numbers needed to override a presidential veto. Any changes will also take time: Newly elected members of Congress won't take office until January. Here are eight ways Democrats’ new congressional majority could affect your money. "Not surprisingly, the Dems are going to be keyed in on affordability with respect to healthcare," said Zach Gaumer, vice president of health policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank. ACA subsidies: Democrats could try to reinstate at least a portion of the enhanced premium subsidies for Affordable Care Act marketplace insurance plans, Gaumer said. Those enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025 , after the Republican-controlled Congress and Trump declined to extend them . Millions of ACA enrollees saw their monthly insurance premiums increase sharply as a result. Medicaid: Starting in 2027, states will be required to implement work requirements as a condition of Medicaid enrollment, due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act the Republican-led Congress passed in 2025. Democrats will likely try to loosen those rules, and thereby avoid a large increase in the number of uninsured, Gaumer said. Long-term care: Medicare generally doesn't cover long-term care services, but Democrats may try to add some LTC coverage to the program's purview, Gaumer said. "That's an interest of several Democrats on the Hill right now," he said. OBBBA made Trump's 2017 tax cuts permanent and added temporary tax breaks. These included new deductions for tip income , overtime earnings , seniors and auto loan interest , which will expire after 2028 without an extension. Democrats may support extending these provisions. But as the Democrat-controlled Congress maps out its agenda, lawmakers will have to address the federal budget deficit. For fiscal year 2026, the budget deficit ballooned to nearly $2 trillion , the Treasury announced in October. Newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Annie Andrews of South Carolina all campaigned on expanding the child tax credit . Earlier this year, Senate Democrats also floated ideas to expand the standard deduction and create income tax exemptions for lower-earning Americans — which are costly proposals, according to Bunn from the Tax Foundation. "I've called these termites in the tax code," he said. "You cannot consistently narrow your base, especially for the income tax, and expect your spending priorities to be well-funded.

events.title: New Flutter CEO bets on FanDuel promotions to win customers as profits suffer
events.summary: Flutter's new CEO Dan Taylor issued his first earnings report as CEO on Wednesday. Third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization missed Wall Street's expectations. Taylor said there's been fierce competition for customers but FanDuel is improving the product and seeing good momentum. Flutter's new CEO Dan Taylor is counting on better products and more generous customer rewards to help convert FanDuel's improving engagement into stronger profits. Taylor's been at the helm for just five weeks and issued his first earnings report as CEO on Wednesday, with third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization missing Wall Street's expectations. The company's stock is down more than 60% year to date. Yet Taylor says the company is now on the right track. "We made some changes to the product," Taylor told CNBC in an interview. "Fundamentally, the way you win this business is by delighting customers, delivering the very best experiences and delivering to them in the way that they want, with the right overall proposition." FanDuel also launched a nationwide rewards program in September that Taylor said has "resonated really, really well." The early customer numbers are improving. Average monthly players on FanDuel's U.S. sportsbook rose 9% in the third quarter, while bet counts increased 15%, Taylor said. Flutter's earnings release showed total U.S. average monthly players up 12%, including 24% growth in iGaming. Sportsbook handle, or the total amount wagered, rose 13%, but sportsbook revenue grew just 4% as promotional spending increased. Taylor said the company plans to keep investing in customer experience. He said Flutter sees room to improve its structural margins over time by changing the mix of products customers use. Flutter has increased its media spend to build FanDuel Predicts, its predictions platform to rival Kalshi and Polymarket, but the cost of sales as a percent of revenue is forecast to be 58% for the full-year 2026 and into 2027. Taylor said there's fierce industry competition for customers but even still, FanDuel trading volume has skyrocketed 271% since July. The FanDuel Predicts app added 140,000 new customers in October, Taylor said. Taylor also defended the long-term opportunity in the U.S., pointing out about half the country still does not have access to regulated sports betting and 90% lacks regulated online gaming. He argued that expanding legal markets is not a partisan issue because regulated betting offers consumer protections and gives tax revenue to states. For the third quarter, Flutter reported an adjusted loss of 18 cents per share, compared with analysts' expectations for a loss of 28 cents, according to LSEG. Revenue rose 2% to $3.87 billion, below the roughly $4 billion LSEG consensus, while adjusted EBITDA fell roughly 25% year over year to $360 million, also below expectations. The company posted a net loss of $1.15 billion, including an $873 million non-cash impairment tied primarily to Brazil, which banned sports betting and online gaming in September. Taylor said the company was disappointed by Brazil's provisional measure, but took the impairment to "set ourselves up to win long-term." The complications in Brazil and unfavorable sports results in the U.S. and internationally led Flutter to cut its full-year revenue midpoint by $300 million to $17.61 billion and lower its 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook by $160 million to nearly $2.5 billion. In the meantime, capital returns are on hold: Taylor said Flutter needs to bring leverage back into its target range of 2 to 2.5 times over roughly the next 24 months before it can consider buybacks again. For now, he said, the priority is organic growth and paying down debt. — CNBC's Mallory Leonard contributed to this report.

events.title: Skincare brand accused of using AI to copy competitors' imagery
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Skincare brand BodyBlendz accused of using AI-edited versions of competitors' imagery A comparison of Lucy Alcorn's image (left) and one posted by BodyBlendz at a later date. ( Instagram: @lucy_alcorn and @body_blendz ) Internationally stocked skincare brand BodyBlendz has been accused of using AI-edited advertising imagery produced by its small business competitors. A Sydney photographer says there needs to be fewer financial barriers to pursuing claims against brands that use others' imagery. Australia is building what it hopes will be a world-leading national framework for AI regulation. An ABC News Breakfast investigation has unearthed multiple accusations the internationally-stocked brand BodyBlendz — which was once promoted by reality star Kim Kardashian on Instagram — has used imagery made for other brands without their consent. One of its accusers, Sydney-based photographer Lucy Alcorn, believes the case demonstrates Australia needs stronger guardrails to protect creatives against a deluge of AI-generated content. "My whole body of work that's online suddenly feels so vulnerable. What would stop anyone else from doing that? It's very scary," Ms Alcorn said. Ms Alcorn alleges several promotional images that appeared on BodyBlendz's Instagram account had been copied from images she shot for another skincare brand, Luna Bronze, possibly using AI. "Especially, the model's face has been shifted," she said. "You can see that it's 70 to 80 per cent my original image. I don't think it would be worth the retoucher's time to do that." Luna Bronze co-founder Maddy Balderson told ABC News Breakfast that a single shoot could cost the brand $30,000 to $50,000 — a large investment the small business had to carve out every year. "It's not just the dollars we spend on the shoot; it's the time. They've skipped making that investment, that creative time." The company has since removed the images. BodyBlendz has not responded to multiple requests for comment from ABC News Breakfast. Others accuse BodyBlendz of using images A UK sunscreen brand has also accused BodyBlendz of using images similar to its own, while an Australian reality TV star has claimed BodyBlendz used their picture without consent. In a statement, Stil Suncare founder Tash Hagan said she was "genuinely mind-blown", and particularly thrown by the fact BodyBlendz's social media post appeared to include an AI-generated face with an uncanny resemblance to her own. After Ms Hagan voiced her concerns publicly on social media, BodyBlendz removed the post and several others, including the post allegedly copying Ms Alcorn's work. She said the brand never publicly responded. But after her friend sent BodyBlendz a private message on Instagram, the brand's team responded, saying they had been unaware and were "genuinely sorry imagery from your friend's original post appears to have been used". The message also said the brand respected the work that had gone into creating the original content and would speak to its marketing team to prevent it happening again. An Instagram direct message from BodyBlendz, apologising for using imagery. ( Supplied ) BodyBlendz has previously been accused of using an image of Married At First Sight participant Martha Kalifatidis without her consent in a stockist's 2019 advertising brochure. ABC News Breakfast has contacted Ms Kalifatidis for comment. Legal action too costly for small businesses and sole traders Neither Ms Alcorn nor Ms Hagan pursued legal action against the brand, saying the costs involved were too high compared with any potential compensation. Ms Alcorn said Australia needed a small claims court to deal with similar cases, brought on by the surge in AI-generated content. University of Melbourne Associate Professor of Law Jason Bosland agreed the legal system would benefit from introducing small claims courts. "With a range of different courses of action, such as copyright and even defamation, it would be good to have simplified mechanisms by which those rights could be enforced," he said. Australia is attempting to position itself as a world leader in artificial intelligence safeguards, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese planning to tackle copyright issues via a national framework. However, a leaked proposal has sparked concerns the government is considering changes to Australia's copyright laws. A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the government was "continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation".

events.title: Voters rebuff data centers in every ballot measure except one during the 2026 midterms
events.summary: 41 data center-related ballot measures were up for a vote in the 2026 midterm elections in 10 states. Voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in nearly every contest with results available Wednesday, with Harwood, North Dakota, the exception. Anti-data-center messaging also featured in major Democratic wins in Ohio and Texas, increasing political risk for the AI infrastructure buildout. The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans. There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia . Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. The City of Harwood voted against a charter rule amendment that would have required additional review before city approval of industrial developments, including data centers. In Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers," 21 local measures were up for a vote, according to Ballotpedia. The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue. OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website . SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year. Nvidia is also backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total. The Ohio governor's mansion also turned blue, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor." Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process. Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder. Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot. In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans. Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030. In one of the biggest results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying he put the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities. Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million. Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, largely came up empty. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X. The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry as a whole. Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath. Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus. "The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath.

events.title: Democratic progressive wing notches win in California Central Valley
events.summary: Campaign focused on cost of living issues and backlash over ICE raids pays dividends for progressive Randy Villegas. Reporting from Bakersfield, California Democratic candidate Randy Villegas has defeated Republican incumbent David Valadao in the race for California’s 22nd congressional district, clinching one of the state’s most closely watched congressional races and notching another win for the Democratic Party’s progressive left. Villegas, an educator who grew up in the Central Valley as the son of Mexican immigrants, ousted the Republican representative after a campaign that won support from figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and railed against the rising cost of living, healthcare cuts, and sweeping immigration raids . list 1 of 3 Surging ICE raids shadow final weeks of California congressional race list 2 of 3 Democratic Party gains US House majority in 2026 midterm elections list 3 of 3 Democrats deliver a historic rout to Republicans in US midterms “I want to take a moment to acknowledge my family. Both of my parents, who I’m blessed to have with me here today. I’ve gotta tell you, the reason I believe in this country, the reason I believe in the United States, is because of the sacrifices that they made,” Villegas said in remarks to his supporters gathered in the city of Bakersfield on Tuesday evening, calling the result a “historic victory for the Central Valley”. “And let me tell you, that victory is not because of me. It is because of us,” he added. Here are some of the key takeaways from the race. The story of the district fits a larger one playing out across the country as votes come in on election night: angry about surging prices that were driven partly by the Trump administration’s decision to launch a war on Iran, and overreach in areas such as ICE raids, voters decided to punish the president and his party. Polls had indicated for months that the president had become deeply unpopular, and that this trend was closely linked to collapsing faith in his handling of the economy and cost of living, issues that had previously helped return him to the White House in 2024. Despite his image as a relative moderate with strong ties to the Central Valley, Valadao did not escape that trend on Tuesday night. Immigration raids trigger backlash among Latino voters Following Trump’s win in 2024, much was made of the Republican Party’s successful inroads with Latino voters despite the party’s embrace of rhetoric vilifying immigrants and restrictive immigration policies. Less than two years later, those promising gains have entirely evaporated. Incensed over the administration’s aggressive and often indiscriminate approach to immigration enforcement and the toll of rising prices, Latino voters across the country swung heavily back towards the Democrats. “We have people who said that they regret having voted for him [Trump], because he has not done what he promised,” a member of the United Farm Workers (UFW) labour union who knocked doors in Latino communities for Villegas, told Al Jazeera on Monday. Residents and officials in the Central Valley said that ICE raids sent shockwaves through immigrant and Latino communities, with arrests of farmworkers and family members cutting against the administration’s claims that it was targeting criminals. Villegas slammed the raids and linked them to Valadao’s support for a massive increase in the budget for ICE, one of the agencies at the centre of the mass deportation raids. A recent survey from the Pew Research Center found that 56 percent of US voters now view ICE unfavourably, making it one of the least popular agencies in the federal government. Progressives make the case for their competitiveness Before facing off against Valadao on Tuesday night, Villegas had to win a hard-fought primary race against California State Assembly member Jasmeet Bains, a candidate aligned with the party’s establishment wing who warned that his progressive positions would be too far to the left in the traditionally conservative region. But Villegas and his supporters challenged that premise. His populist message seems to have resonated in a race dominated by concerns about the cost of living and access to healthcare, and at a time when many feel that politics and the economy are skewed in favour of the wealthy and well-connected. Villegas won endorsements from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and energised supporters from the party’s base, including members of organised labour who pounded the pavement to get out the vote. “We beat the Democratic establishment. We beat the Republican establishment. We beat corporate PAC money. We beat AIPAC!” Villegas told supporters on Tuesday night. Villegas can now add his name to the list of elected officials seeking to prove that progressives can win tough races outside of traditional strongholds.

events.title: McDonald's stock rises as earnings beat, U.S. restaurants show improvement
events.summary: McDonald's quarterly earnings topped expectations, but its revenue fell short of estimates. The chain's U.S. same-store sales declined, but CEO Chris Kempczinski said its domestic performance is improving. McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners. As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expected Revenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expected The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates. The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. "In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well." France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.

events.title: What Republicans' huge loss means for Trump
events.summary: Democrats won sweeping midterm election victories in the House and Senate, shaking up Washington and putting President Donald Trump in a bind. Trump still wields significant presidential powers and has strongly signaled that he plans to veto Democratic bills. Democrats plan to launch a slew of investigations that are widely expected to consume much of the rest of Trump's term. Democrats just put President Donald Trump in a bind. The party is projected to win commanding majorities in the House and Senate after thrashing Republicans in key races up and down the ballot across the country. The blue tsunami will knock Washington on its head and crush the Republican congressional bulwark that both supported and shielded Trump through the first two years of his term. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results The midterm result snuffs out any chance Trump had of passing partisan legislation in the second half of his presidency. And many of the interests he has been able to pursue without Congress' input — including tariffs , the Iran war and an array of Washington-area construction projects — are sure to face sudden pushback from newly empowered Democratic majorities. The paradigm shift hardly leaves Trump helpless, however. As president at a time of executive power expansion , Trump wields singular authorities that could stymie Democrats' efforts to pursue their own agendas. Live updates: Day 2 of 2026 midterm election results A blow to billionaire donors and a reckoning for tech companies — 5 takeaways Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it But with his grip on the Capitol shriveling and his approval ratings scraping record lows in numerous polls, it's unclear how much support he'll be able to muster to fight the coming political battles. Even before Election Day, analysts and pundits had contemplated a Democratic rout so decisive that it would force a reckoning for the GOP, and potentially even pose an existential threat to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. Marc Short, chairman of Advancing American Freedom and onetime chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence , told CNBC on Tuesday afternoon that the GOP has moved away from its conservative foundations. "We need a refresh right now," Short said in an interview. "We've lost our way." Trump has been vague about what he hopes to achieve with the rest of his term. But he has shared a vision of how he might coexist with a Democratic majority, and it involves heavy use of the veto pen. "It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump said in a Fox News interview overnight. "They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them." "And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said, adding, "I have a lot of friends that are Democrats." Trump has previously stated his willingness to veto reams of legislation that Democrats send across his desk. In a New York Post podcast interview released Monday, Trump said that if Republicans don't win, "I veto everything." Pressed to detail his plans for the next two years, Trump touted his record and said, "The most important thing is to keep it going. It's going to get better and better and better, unless people come in that hate our country." If that happens, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said. He may soon get his chance: House Democrats, poised to be led by current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned. The legislative push, first reported by The New York Times, aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries. In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to introduce bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law earlier this year. Democrats also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the war with Iran, or seek congressional authorization to keep it going. But without Trump's approval, those bills may end up as little more than symbolic gestures, as Democrats will lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers that are required to override a presidential veto without GOP help. And there's no guarantee the bills will even make it out of Congress: Despite their landslide victories, Senate Democrats will still end up shy of the 60 votes required to bypass the chamber's filibuster rules for most legislation, giving Republicans key leverage in the minority. Democrats also could feasibly benefit from Trump's vetoes in the long term.

events.title: Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
events.summary: Published 4 November 2026, 00:03 GMT Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse. The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk. A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but has been brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies. Gordon Brothers has previously said Poundland faces multiple economic challenges from rising inflation, increasing staff costs, and "severe levels of shoplifting". Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made. On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers". "He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added. It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units. However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up. Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency. Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece. "We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs." Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday. Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing. "We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said. Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday. Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores". "There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added. The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust. Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales. The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m. Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year. Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they". This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse. Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday. He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company. "Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added. "All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together." Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces. If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed. Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Published 2 days ago If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent. Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.

events.title: Deadly Learjet crash has elites reconsidering private air travel
events.summary: The site where a Learjet crashed in Florida, killing all nine people on board. GREG LOVETT/PALM BEACH POST via Reuters Connect In the wake of the deadly Learjet crash, some are reconsidering flying private. Tech investor Jason Calacanis said ditching private jets for commercial travel. A Learjet 60 crashed in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board. The deadly business jet crash in Florida has some wealthy travelers rethinking the appeal of flying private. Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," said he's done flying on Learjet 60s after one plunged from the sky into a Palm Beach County neighborhood on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard . "Never getting in a Lear 60 again," Calacanis wrote Tuesday in a post on X, adding that he plans to fly commercial instead. "And with commercial being 10x cheaper and 10x safer, I'm only flying the big iron from the majors," wrote Calacanis. Fatal crashes involving private charter aircraft are generally more frequent than those involving commercial airlines, but they remain rare. According to National Transportation Safety Board data , on-demand charter airplanes were involved in two fatal accidents in 2024, representing 0.06 fatal accidents per 100,000 flight hours. Scheduled commercial airlines recorded no fatal accidents that year. (The charter category includes private jets as well as smaller aircraft.) Calacanis also questioned whether flying private is even worth it, saying, "What's the point of saving two hours on average when you have starlink on 50% of @united flight already." Calacanis ended his post with: "See you in the lounge besties." Never getting in a Lear 60 again And with commercial being 10x cheaper and 10x safer, I’m only flying the big iron from the majors What’s the point of saving two hours on average when you have starlink on 50% of @united flight already See you in the lounge besties — @jason (@Jason) November 3, 2026 Texas tech founder Adam Robinson , his wife, and their two young children were among those killed when the Bahamas-bound Learjet they were flying on over the weekend went down. The cause of the crash remains under investigation. Pilots on board reported a buildup of ice and turbulence shortly before the jet nosedived. Seattle-based tech investor Ben Sharpe replied to Calacanis' post, saying he was "thinking the same" about private travel. Was thinking the same Jason. Flying private saves you at most a few hours, costs $50-80k more and has considerably higher chance of failure over commercial airplanes. Had the family opted to fly commercial, they would have been at a restaurant or airport lounge on a layover to Bahamas and alive. The risk of death flying commercial is essentially zero. — Ben Sharpe (@kedlinco) November 4, 2026 "Flying private saves you at most a few hours, costs $50-80k more and has considerably higher chance of failure over commercial airplanes," Sharpe wrote. "Had the family opted to fly commercial, they would have been at a restaurant or airport lounge on a layover to Bahamas and alive," he said. "The risk of death flying commercial is essentially zero." Lost a good friend in a private jet accident, I'd encourage everyone reading this to simply fly commercial whenever possible. Statistically, it's much safer. I know private jets are convenient, but unless you have a good reason, take the big plane, fly with the people — Adam Singer (@AdamSinger) November 2, 2026 Adam Singer, a marketing executive at the platform AdQuick, said in a Monday X post that he "lost a good friend in a private jet accident" and encouraged everyone to fly commercial whenever possible. "Statistically, it's much safer," Singer said. "I know private jets are convenient, but unless you have a good reason, take the big plane, fly with the people." events.title: States agreed to ‘fully, finally, and forever’ release Meta from claims they didn’t know existed — with $459 million for Cambridge Analytica claims
events.summary: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election. But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting . I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare . My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations . I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely. My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data. Investigative failures The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse. The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.” The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data. At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S. A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “ People You May Know ,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse . Meta said it would appeal the decision. Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica. Escaping further scrutiny Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated. In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states. The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed. A decade-old matter – Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal – was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens. From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal , settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime. Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation , but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “ We’re just getting started .” Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “ Facebook’s unjust enrichment .” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement. What price for the harm? The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects. If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win. The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court. Emma L. events.title: America’s grid upgrade hinges on a 400-ton machine designed in the 1800s — and just one U.S. mill makes the special steel inside it
events.summary: Americans have a lot of plans for the country’s power grid. Some people want to expand renewable energy by building solar and wind farms . Others want to add new coal- or natural gas-fired power plants . There are those who want to provide power to some unknown number of data centers processing artificial intelligence algorithms. To accomplish any of these goals, the country will need a significant number of pieces of equipment whose design was invented in the late 19th century: large power transformers . These giant metal structures are about the size of a two-story house and weigh as much as 400 tons – roughly equivalent to a fully loaded Boeing 747 . They convert high voltages used to transmit electricity down to voltage levels people can use in their homes and businesses. And they are made largely in the same way they were when they were invented 150 years ago . Many of the large power transformers in service in the U.S. and around the world are aging beyond their intended lifespans . And there aren’t enough replacements to meet the world’s needs. It can take more than three years for a company’s order to be filled and delivered. Transformers as transport systems Large power transformers are crucial to transporting electricity over long distances . Power plants – whether coal- or gas-fired, hydropower dams, or solar or wind farms – are often far from the customers who need the electricity that’s generated. Transmitting power through wires generates heat , which over a long distance dramatically reduces the amount of energy arriving at the far end. To reduce energy losses, power companies use large transformers to increase the voltage. You can think of this like freight being loaded onto large trucks and directed over interstate highways. They can carry a lot of energy more efficiently than smaller cars could on smaller roads. But the high-voltage power is not safe for a home or business to use right away, just as a semitruck at highway speeds shouldn’t try to enter your driveway. So when the power arrives near a group of customers, it needs to take an off-ramp, going through another large transformer that lowers its voltage to levels regular customers can use. Then low-voltage lines act as local city streets, delivering the electricity the short distance from the highway exit to homes and businesses. Between 2019 and 2025, demand for generator step-up transformers, those that connect power plants to the transmission grid, nearly tripled . And over the same period, demand for transformers to work as off-ramps more than doubled, with costs increasing 80% . These devices are not mass-produced from automated assembly lines. They are custom-engineered to meet specific needs and demands for their intended destinations. If a specialized transformer fails during an extreme storm or heat wave, there aren’t just replacements waiting in a warehouse somewhere. The supply chain trap What these transformers are made of is a big part of the delay. One key ingredient is what’s known as grain-oriented electrical steel . This is not at all average steel. It is manufactured using precise thermal and mechanical processes that position the steel’s magnetic crystals in a single direction. The crystalline alignment allows magnetic fields to pass through the metal with low energy loss, which is crucial for handling large amounts of electricity. However, only a handful of specialized steel mills worldwide have the technology to produce it. Just one mill is in the U.S. Also in short supply is copper , which is made into wires that are wrapped around the core of the transformer , typically made of steel, to achieve the correct voltage adjustment. Work-around has its own problems Because of the transformer shortage, it can take utilities and power producers more than two years to get equipment to connect new power plants to the grid – regardless of whether they are powered by nuclear energy, fossil fuels, solar energy or the wind. To get around that delay, companies that run data centers to power artificial intelligence systems have sought to bypass the grid altogether, by installing dedicated, on-site natural gas power plants to run the computer centers. That move has caused another supply chain problem . Gas turbines burn at over 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,100 C), which is hot enough to melt standard steel. Turbine blades are manufactured with a complicated process out of very specialized combinations of metal and coated with ceramic heat shields . As tech companies have placed more and larger orders, the time between ordering a gas turbine and having it delivered has stretched to between three and seven years . And prices in 2027 are expected to be nearly triple what they were in 2019 , due to the increase in demand and still-rare materials. What can be done? A supply chain built in the 19th century is struggling to reliably serve power to the 21st-century economy. Large power transformers are also key to upgrading the existing grid and reducing its vulnerability to large storms or extended outages . The solutions are both concrete and complicated. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has recommended standardizing transformer designs , rather than having each be custom-built. That would allow manufacturers to produce more units more quickly, with an assembly line-style process. It would also allow utility companies to share emergency spares. The U.S. Department of Energy has recommended deploying what are collectively called “ grid-enhancing technologies .” These methods include sensors that monitor in real time exactly how much power can be transmitted through long-distance wires and advanced software that can find alternative routes by which to distribute electricity from power plants to maximize what’s available to customers. Together, these types of systems can allow the transmission of 15% to 20% more electricity than without them, easing bottlenecks while waiting for new transformers to be delivered. Longer term, the U.S. could produce more grain-oriented electrical steel, process more copper and expand its capacity to build large power transformers. All the ways people want to adapt, improve, expand and modernize the power grid are dependent on this one type of equipment. Without large power transformers, none of the efforts will get very far. In a sense, leaders face a choice either way: solve these hardware shortages or accept the default consequences of grid congestion, delayed projects and rising costs. Resolving the transformer bottleneck would be what turns that passive reality into active choice. Jasmine Garland , Chancellors Postdoctoral Fellow in Civil, Environmental and Architectural Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.
