events.title: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change
events.summary: Published 4 November 2026, 01:14 GMT Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change. Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead. A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before". The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound. Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals. The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them. Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting". "There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them." Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years". "I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk." Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale". The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s. Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before". Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed. When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version. No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada, which are owned by a separate company. Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices. Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company said Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version. "We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said. The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future". The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food. A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates. Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same. However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. It also continues to contain barley-malt extract. Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? Published 21 August Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals. Many parts of the world have been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves this year due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely affect crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice. The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027. That will intensify pressure on food manufacturing companies, already looking at ways to source reliable and affordable ingredients. The original Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023. The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food. The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero .

events.title: The richest 10% outspend the poorest quarter over 13 to 1 per child on childcare, education and activities — up from about 3 to 1 in the early 1980s
events.summary: In 1848, the education reformer Horace Mann called public schooling “the great equalizer of the conditions of men.” More than 175 years later, education scholars are still arguing about whether he was right. Some research finds that a child’s family background shapes their academic achievement far more than schools do . Other work finds that schools narrow academic achievement gaps that would otherwise be even wider . A classic study following Baltimore children in the 1980s found that low-income and wealthier kids learned at similar rates during the school year . Achievement gaps grew over the summer, when some children read with parents, visited libraries and went to camp, while others didn’t have those same opportunities. How much summer learning loss exists is still an open question. But the larger point holds: Gaps between rich and poor children in reading and math skills are already large on the first day of kindergarten , driven by factors outside of K-12 schooling. For a given group of students, those gaps then stay about the same size through the school years. I am a scholar of education policy who studies the different factors that shape students’ learning, including teachers and the quality of their instruction. Instead of measuring how much students learn at school, as is often the case, my colleagues and I recently measured what students receive in and out of school : the school funding, education support services and time that schools, government programs and families put into each child. By some measures, schools really are an equalizer for children from different backgrounds – but this finding has its limits. A gap that starts early in childhood In our 2026 study , we combined data from 10 nationally representative government surveys to track 77 kinds of investments, as we call them, that contribute to raising and educating children. This includes teachers, tutoring, housing, food and childcare. We also measured factors that don’t have a direct cost, such as the time parents and caregivers spend reading with children. We put a dollar value on each factor – valuing parents’ time at the average U.S. hourly wage, for example – so we could add them up and compare what children from different backgrounds receive. Counting government investment, family spending and the time parents spend with their children, the average child in the U.S. receives about US$502,000 from birth to age 18, our analysis shows. The gaps in how much different children receive start early. Before age 5, children from the poorest fourth of families receive about $44,000 less in total investments than children from the richest fourth – marking a gap of 24%. Most of that early difference comes from housing and childcare costs. However, a striking pattern emerges as children transition into elementary school. The gap in total investment between the richest and poorest children is cut in half, from 24% to 12%. For Black children, the benefit of starting school is even greater. Investment gaps between Black and white children shrink from 20% in early childhood years to 7% once kindergarten begins. This matters because research shows that more school spending improves students’ achievement and long-term outcomes , especially for those from low-income families . So why don’t achievement gaps close during the school years? Catching up vs. getting ahead Part of the answer is what money buys. Our research shows that once children are in school, those from the lowest-income families receive 72% more in tutoring and 68% more in special education than those from the highest-income families, and Black children receive more than twice as much tutoring as white children. These services are meant to help students catch up. A dollar spent catching up is not the same as a dollar spent getting ahead. Tutoring has long been one of schools’ main catch-up tools, and since the pandemic, schools have leaned on it more than ever . It’s a reasonable bet. Studies that randomly assign students to tutoring find some of the largest test-score gains of any school program . Schools serving many low-income students have long been able to use federal Title I money for tutoring . Pandemic relief money made a bigger push possible. Congress sent schools nearly $190 billion , and the largest round was divided among districts the same way as Title I money , so high-poverty districts got more. By 2022-23, more than a third of public schools offered “ high-dosage” tutoring , meaning frequent sessions in small groups. Schools serving more low-income students and students of color were more likely to offer it . But for many low-income, Black and Latino students, tutoring wasn’t new. In our data, collected from 2014 to 2021, about 17% of school-age children were being tutored, including 25% of Black children and 19% of Latino children, compared with 14% of white children. For Black, Latino and low-income children who received tutoring, over 75% got that support from public schools. Early in the recovery, at least, the share of students getting tutoring didn’t appear to grow much. A nationally representative survey of parents in fall 2022 found about 15% of students were being tutored. Meanwhile, the pandemic widened achievement gaps. Students in high-poverty districts still trail those in wealthier districts by more than students in the same grades did before the pandemic. Schools leaned harder on catch-up help that low-income, Black and Latino students were already getting. Federal relief money did help high-poverty districts recover . But even with that help, gaps remain wider than before the pandemic. Who gets ahead Catch-up help is only half the picture. Wealthier children also get more of the resources that help them pull ahead, in school and out. Some studies show, for example, that low-income students and students of color are more likely than richer, white students to have newer, less experienced teachers . Our study documents the same pattern. The differences are even starker outside of school. In our data, wealthier families invest far more in music lessons, sports and other activities that can help kids get ahead. Related research shows that by 2024, the richest 10% of families spent more than 13 times as much per child as the poorest quarter on childcare, education and extracurricular activities – up from about three times as much in the early 1980s. Equal spending isn’t enough Our findings show that public education is the main reason the investment gap between rich and poor children shrinks once kids turn 5. But equal spending is not equal opportunity. Much of the extra school spending on low-income, Black and Latino children goes to making up for gaps that opened before they started school. Meanwhile, wealthier children keep getting more of the experienced teachers and enrichment that help them pull ahead. events.title: Trump approved nearly 90% of disaster aid requests from all-Republican states and only 23% from all-Democratic ones
events.summary: Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades . Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again . I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University , I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “ Beyond Common Ground .” The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet. Federal help is less predictable The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades. Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states . Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s . Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the Panhandle, one of his “favorite places .” There, a January 2025 snowstorm was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages. Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, compared with about 42% from states he lost . While the White House has denied that politics plays a role in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025. FEMA owes local governments almost $10 billion in reimbursements for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as 15% of their annual budget . Philanthropies and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps. Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can build cooperation, trust and collective action , which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery. What connected places do In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the EF3 tornado that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors. School administrators turned the local high school into a shelter the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund. That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed. Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them . A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents pay their insurance deductibles . Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together. After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, the figure hit only 45% . The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states. My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll : bonding ties and linking ties. Bonding ties connect neighbors and family. Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans. Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022 . Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan . A low-cost layer of protection In my new book , I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery. Federal aid may go to rebuild some of these spaces, but it rarely pays to keep them open and running when communities need them most. In another study, I found that Japanese communities with higher density of social infrastructure had half the number of deaths from a catastrophic tsunami in March 2011 compared to similar communities with fewer gathering spaces . In my assessment, as federal aid becomes less predictable, these kinds of places people frequent often will have to carry us into the future. The communities that recover best from the next disaster may be the ones that kept their libraries open, their civic halls full of volunteers and their parks full of residents. Daniel P. Aldrich , Professor of Political Science, Public Policy and Urban Affairs, Northeastern University This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. events.title: Hyperscalers and Apple surge after election results remove investor uncertainty
events.summary: Many of the biggest technology companies are surging on Wednesday, after Democrats scored a seismic victory in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate. Tuesday's election results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, and analysts say they are poised to benefit from increased regulation. During trading on Wednesday, Amazon surged 8%, Google rose over 6%, Microsoft rose 4%, Meta was up 3%, and Apple — which faced Trump's tariffs and recently got refunds — climbed nearly 7%. Tuesday's results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." He said the divided government would lead to "moderation in growth, moderation in inflation, less uncertainty, and I think that's all helping the stock market move up today." However, some stocks, particularly those tied to Trump advisor Elon Musk as well as the AI data center buildout, fell on Wednesday. As results came in last night, some observers saw bad news for big technology companies because of their bets to build large AI-focused data centers. There were 41 local ballot measures on Tuesday to place restrictions or clear the way for AI data centers, and voters sided against data centers in 40 of them. In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their voting decision. Analysts said that Democrats who proposed data center moratoriums won gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, raising fears that projects could get snarled in regulation or blocked by politicians. "Recall that backup power emissions, zoning, water, interconnect/grid, and tax considerations are often overseen by state regulators," Macquarie analyst Paul Golding said in a note on Wednesday. Tesla stock fell 2%, and SpaceX was down 3%. Nvidia, which makes the chips for most of these AI data center projects, slipped just over 1%. Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, or the largest cloud providers that also pair massive capex spending with robust free cash flow and have the most experience and capability to construct AI data centers. "We believe higher regulatory barriers entrench incumbents, and increase risks (and raise required ROICs) for new entrants," wrote Needham analyst Laura Martin in a note on Wednesday. "Hyperscalers are AI incumbents." Smaller AI cloud providers, often called neoclouds, got whacked on Wednesday. CoreWeave stock fell 10%. Baird analysts said in a note that the election results create a "sentiment headwind" for neoclouds. Golding, the Macquarie analyst, wrote that he remains bullish on AI infrastructure, and that well-capitalized, high-quality operators stand to benefit the most if projects in some states slow down. "Neoclouds may pay more to lease powered shells for GPUaaS commitments (and pass on costs), while hyperscaler/AI lab capacity needs could intensify competition for even more limited supply," Golding wrote. Tuesday's results could signal restrictions on new data center developments in some states, but it doesn't necessarily signal a nationwide slowdown in construction, Chris Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute , said in an email. Companies are still raising capital, enterprises are spending, and there's still a need for more capacity. Miglino said that increased regulation in some regions could cause investors and customers to look more closely at different cloud computing providers, and opt for those with the capability to deliver capacity, or which offer AI inference to a specific industry niche. "If you've already secured power, have the financing in place and understand how to deploy and operate compute infrastructure efficiently, you're in a much stronger position than a company that's still trying to figure those things out," Miglino said.

events.title: Oil prices plunge after Vance post on Iran war
events.summary: Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Oil prices fell sharply Wednesday as traders weigh signs — including a widely circulated post by Vice President JD Vance — that the midterm election will add pressure on the White House to find an offramp from the Iran conflict. Why it matters: Elections have consequences. Wednesday's price drop — around $8 per barrel — deepened after Vance posted on X that "everyone knows" the war is why Republicans got pummeled and "any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." Sen. Chuck Schumer (D), the likely Senate majority leader in the next Congress, vowed that Democrats will push to end the war. "This crude price drop is entirely about the U.S. election and the belief that Trump will de-escalate rather than escalate on Iran. JD Vance's statement amplified that sentiment," Ben Cahill, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, told Axios via email. What they're saying: Pavel Molchanov, an analyst with Raymond James, said in remarks circulated to reporters that Vance's post was a "key catalyst" for today's oil price plunge. "The market is saying that Congress and members of his own administration are likely to start acting as a constraint on President Trump's war in Iran," Seb Barker, a strategist with the hedge fund, Marshall Wace, tells the Financial Times. Catch up quick: Oil prices were already falling to start the week on signs of new U.S.-Iran diplomacy. What we're watching: "[I]t remains unclear whether Vance's comments signal a more dovish stance toward Iran," Molchanov said. "For oil prices to sustainably move lower, a durable off-ramp is needed," he added.

events.title: Hakeem Jeffries promises ‘affordability’ focus after Democratic midterm win
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Democratic leader says party expects at least 255 House seats and promises to deliver on affordability. Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries has celebrated his party’s sweeping victory in the United States midterm elections, calling the results an “American tsunami” as Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress. “It wasn’t simply a blue wave. It was an American tsunami,” Jeffries said at a news conference on Wednesday, a day after Democrats pulled off upsets in several Republican strongholds. list 1 of 4 House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries hails midterm victory list 2 of 4 Democratic Party gains US House majority in 2026 midterm elections list 3 of 4 Firsts for women and minorities in US midterm elections list 4 of 4 Democrats deliver a historic rout to Republicans in US midterms Jeffries said Democrats expect to win at least 255 House seats once all vote counts are final, giving the party what he described as a historic majority . “The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty,” he said. Jeffries, who is set to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress takes office in January, said the results showed Americans wanted a change in direction. “We’re humbled by the outcome,” he said, promising a “relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans”. Speaking earlier on MS Now’s Morning Joe, Jeffries said Democrats would focus on getting things done rather than seeking revenge against President Donald Trump and his allies. “We ran on affordability. We won on affordability. And now it’s our job to govern on affordability,” he said. Democrats campaigned on bringing down the rising costs of groceries, petrol, housing and healthcare, which have left Americans feeling increasingly squeezed. But with Trump’s threats to use his presidential veto to block legislation he’s opposed to, Democrats may struggle to push through new laws even with a majority in Congress. Jeffries pointed to a bipartisan housing affordability bill passed in July as an example of the types of legislation Democrats could pursue. The bill became law without Trump’s signature after he dismissed it as “a yawn” and “so unimportant”. Jeffries also said Democrats would work to hold the Trump administration accountable for any wrongdoing, even as he acknowledged Americans wanted them to get things done, not “get even”. “There’s a cost to corruption,” he said, adding that Democrats would follow the facts and the law, and “let the chips fall where they may”.

events.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine. On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well. DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated. According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally. On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.” Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong.” Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless. Prove Google wrong. https://t.co/Ta6ibmFdb9 — Kamyl Bazbaz (@KamylBazbaz) November 3, 2026 In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to. The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives. As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns. But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion. Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer. But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether. After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback. It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually. We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced: – Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control… — News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle) November 3, 2026 The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries. DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant. However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says. It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com , where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off. That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Alex Karp casts military software as a force for peace while declaring a moral imperative to dominate the market NHS counts Palantir benefits at trusts that say they're not using it 1 day ago UK government hasn't the foggiest how much it's spending on digital transformation 13 days ago Vendors asking forward deployed engineers to make good on trillion-dollar AI bet 13 days ago Palantir's fondness for French food cooked up tech's latest fad – forward-deployed engineers October 3, 2026 Palantir's Tom Watson lectures MP on accuracy, citing selective data October 1, 2026 Alex Karp, CEO of US spy-tech company Palantir, used this week's historic US midterm election results to claim an unlikely mantle for a military software supplier: pioneer of an antiwar movement. Palantir's Q3 revenue rose 96 percent year-on-year to $2.31 billion, although its shares fell 8 percent following the results, which it reported on Tuesday as US voters were delivering a resounding defeat for Republicans in the voting booth. For Karp, the figures represented "the reality that this moment has become a real focal point of understanding" and might help explain "what is happening in our society." From the CEO's perspective, they not only reflected the company's financial performance, but also its overall "mission." "That mission reason is we support your alpha [above average performance], we support your sovereignty. We support the war fighter. We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money. But we believe we have a moral imperative to be the dominant player in our industry," he told investors. For Karp-watchers, this is familiar self-serving shtick: turn Palantir's work for military and intelligence customers into a moral crusade, and goad its critics along the way. "There's this larger question of what does it mean to have a business that was built around what we believed and believe now is the most important mission in the world, supporting our war fighters, [and] bringing them home," he said. None of this stops him presenting Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter . He expanded on the point during the Q3 earnings call. "Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that, in fact, it's not worth going to war and also to create social cohesion because we're going to bring back our troops healthier, safer, undamaged and that makes our society much more effective," he said. That antiwar pitch sits awkwardly alongside Karp's $1 million donation in December 2024 to MAGA Inc., the super PAC supporting Donald Trump. Trump subsequently launched a US military operation in Venezuela and went to war with Iran, repeatedly promising the latter conflict would be short-lived as it dragged on. Karp did not address either topic on the call. Elsewhere, Karp claimed that Palantir "built products that would protect civil liberties and stop terrorism. If you don't stop terrorism, you're going to get a radical fringe on the right. If you stop terrorism without rights, none of us wants that." That civil liberties pitch also invites scrutiny of Palantir's longstanding relationship with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose treatment of people it targets and detains has drawn criticism from US judges . Karp seems to enjoy the circus of controversy he and his colleagues have created. He also offered investors this insight: "The future is becoming the present and the present is now." Whatever that future holds, he seems confident Palantir has a moral imperative to invoice it. ® Turn your home into a giant crane game with this open source robot Who needs a humanoid to pick up after you when you can suspend an AI-powered claw from cables near your ceiling?

events.title: WHO approves trials for two new Ebola vaccines
events.summary: Vaccines were designed for the Bundibugyo virus that has killed more than 5,300 in the DR Congo. Incredible celebrations as last patient leaves a DRC Ebola centre The World Health Organization (WHO) has approved clinical trials for two new Ebola vaccines, as doctors fight to control the largest outbreak in the history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On Monday, WHO expert groups recommended adding two vaccine trials designed to fight the Bundibugyo strain, which has killed more than 5,300 people, most in the DRC, since May. list 1 of 3 Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case list 2 of 3 Ebola cases in DR Congo surpass 10,000 in fastest-growing outbreak list 3 of 3 Incredible celebrations as last patient leaves a DRC Ebola centre Public health agencies have struggled to contain the Bundibugyo virus, which has a fatality rate of 50 percent due to the lack of a vaccine or treatments designed specifically for the strain. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said a trial that began last month used the Ervebo vaccine, which was approved for the Zaire strain of the Ebola virus but is not designed for Bundibugyo. Tedros said the new vaccines undergoing trials are designed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus. Results from the vaccine trial are expected in early 2027, the WHO reported. The DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research is leading the trial, backed by the WHO and other partners, said Tedros. The vaccine was developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and Moderna. “Vaccines are powerful tools, but they are not substitutes for the proven measures that can save lives now: early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe and dignified burials and trusted engagement with communities,” he added. The African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said 10,444 cases of the Bundibugyo virus have been confirmed, making it the fastest-growing outbreak in DRC’s history. In Kenya , nine cases have been reported, including two deaths. One case has been confirmed in Nigeria , according to the WHO. Tedros urged that travel restrictions imposed by some countries be lifted, warning that they could discourage transparent reporting. “Such restrictions punish countries for doing the right thing, create disincentives for transparency, and harm the response,” said Tedros. The WHO said it is supporting all countries neighbouring DRC to prepare for cases to spread across borders. Meanwhile, a British healthcare worker infected with Ebola is being ⁠evacuated from the DRC to the United Kingdom for specialist treatment, a UK government spokesperson said. In a statement, the government said the patient is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive ⁠in the UK by Thursday, then be transferred to a high-consequence infectious disease unit. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains ‌low, the statement said.

events.title: The 23-year-old founder of Instinct says people are quick to trust AI with their money
events.summary: Instinct founder Noah Shinn (right) at Fireworks AI's Forge conference in San Francisco. Pranav Dixit/Business Insider Nearly 40% of Instinct users connect a credit card within three weeks, its founder Noah Shinn said. Shinn, whose Instinct app went viral this summer, calls it a sign of trust in AI agents. Instinct and rivals like Meta's Muse are racing to do your shopping. Nearly 40% of users of Instinct, the viral AI personal assistant, connect their personal credit cards to the service within three weeks of using it, said its founder, Noah Shinn. Shinn shared the figure on Tuesday at Fireworks AI's Forge conference in San Francisco, describing it as a measure of how quickly people are learning to trust AI agents with their money and sensitive personal information. "That to me is a real sign of trust," he said. Instinct helped kick off a new wave of AI agents that go beyond answering questions to actually getting things done, from booking flights and buying groceries to managing calendars and canceling subscriptions. The more useful these assistants become, the more access they need to people's emails, calendars, payment information, and personal preferences. The race to build personal AI agents is heating up. Meta launched Muse, OpenAI recently introduced Dots , and Anthropic unveiled Claude Duet , a proactive assistant designed to handle tasks on users' behalf. Shinn, a 23-year-old college dropout, said Instinct measures trust partly by tracking how quickly users allow it to make expensive purchases, including transactions exceeding $500 or trips costing several thousand dollars. Shopping has emerged as a major use case for AI agents. Meta recently disclosed that more than a quarter of Muse users had made purchases through the agent, with an average order exceeding $200. Business Insider's Katie Notopoulos wondered what people were buying and whether expensive, tedious purchases, such as flights and appliances, were driving the numbers. Instinct, meanwhile, announced it raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. Shinn said Instinct's usefulness depends on accumulating information about its users, including their private emails, calendars, conversations, and preferences, so it can remember details without being repeatedly prompted. "It's a massive amount of data," he said. At Forge, Shinn also discussed plans for real-time voice interactions and dynamically changing interfaces, and he predicted that most people with internet access around the world would have an AI operator like Instinct in the coming years. events.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
events.summary: Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami. “Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.” HuggingFace is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught. Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too. Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack, but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership, there’s no responsibility for cyber-attack.” In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said. Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems. Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users. Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that HuggingFace has sold 50,000 Microducks , a cute, two-legged robot from HuggingFace that can be programmed using AI. Delangue told the conference that the success of open source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future. “We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI.” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.” Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever-more resources. events.title: Grand staircases, state-shaped pools, and bowling alleys in the basement: See what the governor's mansion looks like in each state
events.summary: Five states don't have a governor's mansion. Carol M. Highsmith/Buyenlarge/Getty Images Forty-five of the 50 US states have official mansions, where governors can live rent-free. Some governors' mansions are open to the public for tours. Arizona, Idaho, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont don't have designated mansions. After a long day serving constituents, governors return home to sprawling, historic buildings. They're welcomed by 20-foot entranceways; their heels ring out on marble floors. If it's been a particularly grim day, they can wash it away with a swim in their state-shaped pool. These official houses, found in 45 of the 50 states, are meant to evoke pride in their areas. Arizona, Idaho, Massachusetts, Rhode Island , and Vermont are the only states without a designated mansion. Life in a governor's mansion is more public than a normal home. Often, visitors can take tours, and security can be heavy. Careful household budgeting is necessary to avoid criticism from the media or constituents. Some governors have chastised reporters for calling it a mansion, telling them to call it a "residence" instead. Following the 2026 midterm results, 21 states are set to have new governors, with Alaska and Kansas still uncalled. Democrats flipped the governorships in five of those states: Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas. The elections also brought many gubernatorial firsts . In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the US' first Black woman elected governor; Texas elected Gina Hinojosa, the state's first Latina governor; and New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, the nation's first Native American woman governor. Here's what the governors' mansions look like in every state that has one. The Alabama governor's mansion is in Montgomery. The governor's mansion in Montgomery, Alabama. Carol M. Highsmith/Buyenlarge/Getty Images. Alabama's state mansion, built in 1907, with a grand staircase and four Corinthian columns, has been the residence of the governor since 1951, according to the Office of the Alabama Governor . The mansion spans two floors and 8,500 square feet. In the 1970s, a state-shaped swimming pool, a guest house, and a water feature were added. The Alaska governor's mansion is in Juneau. The governor's mansion in Juneau, Alaska. John Elk/Getty Images The mansion was built for $40,000 in 1912. To deal with the cold, the 12,900-square-foot house has eight fireplaces for its 26 rooms. Above a winding staircase hangs a large painting of Russian emperor Peter the Great, who was responsible for Russia's exploration of Alaska. The painting has BB-gun bullets near Peter's eyes, and there has been a decadeslong controversy over who pulled the trigger, local news channel KTUU reported. Since 1913, the mansion has opened to the public once a year for a tour at Christmas, according to Alaska's Office of the Governor . Arizona used to have a governor's mansion in Prescott. Arizona doesn't have a governor's mansion. Rosemarie Mosteller/Shutterstock Arizona does not currently have a governor's mansion, but it did once. The historic log cabin on the Sharlot Hall Museum campus was once the governor's mansion in Prescott. It was only used for about two years before the capital left Prescott, KJZZ Phoenix reported. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs lives in her family's private residence in Phoenix. The Arkansas governor's mansion is in Little Rock. The governor's mansion in Little Rock, Arkansas. Arkansas Governor's Mansion Handout/Reuters The three-story mansion, a Georgian Colonial-style building, has been home to the state's governors since 1950. There was no official residence before this one. When it was opened to the public in 1950, 180,000 visitors toured it, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas . The property is 8.5 acres, with six different gardens. Since 1989, the house received nearly $6 million to renovate and expand, the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported. It has antique Persian carpets, a 62-piece sterling silver service from the USS Arkansas, and a grandfather clock from Ireland made in the 18th century. Notable visitors who have stayed the night include former President Harry Truman and actor Gregory Peck. The California governor's mansion is in Sacramento. The governor's mansion in Sacramento, California. Rich Pedroncelli, File/AP The three-story Victorian-style mansion was built in 1877. It has 30 rooms, Italian marble fireplaces, original wood floors, Persian rugs, and a kidney-shaped swimming pool, Curbed San Francisco reported. The governor's mansion took a break for almost 50 years when then-Gov. Ronald Reagan moved out, after his wife, Nancy, called it "a fire trap." From 1967 to 2015, it was a public museum, until Gov. Jerry Brown moved into the property after a $1.6 million renovation, the Los Angeles Times reported. Sacramento-born writer Joan Didion called the mansion "an enlarged version of a very common kind of California tract house." The Colorado governor's mansion is in Denver. The governor's mansion in Denver, Colorado. Hyoung Chang/Media News Group/The Denver Post / Getty The two-story mansion, known as "Colorado's Home," was built in 1908. It has 27 rooms and has been the official residence since 1960, according to its official website. The mansion features red brick and white trim, with mahogany woodwork and oak floors inside. It also has a Steinway piano signed by Liberace, The Colorado Sun reported. In 2014, one notable addition was the installation of a three-handle draft beer system, serving a rotating selection of local craft beers. When former Gov. John Hickenlooper was in office, he didn't always live there, and allowed cabinet members who lived far away to use it as a dormitory. events.title: Key Pentagon priorities in peril after Democratic sweep
events.summary: Tuesday's election was great for Democrats. It was bad for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and some of the White House's most ambitious national security projects. Why it matters: Surprise wins across the map for Democrats — including in the Deep South — complicate a lot for the Trump administration. Republicans have relied on a simple-majority funding mechanism known as reconciliation to pay for marquee projects like Golden Dome . That option is now a long shot over the next few months, and impossible after that. Outrage over the Iran war, well beyond the half-year mark, is sure to turbocharge a long list of congressional inquiries. And lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Reps. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), have suggested impeaching Hegseth. Follow the money: Defense analysts agree prospects for the administration's full $1.5 trillion defense budget look grim. A Wednesday note from TD Cowen's Washington Research Group warned "Trump 'branded' projects are dead." Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and "other signature efforts," it added, "will be curbed." Meanwhile, Todd Harrison, an American Enterprise Institute defense budget expert, said it's unlikely the lame-duck congressional session will pass reconciliation and instead will keep the defense budget operating under a continuing resolution into next year. "They're all at risk," Harrison said of reconciliation-backed programs. "My base expectation is nothing happens on the defense budget." The other side: The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. Between the lines: Some of the most powerful Republican lawmakers on defense matters were defeated or are on pace to lose. Sen. Susan Collins, the appropriations chairwoman, lost to Troy Jackson in Maine . Sen. Darline Graham, also on appropriations, lost to Annie Andrews in South Carolina . Rep. Jen Kiggans, a member of the armed services and veterans affairs committees , lost to Elaine Luria in Virginia . And as of Wednesday afternoon, Reps. Rob Wittman of Virginia, Mike Turner of Ohio, Scott DesJarlais of Tennessee and Jeff Crank of Colorado all trailed their Democratic challengers. What they're saying: Hegseth himself may be on the hot seat. "Secretary Hegseth's chaotic and incompetent leadership has made America weaker and less safe, and now he will be forced to answer for it," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), a member of the appropriations, armed services and intelligence committees, told Axios. "We owe it to our service members, our military families and the American people to make sure that" Hegseth and the broader Trump administration "are held fully accountable," she added. Yes, but: President Trump told reporters he's not considering replacing Hegseth. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," he said. The bottom line: "People do expect there will be investigations and there will be oversight and all that, and certainly that will have an impact," VJ Sahi, a partner at strategic advisory firm Clark Street Associates, told Axios. But the "degree of the impact," he added, remains "TBD." Go deeper: When defense and marketing departments meet

events.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
events.summary: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “ It’s the economy, stupid .” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy , making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think , because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers , with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz , which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food , follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally . Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection . For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record . Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month , and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32% . When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3% , and gas prices were still high . Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “ Whip Inflation Now ,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly . Inflation hit 9% in 1978 . In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats . Inflation continued to climb , and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976 . Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “ Reaganomics ” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum . By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut , lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs . In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22% . In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate . Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40% . Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon . Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon . But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord , under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1% , a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon ; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5% , U.S. oil production rose 3.3% , from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon . On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. events.title: The AI boom has sparked a fiber frenzy, and suppliers like Corning are racing to keep up
events.summary: Corning is investing $585 million in expanding manufacturing in North Carolina. Travis Dove for The Washington Post via Getty Images AI's growth demands denser optical networks, increasing the need for more fiber across data centers. Hyperscalers like Meta are securing fiber supply through long-term deals with manufacturers. Innovations like Relativity Networks' hollow-core fiber can increase data transmission speeds. Data centers have long relied on fiber to transmit signals. But the compute necessary to meet AI's demand requires more fiber than ever before. AI pulls from hundreds of thousands of servers and chips. Lauren Clark, a managing director in Brown Gibbons Lang & Company's infrastructure vertical, told Business Insider that the higher density of fiber, the faster computers can talk to each other— and the faster a large language model can provide a response. And as AI models become more complex and sophisticated, they require denser optical networks, said Mike O'Day, senior vice president and general manager of Corning Optical Communications. Without sufficient fiber, AI chatbots stall and show users a busy signal or error, which is already happening today. Longer-term, a lack of fiber could mean pricier tokens and longer adoption cycles because supplies are constrained, said Gordon Bell, a partner and principal leading digital infrastructure engagements at EY-Parthenon. "You can't have AI for an end user without a powered data center . You can't have it without connectivity," Bell said. "They all need to come together at the same place at the same time in order for everything to work." As AI models become more complex and enterprises and consumers use the technology daily, AI tools will require more infrastructure to respond to chatbot queries. To meet demand, hyperscalers — the companies that provide cloud computing and data storage such as Amazon and Meta — are locking in agreements with fiber manufacturers such as Corning. In turn, fiber suppliers are expanding manufacturing capacity, while some startups are developing technologies to send data at faster speeds. Both strategies reflect the industry's bet that fiber will be critical to keeping pace with AI's growth. "There's just an insatiable demand for optical fiber," said Jason Eichenholz, the cofounder of Relativity Networks, an optical networking and fiber-optics startup. AI changes the fiber game For decades, optical fiber was a quiet corner of telecommunications, Clark said. When ChatGPT launched in 2022 , it brought fiber into the spotlight. "AI is the biggest change factor in data centers and digital infrastructure that we've seen since the origins of the industry," Clark said. That demand is also reshaping how data centers are built . While single mega-facilities exist — like xAI's Colossus data center in Memphis , Tennessee — there are limits to how large one facility can be due to the amount of electricity and water needed to support each data center, Eichenholz said. Communities are also pushing back against this type of data center construction in their neighborhoods, he added. The lack of mega-facilities means companies build multiple data centers with fiber connecting them, Bell said. Fiber gets data from point A to point B and connects GPUs and chips, allowing them to "function essentially as one gigantic computer," Bell said. The challenge to scaling up fiber supply lies in production capacity, Bell said. That includes making the fiber, sourcing connectors, testing the fiber, and the physical labor of laying fiber in the ground. Additionally, non-data-center industries, such as office buildings, industrial sites, and residential homes, use fiber for connectivity — such as fiber-optic internet that many people use at home. "Because of data centers increasing their demand for fiber, it is putting a strain on the overall system," Clark said. "There is definitely a dearth of supply that's going to trickle through the entire market." She said fiber orders today take twice as long to fill compared to roughly three years ago. Solutions take shape Hyperscalers are assessing if they can trust that fiber will be delivered on time and in the quantities they need, Bell said. To solve the crunch, tech giants and fiber manufacturers are signing enormous pre-commitments, Eichenholz said. "You're seeing massive multi-year, multibillion-dollar take-or-pay contracts on a product that was a commodity three years ago," he added. Fiber manufacturers are scaling up capacity, but in a disciplined manner. They're locking in commitments from customers before they increase manufacturing and labor capacity, so that hyperscalers and suppliers share the costs and risks of expansion, Corning's O'Day said. Corning is investing $585 million in expanding manufacturing in North Carolina. This year alone, the optical fiber manufacturer inked long-term agreements to supply fiber and cable to Amazon, Meta, and Nvidia. Last month, the company's optical communications division reported a 44% year-over-year jump in sales , while GenAI product sales more than doubled. Corning's manufacturing facility in rural Midland, NC. Travis Dove for The Washington Post via Getty Images "Our customers are connecting enormous numbers of GPUs, and they need to fit much more fiber and many more connections into the same physical space," O'Day said. Beyond agreements, fiber suppliers are innovating the product itself. O'Day said Corning has developed smaller-diameter fiber and denser cables that put more capacity within the same footprint. The company invented a fiber with a 40% smaller surface area that can bend into 10 times smaller spaces. That led to the development of its Contour Flow Cable, which Corning announced in March. While incumbents like Corning are packing more fiber into limited spaces, new entrants are rethinking optical physics altogether. Relativity Networks, an AI network startup, developed ChronoCore, a hollow-core fiber designed to bypass the physical speed limits of conventional glass. The fiber allows signals to travel at 99.7% the speed of light, Eichenholz said. He calls it "an HOV lane for fiber." By comparison, light moves through glass fiber at two-thirds the speed of light. Relativity is partnering with Prysmian, one of the world's largest producers of fiber-optic cables, to scale production. The difference in speed matters when connecting data centers. Light traveling through traditional fiber has a slight delay, but the hollow core moves at nearly the speed of light, which means operators can build data centers farther apart without harming the performance of an AI model. Relatively completed its first deployment with a major hyperscaler in 2024 and recently landed a $40 million order to connect data centers with the same hyperscaler. Bell predicts the pace of data center buildouts will eventually level off. But they don't see the appetite for fiber shrinking in the near term. "There's a lot of unknowns wi

events.title: Johnson out as House Republican leader after GOP rout
events.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson privately told staff he is not planning on running for minority leader or any other leadership role in the next Congress, according to people familiar with the comments. His decision will kick off a scramble among House Republican leadership contenders in the aftermath of their sweeping losses Tuesday night. Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., are launching leadership bids on Wednesday. Both Jordan and Scalise previously came up short in speakership bids in the chaotic aftermath of Kevin McCarthy’s ouster. Johnson eventually emerged as an unlikely consensus pick among House Republicans then. Johnson had previously suggested he might step back from leadership or even leave Congress as House Republicans’ midterm chances dimmed. President Donald Trump appears to be staying neutral in the race, telling reporters Wednesday, “we’ll stay out of it.” He praised Johnson for his tenure. Republicans could also see other shakeups further down their leadership chain. Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, currently the Republican Study Committee chair, announced in a letter to GOP colleagues Wednesday that he’d run for the second-ranking position. “We need fresh ideas and a leadership team committed to rebuilding a culture with a clear game plan to win in 2028,” he wrote. That sets up a clash with Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., currently the House majority whip. And leading up to Election Day, Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., had received encouragement from other Republicans about running against Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., for conference chair. Democrats are not expecting major shakeups among their ranks. Some progressives have threatened to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, though it’s unlikely to derail his ascension. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Democrats map out an agenda to address affordability and corruption after midterm sweep
events.summary: Likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries and other prominent Democrats are laying out their plans to introduce legislation to address the cost of living, undo President Donald Trump's tariffs and end the war in Iran. They'll have to balance those legislative goals with their plans to investigate Trump, his family and associates, in what could be an antagonistic relationship between Congress, the White House and the business world. The newly elected Democratic majorities in the Senate and the House are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned, and are preparing to tussle with an antagonistic President Donald Trump . The legislative push aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries. In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. Democrats — likely led by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House in U.S. history — also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the Iran war or force Trump to seek congressional authorization to keep it going. Some details of the Democrats' plans had been previously reported by the New York Times. Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns 5 midterm election takeaways: Tech billionaires suffer as Democrats drub Republicans Elon Musk’s record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it But Democrats will need to strike a balance between these legislative priorities and a robust oversight and investigatory agenda that the party is mapping out to scrutinize Trump, his family, cabinet and supporters in the business world. "We haven't evaluated who are going to be the targets of the investigation right out of the gate. We'll have those conversations over the next couple of weeks," Jeffries told CNBC on Wednesday. "But clearly, things aren't going right for the American people. Capitalism is broken in the way in which it is being experienced by so many working-class Americans and middle-class Americans. We've got to make sure we build an economy, a free market economy, that works for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Democrats on the campaign trail for months hammered home a message of affordability . And as corruption emerged as a top issue for voters in the waning months of the election, they tried to connect the Trump administration's perceived bad behavior to Americans' pocketbooks. Already, prominent Democrats are taking a similar tack as they prepare to assume majorities in both chambers. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Wednesday that the panel's top priorities "will be affordability for us, accountability for them." Wyden said the committee would double down on its efforts to make sure billionaires pay their fair share in taxes, address the "corporate chokehold on our nation's health care system" and reassert congressional authority over trade. He also vowed to target the "special interests" that had cozied up to Trump in the past two years. "From the banks that helped cover up Epstein's crimes, to insurance companies that are delaying and denying health care to churn a profit, to the pharmaceutical company CEOs that price gouge while enjoying Trump's hand-delivered windfalls, when I am chair, they will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump's corruption," Wyden said. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, has vowed to take on Trump's family, corporate corruption, Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement overreach and the handling of files related to disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Garcia issued a pointed, two-word statement as results tipped toward Democrats on Tuesday night: "Lawyer up." And Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and member of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees, said in a recent interview with CNBC that she believed Democrats should target figures like Elon Musk , as well as cabinet secretaries like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Attorney General Todd Blanche .

events.title: Fedora 45 is finally finished and fit
events.summary: Fedora 45 is here , after not one but two week-long delays as the team found last-minute issues. Although both the original and second announcements were irksomely non-specific, in general we prefer this "when it's ready" approach to the rigid calendar-based schedule that Canonical favors for Ubuntu. It includes six main editions, five immutable desktop variants, and 12 "spins" with different GUIs. The combined version 45 release notes detail some of the bigger individual component changes and note the hardware requirements. The recommended spec is now a 2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 GB of RAM and 20 GB of disk space, and at least 1024×768 graphics. Fedora 45 supports most display adapters, but 3D acceleration may not work on older GPUs, including Intel models prior to GMA9xx, Nvidia models prior to NV30 (GeForce FX5xxx series), and AMD Radeon models prior to R300 (Radeon 9500). We took a quick look at the beta back in September, focusing on its new next-generation text console, which is a welcome change. We especially liked the ability to zoom in and out on the text console on the fly, which is something we've missed since the superb "Laptop Ultravision" for DOS , about a third of a century ago. (The company is long gone, but we found a downloadable version for all you DOS users .) The desktop flagship editions are Workstation 45 , which comes with GNOME 51 "A Coruña" , and Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop , with KDE Plasma 6.8 . We covered some of the new features in GNOME 51 when we looked at the Ubuntu 26.10 beta , and those changes apply here too – notably, improvements in the Settings app, but removal of some older Nvidia GPU support. Both the big names are Wayland-only environments now, but by our reckoning, X11 fans have seven of the 12 official spins to choose from: Xfce, Cinnamon, MATE, i3, LXQt, LXDE, and Sugar (SOAS) all still use X.org if you prefer. There is also a combined What's New page for all the Atomic Desktops, Fedora’s immutable variants – the main shared feature here being the new web-based installer. The new version of main Fedora is accompanied by Fedora Asahi Remix 45 for Apple Silicon Macs. This is a more notable release than the cross-platform editions, as Asahi 45 brings initial support for M3-based Macs as well as M1 and M2 kit. As The Reg described in September , though, the M3 support is preliminary and limited – for instance, it excludes the M3 Ultra. If you have an M3 Mac, for now, you're better off sticking to macOS. The most important changes in Fedora 45 are under the hood, which is what the Red Hat release announcement focuses on. It now uses RPM version 6.1, with enhanced package signature checking , and blocks the vendor of packages silently changing. The GNOME keyring now uses the oo7 secrets manager . Support for two old VPN plugins has been removed, because the packages were unmaintained. A feature that we are happy to see land at last is better support for Red Hat’s Stratis next-generation storage subsystem. We gave a potted overview of Stratis 3.3 back in 2022: it was on version 3.3 back then. It’s the same main Stratis version 3.9 we saw in Fedora 44, but the installation program now has support for installing Fedora 45 on Stratis storage . Stratis is Red Hat’s rival to OpenZFS. The plan is that Stratis offers similar features and resilience to ZFS, especially in the field of copy-on-write snapshots and simple multi-device logical volume management, but built from all-GPL code. Rather than a whole new filesystem, Stratis integrates XFS, LVM, and the kernel device-mapper functionality. Stratis 1.0 appeared in Fedora 29 eight years ago, and Fedora 45 has version 3.9.3. It's good to see it finally making real progress: if nothing else, we've seen Btrfs irretrievably corrupt a full volume far too many times to ever trust it again, so an alternative is very welcome. When we looked at Fedora 44 , we noted the difficulty of doing custom disk partitioning. It was there, but very well-hidden. Now, the installer can launch the Cockpit web-management tool to make it easier to set up your drives however you want. An interesting side-effect of the delayed release is that Fedora 45 ships with kernel 7.2 – specifically, version 7.2.15, which is the last release of this short-term series . In other words, it’s an end-of-life kernel version. It’s an amusing contrast to its near-contemporary Ubuntu 26.10, which shipped with a pre-release kernel . Our test Ubuntu box was automatically upgraded to the release version by the background automatic updates process , but to our surprise, it didn't receive the kernel update for over a week. This shouldn't be a problem: unlike Ubuntu, Fedora releases routinely receive updates to whole new kernel versions, so we’re sure Fedora 45 users will get kernel 7.3 very soon. We upgraded the same test machine on which we tried GNOME 48 in Fedora 42 early last year. You can skip one Fedora release on upgrade, but not two, so we had to go via Fedora 44 — which took some time, and threw up a minor packaging glitch, but it got there. The result runs surprisingly well, although this 2008 machine is well below the recommended spec. ®
