events.title: The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 US midterms
events.summary: Historic firsts, surprise victories and expensive defeats as Democrats take control of Congress. Democrats had a big night in Tuesday’s United States midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress and pulling off some surprising victories in longtime Republican strongholds. From turning Texas blue to electing the country’s first Muslim senator, there were plenty of historic wins. But the night also brought some major setbacks for US President Donald Trump and his allies, including one who spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing losing candidates. Here’s a look at some of the election’s biggest winners and losers. Annie Andrews: In one of the most surprising wins of the night, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a Republican-held Senate seat in a deeply conservative South Carolina, beating out the Trump-backed candidate Darline Graham. A paediatrician who campaigned on healthcare and affordability, Andrews became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1998, and its first elected female senator. The victory was a major breakthrough for Democrats and helped them take control of the Senate. Abdul El-Sayed: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. The former public health official overcame attacks on his faith and a bitter primary battle against establishment-backed Democrat Haley Stevens, who went on to endorse Rogers. “You chose hate and Michigan chose hope,” El-Sayed told Rogers in his victory speech. Chuck Schumer: After facing criticism from fellow Democrats for not pushing back hard enough against Trump, as well as anger from progressives over his support for arms sales to Israel, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is now poised to reclaim his position as majority leader. Schumer helped recruit candidates including Sherrod Brown and Roy Cooper, who flipped Republican-held Senate seats. He celebrated the victory on Tuesday, saying, “We have five words for the American people: ‘Relief is on the way’.” James Talarico: After years of Democrats trying to turn Texas blue, James Talarico finally pulled off a major upset by winning a US Senate seat in a state Trump had carried by double digits just two years ago. The 37-year-old former middle-school teacher, state legislator and Presbyterian seminarian gained national attention for using his Christian faith to challenge the religious right. But his campaign against Republican Ken Paxton also focused on the cost of living and corruption, including the influence of wealthy donors like Elon Musk, who supported Paxton. Vivek Ramaswamy: Biotech billionaire and Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy lost Ohio’s governor’s race to Democrat Amy Acton in light of a controversial attack ad in which Acton’s estranged mother accused her of lying about her difficult childhood. What the ad left out was that her mother lost custody after Acton’s stepfather was indicted for raping her as a child. The widely condemned ad dominated the final month of Ramaswamy’s campaign, with his team eventually pulling it after spending about $1m to keep it running. Haley Stevens: Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens ended up on the losing side for the second time, after first losing the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, and then endorsing his Republican opponent Mike Rogers just two days before the election. Stevens broke with El-Sayed over his criticism of Israel and an ad linking US military aid to rising grocery prices, which he disavowed. El-Sayed won anyway, while Stevens was left facing a backlash from Democrats and a wave of resignations from her own team. Elon Musk: The world’s richest man spent more than $400m backing Republicans, only to see them lose both chambers of Congress. Among the candidates he supported was Ken Paxton, who lost the Texas Senate race to Democrat James Talarico. Musk now faces possible congressional investigations into his leadership of Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and his companies’ federal contracts, with Democrats gaining the power to subpoena documents and even call him to testify under oath. Donald Trump: Though Trump wasn’t on the ballot, the midterms are a major blow to the final two years of his presidency, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress. Republican candidates backed by Trump lost Senate races in longtime strongholds like Texas and South Carolina. The results mean Trump will spend the remainder of his time in office facing a Democratic-controlled Congress with the power to block his legislative agenda, investigate his administration, and hold his officials accountable for alleged malfeasance.

events.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
events.summary: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

events.title: Democrats' midterm gains could sideline Electoral College by 2028
events.summary: Democrats' sweeping statehouse gains Tuesday have opened a path to effectively replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote in time for the 2028 presidential election — without needing to amend the Constitution. Why it matters: The results could give Democrats the legislative power to fundamentally change how America picks its president, potentially ending the possibility of winning the White House while losing the national popular vote. Driving the news: Democrats have won control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada, enough to push an agreement called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact beyond the 270-vote threshold required to take effect. The compact has been enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C. since launching in 2006, representing 222 electoral votes so far. The agreement only kicks in when participating states collectively control at least 270 electoral votes. The five new Democratic trifectas could bring the total to 283. How it works: Americans don't directly elect the president. Instead, they actually cast ballots to choose electors, whose votes determine the winner every four years. Nearly every state awards all its electoral votes to the statewide winner. Maine and Nebraska also award electors based on congressional district results. But the Constitution explicitly gives states power to appoint electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." Under the compact, participating states would instead award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once the agreement reaches 270 electoral votes. Yes, but: The five states would still need to enact the compact, and it's not clear if it will be a priority for the new Democratic states. The Electoral College would formally remain in place, and the compact could face constitutional challenges, including over whether congressional approval is required. Michigan failed to enact it during its previous Democratic trifecta from 2023 to 2024, and Nevada's then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact in 2019, warning it could diminish his state's influence over presidential elections. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the compact would be unconstitutional without congressional approval, which he contends is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. What to watch: Whether and how legislators in the new trifecta states move forward. Lawmakers in all five states have previously introduced legislation to join the compact.

events.title: Democrats vow Trump investigations, but voters have another priority too
events.summary: Democrats wasted no time gloating and warning the Trump administration about a pending flood of subpoenas and investigations once the 2026 midterm blue wave became clear. Why it matters: Democrats are eager to exercise their oversight powers over the president and his allies, but they must navigate that while addressing Americans' No. 1 election concern — the high cost of living. Driving the news: Before the AP even called the House for Democrats, expected House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said in a statement that the president's allies should "[l]awyer up." He seconded the sentiment in a Wednesday post to X. Sen. Ron Wyden posted on X Tuesday night, "[s]ubpoenas." In response to a post from former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who said the Trump administration was "too successful" during its first year, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) responded, "[w]ant to say that under oath?" The big picture: Voters aren't necessarily asking Democrats to choose between the cost of living and accountability. They want action on both. About half of voters said the high cost of living and government corruption were "crucial" to their votes for Congress, per the AP's Voter Poll. Roughly four in 10 voters said the economy was the top issue facing the country, compared with three in 10 who said it was democracy. Seven in 10 said Congress isn't doing enough to check presidential power. What they're saying: When asked about Wyden and Garcia's comments in an interview Wednesday morning, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) — the overwhelming favorite to become House Speaker — told TODAY that the "American people clearly don't want us to try and get even." "They want us to get things done to make their life more affordable. At the same period of time, what we have seen is unprecedented corruption unleashed on America, the likes of which we have never seen before." "And when you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends, and their donors, it's clear to the American people that that means you have a Congress or White House or Supreme Court not focused on actually addressing the needs of working class folks." The White House didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Democrats have already laid out some of their main priorities for investigation. Garcia vowed Tuesday that House Dems would focus on probing Trump's family businesses, alleged corporate corruption and government contracts. He also said he'll investigate DHS and ICE misconduct allegations, as well as the Jeffrey Epstein files and the administration's handling of them. Other reporting has suggested Democrats might also probe the DOGE effort, or its de facto former leader, tech billionaire Elon Musk. President Trump said on Monday he's open to pardoning his allies and staff if Democrats target them. Reality check: Some legislative priorities Democrats want could also be easily blocked by the president's veto power. Democrats are not currently projected to win the 2/3 majority needed to override such a move on their own. A presidential pardon only erases liability in a federal case; it does not shield a recipient from civil or state-level charges or investigations. What we're watching: Whether Democrats truly pursue an effective oversight agenda and whether Democratic leadership can walk the tightrope of bringing costs down while doing so. events.title: What we know so far on the results for California's Prop. 40 billionaire tax
events.summary: Californians are voting on a proposal that could send a one-time, huge tax bill to the state's billionaires. Lester Cohen/Getty Images It could be days or weeks before a final tally on California's Prop. 40 "billionaire wealth tax." Early results give the "No" vote a commanding lead among both Silicon Valley elites and rural Hispanic counties. It could bring in $100 billion to plug a coming Medicare hole — or lose billions in tax revenue. The morning after the midterms, there's still no answer on California's billionaire wealth tax — and the final results may not be in for days or even weeks. As of around 10:30 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, 44.4% of California voters had thrown their support behind Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time "5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion." With about 60% of the vote in thus far, there's still plenty of time for the results to reverse, but the "No" vote has a commanding lead. More interesting is how support and opposition have played out across the Golden State. The socially-progressive urban strongholds of Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Alameda County (home to Berkeley and Oakland) are favoring the measure with slim majorities. Meanwhile, many of the poorer and majority-Hispanic agricultural communities in California's Central Valley and desert regions have come out against the wealth tax by double-digit margins. Rural California has an unusual bedfellow in wealthy Silicon Valley. Counties representing Palo Alto, Cupertino, and the hilly Peninsula cities that house much of the Bay Area's venture capital and post-exit founder class have come out firmly against the tax so far. Other solid-blue Western states look set to pass narrower progressive tax measures. Washington state, which hasn't voted in favor of an income tax since 1932, went firmly against repealing a "millionaires tax" passed by the state legislature earlier this year. In Colorado, an amendment that would replace the state's flat income tax with a progressive scheme is leading by a thin margin. Amendment 87 would raise taxes on the wealthy and businesses while cutting them for most Coloradans. California's vote is the culmination of a showdown that's been shaking up Silicon Valley executives for months. Google cofounder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Affirm CEO Max Levchin, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kleiner Perkins Chairman John Doerr, and angel investor Chris Larsen have collectively poured millions into an opposition campaign . Brin himself has donated more than $100 million to the "No" team, per Cal Matters. State campaign-finance filings show committees opposing Prop. 40 had reported about $130 million in contributions through October 22, versus about $33 million for its supporters. Meanwhile, other tech executives are preparing, just in case they have to pay up. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg weighed moving out of the state. In October, the company created a new class of shares that would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the vote passes — potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up some of his voting power. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said during a January spot on Bloomberg TV. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it." The vote has also split some regular political alliances. Progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has backed the billionaire tax, while California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, opposes the measure. There are multiple paths to "No" If a majority of voters fill in the "Yes" bubble on Prop 40, roughly 200 people who were California residents on January 1, 2026, could face the one-time tax. That vote has two lurking trap doors — propositions 41 and 42 could ruin the "Yes" team's finale. As of Wednesday morning, the "No" side on Prop. 41 was winning with 52.5% of the vote, while Prop. 42 was up with 54.3% in favor. Both countermeasures were designed to undercut Prop. 40 by imposing new auditor reviews and prohibiting taxes on certain assets. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the billionaire tax could be stopped from taking effect, even if a majority of Californians vote for it. What California's billionaires could owe In broad terms, the measure would tax billionaires based on more than their salary. Taxable wealth would include ownership stakes in businesses, securities, investment accounts, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, among other assets. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be excluded. If the billionaire tax passes, it'll be due in 2027 — though taxpayers could spread out their payments across five years at a higher cost. Supporters say the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. A majority of the proceeds would go toward healthcare, with the remainder allocated to education, food assistance, and the operation of the tax program. The campaign has pitched the measure as a way to help backfill looming federal cuts to Medi-Cal. Overall, Prop. 40 backers have said the tax event would raise over $100 billion for the state. A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper from Stanford economists, published in October, warned that the results could be much less rosy . The initial tax event could bring in around $30 billion before prompting high-earning executives to leave the state, the paper said. That could lose California $38.9 billion over time, the paper warned. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I keep volunteering at my daughter's elementary school even though she no longer goes there
events.summary: The author said she helped teachers prep their classrooms for the new school year at her daughter's former elementary school. Courtesy of Courtney Johnson. I love volunteering at the elementary school my daughter attended. She's moved on to middle school, but I'm staying put. Spending my time there has been a great way for me to connect with other parents and the community. In August, I volunteered at my daughter's former elementary school , handing out back-to-school packets. Excitement and anxiety blurred the halls as kids and parents made their way to classrooms. In the commotion, a boy now taller than me came up and asked, "Do you remember me?" "Of course I do," I exclaimed as a smile came across his face. "Wow," he said. "You always planned the best class parties . I miss those," he said as he walked down the hall with his now fifth-grade sister. With a list of volunteer opportunities in front of me, I am drawn to help at my daughter's elementary school rather than at her middle school. From knowing the lasting impact I have to giving my daughter space in her teen years, I have many reasons why. School gives me a place to connect For my husband and me, our families are mainly in the Midwest and on the Carolina coast, making the daily ups and downs of parenting fall entirely on our shoulders. The more time I spend in the school building, the more comfortable I feel leaning on staff in the been-there-done-that parenting environment. Whether a teacher asks how my daughter is doing or sees I'm digging out of difficult conversations, I know they are "family" I can go to. Volunteering helped me honor my parents Looking back to my elementary years, my mother is central to those memories, volunteering any way she could. Meanwhile, my dad was always the one grabbing the catcher's mitt to warm up the pitcher or donating his time to the Lions Club and other local organizations. The author said spending time at the school has led to some paid work, too. Courtesy of Courtney Johnson. My parents always stressed that the best way to say thank you is with your time . After losing my mom suddenly in February, giving my time has become even more important to me. Every mailbox I stuff, email I send, or event I volunteer at helps me feel close to her. I'm hanging on to my OG mom friends There is something to be said about your original parenting friends , the ones you make when you begin a whole new chapter in your life. In the case of beginning motherhood away from family in a new town, those first friends met at story time, play gyms, and more, and became my first natural friends. Opportunities to connect with OG friends are becoming fewer and farther between as our kids grow up and head in new directions. For now, volunteering at the elementary school gives me a chance to connect with some of the OGs without having to schedule something months in advance. Yes, some of the volunteer mom faces I see are slowly changing at the school, but for now it still remains a place that feels familiar and comfortable to me Volunteering has led to some work When my daughter was in preschool, I started volunteering weekly to help build a bridge between the teachers and me. Without physically walking around with my résumé, I found it natural to strike up conversations with teachers in the hall and in the workroom about my past teaching experience. I quickly became a preferred sub, so I often get texts saying, "Hey, are you available on such and such date to sub?" Without wanting to go back to teaching full time, subbing lets me still get my teacher fix but also the flexibility of time to pursue other interests. With limited opportunities to volunteer and make an impact at the middle school level, I will continue to volunteer at my daughter's former elementary school. Whether I'm sharing my passion for hiking and guidebooks with students or handing out packets at back-to-school night, I fill my cup during school hours without missing time with my daughter. events.title: Democrats took back the Senate in a massive blue wave. See the 7 states that flipped.
events.summary: Seven states elected Democratic senators in the 2026 midterms, with most of the wins in long-held Republican states. Win McNamee/Getty Images; RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images Democrats have taken control of the US Senate in a massive blue wave. They flipped seats in seven long-held Republican strongholds, including Texas and Kansas. Some states hadn't elected a Democratic senator in more than 30 years. The "blunami" has come for the Senate. Democrats have flipped seven Republican-held US Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections so far, either by defeating incumbent Republican senators or winning races in which the sitting Republican senator was not on the ballot. It's a resounding victory for the party and a blow to President Donald Trump. Democrats entered Election Day less confident about retaking the Senate than the House, but they ultimately flipped more seats than they needed to gain a majority, including in historically Republican strongholds like Texas and Kansas. Two close Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are still uncalled, but the new split puts Democrats with at least 54 seats in the Senate. The party also earned a majority in the House of Representatives and will control both chambers of Congress. The election results drew mixed reactions from Silicon Valley . "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who spent $224 million backing Republican midterm campaigns in the Lone Star State, wrote on X . Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," expressed similar sentiment: "I never expected Texas to turn blue," he wrote on X . "Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!" Not all tech leaders were upset. LinkedIn cofounder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman wrote on X that the midterm elections, including the Texas results, were "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies" and that "voters rejected the status quo." Here are the Senate seats that have flipped as of November 4, using vote counts and preliminary win percentages from the Associated Press . We've also included House and governorship flips to show how the states fared in the broader election. Maine Troy Jackson early on Wednesay. Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images Troy Jackson (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins with 53.8% of the vote. Collins had served as one of Maine's senators for 30 years. Ohio Sherrod Brown on Tuesday. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sherrod Brown (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted with 50.0% of the vote. Ohio also flipped the governor's seat, with Amy Acton winning with 52.3% of the vote. She defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and became Ohio's first woman elected governor. Republican Nancy Hollister previously served as governor via succession. Democrats also flipped the 7th and 15th congressional districts. North Carolina Roy Cooper on Tuesday. AM STEWART / AFP via Getty Images Roy Cooper (D) defeated Republican Michael Whatley with 58.7% of the vote, flipping the US Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. The last time a Democrat won the seat was in 2008. Democrats also flipped the 6th, 9th, 11th, 13th, and 14th Districts. Iowa Josh Turek on Tuesday. Scott Morgan/Bloomberg via Getty Images Josh Turek (D) defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson with 50.5% of the vote, flipping the US Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Iowa hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 2008. Iowa also flipped the governor's seat. Rob Sand (D) won the gubernatorial race with 55.5% of the vote, defeating Republican Zach Lahn. Democrats also flipped the state's 1st, 2nd, and 3rd districts. South Carolina Annie Andrews on Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images Annie Andrews (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who took over after her brother Lindsey Graham died in July, with 51.1% of the vote. It's the first time South Carolina has elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998. Texas James Talarico on Tuesday. Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images James Talarico (D) defeated Republican Ken Paxton with 55.1% of the vote, flipping the Texas US Senate seat held by Republican Sen. John Cornyn. He'll be the first Democratic senator from Texas since 1988. The governor's seat also flipped: Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott with 52.8% of the vote. Democrats also flipped the 15th and 23rd districts. Kansas Adam Hamilton on Tuesday. Nick Oxford/Bloomberg via Getty Images Adam Hamilton (D) defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall with 50.9% of the vote. It's been nearly a century since Kansas voted in a Democratic senator — the last time was in 1932. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says ‘founder mode’ cost him almost his entire executive team: ‘They left or they didn’t want to work for me’
events.summary: Long before he cofounded Airbnb—the now-$105 billion short-term rental platform—in 2008, Brian Chesky was practicing being a founder as a kid—designing things, disassembling Christmas toys, and persuading friends to buy what he was selling. By the time he started a company, he figured he’d been preparing for the job his whole life, with 20 years of founder experience under his belt. Stepping into the CEO role, however, was a different matter. “I think I was pretty much naturally a great founder, and I was naturally a terrible CEO,” Chesky told Guy Raz on Monday’s episode of How I Built This . As Airbnb grew, Chesky said he followed advice to hire experienced executives, trust their judgment, and give them room to work. But when he rejected that approach and took a more hands-on role, he was met with resistance. “Almost the entire exec team left,” Chesky said, adding that the departures happened eventually. “They left or they didn’t want to work for me.”  The longtime CEO wasn’t looking to win over everyone—just 10 people willing to serve on his executive team and see whether working his way produced results. That approach later became known as “founder mode.” Y Combinator cofounder Paul Graham popularized the term after hearing Chesky speak at an event for the startup accelerator. In a September 2024 essay , Graham challenged the idea that founders must hand off the details as their companies grow, arguing they should stay involved with employees beyond their immediate reports.  Chesky began changing how he ran Airbnb in 2020, four years before Graham’s essay, as the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the company’s IPO plans and sent revenue down 72% . He turned to former Apple designer Jony Ive, who told him: “You don’t manage people. You manage people through the work.” He then took a page from Apple cofounder Steve Jobs’ playbook and cut layers of management. For Chesky, that meant bringing the employee doing the work and the managers above them into the same meeting. Everyone could make a recommendation, and he could make the final decision without sending an idea through several rounds of signoffs. In August 2025 , Chesky said he treated roughly 50 employees as direct reports, weighing in on decisions to hire, fire, promote, and manage them. Finding people willing to work his way Taking a more hands-on role meant breaking some old habits. Chesky said he often listened to executives with far more experience than he had, even when their advice ran counter to his instincts. “And what do I do when my intuition and their experience collide? Usually I deferred, and that was usually a mistake,” he said. He also shied away from difficult conversations about performance, sometimes taking on struggling employees’ work himself.  “I felt cautious about being a boss,” he said. “I think I was a little bit of a people pleaser. I wanted people to like me.” But that deference came at a cost.  “They’ve gone down a path for two years. Guess what happens? They leave. You might spend five or 10 years fixing or correcting that decision that person made,” Chesky said. As he overhauled how he ran Airbnb, Chesky began hiring people who had worked for founders such as Jobs and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. They already understood his approach and needed less convincing. Chesky has since defended detailed oversight as a way to help employees improve and make decisions faster. But he told Raz staying involved in every detail indefinitely isn’t sustainable. He described reviewing roughly 70 drafts of a single press release to establish the standard he expected. Once employees understood that standard, he could step back. He put it more bluntly in a 2024 interview with Fortune : “If you want to be autonomous, start your own company.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump hammers Fox News, blaming network for GOP losses as ratings slide
events.summary: President Donald Trump hammered Fox News on Truth Social Tuesday night as election results favoring Democrats rolled in. His comments come after Fox News reported a year-over-year viewership decline despite an otherwise strong quarter. Trump is a frequent critic of media companies, especially broadcasters that he views as being biased against him. President Donald Trump turned against Fox News on Tuesday night in a string of posts on Truth Social while Democratic wins rolled in during a historic midterm election. Trump blamed the network, which he's long championed, for Republican losses, saying in one post on his social media network that it "bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition." Democrats took control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, flipping seats in states usually favorable to Republicans, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Trump also pointed to Fox's recent ratings as evidence of the network's decline. "FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It's them, not me," he posted. Fox News did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a press release last week, Fox News reported 1.1 million average viewers for October, down about 27% from the same month a year prior. Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch noted the decline during the company's quarterly earnings call on Monday, citing "viewer fatigue." However, Murdoch said such a shift is expected in the lead-up to a midterm election with a second-term president and said it was not the result of viewers turning to competitors' coverage. "Those viewers are not going to any other news channel. They're not switching to MS NOW or to CNN," he said. "They're just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall." Versant -owned MS NOW and Skydance -owned CNN both reported primetime viewership was up by double digits in October compared with the year-ago period. However, both networks still had smaller total-day average audiences than Fox News. MS NOW had 588,000 average viewers in October across all day parts, and CNN had 402,000, according to Nielsen data cited by Fox. Despite Fox News' year-over-year drop in viewership, the company reported an otherwise strong quarter in what Murdoch called an "outstanding start to fiscal 2027." Fox Corp., which includes the linear TV networks as well as entertainment and sports assets and a streaming business, reported revenue for its fiscal first quarter of $4.57 billion, up 22% year over year. The company pointed to strength in advertising revenue, which increased 47%, buoyed by strong political advertising and the FIFA Men's World Cup, which aired in part on Fox platforms across June and July. Trump is a frequent critic of media companies, especially broadcasters that he views as being biased against him. While he's repeatedly taken aim at NBC and Disney -owned ABC, the president has had a much friendlier relationship with Fox and its networks. Trump appeared on Fox News ' "Hannity" on Monday night ahead of the election. Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

events.title: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant; shares fall 10%
events.summary: CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell more than 12% on Wednesday. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy. "So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added. CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split. In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent. "This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday. One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Who needs a humanoid to pick up after you when you can suspend an AI-powered claw from cables near your ceiling? Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang 22 hours ago GhostBSD 26.2 takes the fright out of FreeBSD with a friendlier installer 1 day ago Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 1 day ago These smart glasses promise to turn your silent mouth movements into text 1 day ago SUSE to cut one in ten employees because of... AI 2 days ago Your new robot servant doesn't have to look anything like a person or walk on two legs. In fact, it might just be a claw that hangs from the ceiling instead. That’s the future envisioned by Nathaniel Nifong, founder of Neufangled Robotics, and its Stringman robot . Put simply, Stringman is an AI-equipped claw suspended from four strings running through the corners of a room (up to 10 meters diagonally). Two motorized anchors adjust the lengths of the strings to move the claw around the room, from ceilings up to 4 meters high down to the floor to pick stuff up. With a payload capacity of around 2 kg, depending on its position, Stringman can move items to designated locations – like a toy box – and perform tidying tasks. Stringman can also be manually controlled if you’d prefer to play a room-sized crane game by yourself. According to Stringman’s documentation site, the device is currently a public prototype that “can self-calibrate in a new room and run policies, but is not yet reliable enough to be called a home appliance.” That said, demonstration videos on the website show it in action, and it’s neat to watch. Stringman is shown picking up laundry and dropping it in a basket, putting Lego bricks and other kids' toys back where they belong, and generally zooming around rooms and demonstrating its agility. One could imagine a properly trained Stringman could even grab the remote you left on the other side of the living room and drop it in your waiting hand if you’re that incredibly lazy. “Our mission is to give people an organized home,” Neufangled says on its future roadmap page . “We prioritize robots that are narrowly effective at something that helps today rather than a general purpose robot that may be in development for years.” The company further describes its goal as designing robots that are low cost and capable of doing things that people hate to do - e.g., pick up after a messy toddler - and making a robot that can do that while camouflaging itself into the home “as well as possible.” As long as you think a foot-long claw robot hanging from the corner of the ceiling is camouflaged, this is the robot for you. Neufangled lists Stringman for $795, which is a lot to ask for a public prototype that isn’t reliable enough to be called a home appliance yet. Luckily for those who’re interested in this sort of niche home automation, it’s fully open source , too. “A complete Stringman is three Raspberry Pis on your Wi-Fi network,” the documentation site reads: One in the gripper, and two in the corner anchor mounts that store line reels and have cameras to track the claw’s location as it moves around the room. A third camera mounted on the claw provides visual feedback. Oh, you'll also need a dedicated PC or Mac to run the robot's motion-control software. As for Stringman itself, to build your own, you'll need a 3D printer, a supplier to manufacture the PCBs, motors, Raspberry Pis, and other components listed in the bill of materials. You'll also need to follow the guides on the documentation site to get it up and running, calibrate it for your space using printed markers, set up drop-off points using visual tags, and program it to perform tasks. But is it safe? One could imagine getting tangled in the lines if you get in Stringman’s way. Nifong admits that can happen, writing in the documentation that he has walked into the lines himself without injury.

events.title: The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions It is getting ever harder for Eurosceptics to deny that it was an economic and strategic blunder for Britain to leave the single market T he EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels. Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integration with the EU’s carbon emissions trading scheme. The agenda was set by Sir Keir Starmer as part of his intended “ reset ” of EU relations. Mr Burnham has since pledged to move further and faster towards closer ties, although he remains bound by his predecessor’s manifesto prohibition on membership of the single market and customs union this side of a general election. What the prime minister can achieve in that space will be determined partly by his judgment of what domestic public opinion will allow, but more immediately by the terms of the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. This legislative package, more commonly called “ Made in Europe ”, mobilises public procurement rules to insulate continental industries from what many EU political leaders see as unfair overseas competition – chiefly from China. Industrial policy and protectionism on such a scale is a symptom of the way a once-globalised trading system has in recent years fractured into rivalry between continental blocs. China’s colossal trade surplus, causing panic among European car manufacturers, for example, is one side of that story. Donald Trump’s capricious tariff wars are another. Britain looks perilously isolated in such a world, which is why Mr Burnham is keen to find some accommodation within the Made in Europe regime. That isn’t straightforward, given that the essential purpose of the new rules will be to benefit enterprises in the single market to the deliberate disadvantage of those on the outside, which includes Brexit Britain. Some compromise is available, with the UK recognised as a “trusted partner”, but that status won’t be accorded simply as a reward for pro-European vibes from Labour. Mr Burnham’s declarations of strategic intent are helpful, but there will be a lot of hard bargaining ahead on the terms of a deal. Without one, Britain’s carmaker and other industries would face crippling new trade barriers. For that reason, the “Made in Europe” question has shot up the government’s agenda. The Eurosceptic opposition parties, meanwhile, are silent on the subject. To acknowledge the existence of a problem would mean recognising Britain’s disadvantaged status outside the single market, which is a refutation of the founding case for Brexit . Mr Burnham will not find it easy to negotiate the next stage of Britain’s reintegration with the EU, but those who resist his direction of travel will find it ever harder to pretend there is any alternative. events.title: How ElevenLabs’ CTO is rolling out AI agents—and why he thinks bigger efficiency gains are ahead for the voice AI startup
events.summary: Alex Holt, the chief technology officer at ElevenLabs, is about as bullish on AI agents as a C-suite leader can get. The AI voice startup has deployed an inbound sales development representative (SDR) agent that has handled over 3,000 customer leads this year, qualifying over 90% of those potential clients in 32 different languages without any human intervention. Yet another AI agent serves as a coach to help new sales team members role-play customers interactions, resulting in faster onboarding for that part of the workforce. There’s also a recruiting agent that conducts first-round interviews with new job candidates, and within the company’s Slack, various agents are quick to jump in and answer any employee questions about internal processes. “I think what’s most exciting about this space is that you know you always feel like you’re on the tip of the iceberg,” says Holt. He says that the efficiency gains ElevenLabs reaps from agentic AI may feel cutting edge today, but “in six months time, you can see even more gains.” Increasingly, CTOs and chief information officers have homed in on agentic AI as a central focus for the value they expect to extract from their frothy investments in the technology. Agentic’s share of AI value grew from 17% in 2025 to 22% this year, according to research published by consulting giant BCG, and is projected to reach 39% by 2030. And yet, most surveys find that businesses are ill-prepared to rethink workflows and orchestrate multi-agent processes, in which one agent autonomously passes along work to another. Holt says most employees at ElevenLabs work collaboratively with agents and a majority have even built their own agents to help handle repetitive tasks. The company’s core business objectives don’t change with AI: sales teams are expected to use AI to generate more revenue at a faster pace; for customer service, satisfaction scores are closely monitored.  “It’s exactly the same business metrics,” says Holt. “This has to be an initiative that the business units themselves are driving and pushing. The agents and tech are a tool that they can leverage to do that.”  Organizationally, ElevenLabs has deployed an engineer to sit on every team across the business, and every group has fewer than 10 people. Within recruiting, for example, two forward deployed engineers work in a pod with HR colleagues with the sole objective of reducing the time it takes to get candidates through the interview process. Today, almost all prospective candidates are initially screened by an AI recruiter when applying for a role at ElevenLabs. “That’s 30 minutes that the recruiter can spend at the end of the process, convincing you to join,” says Holt. Holt joined ElevenLabs in September 2023 as an engineer after spending five years at software and data analytics company Palantir Technologies. He was elevated to the CTO role in June 2026. Three months later, the startup announced that it doubled its valuation to $22 billion . CEO Mati Staniszewski recently indicated that ElevenLabs may begin to plan for an initial public offering in 2028 . The next frontier for agentic AI, says Holt, is to put more effort into multi-agent systems, enabling greater shared context and more complex work handoffs between multiple agents. This is already under development for the company’s sales leads. The SDR agent uses voice AI to determine the seriousness of a prospective buyer, looping in a human representative after that screening process. But recently, one ElevenLabs customer was able to close a sale entirely through an interaction with two agents. First, the inbound request was fielded by the SDR agent, and later an account executive agent handled the legal documents and contracts.  “The value of that is you can now automate that whole chain for customers where it’s the simple, most repetitive mechanical cases,” says Holt. He says employees can dedicate more time to more complex inbound requests or upselling. Holt says embracing agentic AI at this magnitude does require some patience. Is the recruiting agent helping to hire the right people? Are ElevenLabs’ customer service scores improving with AI? “Some of these metrics can take a long time,” says Holt. “We lean on the business owners to identify those leading indicators and the metrics we should be measuring.” There are also instances where AI can act in unintended ways, an issue that’s raised alarm following recent high-profile instances in which OpenAI and Anthropic agents went rogue. ElevenLabs says it has created a human-led monitoring and observation layer to govern its agents. But mistakes can still slip through. One customer service agent erroneously gave a small refund under $30 to a customer and failed to escalate the issue to an employee. ElevenLabs created a test case that simulated the call and the exact chain of thought and reasoning that led the agent astray, then updated the prompts and guardrails.  Holt says tracking every decision that an agent makes in this manner can actually be helpful. If a human made the same mistake, the company likely wouldn’t have noticed. “It’s not just automating processes; it allows you to collect more data,” says Holt of agentic AI. “I expect over the next few years, the trend that we’re going to start seeing is people talking much more about optimizing these processes.” John Kell This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms
events.summary: The Iran war was the reason for the Democrats' blue tsunami that stunned Washington, Vice President Vance said in an X post Wednesday morning. Why it matters: The VP offered a surprisingly blunt assessment of why the GOP got crushed Tuesday night — and started to put at least a little daylight between himself and President Trump as the 2028 cycle begins. Vance's comments come hours after Trump admitted the Iran war partly played a role in pushing Democrats over the edge. Trump's son Donald Jr was quick to apparently endorse Vance's message. Driving the news: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote on X . "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." Vance's comments align with Trump, who told the Wall Street Journal: "Iran was a piece of it," though he did not say he regrets the war. What they're saying: Vance wrote on X that the "Democrat blowout" came despite optimism from within the White House about turnout and people "showing up." But, Vance said, "many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026" instead. The White House and vice president's office did not immediately respond to requests for comments Wednesday morning. Zoom in: Vance said Trump 2024 voters were angry with the administration and chose to embrace Dems. The GOP has to do four things to bring them back, he said: End the Iran war, focus on inflation, "put America First," and "change our relationship to Israel." "To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country," Vance wrote. Yes, but: Voters had other grievances in the election Tuesday night. Cost of living and government corruption were the two top issues in this year's election, per exit polls from AP . Gas prices and grocery costs have skyrocketed amid the Iran war and the president's tariff policies. Trump was also labeled "corrupt" and "dangerous" by majorities of registered voters in a poll prior to the election. The bottom line: Vance's candid response comes ahead of a potential 2028 presidential run. The vice president is already being watched by the pre-Trump Republican faction that never embraced Trump's takeover of the party, which might require him to distance himself from the president's policies. events.title: The Lawyer Holding Big Tech Accountable by ‘Beating the Tar Out of Them’ in Court
events.summary: As social media giants face allegations that they fail to protect users , attorney Mark Lanier is grappling with the question: What would it actually take to hold companies accountable? "I think it just takes beating the tar out of them," Lanier told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the WIRED World Fair on Wednesday. Lanier was the lead attorney in the first social media addiction case to go to trial, which resulted in a verdict against Meta and Google in March. The plaintiff was awarded $6 million in damages —a symbolic victory, but a rounding error in terms of the tech giants’ bottom lines. Lanier said lawsuits in which attorneys general represent their states have the potential to orchestrate significant change, alongside greater financial repercussions. In a case that went to trial in August, attorneys general across several states—including Arkansas, where Lanier’s firm served as outside counsel—accused Meta of failing to protect young social media users. A few days into the trial, Meta agreed to a settlement of up to $16.7 billion , to be paid out to 51 US states and territories. The social-media giant also pledged to make changes on how teenagers use Instagram and Facebook , such as a default two-hour time limit. (TikTok agreed to similar limits as part of a settlement in Alabama in September .) A $1.7 trillion-dollar company like Meta can treat such settlements and verdicts as the cost of doing business, even if the costs climb into the billions. But these cases also have more nebulous repercussions. They impact how the public— and companies’ own employees —feel about the platforms. Lanier said that, in addition to wins in court, change can come from people understanding companies’ actions and demanding accountability. “I am not here because I'm bored on a Wednesday,” Lanier said from the WIRED World Fair stage. “I'm here because I want everybody to know what these companies do—because that type of pressure will help change everything.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: House Democrats are eyeing Trump’s pardons and his family’s crypto deals — the last time they ran oversight, his administration ignored subpoenas
events.summary: Oversight is coming for the Trump administration. That’s been the message of congressional Democrats throughout the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign . Now that the party’s candidates have reportedly won control of the House of Representatives , that campaign promise is likely to be carried out. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told The New York Times in late October that among the potential oversight targets were pardons granted by President Donald Trump, possible corruption in government contracting and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency deals. Routine congressional oversight hearings usually don’t make headlines. That changed during the second Trump administration. When Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, what took place was a contentious, highly partisan, made-for-TV-and-social-media confrontation. Bondi refused to answer many questions from Democrats, instead launching personal attacks against these members of the U.S. Senate. The episode captures a basic tension in congressional oversight: Congress can demand answers, but getting them often depends on the cooperation of the branch it is investigating. That tension is about to sharpen when Democrats control the oversight process. Their hearings will likely be anything but routine. From our perspective as political scientists who study the U.S. Congress , congressional oversight has played an important role in American democracy. Here’s a brief history. Inquisitory powers In simple terms, oversight is the ability of Congress to ensure that the laws it passes are faithfully executed. This generally means asking questions, demanding information, convening hearings and holding the executive branch accountable for its actions. Oversight isn’t specifically mentioned in the Constitution. Article 1, Section 8 , which lists the powers of Congress, includes the power “to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper,” without identifying an oversight role. Once laws are enacted, Article 2, Section 3 , states that the president “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” However, the framers viewed congressional oversight as a key component of legislative authority. They wanted presidents to take Congress seriously and structured the Constitution to ensure that the executive would be accountable to the legislature. As James Madison urged in Federalist 51 , the separate branches of government should have the power to keep each other from becoming too powerful. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” Madison wrote. The framers drew from the examples of the British Parliament and Colonial legislatures . In 1621, Sir Francis Bacon was charged with corruption and impeached as Lord High Chancellor after an investigation by a committee of the British Parliament. And in 1768, the Massachusetts Assembly conducted an investigation of Gov. Francis Bernard that led to a formal request to the King of England for his removal. At the Federal Convention in 1787 that produced the Constitution, Delegate George Mason noted that members of Congress possessed “inquisitory powers” and “must meet frequently to inspect the Conduct of public officials .” Even though this idea was never written down, it was a habit of self-government that early Congresses put into practice. Early oversight hearings Congressional oversight began almost as soon as the first Congress met. In 1790, Robert Morris, the superintendent of finances during the Continental Congress and a financier of the American Revolution, asked Congress to investigate his handling of the country’s finances and was exonerated of any wrongdoing. During this period, congressional investigations were often referred to select committees – bodies created to perform special functions. These panels had the power to issue subpoenas and hold individuals in contempt. Since there was no official record of debates and proceedings , the public relied on newspaper accounts to learn about what had happened. In March 1792, congressional oversight exposed businessman William Duer, who signed contracts with the War Department but failed to furnish the needed military supplies. This shortfall contributed to a stunning U.S. military defeat against a confederation of Native American tribes in the Northwest Territory. Congress eventually removed the quartermaster general from his role for mismanaging the contracts. Throughout the 19th century, Congress continued to quietly exercise this power. Hearings from December 1861 to May 1865 on the conduct of the U.S. Civil War produced a detailed record of the war, exposed military wrongdoing and condemned slavery. In 1871, the Senate created a select committee to investigate Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction . Investigating corruption and criminal acts Congress started to use its oversight power more aggressively in the 1920s with the Senate Committee on Public Land and Surveys’ high-profile investigations into the Teapot Dome scandal . Hearings revealed that Interior Secretary Albert Bacon Fall had secretly leased federal oil reserves in Wyoming to two private corporations and had received personal loans and gifts from the companies in return. The investigation found clear evidence of corruption. Fall was indicted and became the first U.S. Cabinet member to be convicted of a felony . The U.S. Supreme Court helped to shape the legal foundation of congressional oversight. In McGrain v. Daugherty , decided in 1927, the court held that congressional committees could issue subpoenas, force witnesses to testify and hold them in contempt if they fail to appear. Two years later, in Sinclair v. United States , the court ruled that witnesses who lied to Congress could be charged with perjury. These cases granted the judicial branch’s sanction to what had long been an implied legislative power, cementing the constitutionality of congressional oversight. Oversight highs and lows The modern era of congressional oversight has produced some very important reforms – and some truly regrettable spectacles. The most important example of bipartisan congressional oversight came in response to reporting by The Washington Post’s Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward . The two journalists wrote about the 1972 burgling of Democratic National Committee offices in Washington, D.C.’s Watergate Hotel and subsequent cover-up efforts by the Nixon administration – and President Richard Nixon himself . On Feb. 7, 1973, the U.S. Senate voted 77-0 to establish a Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities , which brought together Democrats and Republicans to investigate what came to be known as the “Watergate scandal.” The committee’s work spurred action in Congress to impeach Nixon, leading to Nixon’s resignation in 1974 and to the enactment of legal reforms to provide an institutional check on presidential power. events.title: Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics | Aditya Chakrabortty
events.summary: Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics As tech bosses get richer and ordinary Americans struggle, Democrats put the case against the US’s grotesque unfairness – and voters responded R emember the “vibe shift”? Just last year, columnists and corporate boardrooms alike declared that the second coming of Donald Trump meant the old rules of politics and even everyday civility were roadkill. “I feel liberated,” one top banker told the Financial Times . “We can say ‘retard’ and ‘pussy’ without the fear of getting cancelled … it’s a new dawn.” Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, but to be a billionaire was very heaven. Because in Trump, the tech bosses had a politician who could work magic by forging a forever alliance between them and blue-collar America. This was the very core of Trumpism, the trick that wowed rightwingers around the world: how he could yoke together minimum-wage workers with the 1%; Latinos and black voters with those happy to dabble in a little light racism; the Epstein-haters with the Epstein class (who can forget Elon Musk’s email to Jeffrey : “What day/night will be the wildest party on your island?”). And he did it by alchemising class antagonism into culture war . Forget about that pay rise – have you have heard about those Haitians eating dogs ? Silicon Valley, Wall Street and east coast media owners all saw Trumpism not as a political strategy but as a turn in the entire culture: a vibe shift to the right. They were wrong. Tuesday night was a comprehensive rejection of the president. Before the midterms, ultra-wealthy donors such as Musk poured billions into Trump’s proxies, but the working- and middle-class base were not having it. The relatively new coalition that put the orange man in the White House has been smashed apart by old-fashioned class politics. When election analysts observe that the struggle of ordinary Americans to afford the basics of life now “polls in a tier by itself” , that is class rearing its head. It is a response to the record petrol prices in a car-centred society, the huge swings in everything from eggs to mincemeat, the battle to meet the rent. The squeamish, including within the Democratic establishment, might euphemise these as “economic issues” or “affordability”, but remember that this time last year, the democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani turned affordability from a meme into a platform for winning elections. In late 2026, and going into the next battle for the White House, the New York mayor now wields national influence. Among Mamdani’s achievements has been his reminder to ordinary voters that when they can’t afford the basics, it’s not just because prices are unreasonably high – it’s also because their pay is unfairly low. He has tied the cost of living to an argument about inequality, and rightly so. Over decades – through Reagan and Clinton, Bush and Obama – Republicans and Democrats have changed the tax code to reward ownership rather than earning, so the richest 400 households now pay lower rates of tax than the bottom 50% of Americans. As the radical economists Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster show in their new book, Grand Theft Capital: What Workers Should Know About the Affordability Crisis, the share of national income going to ordinary workers has slumped from 30% in the 1960s to 20% today. This is the destruction of working-class lives and dreams in which Republicans and Democrats colluded. This is the American carnage that in 2016 helped propel Trump into the White House. But the most glaring feature of this era of Trumponomics has been its shameless inequality. The “hottest country in the world”, as the president calls it, relies on AI for growth. For the first half of 2025, the Harvard economist Jason Furman estimated that spending on AI infrastructure made up 92% of GDP growth. These supposedly national gains are getting raked off by a tiny number of people and funds, based overwhelmingly in one strip on the west coast. In October, the fund manager Apollo pointed out that , of the entire S&P index of America’s biggest 500 companies, only the so-called “magnificent seven” tech firms were flourishing. The other 493 were seeing flat revenues and flat profits. Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, wrote: “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America.” Billions for Sam Altman and Dario Amodei and Jensen Huang; a pittance for those outside Silicon Valley. No wonder the most reviled candidate on so many of this week’s ballots was the datacentre : the energy-sapping, water-sucking, community-destroying datacentre that merely aids the processing of humans into appendages to chatbots. Analysis for the Economist showed that Trump supporters with a datacentre on their doorstep were flipping in droves to the other side.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters FLIP reveals a planet hidden in Webb data, boosting detection sensitivity by up to 15 times China outlines plans for moonshot it hopes to land by 2030 13 hours ago Improved asteroid deflection model runs faster, reveals more doomsday worries 1 day ago Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth 4 days ago Voyager 1 gives controllers the silent treatment 5 days ago NASA ponders a Hubble servicing mission or a controlled deorbit 5 days ago Scientists have developed a way to remove starlight from telescope images that improved sensitivity to faint exoplanets by up to 15 times in tests on James Webb Space Telescope data. A team led by Northwestern University's Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez combined a physics-based telescope model with optimization techniques used in machine learning to subtract unwanted starlight. Directly imaging exoplanets remains difficult because their host stars' glare can overwhelm their faint light. Existing techniques subtract modeled or reference starlight, but tiny changes in telescope optics can leave residual glare that hides planets. The team's Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP) framework models how light passes through the telescope, adjusts for optical imperfections, and simulates the glare to be subtracted. Applied to observations from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), FLIP produced the first image of the known giant planet 51 Eridani b at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 micrometers, where conventional processing had failed. Tests showed sensitivity improvements of two to 15 times over conventional techniques, according to the Nature paper . "This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories… potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success," the paper says. Further work includes reducing computational demands and developing ways to handle the much larger data volumes produced by ground-based observations. events.title: Conservative group issues warning on AI
events.summary: AI policy helped deliver Democratic majorities and Republicans need a major recalibration on the issue ahead of the next presidential election, a post-midterms memo from the conservative AI policy group Alliance for a Better Future argues. The group, helmed by former Virginia Republican official Janet Kelly, focuses on pro-family, pro-worker AI policy and has groups like the Heritage Foundation on its advisory council. The memo , which was shared first with Semafor states that “it’s impossible to ignore the strong impact Super Intelligence policy had on this election and how connected it is to economic concerns in particular. … If Republicans recalibrate correctly, [AI] can be an asset in 2028 for both our country and our party.” The memo describes liberal efforts to connect economic concerns to anti-elite populist sentiment related to AI as a “deadly one-two punch.” Those worries drove AI “up the issue grid” so rapidly it flew under the radar for Republicans, it continues, arguing that GOP candidates and their allies also failed to counter Democratic attacks that associated their candidates with a pro-AI and data center message. A full-throated embrace of Trump’s light-touch AI regulatory agenda would be a mistake for future Republican candidates, according to the group, which is pushing for a greater level of AI guardrails than the administration. “It would be political malpractice for Republicans not to course correct their SI policy positions and risk permanently ceding this issue to Democrats,” the memo states. The group recommends passing bills around chatbots and kids, codifying Trump’s voluntary AI accord into law, instituting economic policies that help workers, and pushing companies to focus more on uses like curing disease and less on “experiments that only benefit the developers themselves.”

events.title: A consumer-based AI wave is coming
events.summary: The bulk of investment in the AI boom has gone into enterprise applications — that is, technology that people use for work. But the biggest successes in the tech industry that have carried the entire stock market for decades have almost all started with consumers. Marissa Mayer, who recently started a consumer AI app called Dazzle and joined me on Semafor’s Future Proof, says thatby 2030, consumer AI will be about twice the size of enterprise. Dazzle, an AI personal assistant that doesn’t read your email or calendar like other AI productivity apps, looks almost exclusively at your photo reel to gain information about you. Its capabilities are impressive considering its narrow source of data. And whether it goes on to become a fixture in AI’s future, it is a preview of a new consumer-focused tech wave that hasn’t yet arrived in the industry. Once it does, the public’s perception of AI could change again. Based on Tuesday’s election results, it’s hard to imagine it could get worse. — Reed Albergotti
