events.title: Danish students join European protest wave against education funding cuts
events.summary: Danish government proposes scrapping allowance scheme for students from wealthier families. Thousands of young people in Denmark have demonstrated against a government plan to cut student stipends under a decades-long allowance scheme, adding to a wave of youth unrest across Europe. Organisers said up to 13,000 students marched from Copenhagen’s city hall square to parliament over proposed cuts to free up funds for defence spending on Monday, under the banner “Enough is Enough”. list 1 of 3 Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z protests in more than 30 German cities list 2 of 3 Tension and clashes as hundreds of thousands protest in France list 3 of 3 Police storm Portugal housing protest camp The rally echoed student protests in France that spread to other European countries in recent weeks, and that morphed into wider grievances over the cost of living and housing crises impacting young people across the continent. Student associations said some 40,000 students were on strike at 57 schools across Denmark over the proposed cuts. Since 1970, all students enrolled in schools or university in Denmark over the age of 18 have automatically received the student allowance regardless of their parents’ income. Students currently receive 1,154 kroner ($173) a month for those who live with their parents, and 7,426 kroner ($1,116) for those who live on their own. Under the new government proposal, the allowance would be abolished for students living with parents earning over 700,000 Danish kroner ($105,248). Only students living with parents earning between 419,589 kroner ($63,087) and 700,000 kroner ($105,248) a year would be eligible for the allowance, with stipends staggered based on their parents’ income. Copenhagen police were out in force during the demonstration. Thousands of young people chanted “Broken Promises” and carried signs reading “Save SU”, the Danish acronym for the student allowance, “Less Support, Less Educated” and “Don’t Cheat the Young”. “In Denmark, we get funding and economic support for getting an education, and we’re very proud of this,” said one protest organiser, Danish High School Students Association president Oscar Tonsberg Hoffmann. He told AFP that it would be wrong to dismantle “one of the world’s strongest educational systems”. Kieran Hindshaw, a 23-year-old agronomy student, said he felt betrayed by the government. “I’m infuriated that we finally get a supposedly ‘red’ government in Denmark that includes the left parties … we get cuts to our welfare and to the economies of young people whilst they’re funding corporate tax reductions and warfare,” he said. The Higher Education Ministry said around 14,000 students are expected to lose their stipends, and some 8,000 would see it reduced. The government has also proposed that unemployment benefits for recent university graduates be paid only to those who have worked during 18 of the last 24 months of their studies. Industry Minister and Social Liberal Party leader Martin Lidegaard has meanwhile said the cuts “are not pleasant decisions”.

events.title: My parents gave me 3 storage units as an early inheritance. They collected vintage toys for decades.
events.summary: Steph Krim inherited her parents' collection of vintage toys. Courtesy of Steph Krim Steph Krim grew up surrounded by vintage toys her parents collected for their auction business. Her parents gave her the collection as an early inheritance after years in storage. She drove 1,000 miles to bring it home and is turning it into a new business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Steph Krim . It has been edited for length and clarity. I had always been that weird kid whose family collected things . My parents had a catalog toy auction business . This was before eBay existed. We'd travel all around the world, finding things — mainly toys — for our collection. My mother would photograph the items and paste the photographs into the catalog, and my father would type the descriptions of each item using a typewriter. Then the catalog would be sent out to potential customers, along with a list of how much previous items had sold for. People would call up or send in their bids by mail. We lived in a long, thin house in Massachusetts . Attached to our house was a three-story extension where we stored all the collectibles. Collecting was my life as a child, and I think my parents would have carried on with the business forever if they could have. But when I was about 13, eBay came around , and the industry completely changed. They put the collectibles in storage units for years Not selling as much as they had previously, my parents decided to move house and put the collection into storage units . It would be years before I ever saw the collection again. Steph Krim inherited all her parents' collectibles. Courtesy of Steph Krim Eight months ago, my mother called me — I live in Chicago now — and told me: "It's probably crazy, but if you could figure out a way to drive a truck across the country with this stuff, we would be willing to part with what we have here." I had mentioned to them that I would be interested in offering to buy the collection if they were going to sell, but I didn't imagine that would be for a long time (probably every). I knew it meant too much to them. But when they offered, I jumped at the chance. I had no idea what was in the boxes In July, I flew to Massachusetts with my family and loaded up a 26-foot truck with boxes from three huge storage units. I had no idea what was in the boxes. I genuinely didn't think we would get everything in the truck — there was so much. Then we drove 1,000 miles back to Chicago , unloaded the boxes into a storage unit, and, one by one, I've been unpacking each box. Countless wind-up toys, models, Pokémon, robots, tin toys, dolls, action figures, and so much Disney. Everything from Batman to Cabbage Patch to ET to Star Wars, and tons of stuff from Japan in the 90s. Pop culture everything. Steph Krim was surprised every time she opened a new box. Courtesy of Steph Krim I never know what's going to be in each box. I get surprised every time. It's going to take me a very long time to get through every box, but I don't feel overwhelmed by the amount of stuff there is. I grew up around this stuff. Collections are a way we put on display what we think is beautiful, what we are attracted to. It's intimate and personal — a way to connect with ourselves, but then show that part of ourselves to the world. I love collecting. Although I may not feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of stuff to sort through, I do feel overwhelmed by a personal sense of responsibility to make sure I don't waste this opportunity. It's my family's history. Their life's work. The contents of those storage units could have remained untouched, but instead, my parents gave them to me as an early inheritance. It's a chance to extend our family history of collecting. My parents used to call their business Krim's World. I'm calling this business Krim's Clubhouse in honor of their work and this little universe of toys we've created and get to play in. More than ever, I'm in contact with my parents. My phone is full of messages with both of them — a constant whirlwind of joyful energy and excitement as we discover what's inside. I want to break a world record As a child, I was teased by other kids when I told them we had the world's largest plastic wind-up toy collection, because I didn't have proof to back up the claim. I plan to create the proof. While I'm selling off duplicates of the wind-up toys, I'm keeping at least one of each and attempting to get the collection into the Guinness Book of World Records. Seven-year-old me would have lived to beat this record, so I just have to. And maybe, after all these years, I'm finally going to prove that weird kid right. events.title: These big companies moved to red Texas. Now the state's gone blue.
events.summary: Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Texas Senator-elect James Talerico celebrate their wins. Business leaders may be reconsidering their moves after Texas went blue on Tuesday. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Tuesday's blue wave reached all corners of Texas. A democrat now controls the governorship, while the state house is still tabulating votes. More than 200 businesses have moved their headquarters to Texas since 2019. More than 200 companies flocked to Texas in the last seven years, as Republicans in charge of the Lone Star state advertised a business-friendly aura with lucrative corporate tax incentives. On Wednesday morning, though, the CEOs of those companies woke up to an unprecedented blue wave whose crests reached deep into Texas, from the Rio Grande Valley to Dallas. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, a state representative with a minimal national profile, defeated Gov. Greg Abbott, a prominent Republican running for a fourth term. Hinojosa has signaled that she favors rolling back some of the incentives that lured businesses to the state. "I do think we should wipe clean corporate welfare in this state," she said in an October interview with Kut News, a Texas NPR affiliate. On the national stage, Republican Senate candidate and Attorney General Ken Paxton suffered a stunning loss to James Talerico, another state representative, by more than a million votes. The GOP managed to hold onto the state senate, but results were still being tabulated on Wednesday for a handful of competitive state house seats, according to the Associated Press. While Hinojosa and Talerico gleefully bumped drinks at Whataburger on Tuesday night, business leaders were no doubt busy contemplating whether the economic incentives that motivated their move would stay in place. "I never expected Texas to turn blue," Jason Calacanis, a tech entrepreneur and influencer, said on X. "I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!" Texas levies no income taxes on private individuals or corporations. Though the state charges a franchise tax on companies that post more than $1 million in revenue, Abbott has signed bills expanding franchise tax exemptions. During her campaign, Hinojosa focused her criticism of tax incentives on data centers. Here are some of the largest companies that moved their operations to Texas in recent years, according to a list compiled by Abbott's office. events.title: Netanyahu bet on Trump – but both lost
events.summary: Alongside scramble to form ruling coalition, Israel’s political establishment grapples with US voter rejection of White House ally and own contribution towards it. US President Donald Trump and his Republican party’s resounding midterm defeat has left many in Israel, particularly on the political right, grappling with the scale of the rebuke to those seen as their closest allies in Washington. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray himself as almost uniquely qualified to maintain the unflinching support of Trump, who returned to the White House last year promising, among others, to not start “stupid foreign wars that never end”. list 1 of 4 ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results list 2 of 4 Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win? list 3 of 4 Iran’s Khamenei warns Trump loss at polls won’t end US hostility list 4 of 4 How big is the Republican midterms loss, and is there a silver lining? Yet in late February, Trump joined Netanyahu in ordering a joint military campaign against Iran, prompting immediate Iranian retaliation and raising the spectre of an all-out regional war. With the prospect of renewed hostilities looming, both leaders exchanged effusive endorsements in the build-up to Tuesday’s US congressional election and Israel’s parliamentary vote last week, calling upon the other’s electorate to head to the polls to support their ally. The moves, however, seem to have either backfired or missed the mark dramatically. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition finished the October 27 electoral race with just 53 seats, far shy of the 61 needed to form a government. Trump’s party, meanwhile, lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate to Democratic challengers who made sweeping inroads into traditionally Republican territory, including the strongholds of Texas and Kansas. “Obviously, what we have witnessed is a historic political tsunami that amounts to a total repudiation of Trumpism, so it’s certainly broader than one issue,” Shibley Telhami, of the University of Maryland and director of the Critical Issues Poll, said of the US midterm results. “But foreign policy was central, especially the Iran war and US backing of Israel, as Americans tie these to pocketbook issues,” he added. The US is Israel’s staunchest diplomatic and military backer. Over the years, it has repeatedly used its United Nations Security Council veto to block dozens of resolutions critical of Israel, including several motions calling for an end to the genocidal war against the Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. At the same time, it has been providing Israel with at least $3.8bn in military aid annually, allowing it to acquire the cutting-edge US weaponry that has granted it military superiority across the region – assistance, however, that is carrying an increasingly high political cost. Polling overseen by Telhami a week ago found that a majority of people in the US believed that Israel had influenced the Trump administration’s decision to instigate the costly and protracted war with Iran. The survey indicated that Washington’s close relationship with Tel Aviv had become more of a liability than an asset for many in the electorate, Telhami noted, “with most saying specifically Israel would be a factor in their vote. An even larger majority said the Iran war, which they tie to Israel, would impact their vote”. While Trump acknowledged the Democrats’ midterm win, and reluctantly conceded that the war on Iran was partly to blame due to its impact on energy prices, Netanyahu has spent the days since his own electoral defeat questioning the results. Over the past week, the Likud party leader has falsely accused foreign powers of illegally boosting the vote for Israel’s Arab-led parties and cited his victory among Jewish voters as the basis for a national government. In his most recent echo of Trump’s reaction to his own loss in the 2020 US presidential election, Netanyahu even threatened not to recognise the certification of the results. But as Israel enters a period of coalition wrangling, its political establishment also has to grapple with the routing of its White House ally and its potential culpability in it. On Wednesday, key opposition figure Yair Lapid said almost all of Netanyahu’s actions since the vote, including his call for the internal security service Shin Bet to investigate the leaders of the Arab parties, in conjunction with the US election results, had rendered the prime minister politically noxious. With voting still ongoing on Tuesday, Trump said in a TV interview he had made a deal with Netanyahu that ⁠⁠the US would no longer be providing funding of “$4bn a year” to Israel after the end of 2026. While details remain scarce, the timing prompted speculation that Trump’s comments were part of a bid to stave off public anger over his administration’s support for Israel and a time of mounting domestic economic pressure.

events.title: Women ride midterm blue wave to historic gains
events.summary: Women candidates won enough races Tuesday to set a new record for Democratic women's representation in the U.S. House — among other historic firsts in Congress and governor's races nationwide. The big picture: The spike for Democratic Women's Caucus members in the House alone marks an increase of more than 60% since 2016. At least 100 Democratic women and 16 Republican women have won House seats as of Wednesday morning, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The total is expected to climb for candidates across both parties, with dozens of races still uncalled. What they're saying: "Despite Republican attempts to silence us and take away our rights, we have built a coalition in Congress that is bigger and more powerful than ever," DWC Chairwoman Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) said in a statement. "We smashed through a glass ceiling," she added. "Because of the hard work of so many, Congress will look more like America." The intrigue: Women veterans are poised to make gains in Congress after 38 ran in Tuesday's general election — up from 21 in 2024, per civic organization With Honor Action . Several Democratic women veterans are leading in competitive House races that could flip Republican-held seats. In South Carolina , retired Navy Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore, who was removed as chief of the Navy Reserve under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, leads Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt in the race for former Rep. Nancy Mace's seat. In Arizona, Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza leads Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani. In Ohio, Air Force veteran Kristina Knickerbocker leads Republican Rep. Mike Turner. The AP had not called any of the three races as of Wednesday morning State of play: Democratic women could gain powerful committee chair positions as control of Congress shifts. Currently, just one woman chairs a standing House committee: Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.), who leads the powerful Rules Committee. She's locked in a razor-thin reelection race against Democrat Chuck Hubbard. Among those already likely positioned for gavels: Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) on their chambers' Appropriations committees, which oversee federal spending. Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), currently Democrats' minority whip, could become the first woman to serve as majority leader, two decades after Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) become the first woman speaker of the House. Zoom out: Women are also taking over governor's mansions across the nation. Progressive, pro-women EMILYs List said Wednesday that a record-high number of Democratic women governors are poised to serve in 2027. That includes Keisha Lance Bottoms , who boxed Republicans out in Georgia and will become the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. Deb Haaland , who won New Mexico's gubernatorial election, has become the first Indigenous woman elected governor of a U.S. state, per AP . There were also historic firsts for Republican women: Republican Julia Letlow is Louisiana's first Republican woman elected to the Senate. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) will be Tennessee's first woman governor. What we're watching: There's still plenty of dust still to settle in the wake of a massive midterms shakeup . But one thing is clear: A historic coalition of women is headed to Capitol Hill. Go deeper: Hakeem Jeffries gets the majority of his dreams

events.title: Meta sells first bonds in euros, raises €9 billion
events.summary: FILE PHOTO: Meta's logo and a keyboard are shown in this illustration created on October 19, 2026. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo Meta sold its first euro bonds and raised €9 billion, after a US$15 billion dollar sale, to fund faster AI infrastructure spending. The deal shows big tech is still raising cash for data centres, computing power and cloud growth, even as doubts grow over the AI boom. Meta joins Alphabet in using Europe’s deep bond markets, which can offer lower costs and help firms hedge currency risk. LONDON - Meta Platforms on Nov 4 sold its first bonds denominated in euros, a lead manager memo seen by Reuters showed, with big tech firms pressing on with fund-raising, even as doubts surface over the strength of the AI boom. The multi-tranche bond sale raised €9 billion (S$13 billion), the IFR news service reported. Maturities for the bond sale ranged from four to 38 years, the memo seen earlier in the day by Reuters showed. Meta on Nov 3 raised US$15 ​billion (S$19 billion) through a five-part US dollar bond offering, ‌as the Facebook parent turns to debt markets to help finance accelerating investments in AI infrastructure. The sale adds to a wave of AI-related fund-raising as companies seek capital for data centres, computing capacity and cloud expansion, despite historically relying on strong cash balances to fund growth. Meta is the second big tech company to tap European bond markets this week. Google parent Alphabet on Nov 2 sold €6 billion worth of bonds in a sale that garnered strong demand, with an order book that topped €17 billion. Concerns about the financing required to support heavy spending on artificial intelligence, and the returns needed to justify that investment, have weighed on technology stocks and bonds in recent weeks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5% in October. Meta’s bond sale also took place against the backdrop of the Democrats’ sweep in the Nov 3 US midterm elections, which has fuelled fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny. Issuing debt in foreign currencies also allows companies to hedge the currency risk from their global assets, while taking advantage of relatively lower borrowing costs in markets like Europe. Europe’s deep capital markets offer an attractive source of funding. Meta’s shares were up about 2% on the morning of Nov 4 in New York. Citi and Morgan Stanley were the bookrunners, according to the memo and IFR. REUTERS

events.title: Trump’s politics meet reality
events.summary: David’s view Late on Tuesday night, after he left the victory party for Senator-Elect Annie Andrews, former South Carolina Democratic Party Chairman Jaime Harrison called to reflect on what just happened. Harrison ran against Sen. Lindsey Graham in 2020, and raised more money than any Democrat in the state’s history. He lost by 10 points. Joe Biden tapped him to run the Democratic National Committee, for what both men hoped would be the presidency that ended the MAGA era. Trump returned, stronger than ever, and Harrison went home. Two years later, Harrison watched Graham’s sister fumble away a Senate seat that had been safely Republican since Strom Thurmond left the Democratic Party. Harrison recalled what he told the late senator in 2020: “You better be grateful Donald Trump was on this ballot, because you would have lost.” This was how Democrats thought about Donald Trump for the better part of a decade. The president convinced Democrats that pre-2016 political rules do not apply to him, that he could lead his voters anywhere. When he said he was “on the ballot,” maybe they’d see him there. On Tuesday night, voters revealed that his roughhouse politics don’t work without the perception of a good economy and a world at peace. Trump did nationalize the election, hold his rallies, and summon the party to Dallas for a midterm convention to juice turnout and get the coalition on book. But it wasn’t a majority coalition anymore. In Trump’s first term, his humiliation of the old Republican Party and its mega-donors showed them that there was a new electoral coalition – tough on immigration, ready to use tariffs to bring jobs back to America, and about as socially conservative as the median voter. At the start of his second term, Trump seemed to have found a synthesis between his new coalition and the donors. He could turn out his base with money from people who didn’t understand that base. That didn’t last two years. Trump notched some significant wins, like the end of the old asylum system and a suite of progressive tax cuts, which Democrats are afraid to run against. But the Trump who destroyed ancestral Democrats in the Rust Belt and rural South is gone. He’s built a nationalist project that his opponents feared — right up until sunset yesterday, when the first early votes were counted in the Indianapolis suburbs. Trump hadn’t convinced supporters to pretend he was “on the ballot.” Or perhaps they just didn’t want to. Democrats made a bet that gravity was real, and Trump couldn’t defy it anymore. Their own angst was helpful. They ran many candidates who distanced themselves from “woke” left-wing ideas, now aware of how Trump could exploit them and how his ultra-aggressive GOP — no more John McCains, ripping the mic away from a woman babbling about Barack Obama’s DNA — would amplify whatever he said. Their strategy was much more compelling to voters than to people who write about politics. There probably won’t be baseball caps with the official House Democratic slogan (“Fighting for an Affordable America”) in embossed letters. Running back 2024 in 2026 With the votes mostly counted, the attempts to copy what worked for Trump in good times look downright pathetic. Republicans who believed they could inherit the Trump coalition mostly tried what had worked for him in 2024. Like Trump, Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran for governor in Ohio, went after his Democratic opponent’s personal weaknesses, suggesting she’s a drunk and the mother who abandoned her knew she was a “liar.” In Texas, Ken Paxton tried Trump’s nickname game (“James Talafreako”) and suggested that his opponent harbored a secret sexual desire for transgender children. Both men lost. Vice President JD Vance ran the same plays, just as ineffectively. In Texas, he’d joke about whether Talarico’s “browser history” would reveal a proclivity for child pornography. In Ohio, he said that he wanted to meet Amy Acton at a bar — “I understand that she’s into that sort of thing!” In Kansas, he said that Methodist minister Adam Hamilton wore Christianity like a “skin suit,” and in Michigan, he accused Abdul El-Sayed of harboring hatred toward white people and Western civilization. In two months, Vance will walk to the old Senate Chamber, smile for the cameras, and swear in Talarico, Hamilton, and El-Sayed for their six-year terms. Republicans are already looking at a post-Trump GOP, and the most panicky among them are wondering if there’s some way to avoid it being led by Vance. Democrats have not suddenly found the message or candidate that can win them a new governing coalition. But Republicans simply don’t know what to do. Republicans who built their identity around Trump, believing that he had a magic with working class voters that could be transferred to them on Truth Social, were wrong. Notable Politico’s Jonathan Martin called his shot before the polls closed : Voters wanted to punish the Trump GOP. In The Washington Sun, Elena Schneider, Alex Roarty and Reese Gorman looked comprehensively at the fatal error Republicans made at the start of the cycle: Tying everything to Trump.

events.title: Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it
events.summary: Democrats are preparing to use the next debt ceiling increase to seek concessions from President Donald Trump. The Treasury could reach its borrowing limit in 2027, setting up another deadline-driven confrontation. Democrats may seek to reverse Medicaid and other healthcare cuts enacted in 2025, limit the war with Iran or roll back tariffs. A prolonged standoff could unsettle Treasury markets and increase the risk of missed federal payments. The electoral sweep by Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year: the debt limit . Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market. Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results Past episodes of brinkmanship around the need to raise the government's borrowing limit have involved Republicans in Congress demanding budget cuts from a Democratic president as the price of their vote. This time it will almost certainly be the left seeking concessions from the right. The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if — as many expect — it ends in compromise. Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increase government spending than lower it. With high bond yields weighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging. Live updates: Day 2 of 2026 midterm election results A blow to billionaire donors and a reckoning for tech companies — 5 takeaways Many in the markets are stuck on the outdated idea that Democrats are less assertive than Republicans, said Aniket Shah, head of the Washington policy team at the investment bank Jefferies. "They have this sort of mental image of Biden-Harris 2024," said Shah. "I don't think they realize how aggressively Democrats plan to take 2027." The debt ceiling is a quirk of the congressional budgeting process. It stops the government from borrowing funds that Congress has already ordered federal agencies to spend. And because Congress has run deficits for decades — this year at $1.99 trillion — the pile of debt periodically bumps into the debt ceiling. Congress last set the limit in 2025, when it gave the Treasury Department the authority to borrow $41.1 trillion. The Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by midsummer, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center , a nonprofit that tracks the issue. The Treasury can use budgeting techniques to extend the so-called X-date, when the U.S. would no longer be able to meet all its obligations, to sometime in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to Wall Street estimates. A few technical hiccups aside, the U.S. has never meaningfully breached the debt limit. The results of the U.S. missing payments would be chaotic as damage ripples out across the financial system into the global economy. U.S. default would immediately call into question trillions in Treasury securities that are the lifeblood of the global financial system. Damaging them could send the U.S. and global economies into an economic tailspin with no obvious means of recovery. Because the stakes are so high, Shah and many others on Wall Street have come to believe that the episode will produce volatility but will ultimately be resolved in compromise. Fights under former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden saw Republican congressional majorities use the issue to ram through spending reductions. (The 2025 raise was less contentious, because Republicans held Congress and the presidency. It was passed along party lines.) Still, the risk-taking in those episodes contributed to ratings firms' decisions to downgrade U.S. debt — and could again. President Donald Trump has called for Republicans to resolve the issue in the next few weeks, before the new Democratic-majority Congress is seated. That isn't likely. The 2025 debt limit increase only passed because it was tied to a package of tax cuts and other policy changes. Republican debt hawks complained but held their noses. Republicans may attempt to raise the limit in the coming lame-duck session under a budgeting procedure called reconciliation, which would allow them to move ahead without Democrats' votes. But success would require unity among a fractured, fleeting Republican majority that also faces several other more pressing priorities.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Firms still want kit on-premises, but spike in revenue is as much about increased costs as higher sales Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices 9 hours ago Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits 9 hours ago Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station 1 day ago Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B 1 day ago Marvell wants to be a copper topper, bets $115B on photonics leader to push optical networking 2 days ago On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing. What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent. However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year. Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems. This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI . Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house. According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue. The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC. The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes. "Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph. "The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices." events.title: California’s billionaire tax is a referendum on the tech industry
events.summary: Reed’s view Putting California’s billionaire tax on the ballot, which was trailing in early results but remained too close to call Wednesday, may have felt like a crusade against the rich and powerful. But the measure is also a referendum on the state’s homegrown tech industry, which is confronting an American public who no longer feels that technological advancement is always making their lives better. For decades, tech has been the great forcing function in the American economy: creating competition, spurring growth, and propagating a talent base that drew the top workers from around the world. It benefited no economy more than California’s, which surpassed Japan to become the world’s fourth-largest economy. But despite cool gadgets like smartphones and GPS systems, many Americans are now focused on social media’s impacts on children, anxiety over AI, and the political backlash toward data centers, which ran deep enough this election cycle to turn even the reliably red Texas statehouse blue . If that’s the way Texas went, you can only imagine how Californians are feeling as they see a gigantic transfer of wealth to billionaires behind the Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX IPOs, and question why the rest of the state isn’t sharing in the AI boom’s windfalls. Dinging California’s billionaires with a wealth tax feels pretty good to almost everyone. But catharsis doesn’t necessarily improve people’s lives. And slowing down technological progress isn’t the answer, either. The only answer I can see is ensuring more Americans take part in the massive wealth gains that are going to happen in the coming decades. If the majority of Americans don’t share in the upside, they will see only downside. As we learned Tuesday, an angry populace will stand in the way of tech’s grand plans. Notable The revolt against the tech industry sprawled out beyond California on Tuesday, with more than 40 localities rejecting data centers in ballot measures, Semafor’s J.D. Capelouto reports.

events.title: Kraft Heinz to divest its North American coffee business in $650 million deal
events.summary: Kraft Heinz is divesting its coffee business to One Rock Capital Partners at an enterprise value of $650 million. The move comes as CEO Steve Cahillane works to turn the company around with increased investment and a focus on its core brands. Kraft Heinz also raised its 2026 outlook in its quarterly earnings report and now anticipates a smaller decline in organic net sales. Kraft Heinz announced Wednesday that it will divest its North American coffee unit in a deal that values the business at $650 million on an enterprise basis, as it works to refocus on its core brands. The deal with private equity firm One Rock Capital Partners includes brands such as Maxwell House and Gevalia and is expected to close in mid-2027, the company said in a news release . Kraft Heinz will retain a 30% noncontrolling equity stake in the business. Kraft Heinz said it will use the $500 million of post-tax cash proceeds from the transaction to pay down its debts as it works to prioritize resources where it can accelerate growth. "This transaction is a meaningful step in unlocking value from our portfolio and will further accelerate the momentum behind our transformation," Steve Cahillane, CEO of Kraft Heinz, said in the release. Cahillane joined the company in January and paused work on plans to split the company in two , a move that would have reversed the blockbuster $46 billion merger from a decade ago. He said the problems Kraft Heinz faced were "fixable and within our control." The turnaround efforts have included a $700 million investment back into the business and a sharpened focus on some of its core brands . Also on Wednesday, Kraft Heinz reported third-quarter earnings that beat expectations and raised its 2026 outlook. It now expects organic net sales to be down 0.5% to 1.25%, an improvement from its second-quarter report, which projected that sales could decrease as much as 2%. "Our 2026 operating plan to turn around the U.S. business and accelerate growth internationally is on track," Cahillane said. "Relative to last year, our market share, sales, and volume trends are improving in every region. We are increasingly meeting consumers where they are, and giving them more reasons to choose our brands."

events.title: Presidential hopeful Vance appears to question Iran war after polls debacle
events.summary: Vance cited trusted pollster saying Iran war, Israel ties were top of mind for Trump voters swinging to Democrats. Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the US Congress to Democrats. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote in a lengthy post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, has been a key negotiator with Iran as the two countries search for a way out of the conflict, which has dented their economies and pushed global fuel prices up. His statements on Tehran have been more dovish than those of other key members of the administration, and his post-election note appears to mark the closest he has yet come to publicly diverging from his boss on an issue that looks set to dog Republicans as the war continues. Citing a pollster he describes as “one of the smartest people I know”, Vance said he was told ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given by Americans surveyed who had voted for Trump in 2024 but were planning to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms. In stark contrast, Trump said, in the wake of the rebuke at the ballot box , that he had no regrets about launching the conflict. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again ,” he told the Wall Street Journal.

events.title: Sam Altman joked about AI's thirst for memory with a new social media nickname
events.summary: Sam Altman briefly changed his X name to "Ram Altman" Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sam Altman renamed himself "Ram Altman" on X after his recent comments on the memory shortage. The AI boom has memory in high demand, and Altman has called for discussions on how it is allocated. RAM and DRAM power the GPUs behind data centers, pushing up prices for consumers and businesses alike. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman briefly gave himself a new name on X: "Ram Altman." The change followed a joke about his appetite for computer memory after recent controversial comments on how the much-desired memory is allocated. Responding to an Altman post about people retaining control over AI’s future, an X user wrote "sam come here come here" alongside an image of several memory chips leading toward a cardboard box propped up like a trap. sam come here come here pic.twitter.com/xj6AO6tSXR — Harshith (@HarshithLucky3) November 4, 2026 Altman replied, "i lol’d." When another user asked whether he could rename his account "Ram Altman,” he answered, "OK yeah" — and did. ok yeah — Ram Altman (@sama) November 4, 2026 The change was short-lived. By 11 a.m. ET on Wednesday, the CEO's name had reverted to "Sam Altman" on his X profile. It was unclear why he changed it back and OpenAI declined to comment when contacted by Business Insider. Altman's joke landed after recent remarks about the world’s limited supply of DRAM , a type of memory that is key to both personal computing and the GPUs that power AI data centers. On an October 29 episode of the "Cheeky Pint" podcast , he argued that running AI models on personal computers could leave scarce memory underused. In a market where supply is tight, he said, cloud data centers can use it more intensively. Sam Altman joined John Collison for a pint to discuss the scaling laws of agent teams, proving Navier-Stokes, why hand-written software will soon look quaint, the optics of token pricing, and what computing looks like beyond the keyboard and screen. 00:00:00 Introduction… pic.twitter.com/q7jsLCszLW — Cheeky Pint (@CheekyPint) October 29, 2026 The comments drew criticism from some people who took them to mean consumers should have less access to memory so data centers could have more. Elon Musk, who has feuded with Altman for years, weighed in on Sunday, posting a meme on X with the caption: "The people deserve to have their RAM too!" The people deserve to have their RAM too! pic.twitter.com/q6dwauALw4 — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026 Altman used the X exchange to push back on the topic. but only because...i actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers, and it is fucking annoying that this was taken out of context. i have been arguing for the world to ramp up memory production for a long time. — Ram Altman (@sama) November 4, 2026 He said he wants the world to have "tons of memory" and for people to put as much as they want in their computers. He added that he has long argued for increasing memory production and was annoyed that his remarks had been taken out of context. When another user asked why he wanted their RAM, Altman replied: "I want you to have so much ram let's build more." i want you to have so much ram lets build more — Ram Altman (@sama) November 4, 2026 Altman’s clarification points to the billion-dollar question beneath it: how to meet demand for memory in both data centers and personal computers. His answer, at least on X, was to make more of it. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
events.summary: A recurring subplot of President Trump's term has been a desire to replace Biden appointees to the powerful Federal Reserve Board of Governors — even ahead of their terms ending — with allies. That effort now looks dead in the water. Why it matters: Even if Trump succeeds in his efforts to fire governor Lisa Cook , or to oust any of the other three Biden-era holdovers on the seven-member board, a Democratic Senate will likely block any replacements it views as insufficiently independent from the administration. State of play: The president seeks to fire Cook — whose term runs through 2038 — for alleged mortgage fraud, an effort that has been blocked so far by the courts. The White House plans a hearing over the allegations next month. Former chair Jerome Powell has remained on the board as a governor, a term that ends in January 2028. Michael Barr, whom Biden appointed as top financial regulator, has remained in place as a governor in a term that extends to 2032. Philip Jefferson's term as vice chair ends this coming September, though his term as a governor extends to 2036. Between the lines: It would break with current precedent for those officials to stick around to the end of their terms. In recent decades, Fed governor spots have turned over much more regularly, particularly after their time as chair or vice chair ends. Powell, Barr and Jefferson may feel greater comfort relinquishing their roles as governors before the end of their terms if they are confident the Senate will block any replacements who don't respect the tradition of central bank independence. Of note: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee that must advance Fed governor nominees, and she has assailed chairman Kevin Warsh for being a "sock puppet" of the administration. Only one Senate Democrat, John Fetterman, voted to confirm Warsh.

events.title: Palestinian citizens of Israel face intimidation after election success
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? After winning a record number of parliament seats, Palestinian-led parties face campaign against them. Israel has officially certified its election results – delivering a blow to right-wing claims of a stolen vote – but the record 19 seats captured by Palestinian-led parties have triggered aggressive police raids, arbitrary arrests, and targeted interrogations by state security apparatuses. The electoral gains made by the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) – could give the Zionist opposition to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu the upper hand in forming the next government, if they choose to work with the Arab parties. list 1 of 3 Israel’s election commission rejects Likud’s fraud claims, confirms results list 2 of 3 How big is the Republican midterms loss, and is there a silver lining? list 3 of 3 Iran’s Khamenei warns Trump loss at polls won’t end US hostility Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have portrayed the increased vote share for the Palestinian-led parties as the result of illegality , a+nd say they represent Jewish Israelis. Political analyst Mamoun Abu Amer told Al Jazeera that the political backlash was preplanned. “From the beginning, it was clearly a systematic campaign when Arab citizens mobilised heavily, especially in the villages, the Naqab and the Bedouin areas,” Abu Amer said. He noted that the heavy turnout deeply shocked the Israeli political establishment, prompting Netanyahu to launch a smear campaign to discredit the democratic process. Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al Party – which is part of the Joint List – shared a similar analysis. “There is no indication that the elections were manipulated in the Arab towns, as everyone expected the voting rate to be high this time in advance due to the bad reality created by this government for our public,” Tibi told Al Jazeera. “On the contrary, there was a press report on Israel’s Channel 12 television revealing that the Likud party, led by Netanyahu, had prepared and readied a file before the elections to invent this falsehood when the results were issued, because they know with absolute certainty that they will lose the elections.” The intimidation campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel materialised through aggressive police actions on election day. As reported by The Jerusalem Post, police arrested several Ra’am supporters for alleged vote-buying, which Likud immediately invoked to claim an attempt to steal the election. However, many of the suspects were quickly released, with a judge noting that suspicions had weakened and that investigators had failed to explain why restrictions were necessary. Defence lawyers maintained the seized funds were intended for charitable assistance. “The best proof of this is that the detainees were released,” Tibi said. “We said from the beginning that the mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse.” The security crackdown extended beyond party activists to media personnel. Abd Abu Shahadeh, a journalist and political activist, was arrested on Tuesday night by the Israeli police and the domestic security service, the Shin Bet. Sami Abu Shehadeh, the chairman of the Balad Party, another member of the Joint List, called it an attempt by Netanyahu to “steal the elections”. Human rights and Israeli affairs expert Mustafa Ibrahim argued that Netanyahu’s approach is deeply rooted in discriminatory state policy. Ibrahim pointed to the treatment of Palestinians in Israel since the formation of the state in 1948 – when hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were forced out of their homes in the Nakba – including the period of military rule that was imposed on them until 1966. Palestinian citizens of Israel have always been viewed as a “fifth column”, Ibrahim said, “and they are described as enemies of the state.” Tibi emphasised that the suppression of Palestinian rights in Israel was part of a broader ongoing pattern. “Political intimidation began on October 7 itself, when celebrities from our community were summoned for investigation simply for liking a post or writing a Quranic verse whose interpretation was distorted,” Tibi told Al Jazeera, referring to the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel. He added that the decision in late September by the Israeli electoral committee to disqualify the Palestinian-led parties from the elections – later overturned by the Israeli Supreme Court – was part of that campaign. “The tools multiplied and the goal is one, which is indeed to intimidate us from political work as candidates and voters,” Tibi said. The political pressure from Netanyahu and his allies has engulfed Israeli state institutions. According to The Jerusalem Post, Shin Bet Director David Zini requested to interrogate senior Palestinian lawmakers, including Tibi and United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, over foreign interference claims.

events.title: Global leaders weigh in on America's midterm shake-up
events.summary: World leaders are reacting to Democrats' comprehensive midterm wins, which saw them retake the Senate and flip the House on Tuesday night. Why it matters: The results could reshape President Trump's final two years in office, with major implications for U.S. relations with allies and adversaries alike. Zoom in: As Trump faces competing calls over whether to resume military action in Iran, Iranian officials supported the Democratic victories as a sign of opposition to the war. Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X , "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message." Prior to the election, regional mediators led by Qatar were trying to reach a diplomatic deal to restart negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to avoid reentering the war, three U.S., Israeli and regional sources said, but renewed fighting remains on the table. But while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume fighting in Iran, his political future remains uncertain, with neither bloc securing the 61-seat majority needed to form a government in Israel's recent election. Zoom out: Trump's second-term decisions have significantly strained relationships with U.S. allies and partners, leading countries to increasingly view Washington as unreliable, self-interested and less committed to global cooperation , according to Pew Research Center data. But Tuesday's election results appear to have infused renewed hope about relations from international leaders. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez applauded Americans for voting "against policies that only make people poorer," and against "hate," "sexism," "climate denial" and "elite privilege," in a post on X ." South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters he believes Democratic control of Congress will "introduce a new era in world relations," adding that he hopes for improved collaboration on geopolitics, trade and investment, Bloomberg reported. Trump, who has repeatedly criticized Ramaphosa, and prioritized South Africans for refugee admissions in fiscal year 2026, citing debunked " white genocide " claims — which falsely allege that white Afrikaners face racial violence by the country's majority Black population. The other side: Moscow signaled little optimism about the change in power, warning that Democratic control could further strain U.S.-Russia relations, particularly with tensions in Ukraine. Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov told RIA Novosti news network that Democrats' "approach to relations with Russia is extremely negative." Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning struck a measured tone, saying China hopes to "build a constructive relationship," and continue working with the U.S. Still, the U.S. Army Pacific is closely watching for a potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan in 2027 and beyond, which could quickly devolve into a bloodbath. Yes, but: Some leaders are also questioning how much progress Washington can make amid such deep political splits. Theo Francken, Belgium's Minister of Defense and Foreign Trade, said on X that governing in the U.S. will be "quasi impossible in the coming years with so much internal division and polarized power bastions." European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said she's "cautiously optimistic on Europe's behalf" and how it could benefit Ukraine and global relations. events.title: Sequoia hits rewind, undoing 20 years of expansion
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Sequoia Capital posted a memo to X on Wednesday morning titled “The Sequoia of Tomorrow” that’s full of surprises. The firm has raised roughly $10 billion in new funds, it says. It is also closing its London office, shutting down its Arc accelerator and its Scouts program, merging its early-stage and growth teams into one, flattening its partnership, and killing the Monday partner meeting. The framing is forward-looking, but the messaging is very much about rewinding to an earlier time when the team was smaller and focused more narrowly on Silicon Valley. Sequoia says as much itself. The firm describes coming out of a roughly 20-year expansionary phase during which it built multiple businesses in multiple geographies and says an unintended side effect was hierarchy. Nearly everything being undone here was built during that stretch, under a succession of stewards running from Doug Leone to Jim Goetz to Roelof Botha. One of the most surprising developments is that the firm is killing two programs that put Sequoia closest to young founders. Scouts , which Sequoia launched around 2009 and, anecdotally, half the industry has since copied in some form, gave small checks to founders and operators to invest on the firm’s behalf; it was a way to see deals through people closer to interesting new founders than any partner could be. Jason Calacanis famously pointed Sequoia to Uber through the program. Sam Altman brought Stripe to Sequoia as a scout, too. Other early scouts included Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky and Dropbox founders Arash Ferdowsi and Drew Houston. Arc , launched in March 2022, was Sequoia’s answer to Y Combinator: a batch accelerator for pre-seed and seed founders, running several cohorts a year for seven weeks, with admitted companies getting $500,000 to $1 million up front. Both were bets on being early and being everywhere. Now Sequoia says it wants to put more energy behind fewer people and things. Also gone is the firm’s London office, which Sequoia opened in 2020. Several people will leave the firm as result. “We simply don’t see the need for a local presence,” the memo says, adding that Europe will keep producing “outlier founders” and that Sequoia can support them from the Bay Area. (If founders didn’t already feel pressured to move to the Bay Area or open an office in the region, they will now.) Luciana Lixandru, hired from Accel in 2020 as Sequoia’s first partner in Europe, says she was offered a move to San Francisco and declined. (“Europe is where my family is, and where I want to build,” she wrote on X.) She says she remains a partner and will keep her board seats while investing personally in European founders. For European entrepreneurs, the message is going to be particularly difficult to digest, especially as it follows Andreessen Horowitz shuttering its London office last year and Coatue closing its own in 2024. Sequoia didn’t say it won’t fund Europeans, but it’s definitely reinforcing here that the center of gravity is once again in the Bay Area. The rewind extends to people, too. The memo notes that Carl Eschenbach, the former Workday CEO, is very much back in the fold (he returned as a full-time partner in March). It also says the team has “reinvigorated the GOAT,” Doug Leone. Though the nomenclature at venture firms is all over the place — including Sequoia — the memo makes clear there are now seven general partners who primarily own and operate Sequoia: Alfred Lin and Pat Grady — who are the firm’s co-stewards — along with Andrew Reed, Shaun Maguire, Konstantine Buhler, Sonya Huang, and David Cahn, who joined the firm in 2023. There are other changes as a result. Jess Lee, the firm’s first female partner and an early-stage investor who oversaw its Arc program, is no longer shown on Sequoia’s investor page but rather as an operator in the role of its chief product officer. Stephanie Zhan, an investor who had joined Sequoia in 2015, has meanwhile left the firm entirely, announcing last month that she is launching her own new firm. Sequoia rarely lets anyone go entirely. Founder Don Valentine famously kept turning up at partner meetings for roughly a decade after handing over the firm. Goetz, who stepped back from his management responsibilities in 2017, is still featured on the firm’s site. Botha is the exception. He was voted out as senior steward last fall in a surprise shake-up days after sitting down with this editor — the firm framed it as a handoff to Lin and Grady — and he completely cut ties with Sequoia this summer, around the time he joined SpaceX’s board . The changes are sure to make waves. Still, none of them are completely out of character. Sequoia iterates routinely, including, at times, reversing out of earlier moves.

events.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
events.summary: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.   While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.  Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before. What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto. So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election. There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process. The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump. With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations. Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout. Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4. And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly. We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

events.title: Owono enduring ‘hardest days of my life’ after De Miguel death
events.summary: Tenerife striker De Miguel died on Tuesday as a result of injuries from a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Owono. FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono said he is enduring the “hardest days of my life” after the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel , whom he collided with during a Spanish second division match on Monday. The 30-year-old Spanish footballer died on Tuesday as a result of injuries he suffered in the collision with Equatorial Guinea international Owono , who had raced into midfield to clear an aerial ball. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words, and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club Andorra on Wednesday. “I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. “I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesus.” Spanish police sources told the AFP news agency that an investigation into what happened has been opened, under judicial supervision. Andorra players observed a minute’s silence on Wednesday before a voluntary training session, which Owono, 25, did not attend. Owono received support from the president of the African country’s federation, Venancio Tomas Ndong Micha, in a letter of condolence following De Miguel’s death. “I feel compelled to convey all our solidarity and support at this time to our player Jesus Lazaro Owono,” Micha wrote. “We know that, as the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress. “From the Equatorial Guinea Football Federation, we offer him all our human and professional backing, fully aware of the harshness of this event, which no one in our sport ever wishes to witness.” Andorra defender Lautaro Spatz posted on Instagram in support of Owono, whom he said was “deeply affected” by what had happened. “Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone,” wrote Spatz. “In football, unfortunate incidents can happen, but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences.” Earlier on Wednesday, it was confirmed that Tenerife and Andorra’s Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend would be postponed. Tenerife were due to face Granada away from home, while Andorra were set to welcome Mallorca. “After the tragic news of the death of Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel, the game … this Saturday November 7, at Nuevo Los Carmenes [stadium], has been postponed,” said Granada in a statement. Mallorca said, “At times like this, respect and sensitivity in the face of a situation of profound grief must come first.” The Spanish football federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches this week as a mark of respect following De Miguel’s death. Tenerife plan to hold a tribute to De Miguel at the club’s stadium on Saturday, which supporters can attend, and are holding a six-day mourning period. The club said the first team, board and staff will attend De Miguel’s funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, in the province of Toledo on the Spanish mainland, where he has family roots. A minute of silence was held before Champions League matches on Tuesday in honour of the striker, with the same planned for the rest of the week’s fixtures, organised by European football’s governing body UEFA.

events.title: The new Congress may struggle to push a progressive agenda
events.summary: Major change on key issues, such as Israel-Palestine, will be limited by the president and the Democratic establishment. As the dust settles on the 2026 US midterm elections, two facts are clear: First, the Democrats have achieved a historic victory – and second, Donald Trump remains president for the coming two years. That means Congressional Democrats will have three legislative lanes to pursue: The first is constraining Trump. This includes doing what they can through Congress to bring the Iran war to a conclusion, blocking many of his nominations, particularly to the judiciary, ending ICE’s aggressive immigrant detentions, and pursuing oversight of Trump and his allies’ financial networks and alleged corruption. The second lane will be about demonstrating a positive policy agenda to inform the 2028 cycle, when Trump will be off the ballot. This is more about “messaging bills” focused on social issues, but could also include economic measures such as tax reform proposals, as well as significant reforms of US global defence cooperation authorities and shifts to major foreign policy questions, such as aid to Israel. The final lane will be that – perhaps narrow – set of issues where bipartisanship and cooperation with the White House is possible. Putting guardrails around America’s burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector may fit in that box, although some of Trump’s biggest funders are likely to do what they can to derail progress. Many of the bills that will be put forward in the first and second lanes would be subject to presidential veto. Others will be toned down, as the Democratic establishment seeks to resist the progressive left’s ambitious agenda. These dynamics are likely to make the upcoming Congress less productive. On foreign policy, in particular, Congress is able to pass just a slim set of acts without presidential endorsement, such as war powers legislation, limiting the president’s ability to wage war without Congressional approval; or measures like the recent Senate resolution advanced by Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen to demand reporting on Israel’s human rights record; or committee subpoenas, which can be used to investigate members of the Trump administration for wrongdoing. But they are likely to be ignored or stonewalled by the White House, leading to months, if not years, of fruitless litigation. That is not to say that introducing “stand-alone” bills on issues, such as arms transfers to Israel, would not be important even if blocked by the president. They remain useful both for framing the conversation and for getting members of Congress on the record and establishing consensus positions. In the Senate, where several incumbents are likely to throw their hats into the upcoming presidential nomination contest, such bills could be used to highlight the progressive credentials of some candidates – or to force more conservative members into awkward positions. That might ultimately make a difference in terms of the framing and debate for the 2028 election – and a potential Democratic administration thereafter. But it will not change anything in the immediate term. There are at least three tools available to legislators where a fierce – and perhaps impactful – debate is likely to play out. The first is that enabled by Congress’ constitutional “power of the purse”. If the current Republican majorities do not manage to pass an annual funding bill by the end of this calendar year, the Democrats will have both the current year and the next two years of US government funding under their control. This includes, of course, Israel’s annual allocation of $3.3bn, which Trump himself put into doubt in a surprising and as yet unclarified statement on election day. If nothing else, the president’s call for an end to security assistance to Israel may accelerate what would likely have been a steady reduction under Democratic leadership. The new Congress will also be able to reconsider a range of funding restrictions and requirements, such as the prohibition on funding the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), or the limitations on funding the Palestinian Authority. Passing such bills will not be simply a matter of partisan rancour — we can expect some pretty tough battles to play out within the Democratic caucus itself on some of these issues. Then it is another matter of whether the Trump administration adheres to the law with the funding it ultimately receives. The second area to watch is that of oversight. With the majority in hand, Democrats in the House and Senate can set the agenda – deciding which actions by the Trump administration are ripe for investigation, identifying witnesses, and using the committee gavels to drive the public debate.

events.title: Uber beats on revenue, CEO tells CNBC the company is 'investing significantly' to add drivers
events.summary: Uber reported better-than-expected revenue for the third quarter, but the company missed estimates in its two core units. The mobility business was challenged overseas by rising fuel costs and lower driver availability. Uber plans to have over 2,000 fully driverless vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027. Uber reported revenue for the third quarter that topped analysts' estimates, but the company missed expectations in its two key businesses. Shares of the ride-hailing service rose more than 7% on Wednesday. Here's how the company did versus analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 25 cents vs. 96 cents expected Revenue: $14.77 billion vs. $14.69 billion expected Revenue increased 10% from $13.47 billion a year earlier. The company reported net income of $512 million, down 92% from a year earlier, when the company had a $4.9 billion benefit from a tax valuation release. Uber's core mobility unit, which is its ride-hailing service, saw a 2% decline in revenue to $7.52 billion, missing the average estimate of $7.71 billion, according to StreetAccount. Revenue in the food delivery business increased 23% to $5.49 billion, trailing the $5.51 billion average estimate. Total bookings of $59.82 billion were about in line with the $59.83 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount. Uber's revenue beat was due to growth in its freight division. Sales jumped 34% to $1.76 billion, topping the StreetAccount consensus of $1.49 billion, Elon Musk's record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire Apple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' ways AMD's data center revenue nearly doubles and Lisa Su expects growth to accelerate Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshah i said, in prepared remarks ahead of a scheduled call, that the company's core mobility segment performed slightly below expectations overseas. "Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," he said, adding that Uber is making "targeted investments to strengthen driver supply." In a CNBC interview, Khosrowshahi emphasized that Uber has "more demand" than supply, especially for its mobility services. "We don't want to raise prices on our customers," he said, adding that the company is also doing what it can to avoid longer wait times. Uber is "investing significantly" in bringing more drivers on board in India, Brazil, and the U.S. to meet demand, he said. Uber has also committed about $10 billion in capital to bring more driverless vehicles to its platform, the CEO said, through an array of partnerships and investments in companies including Rivian, Nuro, AVRide and others developing robotaxis and driverless trucks. Near-term, Uber plans to have over 2,000 automated vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027, half operating in the U.S. and half internationally. It expects to have around 700 available on its platform by the end of the year, adding Amazon's Zoox and Motional robotaxis to its platform in Las Vegas this quarter. Uber is also growing its delivery business through acquisitions of Delivery Hero in Germany and ezCater in the U.S. In its Uber Eats business, a recently expanded partnership with Costco in the U.S. is "tracking ahead of expectations," Khosrowshahi said. The company said Costco is now one of its top merchants in terms of gross bookings. For the fourth quarter, Uber sees overall bookings of $64.5 billion at the mid-point of its forecast, in line with the average StreetAccount estimate of $64.26 billion.
