events.title: VMware returns to low-end server virtualization with 'vSphere Express'
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters 128-cores max, sold on distributors' marketplaces, and in with a shot of restoring some trust Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge 1 day ago Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden 1 day ago Tesco replacing VMware with Proxmox in its stores and on the edge 9 days ago Microsoft’s second-hand licensing appeal gets the brush-off 16 days ago VMware is pushing so many patches, it thinks users need new tools to manage the flood 22 days ago As first reported by The Register , VMware has returned to the low-end server virtualization market with a product called "vSphere Express." The product will run on up to 128 processor cores and includes vMotion to allow live migration of VMs, automated restart of failed VMs, a distributed switch, rapid non-disruptive patching, and support for physical and virtual trusted platform modules. "We have been listening to the market at the low end, and they want a basic core server virtualization platform," said Prashanth Shenoy, vice president of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). He explained that each instance of vSphere Express will be discrete, meaning it won't be possible to manage them centrally. "This is tested for small implementations," he told The Register . "We do not want a customer to run this on thousands of cores." Shenoy said the vSphere Foundation (VVF) enterprise virtualization product, and Cloud Foundation (VCF) private cloud suite, are appropriate for users with more complex needs. vSphere Express will, however, match the release cadence of VVF and VCF. Under Broadcom’s ownership, VMware has enormously reduced the number of resellers in its channel program , meaning it no longer has partners who are a good fit for this product. The virtualization giant will therefore sell vSphere Express through its distributors, most of which now operate cloud marketplaces at which affiliated resellers can acquire software – an arrangement channel folk call "two tier distribution." We asked VMware to tell us the price it will charge for vSphere Express. A spokesperson told us it will offer a per-core subscription license at a price "significantly lower" than VVF or VCF but declined to quote a dollar amount. "We encourage interested customers to reach out to their local reseller for information related to pricing and subscription terms," the spokesperson wrote. VMware has also bulked out VVF and VCF a little, by adding disaster recovery and policy-based networking for virtual private clouds that it previously sold as add-ons. Shenoy pitched the additions as demonstrating VMware's intention to add value to VVF and VCF, in part by ensuring the bundles include tools that users are likely to consider represent essential functionality. The Broadcom business unit will also add new features, such as native AWS S3-compatible object storage for its VSAN virtual storage. That update, due in calendar Q1 of 2027, means VSAN will become a more convenient platform on which to store the unstructured data that AI workloads rely on, therefore boosting the utility of VMware's AI Factory. VMware also plans to make its AI Factory easier to implement. "The idea is to focus more on AI, less on setup," Shenoy said. Analysis: A welcome low-end return faces an uncertain reception VMware's return to the low-end server virtualization market may not be well-received, because it has largely ignored users of its existing low-end vSphere Standard product for the last few years, and irritated many by insisting they upgrade to the more expensive and complex VCF. The virtualization giant also cast aside thousands of resellers. When The Register chats with members of the VMware community, we often hear that trust in the vendor has diminished. Your correspondent therefore feels that vSphere Express will get a mixed reception.

events.title: Brent oil slides to $94 on Iran uncertainty after US midterms
events.summary: Oil prices continued to decline on Wednesday, falling to their lowest levels in nearly two months, as the market sought signals on the direction of the US-Iran war after the Democrats resoundingly won in the US midterm elections . Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, slid 8.47 per cent to $94.83 a barrel at 8.58pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, shed 7.5 per cent to $88.88 per barrel. Both have now retreated more than 15 per cent this week. The US held its midterm elections in which the Democratic Party took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, throwing President Donald Trump's agenda into further uncertainty, not least regarding the direction of the conflict in Iran. The results are seen as a message from American voters frustrated at high inflation and soaring gas prices as a result of the war. Oil prices could stabilise if expectations of reduced US military engagement in Iran build, said Aliasgar Tambawala, co-chief investment officer at Dubai-based financial services firm Klay Group. “Sustained progress towards de-escalation and improved security around the Strait of Hormuz would reinforce this relief,” he said. He added that these developments could reduce the need for further tightening from the Federal Reserve. The US central bank last week decided to hold interest rates after it raised them in September in a bid to tame rising inflation. The fall in crude prices came even after Washington confirmed carrying out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm island on Monday. Tehran, on the other hand, said it had intercepted drones in the area. Negotiations between Washington and Tehran have resumed, with mediators including Qatar and Pakistan, but there have been no clear signals on what the next moves may be. Iran was less optimistic, with its supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei reportedly saying that those expecting a shift in US policy towards his country after the midterm elections were “gravely mistaken”. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, meanwhile, warned Washington against further military action, saying the country would not be intimidated by threats or aggression.

events.title: Elon Musk's 'vote red' post vanished after Election Day
events.summary: Elon Musk spent big on the 2026 midterm elections. A deleted X post shows how well those donations turned out. Annabelle Gordon/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images Elon Musk urged Americans to "vote red" ahead of the midterm elections. Then, a blunami. The post was no longer on Musk's timeline on Wednesday morning following the Democratic sweep. Elon Musk posted a simple Election Day message Tuesday: "Vote red today!" Americans largely didn't follow his advice. Then, it seems, he deleted the post. On Wednesday, hours after Democrats surged to tsunami-like wins in the midterm elections, that Musk plea to vote for Republicans vanished from his X timeline. Musk didn't immediately respond to Business Insider's questions about why the "vote red" post was removed. Early on Wednesday, as the results became clear, he appeared to shift strategy and joked on X about his failed midterm spending approach . "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he wrote. In a separate post, he said, "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." The SpaceX CEO was the largest single donor during this midterms cycle, spending more than $440 million to back Republican candidates. He also used X as a platform to deride Democratic opponents. Texas, where Musk has reincorporated both SpaceX and Tesla, was a particular focus. He spent $224 million to back Texas Republicans during the race, per The New York Times, and, on X, called the Democratic now-Senator-elect, James Talarico, a " far extreme leftist ," a " creep ," and " pure evil ." Those posts are still live as of the time of publishing. The midterms could have major regulatory, contracting, and policy implications for Musk — and shares of both Tesla and SpaceX slumped on Wednesday as investors digested the election results. Data center companies are also flashing red. Musk is not the only Silicon Valley-to-Texas tech bro processing the collapse of a longtime Republican stronghold. Some "All-In" podcast hosts and Texas-based AI executives have started publicly mourning the midterm results . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement. The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now. It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said. Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information. Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening . I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built. I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help. But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later. I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to. For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember. One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame. I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading. Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature. This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder. While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons. I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.

events.title: Here’s how the candidates backed by AI super PACs fared
events.summary: This was the biggest year ever for AI super PAC spending. Years ago, the industry barely registered in campaign finance, but this cycle, AI super PACs spent $79 million across 68 House and Senate seats, according to Tech Influence Watch . Most of that money landed early, and the biggest fight came in June’s Democratic primary for New York’s 12th District, where Leading the Future spent more than $8.1 million against Assemblymember Alex Bores, co-author of the state’s RAISE Act, while Public First spent about $15 million to back him. More than $40 million in outside money poured into the race, making it the most expensive House primary of the cycle. Bores lost. And then the money got quiet. As of Oct. 26, Leading the Future had spent only $7.4 million on general-election races, despite having $34 million in cash on hand across its network, according to The Intercept’s analysis of FEC data.  The industry is split into two camps, with Leading the Future on one side. Funded largely by Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen, who each gave $25 million, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, who gave $25 million, according to FEC filings , it wants light regulation and a single national AI standard, according to Axios , and spends through Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans. On the other side, Public First pushes for stronger AI safeguards through Jobs and Democracy for Democrats and Defending Our Values for Republicans. Here’s how the candidates backed by AI super PACs fared in the most competitive races. S enate South Carolina: Darline Graham (R) vs. Annie Andrews (D) — (Andrews won, 51.1%–46.7%) American Mission and Building the Future, a pro-data center super PAC, spent $4,801,981 supporting Graham this cycle, according to Tech Influence Watch . It was the AI industry’s biggest bet on a competitive general election race, and Andrews used it against her, calling her “Data Center Darline.” Nebraska: Pete Ricketts (R) vs. Dan Osborn (I) — (Ricketts wins, 50.3%–43.7%) Defending Our Values, part of the Public First network, backed Ricketts with $274,485, according to Fortune analysis of FEC filings. OpenSecrets reported $262,625 . H ouse Florida’s 25th District: Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D) vs. Scott Singer (R) — (Moskowitz wins, 51.5%-46.4%) Think Big, part of Leading the Future, spent $259,574 supporting Moskowitz this cycle, according to Fortune analysis . CNBC reported $310,000. Defending Our Values, part of Public First, spent $857,426 supporting Singer, according to Fortune analysis . Montana’s 1st District: Aaron Flint (R) vs. Sam Forstag (D) — Flint conceded to Forstag, who led 51.5% to 45.7%. Decision Desk HQ projected Forstag the winner. As of Wednesday morning, The Associated Press has not called the race. American Mission, part of Leading the Future, spent $590,428 supporting Flint this cycle, according to Fortune analysis.   North Carolina’s 1st District: Laurie Buckhout (R) vs. Rep. Don Davis (D) — Buckhout conceded to Davis, who led about 50.1% to 46.8%. Decision Desk HQ and NBC News projected Davis the winner. As of Wednesday morning, The Associated Press has not called the race. American Mission spent $509,067 supporting Buckhout this cycle, according to Fortune analysis . Texas’ 32nd District: Jace Yarbrough (R) vs. Dan Barrios (D) — Yarbrough led, 51.5%–48.5%. As of Wednesday morning, The Associated Press has not called the race. American Mission spent $129,367 supporting Yarbrough this cycle, according to Fortune analysis . Ohio’s 7th District: Brian Poindexter (D) vs. Rep. Max Miller (R) — (Poindexter wins, 54.9%–45.1%) Jobs and Democracy, part of Public First, spent $570,204 supporting Poindexter, according to Fortune analysis . Texas’ 35th District: Carlos De La Cruz (R) vs. Johnny Garcia (D) — (Garcia wins, 55.4%–44.6%) Defending Our Values spent $1,492,321 supporting De La Cruz this cycle, according to Fortune analysis . Pennsylvania’s 7th District: Bob Brooks (D) vs. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R) — (Brooks wins, 56.1%–43.9%) Jobs and Democracy spent $263,250 supporting Brooks this cycle, according to Fortune analysis . Alabama’s 2nd District: Rhett Marques (R) vs. Rep. Shomari Figures (D) — (Figures wins, 53.8%–46.2%) Defending Our Values spent $974,908 supporting Marques in this cycle, according to a Fortune analysis . OpenSecrets reported $959,908. Texas’ 9th District: Alex Mealer (R) vs. Leticia Gutierrez (D) — Mealer conceded to Gutierrez, who led 57.5% to 42.5%. As of Wednesday morning, The Associated Press has not called the race. Defending Our Values spent $647,075 supporting Mealer this cycle, according to Fortune analysis. Trump-aligned No Going Back super PAC spent more than $543,000, according to the Houston Chronicle . The results suggest AI money was no match for the night’s broader Democratic wave. Of the candidates the two networks backed, those who won were mostly Democrats in races their party carried across the country, while most Republicans backed by either network lost, including Graham, the industry’s biggest general-election bet. The exceptions included Ricketts in Nebraska and Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman in Wyoming, whom American Mission backed. Bores, whose primary loss kicked off the AI spending war, is already looking ahead: his new nonprofit, Who Decides, aims to raise $30 million before 2028. events.title: Business leaders react as a 'blunami' sweeps America
events.summary: Brad Gerstner and Reid Hoffman are two of Silicon Valley's most prominent elite investors, hedge fund managers, and venture capitalists. Bloomberg and JP Yim/Getty Images Business and tech leaders across the US are reacting after the Democrats took full control of Congress. LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, Brad Gerstner, and Elon Musk are among those reacting to the blue wave. Data centers and California's ballot measure targeting billionaires are in the spotlight. The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington. Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats. This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny. In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead. Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country: Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman is a Democratic megadonor. JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening. "Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote. "This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued. Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024. Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right. Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development. "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post. Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX. In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state. Lisa Su, AMD CEO Lisa Su. Win McNamee/Getty Images Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI. "At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added. Dara Khosrowshahi, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi at Uber's America250 celebration in July. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Uber Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC. "I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer." "I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out." Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election. Keith Rabois, Khosla Ventures managing director Keith Rabois. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami." It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing. While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted. Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman. Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami. Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner Bloomberg/Getty Images Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections. In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown." But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade." Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds. The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July. events.title: Ousted Good Good marketer sues the company, alleging he was defamed during the Callaway ad aftermath
events.summary: Garrett Clark, one of Good Good's cofounders, was featured in an ad that sparked backlash. Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images Good Good's former marketing VP sued the company, alleging defamation. Jeff Lefkovits' suit says a controversial scene in an ad made for Callaway was added without his knowledge. Lefkovits was one of those ousted after backlash to the ad. Good Good's former marketing head has sued the company and its ex-CEO, alleging he was scapegoated for a controversial promo made for Callaway. The ad was meant to promote a Callaway driver co-branded with Good Good, the creator collective whose golf videos are popular on YouTube. In the ad, one of Good Good's cofounders, Garrett Clark, runs toward a female member of the group, Alexis Miestowski, and shoved her to the ground, saying, "Do not touch my new driver." Then-CEO Matt Kendrick and Clark said at the time that the ad was meant as a riff on the popular horror movie "Obsession." The idea was that Clark had become obsessed with the golf club to the point of insanity. The ad landed with a thud as critics said it made light of domestic violence. Good Good's top two execs, Kendrick and then-president Joe Flannery, left in the wake of the ad, and the company lost a string of partners. The Good Good ad, since pulled, was meant to be a riff on horror movie "Obsession." Good Good Good Good took down the ad and apologized, as did Callaway. Callaway said that while the company was not involved in its production, its review process was inadequate. Both said the ad was inconsistent with their values. In a civil suit filed in Texas, former brand and marketing VP Jeff Lefkovits says that the scene was "conceived of and approved on set," not in the original "lighthearted parody script" he approved. He alleges that the finished ad was "embraced by Good Good's own performers and owners and approved in writing by Callaway." The suit says Lefkovits was falsely blamed for the ad, and alleges defamation by Good Good and Kendrick, the former CEO. It seeks more than $1 million in relief. Neither Good Good nor Kendrick have filed a legal response to the suit. A Good Good spokesperson said the company had no comment on the suit. Kendrick didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. The ad debacle was a striking turn of events for Good Good, which had been widely regarded as a creator-economy success story. The YouTube group, known for its high-energy golf videos, had built a string of retail partnerships and raised $45 million last year. In the aftermath of the ad, Kendrick told Front Office Sports that Good Good's marketing department, which Lefkovits led, was responsible for the promo and that those people had been "removed." Lefkovits' suit alleges that this statement was false and defamatory, and left him unable to find work. The suit goes on to describe the script. The suit says that the script "ended with a comedy twist in which the entire group becomes equally 'obsessed' with the driver and playfully competes to hold it." The suit says the script contained no shoving scene involving Clark and Miestowski, nor any depiction of domestic violence. Lefkovits says in the suit that he was away when filming of the ad was finished and that the shoving scene was added without his knowledge or participation. The suit alleges that Clark and Miestowski were among those who "loved" the edit and that they didn't suggest changes. Clark and Miestowski didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. "Callaway approved both the concept and the final edit in writing," the suit alleges. The suit says that on August 25, Kendrick emailed Good Good's marketing partners, saying he was making changes to the marketing org and blaming the team for the ad. Lefkovits was fired August 26, the suit says. Kendrick left the company on September 2. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: VC firm Sequoia is flattening its partner structure and closing its London office
events.summary: Sequoia Capital said it could support European startups from its Bay Area HQ. via Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Sequoia Capital is closing its London office. It's also flattening a management hierarchy that it said had "crept over into the investing team." The VC firm joins other Silicon Valley giants in embracing flatter structures to reduce bureaucracy. At Sequoia Capital, London is out, and the Great Flattening is in. The Silicon Valley VC firm said Wednesday it has made internal changes to undo a management hierarchy that had "crept over into the investing team." The shake-up also includes the closure of its London office and sunsetting its batch accelerator and Scouts programs, Sequoia wrote in a Wednesday post on X. The London closure means some employees are leaving Sequoia. The VC firm, which made early-stage bets on companies such as Apple, Google, and Nvidia, said it can support European founders and startups from its Bay Area headquarters. The overhaul marks the ongoing change of the guard at Sequoia. In late 2025, Alfred Lin and Pat Grady took on co-steward roles at the firm, as longtime partner Roelof Botha stepped down. By closing its London office, winding down programs for early founders, and flattening its investing partnership, Sequoia is betting that a leaner structure will help it double down on concentrated, founder-led decision-making. In its post, Sequoia said that a two-decade "expansionary phase" has required "real management" to run operations — but management creep into the partner side of the business had become an "unintended side effect." The VC firm is also dropping its Monday partner meeting cycle, and said that its mission of delivering the best possible returns to limited partners remains the same. "We've made several internal changes that have the effect of flattening the partnership,' the investment firm said. "This allows every partner to flourish, and every founder to receive the full benefit of Team Sequoia - regardless of who your lead partner happens to be. Sequoia joins a long list of companies including Meta, Amazon, Google, and Intel that have flattened management layers in recent years. Companies have typically cited a desire to reduce bureaucracy. In other cases, companies have cited AI when cutting back on managers and flattening structures, including Coinbase and GitLab . There have been course corrections. Earlier this year, Business Insider reported that Meta asked some employees in its Applied AI division to become managers again . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories
events.summary: Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy US midterm elections – live updates After US midterms, what will lame duck Trump mean for global economy? US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the midterm elections, lifted by hopes that Donald Trump’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy. The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 gained close to 2% each by midday in New York, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives . The price of oil dropped sharply as traders assessed the impact of the Democrats’ win on the war in Iran. However, the US dollar fell against the currencies of America’s major trading partners, hitting a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields. Investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Trump’s final term in office. The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month, with the pound hitting its highest level since mid-September on the back of a fragile dollar, while the euro also made gains. The dollar also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty. Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%. On two-year bonds it has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise. Across the US, voters rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with the Democrats securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina. Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.” Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors. European markets climbed in early trading, with London’s FTSE 100 rising by 0.2%, Germany’s Dax up by almost 0.6%, France’s Cac 40 0.4% higher and Italy’s FTSE MiB index jumping by almost 1.4%. Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Donald Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%. “Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the UK research director at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats.” Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms , funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger of Musk’s two companies. The price of gold, a traditional haven asset, rose by 2.2%, soaring past $4,000 an ounce. AI-related shares tumbled during Asian trading hours, on expectations that Democrats will want to bring in greater regulation of the sector. Chris Turner, the global head of markets at ING, said: “Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on datacentre buildouts.” He added: “Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets.” Jesper Koll, an expert director at the financial services company Monex Group, said: “The AI momentum has turned negative, with or without the Republicans having a majority. The starting point for financial markets into this election, particularly for the equity market, has been adverse on AI.” Trump’s style of governing through executive orders has prompted some analysts to question whether the Democrats regaining control of Congress will have much change on US policymaking.

events.title: Photos: Iran marks US embassy takeover with rallies against US, Israel
events.summary: Tehran rallies see slogans, flag burnings, and claims of US-Israeli defeats amid historic embassy takeover anniversary. Iran marked the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the United States embassy in Tehran on Wednesday with mass rallies in the capital, as officials used the occasion to hail what they called US and Israeli “defeats” in recent elections and on the battlefield. On November 4, 1979, Iranian students stormed the US embassy, taking 52 American diplomats and citizens hostage for 444 days, a crisis that cemented the rupture between Tehran and Washington, which have had no formal diplomatic relations since. This year’s anniversary comes against the backdrop of a war launched by the US and Israel against Iran on February 28, in which Iran’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed, roiling global energy markets and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Thousands of demonstrators marched through central Tehran, burning US and Israeli flags and chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel”. Effigies and caricatures of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were paraded through the streets, including one showing Trump as a ferocious dog held on a leash by Netanyahu. Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani told the crowd that the US and Israel had suffered a “decisive defeat”, including in Tuesday’s US congressional midterm elections, which was considered a rebuke of Trump’s Republican Party, claiming US weaknesses were the result of Iranian “steadfastness and strength”. Iran’s judiciary chief, Gholam Hossein Mohseni Ejehi, echoed the message in a post on X, saying: “Trump failed both in war and in politics. We will certainly impose even more defeats upon him.”

events.title: GoDaddy's CEO says he won't read work written with AI. Here's how he can tell.
events.summary: The CEO of GoDaddy Aman Bhutani said he has a strict rule for himself about using AI. Brian Stukes/Getty Images GoDaddy's CEO Aman Bhutani told Business Insider he won't use AI for writing. He also said he won't read work that he suspects was written by AI because he values original thought. He said that writing with perfect language and excessively long documents are indicators work may be AI-written. GoDaddy CEO Aman Bhutani has a strict rule for himself when it comes to AI: He won't use AI to write. And he expects his employees to follow suit. "If somebody sends me a document and I can tell pretty quickly it was written by AI, I don't read it," GoDaddy CEO Aman Bhutani told Business Insider. "Because if the person couldn't take the time to write it, then I definitely shouldn't take the time to read it." This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with GoDaddy CEO Aman Bhutani: • The life-changing leadership advice Uber's CEO gave GoDaddy's CEO • GoDaddy's CEO on when small businesses should — and shouldn't — use AI Bhutani said employees can use AI to help them for things like better understanding a word or phrase, but that employees are expected to be able to convey their ideas in narratives that others can understand. This is an important skill because it enables them to continue "practicing the art of iteration," or continuously getting better, he said. "What I'm really looking for is: What was the original observation? What was the original hypothesis? What got you interested in this idea? Why do you think it matters? Right?" he said. "Because AI only knows what the internet already knows. It doesn't know what we know deep inside us, and there are ideas coming from us all the time." Bhutani isn't the only business leader who has a problem with employees using AI to do their writing . Earlier this year, Varun Anand, the cofounder of AI sales and marketing startup Clay, shared his company's AI writing policy on LinkedIn. The policy, which was written by an engineering employee Sophie Alpert, states that "Writing is thinking" and that employees must be able to explain every line that they write. Figma CEO Dylan Field said in an X post in September that his organization requires employees to add the disclosure "written with AI" if they use the tech during their writing process. Bhutani said there are a few signs that indicate to him if something is written by AI. He said that he works with a diverse group of people and English is often not their first language. So if the language is a little bit too perfect, that can be a tell. Another hint for Bhutani is the length of the writing. He said if something is too long, that can be a giveaway. And if it's short, it's often "punchy and clear," which can be another sign. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Scalise, Jordan vie to lead House Republicans reeling from midterm rebuke
events.summary: Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) will announce his bid to lead House Republicans on Wednesday, a person familiar with his plans told Axios, as his party begins to regroup from stunning midterm losses that cost them their congressional majorities. Why it matters: Scalise's announcement sets up a potentially bruising battle for the minority leader post, with Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) also being floated as a potential contender. It's Scalise's second attempt at the top House Republican job. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff that he will not run for minority leader on a Wednesday morning call, a person familiar with his plans said. Driving the news: Scalise pitched himself as a leader positioned to bring Republicans back into the majority "He is a proven and tested leader who is ready on day one. He's spent his career unifying Republicans and he is prepared for the big legislative and oversight battles ahead. The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he's a trusted leader," the person familiar with his plans said in statement. Catch up quick: Scalise defeated Jordan in the Republican conference's secret-ballot vote to nominate a speaker in October 2023, but withdrew a day later after failing to secure enough support on the House floor. Johnson ultimately emerged as speaker after weeks of Republican infighting. State of play: A Scalise-Jordan race would pit two of the House GOP's most prominent figures against each other. Scalise enters the contest with more than a decade of experience in leadership, while Jordan could draw support from the party's conservative wing. But the scale of the loss on Tuesday night has prompted calls for an entirely new leadership slate — a potential stumbling block for Scalise. Three House Republicans previously told Axios that a major midterm defeat could fuel calls for an entirely new leadership team The intrigue: Majority Whip Tom Emmer, meanwhile is making calls to lock down support from him to stay on as whip in the minority, a person familiar with his plans told Axios. Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios in September that he intends to remain in his current role rather than seek a higher leadership position. That could leave the losing candidate in a Scalise-Jordan matchup without an obvious fallback spot in the top leadership ranks. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to elect their next leadership team on Nov. 10, with candidates facing a Friday deadline to declare their intentions. The winner needs a majority of House Republicans in a secret-ballot vote. Trump could play a pivotal role in determining the next top House Republican, and GOP lawmakers are watching closely to see whether he throws his support behind a candidate.

The Commission has a longstanding commitment to understanding and addressing the concerns of small entities. The adopted amendments recognize the substantial growth in the asset management industry over the decades since the asset-based thresholds for identifying “small entities” were initially set. By helping to ensure the Commission’s RFA analyses capture a more meaningful population of investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies that are considered “small entities,” the adopted amendments are therefore intended to minimize the significant economic impact of the Commission’s rules on these market participants. “Updating the SEC’s definition of small entities for investment companies and investment advisers – which has not been done in nearly 30 years – is an important step to eliminate unnecessary regulatory burdens and modernize our rulebook,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “These amendments more accurately capture the types of registered investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies that are considered small relative to today’s market and will help ensure the Commission’s rulemaking is reflective of that reality.” The RFA seeks to, in part, promote the effectiveness and efficiency of regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory approaches, with the goal of minimizing the significant economic impact of federal rulemaking on small entities. The Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small entities, including through performing regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA. Increase the asset-based thresholds under which investment companies, investment advisers, and business development companies are deemed small entities. Update the way that related funds’ assets are aggregated for purposes of defining small entities. Eliminate the investment adviser total assets threshold. Provide for inflation adjustments to the asset-based thresholds by order every 10 years. The adopting release is published on the SEC website and will be published in the Federal Register. events.title: How a Democrat shocked the world in South Carolina
events.summary: The Scoop As soon as Republican Sen. Darline Graham won the GOP nomination to replace her late brother in August, Democrat Annie Andrews made her move. Andrews immediately began spending more than $5 million on advertising in South Carolina’s Senate race at a moment when she largely had the airwaves to herself as her new opponent struggled to raise money. At the time, Republicans were racing to prioritize other competitive races across the country — and most people in both parties still saw South Carolina as a pipe dream for Democrats. But by October, when the rest of the country began tuning into South Carolina — and spending money — Andrews quietly became the frontrunner, according to internal campaign details shared with Semafor following her victory on Tuesday. On Oct. 5, the Andrews campaign received a poll showing her with a 3-point lead over Graham. But the Democrat’s campaign decided against publicly releasing the poll — or any subsequent internal poll — showing Andrews with a lead over Graham, wary of drawing too much attention from national Republicans and jeopardizing a peak at the right time, according to Chas Goldman, a strategist for Andrews. That Republican attention did come, but not in time to save Graham in a state where Democrats hadn’t won a Senate race since 1998. On a Senate map filled with shocking GOP losses, South Carolina stands out: It’s the home of the National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, Tim Scott, and territory on which Democrats tried to compete statewide in 2020 — and lost handily. Former GOP Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., told Semafor on Wednesday that he could feel the anti-Graham sentiment building on the state’s coast but that most Republicans still felt that Graham could “nose it out” elsewhere. Ultimately, though, he said President Donald Trump’s backing of Graham in a crowded primary which included Sanford and Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry “never sat well with folks.” Sanford said Andrews did a good job appealing to disaffected Republicans but also said the rejection of Graham amounted to “a Waterloo moment for Trump.” “The fact that a state as red as South Carolina would go the other way on his hand-picked candidate? This is a person who said: ‘Close your eyes and pretend you’re voting for me.’ OK, they did,” Sanford told Semafor. “They just didn’t like Darline as a candidate and felt it had been forced down their throats by Trump. And they’re like: ‘We’re not doing this.’” Andrews outran her party’s gubernatorial nominee by 4 percentage points, evidence of both her strength and Graham’s weakness as a candidate. Graham ran behind Alan Wilson, the Republican governor-elect, by roughly 100,000 votes. In an interview with Semafor in early September, Andrews said she welcomed help from national Democrats and “anyone who wants to help me win this race, but I am confident I can do it without investment from the national party.” “I’m on TV, she’s not up yet, and that’s a huge advantage,” Andrews said of Graham at the time. “All of the ingredients are in place, and I’ve been gifted with what is frankly an incredibly weak opponent. I’m ready.” turning the red tide Andrews exploited divisions in the Republican Party over Trump’s endorsement of Graham, reaching out to supporters of Norman and former GOP Gov. David Beasley, according to details shared with Semafor. She ran an ad with her Republican dad to appeal to former supporters of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham R-S.C., and worked with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and other Black leaders in the state to juice turnout. Beasley ended up cutting a joint endorsement ad with former Democratic Gov. Jim Hodges while Norman’s son, Warren, warmed publicly to Andrews. By traditional campaign metrics, Andrews swamped Graham. She raised more than $25 million, according to her campaign, and was largely able to keep her own campaign afloat into October, when both national parties began spending in the race. Graham raised nearly $2 million, a sum that meant she would need outside support to win. Ultimately Democrats joined Andrews in the fray. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quietly spent $500,000 there and Senate Majority PAC spent $750,000. Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, said that “Graham brought significant negatives and baggage to the race, that’s undeniable, but Andrews won this race as much as Graham lost it.” Sen. Raphael Warnock, from neighboring Georgia, campaigned for Andrews, but she mostly sought to keep the campaign local. Her coattails extended to a House pickup in the state’s lowcountry as she targeted Republicans and independents in her campaign events. “For 18 months, she traveled all 46 counties, earning voters’ trust one conversation at a time. She worked just as hard to raise the resources to go up on TV early and stay there. Those relationships and that early investment built a lead that she never gave up,” said Brexton Isaacs, Andrews’s campaign manager. Burgess’s view I interviewed Andrews throughout this saga: Once when she launched, once earlier this year when it appeared Lindsey Graham would be her opponent, and once after Darline Graham replaced her brother on the ticket. Each time she explained to me why this wasn’t like 2020, when Jaime Harrison raised gobs of money but lost to Lindsey Graham. I was as skeptical as anyone else that South Carolina was ready to elect a Democrat to the Senate. But over the last couple weeks, the whole country tuned in as national Republicans and Democrats alike poured money in. At the moment it’s the biggest surprise on the Senate map — perhaps until we find out what happens in Mississippi. Notable Graham began thinking about running for a full term in July after discussing it with President Trump, Semafor reported.

events.title: The 2026 midterm elections came with a wave of history-making wins. See every historic first.
events.summary: Gina Hinojosa is the first Latina elected governor of the state of Texas. Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Democrats swept the 2026 midterm elections, securing wins in long-held Republican states. Four states elected their first Black governors, and four elected their first women governors. Abdul El-Sayed became the Senate's first Muslim member, and Chris Pappas, its first openly gay man. The midterms' blue tsunami was full of surprises — and a long list of historic firsts. Democratic candidates for the US House, Senate, and governorships swept wins across the US on Tuesday night, including in many long-held Republican states like Texas and South Carolina. Four states elected their first-ever Black governors, and four also elected a woman governor for the first time. In Georgia, it was both, with Keisha Lance Bottoms making history as the first Black woman elected governor in any US state. For the first time in US history, five Black governors will serve simultaneously, and at least 17 women will serve as US state governors simultaneously. While races in Alaska and Mississippi remain undecided, see the full list of every historic win in the 2026 midterm elections so far. Keisha Lance Bottoms (D), Georgia Megan Varner/Getty Images Democratic Keisha Lance Bottoms is now the first Black woman elected governor in US history after defeating Republican Rick Jackson. She is also Georgia's first Black governor and first woman governor. Byron Donalds (R), Florida Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Byron Donalds is now the first Black Republican elected governor in US history and Florida's first Black governor. Gina Hinojosa (D), Texas Gina Hinojosa at her election-night watch party. Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images Gina Hinojosa is now Texas' first Latina governor , defeating incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and the first Democratic governor elected in the state since Ann Richards in 1990. Xavier Becerra (D), California Caroline Brehman/Bloomberg via Getty Images Xavier Becerra is now California's first elected Latino governor, succeeding Gavin Newsom . Amy Acton (D), Ohio Jeff Swensen/Getty Images Democratic candidate Amy Acton is now Ohio's first woman elected governor after defeating Republican Vivek Ramaswamy . Marsha Blackburn (R), Tennessee Michael Swensen/Bloomberg via Getty Images Marsha Blackburn is now Tennessee's first elected woman governor. She was the first woman elected to represent the state in the Senate in 2018. Amy Klobuchar (D), Minnesota Dymanh Chhoun/Sahan Journal/Catchlight via Getty Images Amy Klobuchar was elected as Minnesota's first woman governor. In 2006, she became the first woman from the state to be elected to the US Senate. Hochul became the state's first woman governor after taking office in 2021. Abdul El-Sayed (D), Michigan Abdul El-Sayed. In his acceptance speech, he thanked his supporters and his husband, Vann Bentley, whom he married in 2023. Annie Andrews (D), South Carolina Annie Andrews on Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images Annie Andrews became the first woman elected to the US Senate representing South Carolina. She defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who was appointed to fill his seat after he died in July. Juliana Stratton (D), Illinois Juliana Stratton. Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images Juliana Stratton is Illinois' second Black woman elected to the US Senate. Alongside Tammy Duckworth, she makes Illinois the first state to be represented by two women of color in the Senate. Her victory means three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time — another historic first. Melat Kiros (D), Colorado Melat Kiros. AAron Ontiveroz/Getty Images Melat Kiros is the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress, representing Colorado's 1st congressional District. She is 29 years old. Adam Hamawy (D), New Jersey Adam Hamawy. DREW ANGERER/AFP via Getty Images Representing New Jersey's 12th District, Adam Hamawy is the Garden State's first Muslim member of Congress. She will represent the state's 2nd District. Five Black governors will serve simultaneously for the first time in US history. events.title: Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia’s Belgorod region
events.summary: Russian strikes also cut power to Ukrainian cities as Moscow claims 700 Ukrainian drones downed across multiple regions. Ukrainian drone strikes have killed three people in Russia’s Belgorod region, while attacks cut power to multiple cities in Ukraine and parts of Russian-occupied Crimea, officials reported. Local Russian authorities in Belgorod, which borders Ukraine, announced the three deaths on Wednesday. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia’s overnight attacks damaged power generation facilities and substations in nine regions leaving emergency outages in many cities. list 1 of 4 President Zelenskyy says US elections will impact war in Ukraine list 2 of 4 Grain under fire: Black Sea attacks threaten global food supplies list 3 of 4 Russia detains minor over alleged Moscow attack plot after US warning list 4 of 4 Russia, Ukraine air raid alert apps hit by cyberattacks after truce ends Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed on Telegram that it hit two power stations in Ukraine’s Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions. Ukraine has repeatedly said Moscow is targeting its energy grid as temperatures drop before winter. Overnight, Russian attacks on critical infrastructure caused hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions. Residents in the capital were urged to use public drinking water fountains, and emergency centres offering hot tea and power points to charge devices were set up in the worst-hit areas. There were also power outages in Crimea, the peninsula Russia seized from Ukraine in 2014, home to approximately 2.5 million residents. Russia’s Ministry of Energy said Ukrainian strikes hit energy infrastructure overnight and that temporary outage schedules were in force. It did not say how many households were affected. But reports also indicated that Russia-held Crimea ordered power cuts after an accident outside the region, a Moscow-installed ⁠official said, according to the Reuters news agency. ‌In addition to the capital, Kyiv, Russia also hit the regions of Poltava, Dnipro, Kirovohrad and Rivne, Reuters reported, citing Ukraine’s emergency service and local officials. In southern Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at a major warehouse belonging to Ozon, known as Russia’s Amazon. The strikes were on an Ozon distribution facility in the town of Adygeysk, in the Republic of Adygea, regional head Murat Kumpilov said. Ozon said all workers were evacuated and no one was hurt, and that it had removed damaged goods from its listings and rerouted deliveries. Russia’s Defence Ministry also said it downed 709 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas. Amid ongoing fighting between Russia and Ukraine, Russia’s Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin hopes United States President Donald Trump will continue his peace efforts after a sweeping Democratic victory in the congressional midterms dealt a blow to the president. “President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking efforts,” Peskov said in a statement. Whether a change in Congress could hinder Trump’s peace efforts, Peskov said, as cited by the state-run Interfax news outlet, that it was “an internal matter for America”. Democratic control of the legislature in January is expected to bring a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress that could pressure Trump to change tack, but there is little hope that the US will return as a major financial backer of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy awarded US First Lady Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olga, which honours women who have contributed to Ukraine, according to a presidential decree on Wednesday. The decree noted Melania Trump’s “significant personal contribution” in providing support for humanitarian aid and children in Ukraine. Ukrainian officials say the US first lady played a pivotal role in organising a six-day local ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, which ended on Sunday.

events.title: James Talarico was a 23-year-old middle school teacher when an 11-year-old inspired him to run for office—now he’s making history in Texas as Senator
events.summary: A “blue wave” hit the U.S. last night as the country tallied the votes of its 2026 midterm election, with key states like Ohio and South Carolina flipping from Republican to Democratic control. One of the most anticipated races took place in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico ultimately triumphed over Republican Ken Paxton for the Senate seat.  The 37-year-old is now the state’s first elected Democratic Senator in nearly four decades—and his unlikely path to Washington began as a public school teacher. Talarico started his working career teaching sixth grade at Rhodes Middle School, a high-poverty area in San Antonio, when he recognized how state policies were hurting his students.  The then-23-year-old educator witnessed the impacts of massive budget cuts that wiped out critical resources from kids living in an already underserved area; in 2011 the Texas Legislature cut $5.4 billion in public school funding following a budget shortfall. The loss of support for the state’s poorest students—and the strife of underpaid and overworked teachers—inspired his pursuit of public office just a few short years later.  “I served my students on the West Side and served their families and really saw the impacts of economic injustice up close and personal,” Talarico told Austin PBS last year. “That experience is what motivated me to then run for office, because I saw students slipping through the cracks, I saw teachers driving Ubers at night to make extra money, I saw teachers selling their own blood plasma to make ends meet. And I knew that was wrong.” The average middle school teacher in Texas makes $63,400 annually, according to USAFacts, and is ranked in the bottom half of U.S. states when it comes to pay. Fortune reached out to James Talarico for Texas for comment. Meet the struggling student who inspired Talarico’s political career Talarico only taught in Texas’ public school system for two years before taking his ambitions to non-profits and politics. Yet one student’s story in his teaching career left a lasting mark—and has been a recurring anecdote during his senatorial campaign trail. The eighth-generation Texan often recounts the story of one struggling sixth-grader named Justin who emboldened him to run for office. The kid had a tough upbringing, was abandoned by his mother, and had just been kicked out of a previous school for bringing a knife and threatening violence against a teacher.  Talarico made an effort to build a connection, and the 11-year-old was making progress, even gifting him a snowflake cup from the Dollar Tree . But then Justin got into another altercation at school—his “third strike.” Talarico remembers him being carried out of school without his feet ever touching the ground; that was the last time he ever saw Justin.  After doing some digging, he found that the school district therapist appointed to Justin had been eliminated amid Texas’ budget cuts. Students who have been exposed to tough upbringings, violence, and trauma suddenly lost their lifelines of support. Talarico described it as a “radicalizing” experience, and set out to pursue a career in public service. “I promised myself right then that if I ever got a little bit of power or a little bit of influence, that I would do everything I could with every fiber of my being to stop that from happening again,” Talarico said in a 2025 episode of The Joe Rogan Experience podcast . Talarico’s rise from middle-school teacher to Texas Senator  After his teaching stint, Talarico went on to become the Central Texas executive director of Reasoning Mind: an education nonprofit focused on math instruction and classroom technology.  In 2017, he launched his first-ever political campaign in running for the Texas House. And the following year, at just 29, Talarico won the special election and the regular election for the district, flipping the seat from Republican to Democrat.  There, he implemented school funding reform and introduced his Whole Student Agenda addressing pupil mental health and various school-related issues.  Talarico has since held onto a seat amid switching to District 50 in 2022, and just last year, announced his Senate bid to challenge the Republican nominee in Texas.  Now, he’s the Lone Star State’s first Democratic Senator elected since 1988, and has the potential to earn a U.S. Senator’s average salary of $174,000. Despite becoming a high-profile political force, he still leads with the lessons from his middle-school teaching days.  “Justin and my students are the ones I think about when I’m at the Capitol,” Talarico continued during the podcast. “They are the criteria that I use to evaluate public policy, not if it’s a Democratic bill or Republican bill, not if it’s going to get me ex-lobbyist support.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Google was met with swift backlash on Tuesday after it announced that schools using Google’s K-12 software will not be able to use Search unless they opt in to using AI tools. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a student’s school doesn’t opt in to using AI tools like Gemini, then students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Even as Google made this announcement on a busy Election Day, several left-leaning politicians took time to speak up about their concerns. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google in an X post of “extortion,” writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said on X that Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.” President Trump claimed that AI oligarchs could regulate themselves because they “love our country.” Now, Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search. That’s not love. That’s extortion. PAUSE AI NOW. — Sen. Bernie Sanders (@SenSanders) November 3, 2026 Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair and staunch advocate against monopolies, also condemned Google’s decision as anticompetitive. “This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” she wrote . “Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.” New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of being a monopoly, commenting , “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.” Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service. Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains… https://t.co/eajJN9yfQF — Lina Khan (@linamkhan) November 3, 2026 While Search is a necessary tool for information gathering, educators worry that its built-in AI overviews could dissuade students from finding answers themselves. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools, using a different search engine isn’t a simple fix. Google says that it’s working on a “Guided Learning” tool for student accounts in Search, which is supposed to walk students through the process of solving a problem or finding information, rather than just handing them the answer. If a student is struggling with a math problem, for example, the feature may prompt them to refresh their memory about the rules for dividing exponents, instead of spitting out a number. In response to the backlash, Google pointed out in a post on X that it had listened to educators by turning off access to AI products by default and noted that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually. We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less. Here’s what we announced: – Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be OFF 🔴 by default. This is based on K-12 schools asking for more control… — News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle) November 3, 2026 “We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google wrote in its statement. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” Topics AI , Google , Google Search When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: I tried Gordon Ramsay's 15-minute Bolognese pasta. Now my family makes it for dinner every week.
events.summary: Gordon Ramsay's 15-minute pasta has been on regular rotation in my family's kitchen. Michael Yarish/WBTV via Getty Images One of my favorite pasta recipes is Gordon Ramsay's tagliatelle with sausage Bolognese. The recipe requires just a few ingredients and only takes 15 minutes. My family loves Ramsay's pasta so much that they make it every week. When my family and I stumbled upon "Gordon Ramsay's Ultimate Cookery Course," we had no idea we were about to discover one of our favorite weekly pasta recipes . The series — which first aired in the UK in 2012 — follows Ramsay as he demonstrates 100 essential recipes for the home chef . It was one of our comfort watches in those early days of the pandemic. And the 15-minute tagliatelle with sausage Bolognese, one of Ramsay's recipes from the show, became our comfort dinner. Six years later, it's still a family favorite. Here's how to make it. Gordon Ramsay's 15-minute tagliatelle with sausage Bolognese requires five main ingredients. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To whip up this delicious dish, you'll need: Dried tagliatelle pasta Sausages (Ramsay recommends fennel or Sicilian) Tomatoes Half an onion A few cloves of garlic If you can't find tagliatelle at your local supermarket, pappardelle always makes for a great substitute. I always start this dish by chopping onions, garlic, and parsley. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider One of the best parts about this dish is that there's barely any prep. It takes me about five minutes or less to prepare everything before I start cooking. While Italian parsley isn't part of Ramsay's recipe, I love adding it if I have any lying around. The herb brightens all the flavors and brings a bit of freshness and color to the dish. I also dice some tomatoes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider This dish can easily be adapted to your preferences and what you already have in your kitchen. On this night, I used cocktail tomatoes, which have a juiciness that works great in the Bolognese sauce . Before cooking, I also prep the sausage. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider You need to peel the casings from the sausages before crumbling the meat. Ramsay recommends slicing each sausage down the middle to help remove the skin. After putting my pasta into a pot of salted boiling water, I throw my onions into a pan. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I let the onions cook for a few minutes before adding the rest of the ingredients. Then it's time to throw in the garlic and parsley. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Ramsay recommends letting the garlic and onions "sweat until they're soft" before you add the meat. After adding the sausage, I use a spatula to break down the meat while mixing everything. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Don't forget to season everything with some salt and pepper! After the sausage has browned, I throw in the chopped tomatoes, plus a can of crushed tomatoes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The first two times my dad and I made this dish, we thought the sauce was a little dry with just the chopped tomatoes. Thick tagliatelle and pappardelle noodles are perfect for thick sauces — they almost seem a little naked without one. Since we already loved the pasta's taste, we didn't want to drastically change the recipe. The extra can of crushed tomatoes gives the Bolognese sauce a bit more oomph in both taste and texture, while still staying true to Ramsay's flavor profile. While the sauce simmers, I check to see whether my pasta is al dente. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider My method is always to catch one of the pappardelle ribbons in a ladle, run it over some cold water for a few seconds, and then bite into it to see how firm the noodle is. I add two ladlefuls of pasta water to the sauce and remove it from the heat while my noodles finish cooking. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Ramsay said the starch from the pasta water helps thicken the sauce and make it stick to the noodles. After draining the pasta, I throw my noodles into the pan and mix everything together. Don't forget to top it with some parsley and grated Parmesan! Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider My parents have had Ramsay's 15-minute tagliatelle pasta on regular rotation since we first tried it years ago. My dad loves how much flavor the sausage adds to the Bolognese sauce, and my mom said she always feels "warm inside" when she eats this dish. "It feels like home," she told me. The sauce is meaty and rich, the flavors are complex, and each bite floods me with comfort. It truly is the perfect quick dinner . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
events.summary: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday. The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft. Advanced persistent threat Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful. Read full article Comments
