events.title: Latest award confirms EuroEyes International as market leader
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] By recently winning the prestigious Zeiss Award for the 10th consecutive year, EuroEyes International has once again been recognised for its pioneering work and, in particular, for performing the highest number of trifocal lens implantations in clinics around the world. Over the years, its team of laser eye surgeons has completed hundreds of thousands of operations, establishing a reputation for fast and effective high-end care, which has made it possible to keep expanding internationally and, through charitable initiatives, to provide life-changing treatment for people in less advantaged countries and communities. In another sense, though, it can also be taken as tacit acknowledgement of the success of EuroEyes’ business model, which has achieved steady growth through a series of astute acquisitions, an early presence in the China market, an entrepreneurial mindset, and insistence on the highest standards at all times. The group’s network now includes laser eye centres or clinics in Germany, Denmark, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and - following a just concluded deal to buy the world number two in the field - the Netherlands. And, with a view to supporting further domestic and regional expansion, a successful initial public offering (IPO) was completed in 2019 in Hong Kong. (stock code 1846.hk) . “For us, growth in China has been driven by rising disposable incomes and the large demographic dealing with myopia or presbyopia,” says Dr Jørn Slot Jørgensen, the founder, chief executive and medical director of EuroEyes, who has spent an average of 10 days a month in China for the past 10 years, barring the Covid-19 period. “Overall consumer confidence may be down slightly at the moment, but people in the higher income category are still willing and able to invest in their own long-term health and well-being.” As a trained ophthalmologist who still performs more than 1.000 individual operations a year, Danish-born Jørgensen runs counter to the stereotype that doctors have little or no interest in business. His father showed the way as a medical practitioner who also played the stock market, and his own inclination was always work outside the usual, somewhat restrictive, hospital environment where it would be possible to branch out and build something special. That began with outpatient work in Hamburg, treating cataracts and other conditions, which led in due course to being an early adopter of laser surgery, which proved genuinely transformative. It was fast, safe and, crucially, eliminated the need for hospital stays which would previously last up to six or seven days. “When I saw no one else was doing this, I went to Berlin, Munich and found partners in Copenhagen,” Jørgensen says. “Then so many people in China started finding us on the internet and coming to Germany for treatment, it was an obvious move to open a first clinic in Shanghai.” “One key reason we went to China is that roughly 90 per cent of Chinese people are myopic, but it can be corrected,” Jørgensen says. “That explains why Lasik (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) is now one of the most performed treatments in the world of medicine,” He adds that demand for fixes for presbyopia also seems sure to rise, as life expectancy increases and people give more attention to personal maintenance. In such cases, the basic problem is that the optic in the lens no longer works as before, making reading glasses a necessity. However, advances in technology have made it possible to take measurements by computer, get precise patient feedback, and then come up with fully customised solutions. The next steps in this direction will include greater use of AI, in particular to do preliminary checks of the retina for people suffering from diabetes, and of OCT (optical coherence tomography), a type of non-invasive imaging that uses light waves to capture cross-sections of the retina and optic nerve. “As a surgeon, you always welcome ways to do things better,” Jørgensen says. “Once you have learned the methods and techniques, it becomes easy and enjoyable. Nowadays, when I operate, it is like playing the piano.”

events.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phones are up to 27 percent off
events.summary: You can save a heck of lot of money on Google’s Pixel 11 phones through November 8th, whether you want the best-for-the-least Pixel 11 , or the slightly pricier Pixel 11 Pro that takes better photos. Even the big Pixel 11 Pro XL with a longer-lasting battery is hundreds off its original price. The Pixel 11 Pro deal is the most attractive of the bunch, as the $1,099.99 phone with 256GB storage and 12GB of RAM is down to just $799.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and at the Google Store , beating its October Prime Day price by $50. It’s $100 less than the base Pixel 11 model sold for at launch, and it’s the phone to get if you want great camera performance, plus extra features like HiLight that, while cool, weren’t really worth paying a premium to access. I’d be very surprised if the price dropped more for Black Friday. Google Pixel 11 Pro Where to Buy: $1099 $799 at Amazon $1099 $799 at Google $1099 $799 at Best Buy There’s absolutely nothing wrong with opting for the Pixel 11 instead, especially at its attractive $699.99 ($200 off) price that now matches the cost of the iPhone 17E, following Apple’s September price bump . The Pixel 11 is the most affordable phone that supports Google’s software features that are exclusive to this year’s phones, including Magic Capture, Camera Looks, and Proactive Assistance. It has fast 25W wireless charging (up from 15W with the Pixel 10), and has 12GB of RAM, like the Pixel 11 Pro. Google Pixel 11 Where to Buy: $899 $699 at Amazon $899 $699 at Google Store $899 $699 at Best Buy I’m still happily rocking my Pixel 9 Pro, but if I were going to upgrade right now, I’d get the Pixel 11 Pro. Yes, I want the better cameras and HiLight. But really, the main reason I’m lured to the Pro is because the trade-in offers are really generous right now. It’s just $10 more to opt for the Pro over the base Pixel 11. My base Pixel 9 Pro with 128GB of storage can fetch $530 in trade-in credit at the Google Store and $525 at Best Buy, which seems great.

events.title: Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans in fierce midterms
events.summary: Americans are electing members of Congress, which is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 House seats are up for election. In the Senate, only 35 of 100 seats are being contested because senators serve six-year terms. This results tracker shows both the races being decided now and the 65 seats that are not up for election this year - 34 held by Democrats and 31 by Republicans. Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results Published 4 November 2026, 13:43 GMT Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk. According to the Financial Times , external , the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The money was not enough to stop the seat from turning Democrat for the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas." "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokingly wrote on X , external . While stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning following the election outcome, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively. Many Democrats had been vocally outspoken against the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres on the campaign trail. Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US . Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site. As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October. "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response. On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall , contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates. Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns. Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations. Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate. Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign. A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around. events.title: Russia is giving some of its missiles greater range and larger warheads, Ukraine says
events.summary: Russia is increasing the range of some of its missiles, Ukraine's military intelligence agency said. REUTERS Ukraine's military intelligence agency has released details about Russian missile capabilities. The assessment said Russia is increasing the range of some ballistic and anti-ship missiles. It also said Moscow has stockpiled thousands of ballistic and cruise missiles. Russia is working to increase the range of some ballistic and anti-ship missiles, giving the latter a more powerful warhead, according to a new assessment from Ukraine's military intelligence agency. The assessment comes as Ukraine endures worsening Russian missile and drone attacks, while facing a shortage of interceptors and other air defense equipment to stop the deadly bombardments. The agency, also known as the GUR, said on Wednesday that Russia is developing a modernized variant of its 9M723 "Iskander-M," a tactical ballistic missile, with a projected range of 340 to 440 miles — roughly 100 farther than its predecessor. The GUR said in August that Russia had used an upgraded "Iskander-1000" missile for the first time over the summer. It was modified with a larger engine and launcher to increase its range. Russia has also armed its 3M55 "Oniks" anti-ship missiles with larger warheads and increased their range "to enhance their effectiveness against ground targets," the GUR said. It did not disclose specifics, but said Moscow has produced dozens over the past seven months. Russia's defense ministry and its US embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the GUR's assessment. The assessment comes as Russia has ramped up its missile and drone attacks in recent months. As winter draws near, strikes on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure in particular have civilians bracing for yet another brutal stretch. Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles and thousands of cruise missiles, the GUR said. REUTERS Complicating matters is Ukraine's perpetual shortage of interceptors needed to defend against the Russian attacks. Kyiv has repeatedly lobbied for its allies to transfer more air defense missiles to shield cities from the bombardments. On Monday, Russian strikes against Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 33 people, according to Ukrainian officials. Meanwhile, the GUR said Russia "maintains significant stockpiles of long-range missile weapons and continues to increase its production rate, despite international sanctions." Russian reserves include up to 700 ballistic missiles and thousands of cruise missiles, the GUR said, adding that Moscow's defense industry is capable of producing more than 200 of these weapons each month. The inventory includes the Iskander-M and Oniks missiles, as well as RM-48U missiles for the S-400 air defense system , the 3M22 "Zircon" anti-ship and land-attack missile, and 3M14 "Kalibr" cruise missiles . The GUR said "technical defects" — specifically, an issue firing from aircraft — have been detected in the X-101 cruise missile that Russia frequently uses to attack Ukraine. "Consequently, some batches are being returned to factories for repairs," the agency said. Manufacturing for the X-47M2 "Kinzhal" ballistic missile remains suspended because of accuracy issues, the GUR said, adding that the existing production capacity has been redirected to other missiles. events.title: Wall Street rallies after Democrats win Congress; data centre stocks slide
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange at the opening bell, in New York City, on Nov 4. Democrats won both Congress chambers, easing fears of big policy shifts and lifting US stocks. Citi’s Scott Chornert called it a “clearing event”. Big tech rose, led by Amazon, Meta and Alphabet, but AI data-centre stocks fell as investors worried about tighter regulation and slower build-out. Defence shares dropped on concern over Trump’s US$1.5 trillion budget request, while solar and clean energy stocks gained on hopes of continued federal support. NEW YORK – US stocks rose on Nov 4 as investors bet a divided Washington after the Democrats’ midterm sweep could limit sharp policy shifts, though data centre stocks were under pressure as concerns over tighter AI regulation weighed. Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, scoring stunning wins in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations in a broad voter backlash against President Donald Trump. The prospect of fewer sweeping legislative changes lifted some large technology stocks, but companies tied to the AI infrastructure buildout fell. “The general view is that this is a clearing event, so the uncertainty related to the elections is now behind us,” said Scott Chornert, head of US equity strategy at Citi Research. Among hyperscalers, Amazon.com jumped 7.1%, while Meta Platforms added 1.6% and Alphabet gained 3.4%. At 09.46am ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,203.07 points, or 2.3%, to 52,989.79; the S&P 500 gained 129.88 points, or 1.72%, to 7,698.80 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 540.38 points, or 2.13%, to 25,912.39. The dollar weakened against most currencies and yields on long-dated Treasuries moved lower. Trump acknowledged that the US-Israeli war on Iran played a role in his party’s defeat in the elections. Elon Musk-led SpaceX and Tesla were among the laggards, down 1.9% and 3.9%, respectively. Musk had spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, including efforts to keep Republicans in control in Texas, the home state of both companies. Eight of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were trading higher, with consumer discretionary leading gains. The AI trade will be in focus after Democrats made gains in key data-centre states including Texas and Georgia, where public opposition to the industry’s rapid expansion has been growing. “It’s pretty clear that the AI trade will face some headwinds there... If you push out the pace or change the pace of the data centre buildout, you begin to change the fundamental trajectory for many of those suppliers,” added Citi’s Chornert. The AI trade has come under some pressure recently as investors grow wary of Big Tech’s soaring AI spending and little evidence of adequate returns. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index confirmed a technical correction on Nov 2. Chip stocks were muted despite AMD forecasting faster-than-expected 2027 growth as its data centre sales surged. Shares of the chipmaker were last up 4.8% in choppy trading. Defence stocks Northrop Grumman, RTX and Lockheed Martin fell sharply, as Trump’s US$1.5 trillion (S$1.9 trillion) budget request could now face a tougher road in Congress. Solar and clean energy-related companies moved higher, as a Democratic sweep could reinforce expectations of federal support for clean-energy development to remain in place. The Invesco Solar ETF climbed 8.3%. McDonald’s gained 3.9% after the fast-food chain beat quarterly profit estimates, while Block jumped 15% after the payments company raised its full-year gross profit outlook. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.6-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 3.49-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 42 new 52-week highs and three new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 105 new highs and 54 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: US markets rise as Democrats sweep midterm elections
events.summary: Nasdaq, Dow, and S&P 500 open higher after Democrats sweep US midterms and Trump accepts election results. US markets are trending upwards after Democrats swept the midterm elections , taking control of both the House and Senate on Tuesday. The Nasdaq opened on Wednesday up 1 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 1.8 percent and the S&P 500 up 1.1 percent as markets opened at 9:30am ET (14:30GMT). list 1 of 4 Iran’s Khamenei warns Trump loss at polls won’t end US hostility list 2 of 4 Gaza volunteer Adam Hamawy wins historic US Congress seat list 3 of 4 How big is the Republican midterms loss, and is there a silver lining? list 4 of 4 Why is the western US still counting votes after election day? Retailers that rely on imports, such as Walmart and Target, are up 1.3 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively, amid possible changes in tariff policy. Health insurance provider UnitedHealthcare is down 2.9 percent, while CVS Health is down 12 percent. However, Cigna went up 1.6 percent. Investor sentiment was also buoyed by United States President Donald Trump’s social media post saying he would accept the results, easing political uncertainty and pressure on markets. For companies involved in the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, the outlook is different as the Democrats have been more critical of the sector. Oracle and Nvidia both opened the day lower, although Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is on the upswing, up 3.5 percent at the opening bell. “There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Dan Ives, managing partner of Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Wednesday. “We estimate 10% of datacenters will not happen now,” Ives added in a post on X. Democrats performed well in states where the AI buildout is pronounced, including Ohio, where Sherrod Brown flipped the Senate seat; Texas, where Democrats took a Senate seat with James Talarico; and the governor’s race, which Gina Hinojosa won, also flipping the seat. Oil prices are also on the decline. The global benchmark Brent crude oil futures are down $3.20, or 3.09 percent, to $100.40 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude is down $3.01, or 3.13 percent, to $93.08. While oil prices are reacting to the midterm results, investors are also watching to see whether the war with Iran and the one between Russia and Ukraine will end amid reports of talks, following the previous session, which saw oil prices hit their lowest levels in four weeks.

events.title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
events.summary: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023. Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began. The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters. Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia. Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors. According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information. Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government. Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023. The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials. On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000. "Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

events.title: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?
events.summary: The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues. At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and if you want to retrieve something, you’ll need to pay again. At north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 (though they’re reusable with no extra fee). At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised? The price rises are helping to push average spending per head on a night out from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to Night Time Industries Association. “For years, nightlife businesses have faced relentless increases in the cost of operating, from energy and employment to taxation, business rates and supply chains,” says chief executive Michael Kill. “Many have had no choice but to pass some of those costs on to consumers simply to keep their doors open. But the reality is that consumers have now hit an affordability ceiling.” With consumers spending less on alcohol, locker systems and cloakrooms offer premises a way to make some of that money back, but, Kill says, “the consumer cannot be the industry’s financial shock absorber indefinitely”. UK storage policy changed after the 2017 attack at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester Arena which killed 22 people and injured more than 1,000. “Martyn’s law” legislation requires “appropriate public protection measures” at public events to reduce the risk and impact of terror attacks. It led to many venues – including the nationwide network of 18 Academy Music Group sites – banning bags over A4 size entirely and offloading them to external lockers or storage partners. In London, these are often kebab shops, restaurants and barbers. Carrie Wang, a London-based spin instructor, was buzzing to see Hot Chip at O2 Academy Brixton until she learned her near-empty tote bag had to be stored in a kebab shop round the corner. “I was fuming,” Wang says. “They charged me £10 and it wasn’t a proper facility, it was just a random storage room – it’s not like they had lockers and my things were actually safe there.” Academy Music Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Ahmed Khan is the owner of Kentish Delight, a kebab shop in Kentish Town. He says that in 2022, O2 Kentish Town Forum’s management asked if he had any spare space in the takeaway. “They had a look and said my premises are perfect and secure for the customer – and I said yes, why not?” Khan charges £5 per bag and says nothing has ever gone missing. “Although the bag people never buy kebabs.” The high costs and added logistics mean that some people are taking risks with their belongings. At an AEW wrestling event at Wembley Arena, fans were directed to a nearby Premier Inn to stow their bags, at £10 a pop with long queues. Soul singer Danny Toeman decided to stuff his rucksack behind a carpark vending machine. “I could stuff most of the valuable contents into my pockets,” says Toeman. “So I thought: let’s just stash it somewhere and if it gets stolen, so what?” That in itself is a security risk – if staff had seen Toeman’s backpack, the venue could have been evacuated. But it’s become commonplace. One Reddit user opted to hide their bag outside the O2 Academy in Southampton. “They will literally not let you in,” they wrote. “I was forced to leave it outside the building entirely and it was stolen when I came out.” Willem Pelle is head of sales at eLockers, a Dutch company working with many UK nightclubs including Drumsheds, Fold and Warehouse Project. “When we expanded into the UK, we saw that many venues were facing staffing challenges following Covid, making traditional cloakrooms increasingly difficult to operate,” Pelle says. London is their main UK market, with Manchester a close second. Pelle says there is typically no upfront cost for the venue, which gets to share the takings with eLockers, adding: “It’s important that the pricing works for both the venue and its customers, while creating a sustainable additional revenue stream.” Some clubbers have reported benefits to lockers, such as those at Drumsheds, where you can put stuff in and out – allowing for outfit changes during an event. But not all venues opt to install expensive locker systems. At Hackney Bath House, the cloakroom is free.

events.title: Don’t let Poundland owner maximise its return at our expense, suppliers say
events.summary: British companies that supply US-owned budget retailer face millions of pounds’ worth of losses if it collapses Suppliers facing millions of pounds in losses if Poundland collapses have said the chain’s US owner should not be permitted to maximise its return at their expense, as ministers attempt to intervene in the situation. The fate of the retail chain, its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday. The US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, which bought the now 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer , remains in talks with at least two possible buyers for the company. They include Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, whose offer has been backed by the retailer’s management team. Gordon Brothers executives are understood to be meeting Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, on Wednesday while Poundland’s management team have a separate meeting with Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, and the shop workers’ union Usdaw amid political pressure to find a rescue deal . However, Gordon Brothers is understood to prefer the option to break up Poundland, sell off its stock and parcel up stores for sale to other retailers, including Tesco and the owner of Poundstretcher, because this would pay off more of a £30m shareholder loan. This route could save some retail jobs but would leave suppliers with unpaid debts and millions of pounds’ worth of stock without a retailer to sell it to. Karan Shah, a director of Universal Toiletries, a fragrance and toiletries supplier to Poundland, told the Guardian the company faced a financial risk of about £1.5m, including almost £700,000 in stock already delivered but yet to be paid for, and the rest in undelivered stock and components. “Gordon Brothers should not be permitted to maximise its own financial return at the expense of suppliers without exploring all the alternatives of a solvent deal,” he said. Shah suggested the timing of the potential administration appeared “very advantageous” to Gordon Brothers, “at the busiest time of year when the warehouses are full of stock”. This could leave millions of pounds’ worth of stock that could be sold off by any administrator to pay back the loans held by Gordon Brothers if Poundland is broken up. Shah’s company worked with the chain for about a decade but stopped supplying stock in recent weeks amid concerns about payment. “We are unfortunately significantly exposed,” he said, adding that Poundland was its biggest UK client and “we are a family business, not a multinational that can afford to take a hit”. Andrew Kay, the chief operating officer of the Oldham-based toy ball supplier John Leisure, said he would have to “rehome” more than a million products, many of which had already been manufactured and were in transit for next spring. He said doing so would be difficult because many items had been made specifically for Poundland, and other retailers would not want the same sizes and quantities. “It is going to be a nightmare that will hurt me badly to deal with all that inventory,” he said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning While Kay has only a relatively small amount of stock for which he has yet to be paid sitting in Poundland, he said Gordon Brothers had questions to answer about its treatment of suppliers. He felt the investment firm seemed to be “making money off the back of others” by attempting to put Poundland into administration at a time when it was filled with stock that had yet to be paid for. He said Gordon Brothers’ aim to save stores and retail jobs by selling off groups of Poundland’s stores would not help suppliers. Adam Turner, the sales director at the confectionery supplier Highcrest Retail Brands, based in Bradford, said he was set to lose millions of pounds in payments on stock the company had already supplied if the retailer went bust. He said Highcrest had managed to find alternative buyers for some of its stock and had some insurance but was likely to lose out on payment for stock already provided and for investments in new products for Poundland. But “we can stomach it”, he said. Shah, Turner and Kay said they were concerned about the future for their own suppliers if they missed out on Poundland orders. “This affects everyone in the supply chain,” Shah said. “Situations like this can wipe businesses out.” It is estimated that Poundland’s collapse could affect up to 30,000 jobs when its supply chain is accounted for. Gordon Brothers has been contacted for comment. It has previously said Poundland “faces multiple economic challenges, including rising inflation, increasing staffing costs and shrinkage from severe levels of shoplifting”.

events.title: Elon Musk’s record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire
events.summary: Elon Musk spent at least $474 million on the 2026 elections, including $224 million in Texas, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. The results leave Musk with fewer allies in Congress and could create new political obstacles in Texas, where Tesla, SpaceX and other Musk ventures have major operations. Data centers became a major campaign issue in the midterms, with $173 million spent on almost entirely negative advertising nationwide, according to AdImpact. Democrats' sweeping midterms victory marked a major rejection of Elon Musk and the artificial-intelligence industry, as a broad backlash against U.S. President Donald Trump and his tech allies put their political influence — and the debt-fueled data center buildout — under sharper scrutiny. Musk, who spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms, funneled $224 million, or nearly half, into Texas alone, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records, only to see his favored candidates, Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott, trounced in a Democratic wave. The defeats rattled markets overnight, sending SpaceX and Tesla shares lower, both of which have long flourished under Abbott's business-friendly policies. Meanwhile, broader tech stocks came under pressure as Democrats secured control of Congress. Across the country, voters pushed back against billionaire influence and the growing power of technology companies, electing critics of the AI industry and approving restrictions on data centers fueling its expansion. "We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections," Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico said in his victory speech, without naming Musk. "We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%." J.C. Lintzenich, a visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, pointed to Musk's massive spending in Texas, telling CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the results were "clearly a rejection of the Elon Musk aspect that has found its way into the Trump orbit." Texas has grown to be homebase for much of Musk's Empire. Tesla operates its largest U.S. vehicle factory outside Austin, SpaceX launches rockets from its Starbase complex in South Texas, and Musk is pursuing additional investments in AI and semiconductor manufacturing. These operations rely heavily on state decisions regarding electricity, water, environmental permits, infrastructure, and tax incentives. Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned against generous corporate subsidies, and Musk himself — will wield significant influence over those decisions. Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new data centers, an end to industry tax breaks and requirements that developers cover their full electricity costs. In her victory speech Tuesday, she vowed to take power from the "powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state." Republicans still control the Legislature, limiting Hinojosa's ability to overhaul state policy. But her administration could complicate Musk's expansion plans with a tougher approach to permitting and business incentives. Nationwide, Musk's America PAC spent nearly $87 million across 44 federal races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. By Wednesday morning, Republicans it backed had lost 29 contests and won just three, with 12 still uncalled. More than $80 million — or 93% of its spending — went toward races Republicans lost. The outcome leaves Musk with fewer allies in a Democratic-controlled Congress that could investigate his federal contracts, his past leadership of Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his companies' ties to Washington. Congressional scrutiny may slow SpaceX's lucrative and fast-growing government contracts , but Trump still controls executive agencies and holds veto power, limiting Democrats' ability to reverse policies that benefit Musk's defense-tech businesses. The defeats aren't the first time that Musk's political spending has failed to produce his desired result. America PAC backed eight losing congressional candidates in 2024, and last year Musk spent over $20 million trying to elect a conservative in Wisconsin. Though Musk promised last year to spend "a lot less" on politics, he ultimately became the biggest known donor in the 2026 midterms. Longtime Tesla investor Ron Baron warned in March 2025 that Musk's political activism risked driving away customers, telling CNBC : "I don't think it's a great thing to alienate half the population." Others cheered Musk's close relationship with Trump, and his influence over everything from regulation to Pentagon tech spending. Musk was not the only tech figure who spent big. OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, contributed $25 million to Leading the Future, a political operation seeking to shape AI regulation, according to FEC filings.

events.title: Trump says Iran war justified despite polls drubbing
events.summary: President Donald Trump has acknowledged the impact of the United States’ attack on Iran and a sharp rise in prices on stunning Republican losses in midterm elections on Tuesday, but said the move was justified and denied responsibility for the rout. “We actually have the greatest economy, but because of the gasoline price, people don’t see it as much as they would have without it. And the gasoline was caused by Iran,” he told Fox News in a televised phone interview late on Tuesday. “People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline. I understand that. I don’t agree with it.” Speaking to The Wall Street Journal about the Republican defeats , Trump said about the Iran war: “I did the right thing. I would have done it again.” But Vice President JD Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, appeared to diverge from Trump’s thinking on the wisdom of the conflict. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Republican strategist James Davis said the war contributed to the setbacks for the party but also to a lack of clear messaging. “The war was definitely part of it and has helped shift the electorate toward Democrats. But the biggest issue was not the war itself, but the clear articulation of a strategy that gives people confidence in that strategy,” Davis told Al Jazeera. The economic fallout from the conflict, including higher energy and especially diesel costs, had affected all sectors of the economy and intensified Americans’ concerns about affordability, he added. Trump did not acknowledge any failings in his strategy, citing his absence from the ballot as the reason Republicans struggled to mobilise voters and blaming the defeated candidates themselves. “I wasn’t on the ticket,” Trump said in an interview with The New York Times. “And because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote.” Trump faulted the losing Republicans, many of whom he had handpicked and held multiple rallies for. “Some of the candidates that I endorsed fought me,” he said, adding that “some of them had a lot of flaws, and obviously they were not acceptable to the voters”. Commenting on the shock defeat of Texas Governor Greg Abbott, Trump lamented that his longtime ally had become a “Republican in name only,” without elaborating. “If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” he said in a post to his social media platform Truth Social. In a preview of his likely governing style over the next two years, the president also posted a picture of his trademark red cap emblazoned with the word “veto” to convey his determination to block legislation carried by the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress. In the run-up to the losses, Trump repeatedly said presidents tend to lose midterm elections and had brushed off the suggestion that his policies had turned off voters. Speaking to Fox News, Trump said he did not plan to make any changes to his cabinet after the rebuke from voters. “It had nothing to do with my cabinet. It’s just a point in time. There was a mood in the air, I guess.” In a conciliatory note, Trump said he wanted to work with Democrats but warned he would stand his ground as well. “I think we’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll get along very well with them. If we don’t, we’ll be very tough on them; they’ll be very tough on us,” he said. “Could I work with them on transgender mutilization of children?” he added. “No, I don’t think so. But I could work with them on many things.”

events.title: Prologis CEO says warehouse demands are shifting fast. Here's how he's keeping up
events.summary: According to a new survey from Prologis, in partnership with the Harris Poll, 91% of company leaders said retailers and logistics providers "urgently" need more decentralized fulfillment networks to meet delivery expectations. According to the survey, fewer companies plan to keep their existing global footprint, with the share falling 14 percentage points from a year ago to just 36%. Companies are seeking faster delivery, first and foremost, as consumer expectations escalate. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. There will always be some need for massive, centralized warehouses, but rising demand for faster deliveries and resilient energy supplies have companies rethinking where their warehouses should be. In fact, 91% of company leaders said retailers and logistics providers "urgently" need more decentralized fulfillment networks to meet delivery expectations, according to a new survey from Prologis , in partnership with the Harris Poll. Responses came from more than 1,800 business leaders in the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, China and Mexico. "Our focus is the consumption end, so we have really narrowed our focus into being in not only the most dynamic consumption centers, most dynamic population centers around the world, but we're very specific what sub markets in those cities that we want to focus on? Because it is all about being closer to those rooftops," said Dan Letter, CEO of Prologis. According to the survey, fewer companies plan to keep their existing global footprint, with the share falling 14 percentage points from a year ago to just 36%. They are seeking faster delivery, first and foremost, as consumer expectations escalate. Same-day delivery is the goal, with the share of companies offering it doubling since 2019. Speed tops price when it comes to securing a competitive advantage, according to the survey. As a result, companies are mixing up their relocation strategies, with more than half both diversifying and regionalizing and about a third nearshoring and reshoring. "That's why we've been very focused on where our portfolio is. We talk a lot about the size of our portfolio, but we've actually sold a fair amount of property over the last 15 years as well. Just property that we heard from our customers that that's not their long-term vision. So, despite having 1.3 billion feet, we actually sold over 200 million feet as well because it wasn't what our customers were looking for," Letter explained. Energy infrastructure is also increasingly driving strategies, with energy resilience a leading concern due in part to artificial intelligence. Power reliability ranks number one in logistics location decisions. Just over a quarter of executives surveyed said they expect industrial landlords and developers to lead or fund on-site energy resilience infrastructure. That includes solar, energy storage and fleet charging. "We really doubled down on the energy side about five years ago, and we turned it into a business," said Letter. "We have over 1.4 gigawatts of power that we generate from our solar and our storage business. And then we have also been focusing on how do we help our customers electrify their fleets." AI is helping companies become more competitive, specifically when it comes to logistics and warehousing. Demand forecasting and agentic AI systems, respondents said, are some of the most "transformative technologies" when it comes to reshaping supply chains over the next three years. Three-quarters of those surveyed said they are planning big investments in AI demand forecasting as well as inventory replenishment. "As they've gotten deeper on AI, we've gone deeper with them as well," said Letter. "We've been making investments alongside our customers to just understand what's next, and that helps us in all aspects of our business and be way out in front of our customers." events.title: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
events.summary: CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates. In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy. A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people. The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year. A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies. The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week : “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.” He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions. At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown. Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.” David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business. “Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement. That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”. The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation. CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

events.title: ‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?
events.summary: It’s 20 years since Jo and Richard Hill bought anything in Rotherham town centre. Why have they and so many locals abandoned it for the nearest retail park – and what would it take to change their minds? O n 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher. Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday. Gordon has lived in Rotherham for 24 years. “A lot of people come to outlets like this. It’s very rare we go into the town centre and, if we did, we’d go to Sheffield,” he says. He is hardly an outlier. Almost half of Britons don’t visit their high street weekly. Instead, shoppers are opting for retail parks . Business is so strong, retailers are scrambling for spots, even paying extra to secure their place. By the end of 2025, only 4.8% of retail park lots in Britain were vacant, according to real estate consultancy Knight Frank – the lowest level on record. Vacancy rates for UK high streets, on the other hand, sit at 13% , reports Savills. Gordon remembers a time two decades ago when you “couldn’t move” in Rotherham town centre, especially at the weekend. “It was packed and all the local shops were busy. Now these big outlets have taken over.” He admits his shopping habits come at a cost to the local community. “We are part of the problem,” he says. “It’s not progress. You used to meet people, but now you’re lucky to see anyone you know. Most people will come here and shop, get what they need and go back home.” Jo Hill, 59, and her husband Richard, 65, are also Rotherham locals. Until recently, they hadn’t set foot in the town centre in nearly two decades. “What you see is either vape shops, nail shops or charity shops,” says Jo, who is semi-retired. Rotherham town centre is bookended by Parkgate at one end, and Meadowhall – one of the UK’s largest indoor shopping centres – at the other. The couple were visiting Parkgate to buy a printer from Currys. “For the big stuff, it’s either here or Meadowhall,” says Richard. A short journey away, in Rotherham town centre, the picture is different. About 70 retail units, 24% overall, are vacant , far higher than the national average, and it is immediately apparent. One of the first things you see when leaving the train station is a derelict branch of BrightHouse, a rent-to-own retailer selling large appliances and furniture, which shut down in 2020. Further up is an anonymous-looking shopfront with smashed windows, graffiti and empty panelling where a shop sign should be – another shuttered chain, Fultons Foods, which closed in 2022. The only identifying mark is a window sticker: “There’s always change at Fultons.” Vape shops, discount chains and charity shops dominate the street. The arrival of Parkgate Retail World nearly four decades ago wasn’t without friction. Even then, market traders expressed fears about the impact on business and, in Westminster, parliamentarians warned that these mini shopping metropolises would drain jobs from the high street, “ disembowel towns and villages ” and disadvantage those unable to drive . Donna, who owns a furniture shop, and Saj, who runs a sandwich deli, are on their lunch break when I stop them. “It’s declined totally. I really wish it hasn’t, but it has,” says Donna. Nowadays she usually serves about four or five customers, and her daily takings have declined to “virtually nothing”, she says. Saj agrees that footfall is nonexistent. The pair say safety is one reason that locals, especially elderly people, are staying home. “People have had their bags stolen, or been followed into banks; you’re watched when using the cash machines,” says Donna. “People will only come if they feel safe. It was always the older generation that came into the shop buying beds. Now their families won’t let them come out.” In 2023, a government analysis found that the number of crimes carried out per 1,000 people in Rotherham town was 160, 72% higher than the national average at the time.

events.title: Mike Johnson bows out of leadership after crushing House GOP defeat
events.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) plans to step down as the House's top Republican after his party's epic midterm election losses wiped out their majority, according to a person familiar with his plans. Why it matters: Johnson's exit touches off a potentially contentious scramble to replace him with Republicans days away from choosing their next leaders. Johnson told staff on a Wednesday morning call that he will not run for minority leader, the person familiar with his plans said. Driving the news: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) have been floated as potential successors, setting the stage for a bruising leadership battle. Johnson's political future remains uncertain, with questions swirling over whether he will remain in Congress or leave the House altogether after three years as speaker. The Louisiana Republican had spent months traveling across the country and raising millions of dollars in a last-ditch effort to preserve the GOP's majority. Flashback: Johnson ascended to the speakership in October 2023 as a little-known lawmaker after weeks of GOP turmoil following Kevin McCarthy's historic ousting . Johnson spent much of his speakership navigating razor-thin Republican majorities, managing persistent GOP infighting and repeated conservative rebellions that brought legislative business to a standstill. But he also emerged as a prolific fundraiser and close Trump ally, helping shepherd the president's legislative agenda through a fractious Republican conference. Yes, but: Johnson had publicly insisted he intended to remain in Republican leadership even if the GOP lost control of the House. After suggesting to Fox News that he could return to Shreveport and start a lawn care business if Republicans lost the majority, Johnson told CBS News in October that he planned to remain the top House Republican regardless of the election's outcome. His political future had become the subject of private speculation among Republicans, with many lawmakers skeptical he would run for minority leader after a GOP loss. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Nov. 10, with candidates facing a Friday deadline to declare their intentions. The race will be decided by a secret ballot of Republican members, requiring only a majority of the conference to win. Trump could play a pivotal role in determining Johnson's successor, and Republicans are watching closely to see whether he throws his support behind a candidate.

events.title: Iranian leaders welcome US midterm results, but Trump may still attack
events.summary: Tehran views midterm results as a rejection of Trump’s ‘war on Iran’, signalling US frustration with foreign policy. Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities are painting the sweeping midterm election defeats for United States President Donald Trump’s Republican Party as a repudiation by the US public of the war on Iran. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” said Iranian parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who led the Iranian delegation in talks with Washington that led to the signing of a short-lived memorandum of understanding in June. list 1 of 3 Who determines Iran’s fighting and negotiating position amid US threats? list 2 of 3 America is heading for two years of constitutional brinkmanship list 3 of 3 How big is the Republican midterms loss, and is there a silver lining? “If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” read a post on his X account on Wednesday. Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei, the head of the Iranian judiciary, said: “Trump was defeated in both war and politics” and promised that the Islamic republic will impose more defeats. Analysts said the sweeping victories for Democrats, which complicate the president’s remaining years in office, would only serve to make the leadership of Iran more adamant about their demands for ending the war started by the US and Israel on February 28. Trump has been talking about the possibility of attacking Iran for weeks, but says he hasn’t made a decision yet, as a US naval blockade, sanctions and trade disruptions are also heavily pressuring the country. Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, said the electoral defeat of Trump’s Republican Party will increase pressure to end the Iran war, but it does not rule out further strikes. “He needs a diplomatic victory or at worst an off-ramp, yet in the face of defeat he may be reluctant to appear weak,” she told Al Jazeera. Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the sense of victory being displayed by Iranian decision-makers will likely make them more uncompromising on core demands. Those include seven conditions set for the partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, as well as a requirement for the US to take the first step. “The likelihood of Iran making concessions on the nuclear issue could also become even lower than before,” he told Al Jazeera. Wednesday marked the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran by Iranian students, triggering a hostage crisis that set the tone for relations in the decades since. In Tehran, the authorities organised demonstrations and speeches around the embassy building and other downtown areas to denounce US-led “global arrogance”. State-organised marches and events were also held in Bandar Abbas, Mashhad, Qom and numerous other cities. State television also showed pro-government events for schoolchildren . A statement attributed to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was released to mark the day. “Now, the stage of the Persian Gulf, especially the Strait of Hormuz, has invalidated the myth of American invincibility,” read the statement from Khamenei, who has not been seen or heard publicly since becoming supreme leader in early March following the killing of his father. He asserted that some still harbour hope that partisan changes in the US or granting concessions to Washington would stop their “enmity” towards Iran, but “they are harshly mistaken”. Khamenei said the only way to attain “absolute deterrence” was to pursue strength. In Tehran’s Enghelab Square, a giant billboard depicting Trump behind prison bars was unveiled on Tuesday. “We will kill Trump,” read the accompanying message. State-linked media also closely followed the US elections, and cheered for some of the bigger losses for hawkish Republicans. “Trump’s nightmare,” read the reformist Sazandegi newspaper’s headline on Wednesday, accompanied by a full-page picture of Abdul El-Sayed, who has become the first Muslim senator after winning his race in Michigan, and attacked the pro-Israel AIPAC lobby – which had spent tens of millions of dollars against him – in his victory speech. Iran and the US continue to fight over control in and around the Strait of Hormuz, while the Trump administration also counts on changing the behaviour of Iran’s authorities through imposing a blockade and economic pressure on 90 million Iranians. Chatham House’s Vakil said she expects intensified diplomacy alongside continued military threats over the coming weeks, with limited military strikes still a possibility. “An interim agreement over the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the blockade appears more realistic than a comprehensive settlement,” she said.

events.title: What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump
events.summary: From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference? For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections , one issue ranked above all others: the economy. So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go? Market reaction: Is it all about AI and data centers? Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory. With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance. "The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note. "I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind." Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates. Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition . Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom. "This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted." If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said. What about Trump's tariff policies? According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center , 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive. That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada. Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy. "Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office." Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies. Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation. What about the war in Iran and surging oil prices? Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans ' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy. Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

events.title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
events.summary: Mich. Dist. 7 Projected winner William Lawrence • D 1 hour ago N.Y. Dist. 4 Projected winner Laura Gillen • D 1 hour ago Election 2026 live results: Trump defends Iran war after Vance blames it for GOP losses French authorities have thwarted a cyberattack on blood banks that aimed to dangerously raise storage temperatures PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said. The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros). The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said the temperature, which was usually set to minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit), went up to 110 C (230 F). “No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said. “Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said. The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare. The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident. “The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.” France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident. One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros. “While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings. The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States. events.title: Gulf and 'Blue Wave'
events.summary: Mohammed’s view The anticipated blue wave in the US midterm elections turned into a tsunami, and its political ripples will reach the Gulf. The election was a rebuke to President Donald Trump over rising living costs, the Iran war, and his conduct in office. But whether that makes him less inclined to escalate the Middle East conflict is another matter. As Amos Hochstein, a former senior Biden administration adviser, put it in Abu Dhabi this week, Congress can control budgets, hold hearings, and demand answers — but “the president of the United States does foreign policy.” Gulf states face two risks. Trump, frustrated by domestic constraints, could use more force against Iran to try to secure his legacy. At the same time, Democrats could use their congressional powers to expose uncomfortable details of deals between Gulf investors and the president’s relatives and associates, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff’s family. There is also some upside, though. The Gulf barely featured in the election, and voters’ demand for lower prices aligns with regional efforts to end the war and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Gulf monarchies have the luxury of planning decades ahead without the nuisance of elections. This allows them to build deep, institutional relationships in Washington that span both parties. Sovereign wealth funds deployed billions during the Obama and Biden administrations, and some of today’s AI cooperation was negotiated before Trump returned to office. One election issue could even favor the Gulf: As US voters embrace data center NIMBYism, Gulf states can offer cheap energy, empty land, and faster permits. Finally, the Gulf’s human rights records weren’t a campaign issue, unlike Israel’s war in Gaza and its treatment of Palestinians, which have attracted bipartisan criticism. But this issue could resurface if investigations into Trump’s circle put Gulf connections under scrutiny. Notable Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, became the US’s first muslim senator, after he won a contentious race in the battleground state of Michigan .

events.summary: Most of Qatar’s gas remains trapped in the Gulf, but Doha is finding ways to export more of it while securing US supplies to meet some of its commitments.
