events.title: Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened.
events.summary: Cyanobacteria blooms in a tributary of Lake Champlain in the town of St. Albans, Vermont, in August. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone toward Lake Champlain. “I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the board’s chair. Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten for all that money. But that study was never done. A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain. Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms. Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you. Get In Touch Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms, roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality, enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.  Now, halfway through a 20-year cleanup effort mandated by the EPA, some lawmakers worry they don’t have enough information to ensure that the state is pursuing the most cost-effective cleanup strategies.  When lawmakers approved the clean water law, they took the major step of establishing a fund to pay for the cleanup and a board to administer it. Since 2016, Vermont has disbursed $928 million — $755 million in state funding and $173 million in local and federal dollars — on water quality projects and programs. That’s nearly as much as what Vermont has spent on paving and resurfacing state highways over the past decade. As part of the law, the legislature also required the board’s leaders to provide it with a full program audit by January 2021. But the board received no responses to an initial request for proposals in 2020. Lawmakers extended the deadline to 2023. Yet again, no outside firms bid on the audit.  Farnham said the board received informal feedback from some firms that the audit’s scope was too broad and complex. He reported back to fellow board members that he and Julie Moore, secretary of the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources, had asked legislators what to do next but didn’t receive any clear suggestions. The board never issued a new request or revisited the matter (until Seven Days and ProPublica recently asked about it), and Vermont’s legislature never followed up to narrow the scope. Water with particles of cyanobacteria, collected in mid-August from Lake Champlain in St. Albans Lake Champlain Committee monitor Jon Twombly, courtesy of Lake Champlain Committee St. Albans in late August during a high-alert bloom day Volunteer photo courtesy of Vermont Department of Health Former state Rep. David Deen, who sponsored the clean water law and retired in 2018, said he was dismayed to learn that the audit never happened.  “Personally, I find it amazing that they haven’t done that audit and that somebody in the legislature did not hold them to account to conduct that audit,” he said. Rep. Amy Sheldon, the longtime chair of the House Committee on Environment, recalled hearing about the audit challenges but noted that it’s difficult for the legislature to follow up because Vermont’s lawmakers don’t have staff. In the other chamber, former state Sen. Chris Bray, who chaired the natural resources committee until 2025, said he did not recall hearing about the missing audit. In an interview, Farnham acknowledged that an outside audit would be helpful. But he said the board already has robust tools for assessing progress through a yearly performance report compiled by the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, which coordinates and tracks most of the state’s clean water spending. “We’ve got enough eyes coming at it from different angles that I think that mutes the need for that comprehensive audit,” he said.  The annual reporting process has improved greatly since the audit was mandated, and the DEC’s website “provides a lot of transparency,” about how the state is spending clean water money and the results, said Emily Bird, director of the department’s Water Investment Division. But some current and former state officials say that approach isn’t a substitute for an audit to determine whether Vermont is getting adequate and cost-effective returns on its huge water quality investments. The last independent assessment of clean water spending was a 2019 report from the state auditor. It found that a disproportionate amount of money was being spent on wastewater treatment plants, which contributed by far the smallest share of phosphorus pollution, instead of targeting bigger sources such as agriculture.  That mismatch persists seven years later. Agriculture is the largest source of phosphorus runoff, yet agricultural water quality programs receive less than a third of the total clean water funding in the current budget. “I’d like to think they’re getting something done,” said Doug Hoffer, state auditor since 2013, referring to state agencies and legislators. “But the only way to know that is to hire someone who is independent to study that. And it’s really concerning that hasn’t been done. It really raises questions about accountability on both sides.” Vermont Auditor Doug Hoffer says the lack of an independent audit of Lake Champlain’s cleanup efforts “raises questions about accountability.” Jeb Wallace-Brodeur/Seven Days An audit would do a few key things that the department’s performance reports do not, Tee Thomas, a former water finance director for the state of Vermont who now runs her own environmental consulting firm, noted via email. The reports rely on models for how effective each type of project is at reducing phosphorus. An audit would analyze water quality monitoring data from rivers and lakes to check those estimates. It would also scrutinize how well Vermont has managed projects and whether it’s gotten results, she said.  The Clean Water Fund gets, on average, $25 million to $30 million each year from the state’s rooms and meals tax, a surcharge applied to some property transfers and deposit money that consumers pay on cans and bottles. events.title: The worst two words in the dead of night? ‘Motorway closed’ | Adrian Chiles
events.summary: The worst two words in the dead of night? ‘Motorway closed’ You are shunted into side streets, crawling along, united with your fellow drivers in wordless despair. Last week, at 2am, my spirit broke T he worst three words in the transport lexicon are often said to be “rail”, “replacement” and “bus”, in that order. But there’s worse. “Motorway closed” is worse. At least with rail replacement buses you get fair warning, on booking apps and whatnot. You can resolve to embrace the pain or, more likely, abandon the journey. Motorway closures, in the dead of night, invariably come as a nasty surprise. Waze, Google Maps, Apple Maps, etc can reliably get you from a car park in Penzance to a cul-de-sac in East Kilbride, but often can’t tell the difference between an open motorway and a shut motorway in the middle of the night. Football fans know all about this. You travel across the country for an evening match, and you lose. The prospect of a long drive home blackens your mood further, but as you slope away from the ground you cling to one consoling thought: at least there won’t be much traffic on the road. And this is true, but light motorway traffic looks rather like heavy traffic once it’s bullied on to side roads. Out of nowhere come the sign, the cones, the arc lights, and off you go, ushered with the other hapless nightbirds into the slow, black void. Dispossessed, demoralised, you crawl along unfamiliar roads, united in wordless despair. To be fair, you can do some pre-planning on the National Highways , Traffic Wales and Traffic Scotland sites – if you have a knack for navigating not-especially-intuitive internet offerings. But as for satnav, often as not, when you need it most it lets you down. Last Thursday night, for reasons too complex to go into, I had to get from Malta to Gatwick to the West Midlands and thence to Liverpool by Friday morning. The flight was an hour late and, deliciously, there was then a half-hour wait for a bus to the terminal. Bowed but not yet beaten, while my suitcase took its sweet time reaching the carousel, I checked all the map apps available to me and they all gave my route a clean bill of health. No closures. Great. It had gone midnight when I set off. As soon as I got on the M23 an electronic sign came leering out of the mist: M25 closed after Reigate. Surely not. Please let it be just a rogue sign on the blink, which has been known to happen. But no. Off the motorway I was firmly ushered into deepest darkest Surrey, ignoring persistent entreaties from two different satnavs to stop being so silly and return to the M25. I yelled at the screens, something along the lines of, “I’d love to get back on the bastard motorway, you useless morons, but they won’t let me!” If AI is so clever – and I assume it has a hand in the operation of satnav services – then how come it doesn’t know the M25 is shut overnight? Come the zombie apocalypse, with AI warrior goons on the rampage, we should entrust our defence to the people who execute these night closures. Truly, it is miraculous how they can muster a battalion of heavy machinery, an army of hi-vis’ed workers and a million cones, all without AI seeing any of it. Now that’s what I call a stealth operation. Relations with my satnavs now having broken down, I had no choice but to trust the signs advising me to follow the yellow triangle. Or was it a circle? Or a square? I’ve always wondered what those things were for. It was at 2am, lost and alone, groping my way around Epsom, that my spirit broke. At a filling station I bought pastries and crisps, ate them, felt a lot worse, and soldiered on into the night. Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Caitlin Clark signs as first-ever brand partner with Dick's and Foot Locker
events.summary: Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark has signed a multiyear deal with Dick's and Foot Locker. The deal comes one month after the release of her Caitlin 1 signature shoe by Nike. Clark is the WNBA's most marketable star, according to a new report from SportsPro. Caitlin Clark has signed a multiyear deal with Dick's Sporting Goods and Foot Locker. The deal marks the first time either brand has signed an individual athlete, man or woman, as a partner. As part of the partnership with the sports retailers, Clark will work with both brands on custom promotions to support her signature footwear, apparel and product lines. She will also be involved in activations and community events. The new deal follows the Oct. 1 global release of Nike and Clark's first signature shoe, which was the largest women's signature shoe launch in the company's history. The release also included an 18-piece apparel assortment. The shoe has received widespread acclaim and drawn strong consumer demand, with inventory selling out within hours on Nike.com and other sneaker retail sites. Clark pointed to the brands' deep roots in sport and basketball and their ability to connect with fans all over the world. "Dick's Sporting Goods was always a stop before the start of any sports season when I was growing up," Clark said in a statement. "Being the first ever brand partner for both them and Foot Locker is a really special full-circle moment. " The Clark partnership also marks the first joint athlete partnership between Dick's and Foot Locker under Dick's Inc. Both Dick's Sporting Goods and Foot Locker have previously worked with athletes on marketing campaigns, in-store events, and other ventures but never at the brand level. Dick's CEO Ed Stack said he looks forward to building on the energy that Clark has brought to playing basketball and winning new fans. "This partnership offers new ways to come together around a shared passion for sport, and the possibilities it creates," he said in a statement. Clark remains one of the WNBA's biggest stars, even after the Indiana Fever's first-round elimination from the WNBA playoffs. She has yet to win a title. A recently released marketability ranking by SportsPro finds Clark is the most marketable player in the WNBA today and the No. 15 most marketable athlete worldwide. Clark has long-term endorsement deals with several other major brands including Nike, Wilson, Gatorade, State Farm and Panini. "Caitlin's influence reaches far beyond the court. She has captivated fans, inspired a new generation, and brought new energy to the game," said Brett O'Brien, senior vice president and chief marketing officer of Foot Locker North America. events.title: Titan OS raises $46 million to expand its smart TV OS internationally
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Barcelona-based smart TV operating system maker Titan OS has raised $46 million in new funding, consisting of both equity and debt, the company announced on Wednesday. The money comes from debt facilities provided by funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, along with existing investors like Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners. The startup, which secured $58 million last year , has now raised $110 million in total. The company said that it could have chosen not to raise money and grow slowly, but it wants to be more ambitious to create more partnerships and expand into more geographies. Titan OS’s promise to TV makers is that it offers better value from their unit sales by loading an operating system where they can generate money through partnerships with FAST channels (free ad-supported television) and ads on different screens. The company now serves 30 million users, up from 18 million last year. This includes being a sales partner for TiVo in some regions, along with Tubi in the U.K. Compared with last year, the startup has also added Sharp, AOC, Vestel, and Skyworth as partners. Its partnership with Philips has been a success, as the Dutch electronics maker has switched to Titan OS and ditched Google TV for its 2026 models . The extended coverage means that it has a bigger advertiser footprint and better audience engagement metrics to offer to marketers. “Our bread and butter is the monetization of our inventory on our own network. But the point is that we’re going beyond that. That’s why our reach has increased significantly, which then triggers the flywheel effect by also attracting more sales partners and more agencies that want to spend on our platform, whether it’s owned and operated or via our extensions,” Hyoung-Ung Kim, the company’s newly appointed CFO, told TechCrunch over a call. In the last year, the company has increased its headcount to 250 people, and also opened an office in London to concentrate on advertising. It already has offices in Barcelona, Amsterdam, and Taipei. With the new money coming in, the company wants to focus on a few areas. First is content discovery. It still takes everyone a long time to find something to watch. For that, it is using interface tweaks and AI to boost discovery, alongside partnering with more content providers like FAST channels. “What differentiates us here from the walled gardens is that we do not have our own content offering. Like Google is trying to channel people to YouTube. We do not have that, and we are impartial in our role in content discovery. We are working and trying to reduce time spent searching,” Tobias Pfalzgraff, SVP of people and marketing at Titan OS, said. Pfalzgraff also emphasized that the company is using AI to improve its ad recommendation and segmentation. While the company is dominant in Europe, it thinks that there are only a few manufacturers creating their own operating systems; more set makers would like to adopt its operating system, just like Philips did. The company also said that with increasing costs of hardware due to AI, manufacturers are thinking about long-term revenue generation opportunities as gadget sales slow down. “The TV hardware industry is not a very profitable business. That’s why they are so reliant on partners like Titan OS that share revenue after the sale of the TV. But now, of course, the chip sets, the chip prices are increasing more and more. Right. events.title: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
events.summary: Jeff van den Noort collects a sample outside his home in North Hero, Vermont, for the Lake Champlain Committee’s cyanobacteria monitoring program. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum. It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear. But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.  Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database. Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.       “I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.” A cyanobacteria bloom mixes with duckweed on the shoreline of Lake Champlain in the town of St. Albans, Vermont, in early August. Courtesy of Lake Champlain Committee Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015, then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.  The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036. But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace.  Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants, represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days and ProPublica. The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go zones. Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of oxygen.  While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast arm. People enjoy the water at North Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington, Vermont, on Labor Day weekend. Algae blooms sometimes force the city to close the beach. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023. Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body. Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest amount of phosphorus per acre. State agencies have repeatedly delayed taking more difficult and politically fraught action to crack down on pollution from farms, businesses and housing developments. Policies around them have encountered resistance from the dairy industry, property owners and lawmakers sympathetic to their interests. The challenges in cleaning up Lake Champlain raise a salient question: If a small, conservation-minded state like Vermont can’t tackle this problem, what does that mean for other areas of the United States grappling with algae blooms in the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico? State officials counsel patience as they remind Vermonters it will take more time to solve the problem.  “We are moving apace with the commitments we’ve made, in terms of the projects, but it isn’t manifesting itself nearly as quickly in the lake monitoring data,” said Julie Moore, Agency of Natural Resources secretary. “This is a complex ecosystem, and we need to come at this work with a whole lot of humility.” Leaders of the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets said it will take time for investments, such as programs to reduce soil erosion and help farmers upgrade their manure storage equipment, to pay

events.title: Abu Dhabi's Ta'ziz raises $1.39bn for two Ruwais projects
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's Ta'ziz has raised $1.39 billion for two projects in Ruwais, with both transactions oversubscribed as the emirate's industrial growth strategy progresses . The terminal project raised more than $928 million, including $225 million of Islamic financing, while over $460 million has been raised for the ammonia project, the company said in a statement on Wednesday. The terminal project, a joint venture between Adnoc and Advario Star Energy, will serve as the primary logistics gateway for the Ta'ziz Industrial Chemicals Zone. It will provide liquid chemical storage capacity and export capabilities to regional and international markets. Meanwhile, the ammonia project, a joint venture between Ta'ziz, Fertiglobe, Mitsui and GS Energy, is developing one of the largest ammonia production facilities in the region, with a capacity of one million tonnes per annum. Set up in 2020 as a joint venture between Adnoc and Abu Dhabi's investment and holding company ADQ , Ta'ziz is a manufacturing, industrial services, logistics and utilities company that supports the production of chemicals and transition fuels. It plays a vital role in supporting Adnoc's plans to become a top three global chemicals player and of Abu Dhabi’s industrial growth strategy. The Ta'ziz industrial zone is set to produce 4.7 mtpa of chemicals, including low‑carbon ammonia, methanol and PVC, once the first phase is completed at the end of 2028. The latest transactions follow the $2 billion financing secured in April by Ta'ziz for its methanol project. “Securing more than $3.39 billion, including the methanol financing announced in April ... demonstrates the strong confidence that international investors and lenders have in Ta'ziz, our partners, and Abu Dhabi’s long-term industrial vision,” said Mashal Al Kindi, Ta'ziz chief executive and chairman of both projects. “These projects will play a critical role in establishing a globally competitive chemicals and industrial ecosystem in Ruwais while supporting the UAE’s economic diversification objectives.” Both the ammonia and terminal projects are progressing, Ta'ziz said. The engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) works for the ammonia project, awarded to Tecnimont, are more than 90 per cent complete and the EPC works for the terminal project, awarded to Rotary Engineering, are around 70 per cent complete. “The 1 mtpa [ammonia] facility is well advanced, and this financing underpins the final phase of delivery,” said Ahmed El Hoshy, chief executive of Fertiglobe. Japan's MUFG acted as financial adviser on the terminal financing, bringing nine regional and international banks on a long-term non-recourse deal. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation was the exclusive financial adviser for the ammonia financing, with participation from seven banks from China, Kuwait, Spain and Singapore for a six-year term facility. The first phase of the Ta'ziz ecosystem is expected to contribute $50 billion to the UAE economy, creating 20,000 construction jobs and 6,000 operational roles, the company said. In May, Ta'ziz also signed a deal with investment conglomerate Alpha Dhabi, aiming for $10 billion in capital investment in its new industrial chemicals ecosystem .

events.title: Borouge International raises 2030 annual target on rising UAE ethane production
events.summary: Abu Dhabi chemicals maker Borouge International has boosted its global annual capacity target to 13.8 million tonnes by 2030, as it expands its ethane production capabilities in the UAE. The global polyolefins company, backed by Adnoc's international investment arm XRG and Austria's OMV, had a previous annual output target of 13.6 million tonnes. The company, formed this year through the combination of Borouge, Borealis and Nova Chemicals, is now raising capacity across its 30 global manufacturing sites. Borouge International signed an agreement with Germany's Linde Engineering to expand one of its ethane crackers in the UAE, the company said in a statement on Wednesday. The move would add 230,000 tonnes to the company's production per year. An ethane cracker is a production facility that converts ethane into ethylene, which is a vital material for plastics and other synthetic products. Borouge International has three ethane crackers, all in Abu Dhabi. Bavaria's Linde, the original licenser of Borouge's second cracker, was also awarded a contract to upgrade the third cracker. Additionally, Borouge International is moving forward with the expansion of the Borouge 4 project in Ruwais. It will add 1.4 million tonnes of polyethylene capacity once fully operational, making Ruwais the world’s largest single-site polyolefin complex. The company is also accelerating its projects in Europe. In Belgium, Borouge International’s second propane dehydrogenation plant, which has an annual production capacity of 750,000 tonnes, has reached mechanical completion, with operations expected to start in the first half of 2027. In Germany, Borouge International is expanding its Borstar Nextension polypropylene project, while in Austria it recently opened its Schwechat speciality polypropylene compounding plant following a €100 million ($112.6 million) expansion. Polyolefins, including polyethylene and polypropylene, are versatile, making them among the most commonly used kinds of plastics globally. They represent nearly 50 per cent of plastics consumption in Europe, according to the Plastics Europe trade association. “We are unlocking new capacity through our strategic growth and expansion projects, strengthening our global polyolefins platform and generating long-term value for our shareholders,” said Hasan Karam, chief operating officer of Borouge International. In May, Borouge and AD Ports Group signed an agreement to study the concept of an alternative export hub at Fujairah on the country’s east coast. The move is aimed at boosting the export resilience of Borouge , allowing the company to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping activity has been severe disrupted amid the US-Iran war.

events.title: Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.
events.summary: People enjoying the water at North Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington, Vermont. The beach occasionally gets closed because of algae blooms. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica Despite being an iconic part of Vermont’s landscape and a large source of the state’s drinking water, Lake Champlain has been polluted for decades. Phosphorus runoff from farm fields, rural roads, parking lots, stormwater drains and wastewater treatment plants flows into the lake, fueling algae blooms that frequently choke its bays and shorelines. Vermont is halfway through a 20-year effort to clean up the lake. In 2016, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established new, stricter requirements for reducing phosphorus runoff that the state must meet by 2036. But more than a decade in, after spending nearly a billion dollars, the state is lagging behind. Water quality has not improved dramatically, and in some parts of the lake, it is getting worse. This past summer algae blooms shut down swimming at public beaches in St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of the lake. Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to understand the reasons behind this lack of progress . We want to know how pollution in the lake is affecting Vermont’s economy and the lifestyles and livelihoods of Vermonters and visitors alike. We’re also interested in learning more about how persistently poor water quality in Lake Champlain affects Vermonters’ health, well-being and finances. Do you live, play or depend on Lake Champlain? We want to hear from you. Your perspective will help us understand how longstanding pollution affects a wide range of issues, from drinking water quality to tax revenue from tourism around the lake.  We’re gathering these stories for our reporting, which can take several weeks or months. We may not be able to follow up with everyone, but we will read everything you submit and it will help guide our project. Please fill out this form. The post Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Please enter a search term. In the chair’s absence, the meeting was chaired by the Bank’s Head of Payment Delivery, who noted this was the second RTGS CHAPS industry forum. Minutes of the June meeting had been published. The Bank provided a brief update on its approach to tokenisation and the work underway across the Bank, HM Treasury and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The Bank highlighted the potential for tokenisation to support greater efficiency through shared ledgers, enable new products and functionality, and potentially strengthen resilience. Work is underway considering the full lifecycle of tokenised assets, from issuance and use, through to payment and settlement. The Bank noted that feedback to its joint call for input alongside the FCA showed a desire from industry to move beyond piloting the approach towards live activity. A cross-authority roadmap is planned for Q4 which will set out the work underway to support this transition, including work to enable digital asset issuance, collateral use and innovative settlement in central bank money. The RTGS initiatives covering extended settlement hours and synchronisation were highlighted as important contributors to this workplan. Item 3: Extended RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours The Bank provided an update on feedback received in response to its recently closed consultation on further extensions to RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours . Respondents had broadly supported the strategic direction and the use cases for longer settlement hours, though there was some difference of opinion on how this should be achieved. Notably responses indicated a preference for further weekday extensions before the addition of Sundays and bank holidays. The Bank has yet to reach conclusions on sequencing. The Bank noted the work around extended hours involved three principal drivers: innovation; cross-border payment enhancement; and liquidity and risk management. Members discussed a number of issues that will need answering as the design develops including liquidity, optional participation, operating costs, incident management, planned downtime and operational support. Key discussions focused on the appropriate approach to value-date rollover, including the relative merits of retaining the existing rollover (with CHAPS closing at 6pm) or aligning this more closely with the calendar day. The Bank acknowledged that further work is needed on this. The Bank plans to publish a response to the extended hours consultation in early 2027. In response to a question, the Bank confirmed that work on implementing CHAPS opening from 1.30am is already underway and progressing well. Initial estimates suggest around 20% of CHAPS payments by volume will settle before 6am. The Bank provided an update on its work to introduce synchronisation functionality into RTGS. This would enable atomic settlement of external asset ledgers against sterling central bank money, conditional on all elements of a transaction settling together or not at all. Potential uses include both tokenised asset transactions and more traditional applications such as margin and collateral optimisation. The Bank noted the need for ecosystem readiness and the challenges of scaling services. There was discussion of the practical arrangements needed to support a live service, including the role of synchronisation operators, participation, architecture, regulatory expectations and operating arrangements.

events.title: AI data center stocks and Musk's SpaceX decline as Texas governor result raises risks of a slowdown
events.summary: Several AI-linked stocks fell as election results came in showing a convincing win by Democrats of both houses of Congress. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race after campaigning for tougher limits on data center development. Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets. AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said. He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red. Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%. The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

events.summary: DR Congo ordered an investigation into suspected illegal mining, after authorities seized thousands of tons of copper and cobalt. The justice minister said police, soldiers, and mining officials confiscated more than 500 trucks and machinery at several sites in the country’s southeast. DR Congo, the world’s largest cobalt producer and a major copper supplier, is courting investment in metals used in electric cars and electronics and seeking greater economic benefits from its mineral wealth. events.title: Senegal budget row extends IMF deal uncertainty
events.summary: Senegal’s parliament rejected a revised budget on Tuesday, complicating the heavily indebted West African country’s efforts to restore financing from the International Monetary Fund. A long-standing row over spending policies and relations with the IMF has created instability at the top of Senegalese politics, threatening to undermine creditors’ confidence and delay IMF approval. The government’s $13 billion plan included a cut to public investment in order to cover extra costs after high oil prices made energy subsidies more expensive. But Pastef, the majority party led by parliament speaker and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko, argued that households and essential public services would bear too much of the burden. The country is seeking final approval for a three-year, $2.2 billion IMF loan program intended to ease budget pressures and unlock other financing. events.title: ‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Wants to Know if Democrats Can Now Hold Elon Musk Accountable
events.summary: Musk Director Alex Gibney Wants to Know if Democrats Can Now Hold Elon Musk Accountable As the US Congress prepares to usher in a Democratic majority , Musk director Alex Gibney wants to know if there will be renewed interest in government investigations into Elon Musk’s business practices. “Is our political system capable—assuming the Democrats win the House and the Senate—of ignoring the power of money … to hold really tough investigations?” Gibney asked WIRED contributing editor Zoë Schiffer following a screening of Musk at the WIRED World Fair just before many of the major congressional races were called for Democrats. Gibney’s sweeping documentary highlights United States government agencies’ multiple investigations into Musk, positing that these actions partially motivated Musk’s support for Donald Trump and other Republican candidates in recent years. On Tuesday, Gibney pointed to the more than $474 million Musk has donated to Republican political groups this election cycle, adding that, “Last I looked, things weren’t going Elon’s way, particularly in Texas.” Not long after those remarks, James Talrico was declared the winner of his Senate race and Gina Hinojosa was elected the state’s governor, some of the first Democrats to win a Texas statewide election in more than three decades. Musk, who has enjoyed close relationships with Texas bigwigs for years, donated at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Talrico’s opponent, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton. Musk “now has such an extraordinary amount of money that dropping $500 million on an election means nothing to him,” Gibney says. However, much of that money is tied up in his companies’ stock. “The question is: What if that stock begins to fall?” While making Musk , Gibney spoke with tech entrepreneurs, former employees, and, in two particularly damning interviews, Musk’s exes—his first wife, Justine Wilson, and ex-girlfriend, Ashley St. Clair. Musk also features interviews with Schiffer and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond. Musk declined to be interviewed for the film. Instead, Gibney’s team used Musk’s past public comments to create a simulated version , pairing actual quotes with a tanned, chiseled avatar wearing a leather jacket. On X, Musk has decried the documentary as a “hit piece.” In September, Alex Spiro, an attorney for Musk, sent Gibney’s Jigsaw Productions a letter threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release. The rollout for Musk has been complex. In early October, independent film distributor Bleecker Street—which owns Musk’s domestic theatrical rights— moved up the release date by a week, following strong festival reviews. According to The Hollywood Reporter , YouTube, TikTok, and Meta all initially declined to advertise the trailer for Musk leading up to the film’s debut; X did not advertise the trailer at all. Musk will be available to rent or buy starting November 6 , at which point it will no longer play in theaters. events.title: Revolut’s valuation jumps 53% to $115B in new share sale as it prepares to launch US bank
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Revolut’s investors have completed a secondary share sale that values the British fintech at $115 billion, 53% more than the price tag it had gained in another share sale a year ago, as the company prepares to launch a U.S. bank in 2027. Investors including Glade Brook Capital Partners, Coatue, Durable Capital Partners, T. Rowe Price Associates, and Baillie Gifford led the share sale, which brought no new money into Revolut. The company declined to say how much stock was sold. Founded in 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko, Revolut has grown from a money-transfer app into a financial services platform with more than 80 million retail customers across over 40 countries. It has established banking operations across Europe, and launched banks in the U.K., Mexico, Australia, and New Zealand this year, as well as secured banking licenses in France, Colombia, and Argentina. The company also began rolling out financial services in India earlier this year, and has received conditional approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish a national bank, which it plans to launch in the first half of 2027, subject to final regulatory approval. The London-based company has grown increasingly profitable, achieving profit margins of 38% on revenue of $6 billion in 2025. Even though Revolut has built much of its business around consumers, its business banking division, launched in 2017, has become an increasingly lucrative endeavor. The division accounts for about 20% of Revolut’s gross profit, James Gibson, head of Revolut Business and a partner at the company, told TechCrunch in a recent interview. Available across Europe, the U.K., Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S., Revolut Business processes more than £36 billion (about $48.6 billion) in transactions each month, including over £1 billion (around $1.35 billion) in the U.S. alone. The division generates more than £950 million (about $1.28 billion) in annualized revenue and holds more than £18 billion (roughly $24.3 billion) in customer deposits, the company told TechCrunch. Nearly half of Revolut Business’ new customers in the U.S. are newly incorporated companies, the company said. Revolut is looking to bring its business banking services to more markets, including Mexico, Brazil, and India, Gibson said, though he did not specify when the company expects that to happen. The fintech also aims to grow its business customer base from over 800,000 businesses to a million by 2027, he said. The company’s rising valuation comes as it weighs a public listing. Storonsky has considered a dual listing in New York and London and indicated a preference for a primary listing in the U.S. However, an IPO, which could reportedly value Revolut at $200 billion , would come no earlier than 2028, depending on market conditions. events.title: Essential workers being priced out of rental market, report shows
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Essential workers struggle to afford vast majority of rental listings, report reveals A new report has found almost all rental properties are unaffordable for essential workers. ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) Anglicare's annual Rental Affordability Snapshot has revealed key professions can only afford a small percentage of rental listings across Australia. Of 16 occupations surveyed, only three saw an increase in affordability since last year. Anglicare is calling on the federal government to deliver more social and affordable housing. Essential workers are being priced out of Australia's private rental market as affordability plummets, new research shows. Anglicare's annual Rental Affordability Snapshot has revealed key occupations, including retail workers, social workers and cleaners, can afford fewer than 1 per cent of rental listings. Other essential jobs, such as nursing and teaching, are not faring much better, with just 1.1 and 3.3 per cent of listings deemed affordable, respectively. Social worker Allie Thompson is about to move into a new rental in inner north Brisbane for $740 per week, which will take up about half of her income. The single mother has chosen to stop taking some of her medications to be able to afford the shift. "I just avoid going to the doctor's as much as I can unless it's absolutely urgent, and I haven't been to the dentist in probably 10 years," she said. "My son is the priority, so he gets the dentist, he gets the medical appointments and the mental health appointments. "I'll choose that any day, but that means I've had to cut back on those other things that are still important." Nurse Silvia Laing says she has cut back on luxuries to afford rent. ( Supplied. ) Silvia Laing has worked as a nurse for more than 40 years, and now supports cancer patients living at home. The 64-year-old pays $550 a week for rent in Albany, WA, which she splits with her partner. Ms Laing said that constitutes about a third of her income. "Holidays are one thing that I've had pretty much cut, and going out for meals has reduced considerably," she said. "Accommodation and health are on the top priority list, and everything that's somewhat luxury is just not going to be afforded." Anglicare's own staff are not immune to the impact of rental prices in the north west of WA. Meenaaz Adams is the organisation's new Pilbara Service Manager and has only just found a rental, eight weeks after moving to the town of Karratha. Ms Adams was provided with a month of accommodation but did not realise how difficult securing a long-term home would be. Meenaaz Adams works for Anglicare and has also found difficulty securing a rental. ( ABC News: Amy Rossbach ) "We thought that 'oh we'll secure something in four weeks'," she said. "No, we were declined three times, something I've never experienced." Increased demand from resource companies had put pressure on the local market, with the average weekly rent sitting at around $1,700. The Anglicare report surveyed 48,776 rental listings across Australia, measuring each property against the full-time minimum wage for workers in 16 essential occupations. There are no affordable rental properties for a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, the report shows. ( ABC News: Monish Nand ) Of the jobs included in the research, only three saw an increase in affordability compared to 2025, while the other 13 either decreased or remained stagnant. For a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, there are no affordable rentals available in the state. Elsewhere, only 338 listings remained. Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers said wage growth had not kept up with rent increases in recent years. Kasy Chambers says wages have not increased at the same rate as rents. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) "We would have had a social contract or an understanding some years ago that if you worked full-time, if you trained for these kinds of jobs, you would be able to find affordable housing," she said. Data from real estate analyst Cotality showed unit rents have increased by 44.3 per cent in the last five years, while house rents have gone up by 36.6 per cent. Ms Chambers said wages have increased by less than half that rate in the same period. "For those who are paying in the private rental market, sadly, most of that increase has just been swallowed up by rents." Ms Chambers said the growing disparity between wages and rental affordability was due to an over-reliance on the private market to deliver housing. "Over the last 40 years in Australia, consecutive governments have stopped building and funding housing," she said.

events.title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
events.summary: American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway. Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons . Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “ compute campuses ” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: UK interest rates increase expected after services sector activity accelerates
events.summary: Purchasing manager’s index at eight-month high, bolstered by spending on AI as firms regain momentum lost to Iran war The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a closely watched survey showed growth across the UK’s services sector leapt last month to an eight-month high, bolstered by spending on artificial intelligence. S&P Global’s survey of the services sector in October showed businesses regained much of the momentum they lost after the start of the Iran war, but also felt the impact of a renewed spurt of input price inflation, which accelerated to a five-month high. Officials at the Bank have become concerned about inflation after the consumer prices index (CPI) rose from 3.1% in August to 3.5% in September . While the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC), which sets interest rates, has been split in recent months , a majority is expected to vote on Thursday for 0.25 percentage point increase to 4%. Tim Moore, the economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a survey of the manufacturing sector earlier this week also showed businesses facing strong price pressures. He said: “These signals underscore the near-certainty of a Bank of England rate hike in November and collectively raise the likelihood of further Bank of England policy tightening into 2027.” Financial markets expect three further increases in the cost of borrowing, although most City economists believe inflation is likely to peak in the spring of next year, allowing the Bank to limit the number of extra interest rate rises to one or two. Moore said service providers indicated the fastest upturn in activity since February and “a solid rebound in new orders”. The S&P Global services purchasing manager’s index (PMI), which gauges growth across sector, rose from 52.1 to 52.8. A reading above 50 indicates a period of expansion. Bigger workloads prompted businesses in the services industry to take on additional staff in October, the survey found. This ended two years of continuous job cutting across the sector, with many businesses during that period saying that they were responding to higher labour and business costs, or not replacing employees who left. Moore said the survey suggested an “increase in economic resilience despite challenges from geopolitical tensions, elevated cost pressures and subdued consumer confidence”. “Greater workloads were attributed to an improved pipeline of sales opportunities, particularly those linked to AI investment spending,” he added. The sector has benefited from the demand for AI applications and software services associated with the boom in datacentre construction. Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the economic forecasters the Item Club, said official data also pointed to a surge in activity in the IT and professional services sectors. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He cautioned that growth in business-to-business services was not being matched on the high street, which has continued to be badly affected by a dip in consumer confidence. “With at least some of that strength reflecting businesses’ rapid adoption of AI technologies, we expect pockets of strength to sustain momentum into next year. But in a two-speed economy, consumer-facing services will come under increasing pressure as households’ spending power is squeezed,” Swannell said. He added: “An interest rate hike looks nailed on at tomorrow’s MPC meeting. And today’s data only adds to the weight of evidence.” Moore said about four in 10 of the services sector survey panel reported an increase in their input prices, while only 1% experienced a decline. It is unclear how much services firms will pass on higher input costs to consumers, pushing up inflation. Some members of the MPC have said they are prepared to wait for more evidence while others have indicated they will vote to quell even modest increases in prices. Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said there was a sign that services businesses were absorbing costs, but not by enough to prevent a rate rise. The services output price balance dropped to 56.9, from 57.8 in September. “We estimate this is consistent with underlying services inflation rising about 4.1%, down from the latest official reading of 4.4% but still too high for the MPC to stand pat,” Wood said. Meanwhile, inflation in the eurozone rose to a three-year high of 4% last month on surging energy and food costs, up from 3.8% in September. The increase makes a rate rise in December by the European Central Bank more likely after it left borrowing costs unchanged last week.

But it’s one thing to bring in revenue, it’s another to do what the prediction markets say they do well: predict. — Jake Angelo

events.title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
events.summary: For the last two years, the UK government has been telling the British public that the country could receive an economic boost of £400 billion ($538 billion), thanks to AI, a figure intended to calm fears that the technology would lead to sweeping job losses and even an economic crash. But the UK AI minister admitted last week that figure was significantly higher than the government’s actual projections after it was revealed that the assessment came solely from a report commissioned by Google and that its own estimation of AI’s economic benefit was less than a third of that £400 billion figure. AI minister Kanishka Narayan, answering a parliamentary question on the issue, said that AI adoption and data investment could add £55 billion to £140 billion to the UK economy by 2030, bringing the central estimate to £120 billion. But even this “more recent assessment,” he said, was a “hugely uncertain” estimate. Narayan said the £400 billion figure “was drawn from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First,” a British consultancy firm now referred to as PF Global. Responding to WIRED’s questions about the difference between the figures, PF Global’s head of economics, Jonathan Dupont, said the disparity was partially because of what they saw as the government’s slow adoption of AI. “AI is a very fast-moving technology, and, as we learn more, we inevitably have to update the assumptions lying behind our models. Compared to our older model, the numbers the government uses assume a much slower rate of adoption than looked possible back in our model that was created in 2023.” Government departments and agencies used Google’s £400 billion figure for almost two years, under two governments. Ministers have had the lower estimate since at least November 2025, almost a year before this week’s admission, yet Skills England, a government agency responsible for apprenticeships, was still publishing the old figure four months later. Nayaran’s parliamentary answer is the first recorded evidence WIRED could find of the government setting the two numbers side by side, or saying that the report was commissioned by Google. The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong. Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, told WIRED: “The government is right to promote the potential for technology like AI to improve public services. However, these reports highlight one of the central barriers to delivering the digital transformation of public services my committee has identified: hype. “Economic projects inevitably rely on assumptions, but overstating the benefits of technology risks undermining the case for change. The government needs to be realistic about what technology like AI can deliver and be transparent with the public about potential savings.” PF Global highlighted more top-down adoption of AI and integration into civil service workflows as examples of how take-up could improve. “While we haven’t changed our view on the overall potential of technology, given the slower rate of adoption we’ve seen in practice, our central estimate for the amount of potential likely to be achieved by 2030 is much closer to the Government’s number—with growth ramping up in the next few years after that.” Lord Holmes of Richmond, the Conservative peer who asked ministers in January 2025 about the origins of the £400 billion claim but did not receive a response, told WIRED: “It is unfortunate that the figure used repeatedly by the government, and then, unsurprisingly, by multiple other organizations, has now been significantly and rightly adjusted. It would have been better for the government to clarify this much sooner and more directly.” He added: “Robust data is critical, not least as billions of pounds of our money and how the government chooses to deploy it depend on it.” The spat over these two numbers—£120 billion and £400 billion—is part of a wider debate over the line between government support and boosterism. Former technology minister Peter Kyle also used the £400 billion figure while promoting the benefits of AI, while many parliamentarians outside of government raised questions about potential issues around the technology. “The government’s revised estimates for how much AI could add to the economy are welcome—but it’s concerning that they come after almost two years of ministers citing a figure from research that was paid for by Google,” Sumedha Deshmukh of the Ada Lovelace Institute told WIRED. “This reflects a wider pattern. Figures about AI that look precise often have assumptions and incentives built into them, and industry often funds or shapes the research behind them. “The government should test the numbers it is given before it builds policy on them, fund independent research, and measure whether promised gains are delivered.

events.title: How big money lost the 2026 midterms
events.summary: Liz’s view After the presidential election exactly two years ago, Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy rode into Washington as protagonists of a new type of politics, running the short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. Last night, both suffered the worst defeats of their political careers. Musk had moved many of his businesses to Texas and spent more than $200 million to hold the state for Republicans — part of a 2026 blitz that dwarfs any political spending by a single donor in a single election cycle — with returns that were diminishing, if not outright negative. Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s numbers faded the more Musk spent. Ramaswamy lost his bid for Ohio governor, where his Republican predecessor won four years ago by 25 points, a bigger swing than can be explained by Trump’s unpopularity and the blue wave that crested nearly everywhere. The two seemed to embody a new type of hard-edged conservative politics that lives at the intersection of Twitter and money, driven by wealthy and successful businessmen who believed their wealth and success would translate into political victories and personal popularity. I watched last night’s results from Ramaswamy’s gloomy election night party at an upscale Marriott in Columbus, Ohio, where a prayer circle was going in the women’s bathroom by 9:45 pm. The outcomes suggest that money and its purest embodiments will be forced to slip politely back behind the curtain, to support more relatable public figures. Ramaswamy’s fellow anti-woke traveler and fringe Wall Streeter, James Fishback, lost even earlier, in the primaries for Florida governor. The biggest money in American corporate history — the huge new investments in AI — also had a hard night, as Trump’s embrace of the technology helped doom his party. Now they have to find new ways to recast their projects as pro-worker and community-friendly to make sure the AI buildout actually happens — and to find spokespeople more appealing than the DOGE twins. Notable Shares in Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX slide about 5% in pre-market trading Wednesday after Democrats won in Texas, where both companies are headquartered.

events.title: Democrats’ win won’t mean a major US-Africa shift
events.summary: Yinka’s view Last night’s sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections heralds a shift in vibes rather than policy. As John “JT” Tomaszewski, the National Endowment for Democracy’s senior director for Africa, told me, African countries will “still struggle” to get on the agenda because of the competing domestic priorities battling for lawmakers’ attention following a chastening electoral rebuke to President Donald Trump. There will, however, be more scope for congressional scrutiny of his administration’s policies. Democrats will likely be keen to use hearings and investigations to revisit the dismantling of USAID and the human costs of cuts to foreign assistance. Some of that would be welcomed because there are still key questions about the administration’s decisions that probably deserve public answers. They will certainly embarrass the White House, which is kind of the point, says Cameron Hudson, a George W. Bush-era official. But I am less convinced that the theater of hearings will translate into meaningful changes in US-Africa policy. Veteran Democrats understand this challenge. A former US ambassador under Joe Biden told me he would like to see — but doesn’t expect — a more assertive Democratic agenda setting out what the US relationship with Africa should actually look like. But, this person suggested, there isn’t any political appetite left for restoring traditional development assistance: “Everybody’s moved on from that.” Meanwhile, African governments have more immediate concerns. One African ambassador, who asked not to be identified, noted visa bans and restrictions currently affect more than half of sub-Saharan African countries , questioning how Washington can keep promoting “commercial diplomacy” while making it harder for African business leaders to travel to the US. “How can the US keep talking about moving to do commerce with Africa when its business leaders can’t visit?” the ambassador asked. There may be a new mood in Washington, but for now, African governments will have to judge Washington by what it does, not what Democrats say about what Trump has done. As the ambassador said: “We’ll welcome the changes so we can have more soberness.” Notable South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the outcome of the US midterm elections signals a shift in the geopolitical landscape that could open the way for a reset in Pretoria’s strained ties with Washington.

events.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
events.summary: Repeated giving may give the impression that companies care more. useng/iStock via Getty Images Plus People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people . The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team. Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal , a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke , a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations . This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder , a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. Yanyi Leng does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

September imports were $426.6 billion, $5.2 billion more than August imports. The September decrease in the goods and services deficit reflected a decrease in the goods deficit of $0.7 billion to $135.9 billion and a decrease in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $30.9 billion. Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $297.3 billion or 11.6 percent. Imports increased $204.9 billion or 6.2 percent. Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2) The average goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the three months ending in September. Average exports increased $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion in September. Average imports increased $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion in September. Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $36.5 billion from the three months ending in September 2025. Average exports increased $28.9 billion from September 2025. Average imports increased $65.4 billion from September 2025. Exports of goods increased $5.1 billion to $211.0 billion in September. Exports of goods on a Census basis increased $5.0 billion. Capital goods increased $3.8 billion. Computers increased $1.3 billion. Computer accessories increased $0.8 billion. Civilian aircraft increased $0.7 billion. Industrial supplies and materials decreased $1.0 billion. Nonmonetary gold decreased $3.4 billion. Crude oil increased $1.2 billion. Net balance of payments adjustments increased $0.1 billion. When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “ How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts? ” and “ How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts? ”. Exports of services increased $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion in September. Charges for the use of intellectual property increased $0.1 billion. Imports of goods increased $4.4 billion to $346.9 billion in September. Imports of goods on a Census basis increased $8.0 billion. Capital goods increased $11.6 billion. Computers increased $7.6 billion. Computer accessories increased $5.7 billion. Semiconductors decreased $1.2 billion. Consumer goods increased $2.4 billion. Pharmaceutical preparations increased $2.9 billion. Industrial supplies and materials decreased $3.7 billion. Nonmonetary gold decreased $2.7 billion. Crude oil decreased $1.3 billion.
