events.title: Democrats win chance to take on energy costs
events.summary: Democrats' big night gives them a chance to turn voter anger over high energy prices into legislative action and congressional oversight, but divisions within the party could complicate their plans. Why it matters: This was an energy election . High gasoline prices, record diesel costs, and rising power bills fueled discontent with President Trump and his party. Voters' rebukes of data centers could slow the buildout of power-hungry AI infrastructure. The latest: Stunning Senate wins in red states and House wins nationwide propelled Democrats to control of both chambers, and flipped several governor's mansions. Energy costs were prominent in key races, such as Democrats hitting GOP rivals over farmers' bills in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) bashed Greg Abbott (R) over his prior embrace of data centers in the state where developers are planning big projects. The data center backlash also featured in Ohio and Pennsylvania, where Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) and Paige Cognetti unseated Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R). Both Republicans faced criticism over their support for data centers. State of play: A detailed Democratic energy agenda hasn't emerged, but there are early clues. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer tied Republicans to electricity costs in his first comments after returns came in. Likely Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has vowed to quickly push an affordability agenda, with energy as a key pillar. He tasked Reps. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.) and Mike Levin (D-Calif.) with leading a "Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group" that crafted ideas, though they remain under wraps. Another potential source of ideas: Hundreds of proposals backed this year by the 100-plus member House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition. Some could gain bipartisan backing, like support for advanced nuclear power. But other areas would be largely symbolic, like restoring some IRA tax credits. Catch up quick: In the Senate, Schumer has offered broad areas of focus around grid development, affordability and consumer protections, and clean energy. He has vowed to restore clean energy tax credits, while pledging "systematic protection for consumers from rising prices." Other ideas include more support for energy efficiency and greater transparency in utility bills. The intrigue: Democrats did not make climate change a midterm messaging focus. Watch whether progressives push to revive an explicitly climate-focused agenda. My thought bubble: Don't expect Democrats to bring back their select committee on climate change, which Republicans disbanded after winning House control in 2022. There has not been a decision announced. But the party's shift away from messaging focused on climate is reason to be doubtful, even as global warming marches on. What's next: The most immediate thing to watch is how the results may affect the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal in the lame duck. Some House progressives have argued that Dems could get a permitting deal more to their liking next year. But backers of the current bill see almost no chance of a political opening to craft a more liberal bill that Trump would sign or could even clear the Senate. The permitting fight has also opened rifts within the Democratic coalition, with multiple unions and the clean energy industry backing the bill, while many environmentalists are undecided or flatly opposed. The debate also highlights broader divisions between the "abundance movement" and progressives who want a harder line against fossil fuels Those divisions could extend well beyond the lame duck permitting fight, influencing future legislative priorities and the policy agendas of presidential hopefuls as 2028 jockeying begins in earnest. The bottom line: One thing already clear is that Democrats are lining up energy-focused oversight of Trump's diesel agreement with Moscow, offshore wind policies and much more. events.title: America unites on one issue: Reining in datacenters
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The results were particularly stark where voters got to weigh in directly Boffins use machine-learning tricks to create a starlight dimmer switch 1 hour ago Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits 10 hours ago Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang 22 hours ago British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted 23 hours ago AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization 1 day ago Datacenter restrictions found broad support in this week's US midterm elections. Data Center Watch, which tracks grassroots opposition to compute sheds across America, examined the public positions of 74 selected candidates across the 36 states that elected governors in the midterm elections on November 3. It found that 43 percent of those candidates supported a ban or moratorium on new projects, while another 51 percent backed further regulation or conditional development. Only about 5 percent had no stated public position. Support for bans or moratoriums crossed party lines, although it was more common among the Democratic candidates examined (60 percent) than Republicans (30 percent). Candidates from both major parties backed restrictions in eight states: Maryland, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, and Texas. Texas has experienced a boom in data campus development recently, thanks to its ample energy resources and light-touch regulations, although outgoing governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause earlier this year while audits of energy and water use were carried out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who supports a temporary moratorium on datacenter buildouts and has vowed to " stop the data center takeover ,” defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election and will take office in January. These positions matter to developers because governors can shape state regulation, energy policy, and permitting, although approval powers vary by jurisdiction. However, temporary pauses and targeted construction restrictions do not necessarily amount to opposition to all datacenter development. Things were even starker where folks got to vote directly on the issue, with measures regarding datacenters appearing on the ballot as well as candidates. Data Centers on the Ballot , which tracked many of these, found that 43 out of 46 municipalities where tighter restrictions on server farms were up for a vote had approved those at the time of publication. Only in one case, the City of Harwood in North Dakota, had restrictions been rejected, and 2 had yet to post results. AI-related campaign spending has also come under scrutiny. Guardrails Alliance, a labor-backed pressure group, described Leading the Future , a super PAC network opposing AI regulation, as "largely a non-factor" in the elections . It alleged the network avoided the most competitive races because "they know their money is politically toxic." Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the US in response to the facilities popping up in people's backyards, often without them having any say in the process. A Gallup survey earlier this year discovered that more than 70 percent of Americans would be against the construction of one in their neighborhood, while a Pew Research Center survey found that Americans increasingly believe datacenters are bad for the environment and blame them for rising household energy bills. Pew also found that advertisers spent almost $12 million on Facebook and Instagram political ads mentioning datacenters between July 27 and October 24. Among those running in October through the study's cutoff, 57 percent opposed datacenters and just three percent supported them. Common themes included corporate interests, energy use, environmental effects, and water consumption.

events.title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat  In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat. Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef . —Meghan McCarron This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones. Find out how the sight-restoring implant works . —Linda Marsa MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback The results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. ( CNBC ) + Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. ( Wired $) + Several winners promised to restrict data centre construction. ( FT $) + Stock futures slid as Democrats won big. ( NBC News ) + The tech left said it’s ready to “wipe the floor.” ( Vanity Fair $) 2 Google is shutting off Search for schools that reject AI The company said AI and Search can no longer be untwined. ( CNN ) + Critics accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI. ( NBC News ) + AI is the end of search as we know it. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The Binance hackers used fake job interviews in their record heist They targeted an engineer through LinkedIn. ( NBC News ) + Researchers had repeatedly warned about the tactics. ( TechCrunch ) + The breach could boost demand for specialist crypto custodians. ( CNBC ) 4 Materials maker 3M will pay $7.35 billion to settle “forever chemicals” lawsuits The suits involve PFAS in firefighting foam. ( WSJ $) + New tech could help rid water of PFAS. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Finland is opening a nuclear waste vault built to last 100,000 years It will bury spent fuel 400 metres underground. ( New Scientist $) + It’s time to make new plans for nuclear waste . ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Russia wants underground data centers after Ukrainian strikes Drone attacks have disrupted services used by millions. ( Ars Technica ) 7 Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity FlashProve uses cryptography to verify a model’s outputs. ( TechCrunch ) + “Personhood credentials” could prove you’re human. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Old jet engines are being scavenged to power data centers But environmentalists warn they will produce more pollution. ( NYT $) 9 Dinosaur blood has been found in fossils for the first time The discovery advances research into ancient biomolecules. ( Guardian ) 10 Chernobyl’s dogs appear to be evolving Scientists found differences linked to DNA repair and immunity. ( Wired $) Quote of the day “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time ” —Elon Musk tries to laugh off a costly loss on X after the Republican candidates he spent record sums supporting got drubbed in the US midterm elections. One more thing Want to understand the current state of AI? Check out these charts. If you’re following AI news, you’re probably getting whiplash. AI is a gold rush. AI is a bubble. AI is taking your job. AI can’t even read a clock. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index—the field’s annual report card—cuts through the noise.  The data reveals a technology evolving faster than we can manage. From the China-US rivalry and model breakthroughs to public sentiment and the impact on jobs, here are the index’s key findings on the state of AI today . —Michelle Kim We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A 99-year-old woman has become the world’s oldest wing walker . + Strap in for a rider’s-eye view of the fastest urban downhill mountain bike run in history. + From a bodybuilding Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 images changed how we see men (for good and bad). + 50 years after the Ramones’ first LP dropped, members of Green Day, blink-182, and Rancid played a concert honoring the legendary band.

events.title: Visits to US McDonald's locations falls as customers struggle with cost of living
events.summary: Mich. Dist. 7 Projected winner William Lawrence • D 1 hour ago N.Y. Dist. 4 Projected winner Laura Gillen • D 1 hour ago Election 2026 live results: Trump defends Iran war after Vance blames it for GOP losses Traffic at U.S. McDonald’s restaurants fell during the third quarter as customers struggled with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living Traffic at U.S. McDonald’s restaurants fell during the third quarter as customers struggled with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living. U.S. same-store sales – or sales at locations open at least a year -- fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald's since early 2025. McDonald’s restored in-app deals and its marketing was focused on value during the quarter, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant. “This is the environment that we’re in right now. events.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
events.summary: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. events.title: Watchdog sticks probe into Capita's handling of 1.7 million member civil service pension scheme
events.summary: Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid. So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP. As The Register exclusively revealed , the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023 . Capita ran to Microsoft for support , and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027 . The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco. The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement: "In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract. " Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee." The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. ® Updated to add at 1407 UTC: Capita has been in touch to say how "deeply sorry" it is about the "frustration" that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme "has caused members and their families." It said it had "made progress," but had a lot more to do. It said its teams are working to resolve outstanding cases "as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

events.title: Riyadh parents stuck in war-time limbo
events.summary: The Scene Houthi strikes on the Saudi capital have created an eerie echo of the COVID-19 period: Schools have gone online and many businesses have sent staff home, spurring an economic slowdown similar to that during the pandemic . And like six years ago, there is no foreseeable end. Parents in Riyadh have been stuck in limbo for almost a month, waiting and wondering when they will be able to send their children back to school so they can get on with work. The frequency of strikes on the city has not slowed over the past month since that side of the conflict started, with missile alerts still ringing multiple times a week, sometimes multiple times a night. There was a brief moment of hope last week when authorities tried to bring students back to classrooms. The education ministry divided Riyadh into 10 zones and planned a staggered return, which would have seen schools reopening neighborhood by neighborhood. The experiment lasted just three days after which officials reversed course, sending students back online without offering a new date for schools to reopen. The decision is now up to individual schools, with the majority opting to remain online. Meanwhile, the city’s business hub, King Abdullah Financial District, remains largely deserted, and office towers above 10 floors are still closed. Some expats who asked to work from abroad were told that there was no need to leave. The message: Keep calm and carry on — things are fine. But the restrictions have made it impossible for many to work from their offices and nobody seems to know how long this arrangement will last. For months, Riyadh maintained a veneer of business as usual despite the war, but this has become harder to sustain with the city postponing events, from tennis tournaments to conferences, and now doing a U-turn on schools. For residents, the question is no longer just whether the Houthi attacks will stop, but how long will this suspended version of life continue. Saudis are coping with humor, as they have throughout this war and past ones. One joke circulating online describes remote schooling as a wise precaution with one unintended consequence: The Houthis now face their deadliest threat yet, mothers trapped at home with their children, directing their prayers against them. Notable Consultants are driving into Riyadh from Oman and Bahrain to keep face time with Saudi clients as flights falter , and the attacks may be speeding up what the kingdom’s headquarters policy always wanted, fewer Dubai commuters, and more staff living in the kingdom , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: McDonald’s US sales decline for first time in six quarters despite value push
events.summary: Over the last two years, McDonald’s has rolled out a series of offers such as an under-US$3 (S$3.80) menu and a US$4 breakfast meal as higher living costs force consumers to opt for cheaper alternatives. McDonald’s US comparable sales fell 0.2% in the quarter to Sept 30, its first decline in six quarters, as cash-strapped diners cut back on eating out. The chain has pushed value deals, including an under-US$3 menu and a US$4 breakfast meal, but traffic still fell 4.6% and stayed weak in October. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company was “encouraged by improvement” after value changes. Global sales rose 1.5%, and adjusted earnings increased to US$3.57 a share. McDonald’s reported a bigger-than-expected decline in US sales as financially stretched consumers cut back on dining out, extending a slowdown that has tested the burger chain’s efforts to win back lower-income diners with value meals. Over the last two years, McDonald’s has rolled out a series of offers such as an under-US$3 (S$3.80) menu and a US$4 breakfast meal as higher living costs force consumers to opt for cheaper alternatives from rivals, convenience stores and home-cooked meals. Comparable sales in McDonald’s largest market fell 0.2% in the quarter ended Sept 30, missing analysts’ expectations for a 0.1% fall, according to data compiled by LSEG. It was the company’s first such decline after five quarters of growth. Customer traffic remained under pressure in the third quarter, and visits to McDonald’s restaurants fell 4.6% in the three-month period from a year earlier, according to data firm Placer.ai. Traffic also remained below year-ago levels in October despite the return of McDonald’s Monopoly promotion and Halloween-themed Boo Buckets. CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement on Nov 4 that the company was “encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value.” Chief financial officer Ian Border had told investors at a Sept 23 event that US sales would likely be negative for the quarter, but that September would likely be positive. Rival Burger King’s parent Restaurant Brands International topped sales expectations last week, helped by discounts and promotions. Yum Brands said on Nov 3 that Tex-Mex chain Taco Bell’s sales have returned to growth following a food safety-related hit. McDonald’s global comparable sales rose 1.5%, in line with expectations. Adjusted earnings rose to US$3.57 per share from US$3.22 a year earlier, helped by a roughly 4% decline in operating costs and expenses. REUTERS

events.title: M&S boss bemoans last week’s budget as ‘whole lot of nothing’
events.summary: Stuart Machin hits out at Labour but welcomes expected UK-EU food deal as retailer reveals half-year results The chief executive of Marks & Spencer has called John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a “whole lot of nothing” and bemoaned an “onslaught of taxation and regulation” from the Labour government despite welcoming an expected deal on EU border checks. Stuart Machin said he was disappointed at last week’s budget statement, adding that it “didn’t really address the issues we need to focus on growth”. He said the chancellor’s “real terms” freeze on business rates, for example, would lead to an additional £10m on M&S’s existing £170m rates bill. Machin also criticised plans for the “most ridiculous” deposit return scheme under which retailers must install machines for the return of cans and plastic bottles in stores in England and Scotland from next October in order to drive up recycling rates. In Wales, the scheme is to also include glass bottles. The M&S boss said he was “very supportive” of a new food trade deal between the UK and EU , which is expected to be completed later this month. Machin said this would help reduce a £10m post-Brexit hit to the retailer caused by the paperwork, packaging and logistical costs involved in sending goods to the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. He added that the deal would also help UK exports of food to mainland Europe. The comments emerged as M&S said a sustained cyber-attack that forced it to shut down its website last year had continued to hurt clothing sales over the past summer. The retailer said profits bounced back to a better-than-expected £355m in the six months to 26 September from only £3.4m a year before, as it partly recovered from the hack. The attack, which began over Easter 2025, forced M&S to shut its website, which sells clothing and homewares, for more than six weeks. Total sales over the half year across the food to fashion group rose 16.2% to £9.2bn. M&S said sales and profit from its clothing and homewares arm remained below that of two years ago as “availability was constrained due to the longer-than-expected impact of manual ordering processes following the incident, while profitability was diluted by an increased mix of online sales, which have higher fulfilment costs”. The retailer has previously explained that its team of buyers had to calculate demand and make orders to suppliers without the help of their usual technology and detailed information last year. Machin said: “We are broadening our appeal and the brand is in good health, but the results fell short of their potential and show there is a lot more to do.” He added that the manual ordering meant that in some clothing categories M&S did not stock enough everyday products, such as denim and knitwear, over the summer. Profits were also hit by more people shopping online during the “long hot summer”. Machin said the impact of the cyber-attack “lasted longer than we expected”, but added: “That’s now behind us.” M&S said it had been able to take its biggest ever share of a declining clothing market despite the availability problems, which were now resolved but added: “Market conditions remain challenging.” Machin said the UK clothing market was down by 11%, with £1bn in clothing sales lost across the industry in the last six months as the hot weather, low consumer confidence and a shift away from spending on nonessentials hit sales. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He added that the industry was still “heavily discounting” and M&S was trying to avoid that trend by pricing its goods affordably. M&S clothing, beauty and homewares sales rose 17.5% to almost £2bn in the half year compared with the same period last year, which was affected by the hack. Performance is expected to improve in the second half as M&S said availability has now recovered “creating a better balance between core and seasonal stock”. Its food business powered ahead, increasing sales by almost 14% to £5.2bn in the half year as it opened seven new stores and expanded or refurbished others. The group’s Ocado joint venture also swung to a half-year profit of £25.6m from a loss of £3.1m a year before as sales rose 16% and it improved the efficiency of its deliveries M&S said it expected to cut £120m in costs this year across technology, logistics and stores. Machin said the retailer would not be making redundancies but was likely to be cautious on hiring new workers as it tried to offset new costs, including £35m related to a new packaging levy.

events.title: AI-generated data found on Nigeria voter roll
events.summary: The News Nigeria’s election authority is under pressure to address the discovery of AI-generated voter information and ID photos on a draft electoral roll, which has sparked concerns about the integrity of January’s presidential vote and risks further undermining faith in the politics of Africa’s largest democracy. With just over 10 weeks to go until the vote, President Bola Tinubu is locked into a re-election battle against a slate of familiar rivals in campaigning that revolves around economic and security issues . More than 103 million Nigerians registered to take part in the poll, according to the Independent National Electoral Commission, but its numbers and overall preparations have come under intense scrutiny. Advocacy groups, technology analysts, and former INEC officials have led calls for an independent inquiry to identify how fabricated information came to be included. Many have warned that the false data would add to the cynicism about the organizer’s commitment to a fair election and weaken voter participation. Nigerian elections have often struggled with low turnout: At just 27%, the 2023 vote saw the lowest turnout since the country’s return to democratic government in 1999. INEC, responding to the backlash, said the contentious register is a temporary document open to review for errors, and that it would look into “possible technical or procedural lapses ” that allowed AI intrusions. A senior official blamed rogue staff, and said the commission “ doesn’t know why ” they would use their logins to tamper with the roll. Know More These responses have been unsatisfactory given the gravity of the situation, analysts say. “INEC wants to make light of it to say that they are doing a cleanup,” Kolawole Oluwadare, a senior official at Lagos-based rights group SERAP, told Semafor. “This goes beyond what INEC can handle in house, which is why we are calling for an audit” by an external body, he added. Martin Uwakwe, a US-based technology analyst who reviewed the draft roll, found several errors in the register beyond the AI-generated issues, including duplicates and the presence of people who had died. He said the electoral commission could use Nigeria’s existing identity database to authenticate voter data and ensure integrity. “These things are very easy to do but I don’t know why we are still having this conversation in 2026,” he told Semafor. Resolving issues with the register is critical for voting to be credible on election day. With each election cycle, Nigeria has increased the role of digital technology, including biometric tests, in the voting process to improve transparency and efficiency. But the present qualms around AI manipulation of voter data may make people skeptical of the reported outcome. For example, the portable electronic devices that will be used to accredit voters on election day (known as BVAS) could be manipulated by those who have access to the back end potentially disenfranchising unwanted voters. “If the people with access are compromised, it becomes an issue,” Uwakwe said. Step Back The hope that technology would drastically transform Nigerian elections to make them vastly more credible did not materialize in the 2023 election. BVAS devices malfunctioned en masse, while poor cell signals and other system failures delayed voter accreditation and result availability across the country. Only around a third of results could be viewed on INEC’s website two days after voting ended, fueling tensions that threatened to spill over. Legal challenges to Tinubu’s victory ultimately fell through because courts determined that it was not mandatory for INEC to publish results electronically. A repeat of these issues could have damaging long-term effects on Nigeria. “When citizens perceive elections as flawed or manipulated, confidence in democratic institutions diminishes, leading to political apathy , protests, and even violence,” Agathus Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, a Nigerian political analyst, wrote for the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development in a recent post. Notable INEC boss Joash Amupitan said his agency embraced the use of AI but warned that bad actors could use the technology to impersonate officials by, for example, making false announcements.

events.title: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown. The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth. “Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote. Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth, and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving toward hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week. The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year. Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations. events.title: BMW warns on profits as it counts cost of plan for 8,000 job cuts
events.summary: German carmaker slashes profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year in face of competition from China The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming the costs of a restructuring programme including significant job losses in the face of continuing competition from China. The company is the latest to issue a profit downgrade in the German car sector, after Mercedes-Benz last week cut its profit outlook. Western automakers have struggled to keep pace with lower-cost Chinese rivals, which has led to reduced sales in China and a rise in Chinese exports to Europe . BMW signalled a potential for losses after slashing its profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year and blamed fourth-quarter costs tied to the restructuring that includes 8,000 job cuts in its home market . At the beginning of the year, BMW had considered a margin of 4-6% would be possible. It reported an 11% drop in third-quarter pre-tax earnings on Wednesday to €2.1bn (£1.75bn). Sales in China fell 22% in the first nine months of the year, which BMW said was in line with a broader downturn ⁠in that market. The chief executive, Milan Nedeljković, said: “Current developments in our industry call for decisiveness and swift implementation. We will therefore specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures.” China “remains a key focus”, Nedeljković added, with the group’s Neue Klasse ​revival of its model offering beginning in ​China this month with the launch of the iX3. BMW follows Volkswagen in making painful restructuring costs caused by the rapidly changing market. Because of the rapid launch of its new generation of electric vehicles, the company is writing off parts of its previous vehicle and technology generations and pricing in the costs of the redundancy programme. The operating ‌margin in BMW’s core ‌automotive business narrowed to 3.4%, beating analysts’ forecast of 3.1% but declining from 5.2% a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges, the margin would be above 2%, within its previous forecast range, the company said. BMW said it planned to cut management functions more quickly under its restructuring drive. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Attackers reportedly set cold-room controls to 110°C, but safeguards prevented stock losses FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers 2 days ago Japanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned 8 days ago Ransomware gets personal: 'We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff' 21 days ago Imagine there's no Shiny Hunters – AI could make human hacking crews obsolete 23 days ago FBI confirms 'multiple' arrests related to ShinyHunters hack October 5, 2026 Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others. Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear. Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment. CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August.

events.title: Democrats will face a health care stress test
events.summary: Democrats will be able to take plenty of messaging votes on health care after their blowout wins Tuesday — but they'll face too many limits and internal disagreements to force all of the big policy changes they want. Why it matters: They'll have a tough time repealing Medicaid cuts or restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies while President Trump is still in office, and their own divisions will hold them back on other issues. And Medicare for All ? Last night gave the idea a big boost, but don't hold your breath. Friction point: With control of both the Senate and House, Democrats will have powerful new leverage — but that leverage will also expose fault lines. Until now, progressives backing Medicare for All and centrists favoring more incremental changes were united in opposing Trump administration policies and blaming the president and the Republican Congress for the health affordability crisis. They'll try to use their power in the next Congress to promote sweeping changes with an eye toward the 2028 elections while also advancing more piecemeal policies, hoping to force some deals with Republicans. But they'll still face divisions over how to expand the federal government's role in the health system, or how to bend the steep health cost curve. Driving the news: House Democrats have already signaled their opening moves with a 100-hour/100-day agenda agenda that prominently features health policies like reinstating the enhanced ACA tax credits that expired at the end of 2025. There will also be votes to roll back the steep cuts to federal Medicaid spending that Republicans included in their "One Big Beautiful Bill," per an 84-page memo from a health care working group to Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.). Other near-term agenda items include expanding Medicare drug price negotiations to private insurance, restoring withheld National Institutes of Health research funding and ending the use of AI in authorizing certain services in traditional Medicare. Within the first year, the blueprint also envisions votes on Medicare for All, a government-run public insurance option and plans to let many Americans under 65 buy into Medicare. There will also be a heavy dose of oversight, with multiple committees intent on using their subpoena power to examine details of Trump's drug pricing deals and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s vaccine policies. Reality check: Little of this would reverse the rising cost of care. And Democrats could spend a lot of energy next year playing whack-a-mole trying to target various expenses, like hospital spending, insurance premiums and the cost of insulin. Some policies, like site-neutral hospital payments , could generate billions in new savings to pay for coverage expansions, and even generate some bipartisan support at a time when more lawmakers are fed up with hospital consolidation and prices. There's also growing interest in how surprise billing disputes are driving up costs. But Democrats won't be the only ones looking for fixes. An aggressive Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services under administrator Mehmet Oz is sure to continue pursing fraud and waste in federal health programs and cutting federal spending on subsidies. Between the lines: The biggest winner Tuesday may be the progressive wing of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Strengthened by the Senate victory of left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the critical swing state of Michigan, the progressives can make a national case for Medicare for All — though the definition may be squishy. Expect many lawmakers to offer assurances that Americans can keep their health care if they want it, with a consensus likely forming around compromises like a Medicare buy-in. Actual dealmaking will largely be driven by big legislative vehicles, like bills to keep the government funded and address the debt ceiling, that could be magnets for health policy changes. There also are certain must-do's, like a "doc fix" to shield physicians from scheduled Medicare reimbursement cuts and a reauthorization of Food and Drug Administration user fees to fund new product reviews. The latter could also be a way for Democrats and Republicans to respond to growing concerns about China challenging U.S. dominance in drug development. What we're watching: Whether a "govern from the center, message from the left" strategy binds a caucus that isn't truly aligned on health care, or whether it quickly exposes rifts between establishment Democrats and the ascendant populist wing.

events.title: South Africa downplays AGOA blow
events.summary: The News South Africa moved to contain fears of major economic damage after the White House’s decision to exclude it from a US preferential trade program, saying its biggest mineral exports never relied on the duty-free program and the tariff increase on affected goods is manageable. Washington announced plans this week to remove South Africa , along with Rwanda, from the African Growth and Opportunity Act from next year. South Africa’s fruit and nut exporters have benefited from the 26-year-old program that allows thousands of products from eligible sub-Saharan countries to enter the US market duty-free. The US, explaining its latest move, cited concerns ranging from barriers to American trade and investment to corruption and foreign policy. Farmers and exporters warned, however, that the wine and citrus sectors could face job losses as their products become less competitive The decision deepens a rupture between Pretoria and Washington, entangling a trade dispute with the two countries’ wider political differences, raising the prospect of a prolonged standoff that gives South African an incentive to pursue opportunities in markets including China. It comes weeks after the US imposed travel restrictions on unidentified officials. These were introduced over South Africa’s race-based business and land policies, which seek to address the inequities of apartheid, as part of an escalating campaign that has included false claims by US President Donald Trump of a genocide against Afrikaners. Even so, South African government officials say much of the country’s biggest trade with the US is already outside AGOA protection. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s agriculture envoy Wandile Sihlobo told Semafor that losing the program was not a “train smash.” The country’s exports already face a 12.5% US tariff, meaning the loss of duty-free access adds an estimated 3.4 percentage points to the average levy, Sihlobo said. “It’s not necessarily as catastrophic as we have faced in the past,” he wrote in a note shared with Semafor. Eckart Naumann, an economist at Trade Law Centre, a South African policy think tank, struck a similar note, calling South Africa’s removal from AGOA regrettable but “ does not spell doom for South Africa ”. South Africa exported about $1.7 billion of goods to the US under AGOA in 2025, representing around 10% of the country’s sales to the country and roughly 1% of its global exports. But some of South Africa’s largest exports sit outside AGOA. Platinum group metals, which account for roughly a third of exports to the US, already enter duty free because they are deemed important to the economy. A Trade Law Centre analysis found that about 80% of South African exports by value are exempt from the current 12.5% tariff . South African-built cars effectively lost much of their AGOA advantage when Washington imposed a 25% tariff on vehicle imports in 2025. Addressing the diplomatic dispute, Deputy Trade Minister John Steenhuisen told a local radio station that South Africa had been “very generous” in trying to resolve the tensions but some US objections collided with Pretoria’s red lines. He said land reform and racial transformation were non-negotiable. The latest US demands extended to corruption, and “who we trade and do business with in the rest of the world,” Steenhuisen said. “It’s been pretty much a moving target. Trade and politics have collided and are so deeply enmeshed that it’s going to be difficult to separate them.” The pressure could push South Africa further into China’s orbit. Trade Minister Parks Tau, in a statement, said the loss of AGOA would accelerate South Africa’s search for opportunities in other markets including China, even as the US cited Pretoria’s relations with “governments of concern” among the reasons for withdrawing AGOA benefits. Know More Pretoria has for the past 18 months tried to mend relations with the US, appointing an Afrikaner as an ambassador to Washington, offering to buy up to $12 billion of US liquid natural gas over 10 years, and lifting the avian-flu related ban on US poultry. But the dispute has increasingly moved beyond trade, with Tau saying Washington had introduced “new issues” that had not formed part of negotiations that began in 2025. “This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States, however a solution depends on the willingness of both parties to find solutions,” Tau said. Steenhuisen acknowledged the US decision would have “sectoral impacts — particularly in some parts of the agriculture sector.” The government has promised to support affected industries, but has yet to spell out what that assistance will entail. Washington’s decision to eject South Africa from AGOA came on the eve of the US midterms, after Trump spent much of his second term tuning his false Afrikaner-genocide narrative which plugs into pre-existing politics of white victimhood on parts of the American right. Tiisetso’s view South Africans can probably live without AGOA. The more troubling question is whether the country’s deteriorating relationship with the US stops there. It hit a low point with the May 2025 Oval Office showdown and went downhill from then. The preferential trade program was already losing economic significance for South Africa, with only 1% of its total exports going to the US under AGOA last year. Cars, previously among the biggest beneficiaries, have their own 25% tariff problem. PGMs, which account for a far bigger chunk of US-bound exports, don’t rely on AGOA for favorable access. So far, so manageable. But Washington has advertised its willingness to go further. When the US imposed visa restrictions in September, Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III called them the “first step in a series of escalatory measures.” Seven weeks later, Washington moved to remove South Africa from AGOA, citing, not only trade and investment barriers and corruption, but US national security and foreign policy interests. It would be a leap to conclude that Washington intends to target South African mineral exports next. Nobody is saying that. But once trade policy becomes part of a wider political fight, their favorable treatment becomes more interesting Losing AGOA may turn out to be the tariff fight Pretoria could afford to lose, but the biggest risk is discovering that Washington has not finished looking for pressure points. Room for Disagreement The Citrus Growers Association, a Cape Town-based trade body, described South Africa’s exclusion as a “serious blow,” and warned of employment losses. Meanwhile, the Exporters Western Cape, a lobby group, told Ramaphosa before the decision that the province’s exports to the US had already fallen 41% with particularly steep declines in juice, grapes and citrus. Notable South African vehicle exports to the US fell 83% in 2025 after a 25% Section 232 tariff, which Naamsa says “nullif[ies]” AGOA’s benefits, Freight News reported.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: The Trump obliteration
events.summary: Make no mistake: Democrats won by epic, sometimes historic margins across red and blue states, up and down ballots, obliterating almost everything President Trump, and a Republican Party remade wholly in his image, built over the past decade in American politics. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans are left with a mostly white, mostly old House and Senate minority, confronting a younger, more diverse ascendant Democratic Party with power and margins it hasn't held in 18 years, since the dawn of the Obama era. The results speak louder than any words we can write: Democrats won Senate races in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio, and perhaps Mississippi en route to what could be a 55-seat majority. Democrats won swing districts all across red America, with national average margins of victory of roughly 13 points, according to a New York Times estimate . Texas is now a Democratic state, top to bottom — unthinkable mere months ago. James Talarico crushed Ken Paxton ( 55% to 43% ) like it was Connecticut. State Representative Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 32 years . Pastor Adam Hamilton is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years. North Carolina looks like a true-blue state after Democrats flipped the Senate seat and likely ousted Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) — meaning he led the GOP drive to keep the House. North Carolina's congressional delegation could swing from 10R-4D to 5R-9D. Georgia was even worse for Republicans, where they lost all power at the state and U.S. Senate levels. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) predicted on X that the losses were so widespread, so deep, so severe that Republicans might not "have a shot at Senate control until 2032." How to think about last night more broadly: This is a 50-50 nation with fast, whiplash shifts in power at the federal level due to persistent discontent with the party in power. So, on one hand, this isn't terribly surprising. On the other, Republican losses were so deep, so wide, so everywhere that it would be foolish to see this as anything but a massive repudiation of Trump, his agenda, his style, his rhetoric and his presidency. If anything, what's left of the Republican Party is more pro-Trump and less likely to challenge him. His critics, even the timid ones, were ousted long before the general election. So Republicans are left with two more years of riding a very unpopular leader managing a very unpopular war. A trapped, embarrassed Trump is even more unpredictable. Democrats have the numbers to investigate Trump, his family and supporters, and the power to set the agenda in the House and Senate. The bottom line: Voters nationally said government corruption was a "crucial issue" in their vote for Congress. Democrats will spend months trying to rehab a party that, despite its victory, remains deeply unpopular as a brand. Expect a vigorous fight between Mamdani-like socialists and Schumer-like center-leftists. Top takeaways from Axios' Zachary Basu.

events.summary: Report reveals financial support promised by rich nations for adaptation measures is well behind the pace that is needed Flows of money to help poor countries cope with the climate crisis have been flat or falling since 2022 , despite growing impacts from extreme weather and warnings from scientists that global heating may be accelerating . A new UN report has revealed that financial support for adaptation – which includes measures such as stronger infrastructure, early warning systems, flood protection and drought-resilient irrigation – is woefully short of what is needed and far behind even the inadequate promises that rich countries signed up to in 2021 in recognition of their far greater responsibility for the crisis. The world’s 155 developing nations will need $305bn (£226bn) annually by 2035 to adapt to heatwaves, fires, floods, storms, droughts and rising sea levels that are made more intense or more frequent as a result of decades of burning fossil fuels, mostly in wealthy global north nations, according to the UN Environment Programme . Yet finance flows from rich to poor countries were at most $32bn in 2024, the latest year for which data is available. That was only a billion up on the previous year, and down from the peak of 2022, partly because many governments in Europe are devoting more of their budgets to defence spending. This is well behind the pace required to meet the goal of hitting $40bn by 2025, though some of the shortfall is expected to have been made up last year by multinational development banks, the report said. At the Cop30 global climate talks in Belém , Brazil, last year, wealthy nations agreed to triple adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035. This increase to between $85bn and $120bn would reduce the gap, but still meet only 20-29% of needs, the report said. The world’s least developed countries (LDCs) and small island states are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis and least able to pay for upgrades to infrastructure, such as more sea barriers and firefighting equipment. The UN estimates these countries need $40bn to $50bn each year in adaptation finance, which is about 3-4% of their gross domestic product – double the relative burden for upper-middle-income developing countries. Despite this, LDCs received 16% less in adaptation financial support in 2024 than two years earlier. Between 2020 and 2025, low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of all the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides. Some of the worst impacts on human health and natural life support systems are unaccounted for because developing nations are less likely to have monitoring systems in place to assess heat-related deaths or damage to ecosystems. A recently established loss and damage fund is already overwhelmed. In its first round, 119 developing countries submitted requests totalling $2.8bn, far outstripping the initial funding of $342m. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Inger Andersen, the UNEP executive director, said a global temperature overshoot of 1.5C above preindustrial levels was now locked in, making climate impacts more intense, frequent, and unpredictable. “For the countries that contributed the least yet suffer the most, this is an unavoidable reality,” she said. “Adaptation finance is a vital investment in global resilience. Delivering on these commitments protects frontline communities, prevents forced displacement, safeguards global food security, and ensures no one is left behind. Now is the time to honour commitments in full. Delays not only increase long-term costs, they also strain our near-term capacity to cope as our systems reach their limits.” Climate justice groups say adaptation finance is the most urgent issue at the upcoming COP31 UN climate summit, which will be hosted in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November. As well as a faster, bigger flow of funds, the priority, they say, is for grants or concessionary loans rather than high-interest loans, which are difficult to pay back on sea walls, heat shelters and other projects that do not generate direct revenue. The UN report underscores this, noting that debt and equity costs can more than double the budgets of adaptation projects. While wars are diverting resources and attention away from climate action, Anderson said it was important to view the interlinked nature of the world’s crises: “While some might view climate action as a separate issue, ignoring it only increases national and regional vulnerability, especially as many climate impacts unfold beyond national borders. Failing to invest in mitigation and adaptation only exposes nations to greater risk. Climate change directly threatens people, economies, and the ecosystems that sustain us – and why adaptation is a direct investment in national security and resilience. The two are fundamentally inseparable.”

events.title: Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop
events.summary: Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school. Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme. Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too. This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around. Trinity is back The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7 , with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray." Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023 . ®

events.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
events.summary: Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting. Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings. Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe. Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people. What are interest rates and why do they change? An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it. The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings. The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%. When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up. The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation? The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting. Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025. It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026. Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target. The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices. The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally. What is happening to UK prices? Published 21 October What is expected to happen to UK interest rates? At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April. However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed. Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently. Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates? Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external . About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise. But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are. Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in any rates being offered. As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts. The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%. About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply. events.title: BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount
events.summary: BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China. German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry. Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said. The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China . Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China. BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3. CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures." BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market. Germany's auto industry struggling because of weak demand and competition from China German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures. Volkswagen , the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market. BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs. The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on? The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October. It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027. On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028. According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany. German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division. events.title: Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices
events.summary: Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes. In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers. Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert. "What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive." Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. " My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said. "In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control." Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton. Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027 , ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent. " Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call. Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units , down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions coupled with rising memory costs mean tough times for the PC industry. Omdia – which owns Canalys – said: " The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly." Reg readers know why component costs are going up. The datacenter construction frenzy meant memory chip makers could make more money from higher-margin HBM than conventional DRAM, prompting them to prioritize production of the former . But AI PCs have been a tough sell from the start , as higher prices and a lack of killer applications meant many customers delayed purchases. Microsoft has to convince the market of the benefits – including trade customers as well as those in charge of procurement at enterprises. Once more, the pitch for AI PCs Back at the Canalys Forum, Microsoft's Linton claimed customers mulling AI PC purchases want better productivity, to reduce costs, to innovate, and to be able to use these computers securely and at scale. Microsoft is going to invest heavily in Windows from both the platform capability and security to enable these ends. So, if you are a Microsoft partner, you'll be able to run Windows and secure agents at the operating system level with Agent 365, with Intune, or with Entra. Linton added: " We announced in June some of the technology in Windows, in particular Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). And so essentially you can virtualize agents, and then you can use Intune to give them policy. And so other platforms, you have to manage agent by agent. Windows, you'll be able to do it policy-based, much like you manage people and network resources. " You will have agents for all, and you need to know how to manage them, track them, audit them, and then ensure that they're contained in the right way. So we're doing that at the operating system primitive level." Some of the quality control issues that have dogged Windows may give some sysadmins pause for thought about the grand claims made by the Windows exec. Still, Microsoft is on a mission, and it knows how to attract thousands of resellers by dangling financial incentives in their direction. Linton said it is pumping money into channel programs, including AI-readiness funded headcount with "top partners" to "get this hybrid AI story moving." Microsoft wants the channel to deploy AI internally too, "especially for your sales team" because "if they're using it, they're able to sell it." Dell isn’t hopeful of an uplift in PC demand this year. David Kennedy, chief financial officer, said sales will remain "compressed." "The reality is most enterprises this year for their IT budgets are sweating those assets out a little bit more and what dollars they have, they're trying to build out their infrastructure side," he told the Citi TMT conference in September. "As we go forward, I think you'll see it [become] a little bit more robust. Our main focus will be on those higher ASP (average sales price) commercial boxes as part of the AI storyboard that's there." He reckons there are more than 400 million PCs owned by customers that are "over four years old", and with the "cheapest token being closest to the data, none of those installed base PCs will have the battery life or the power to do AI workloads on them. So there is a pent-up demand that we believe will come once it stabilizes and once IT budgets get a little bit more settled and expanded." Will 2027 be the year of the AI desktop? The Reg suspects not, though readers can do what they always do and speak their brains in the comments section. ®
