events.title: "What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake": Voters revolt against tech at polls
events.summary: Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom. Why it matters : In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities. The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead-set on winning. "What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake," Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers." Driving the news: Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout. Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on data center construction in place until the state passes legislation tackling impacts on water, electricity, air and property rights in the legislative session that ends in mid-2027. While most 2027 U.S. data centers expected are already under construction, a hold for more than six months would bring extended delays to Texas, which accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis. Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape. Between the lines: All told, nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face delays, although most political analysts don't see Democrats permanently blocking construction. What they're saying: A host of candidates and politicos called out AI as one of the most important issues in the blue wave, an important signpost ahead of a momentous 2028 presidential race. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), a 2028 contender who won reelection by a wide margin, called out "the titans of Silicon Valley" in a victory speech, saying they "dig bunkers for themselves" even as they warn "that the artificial intelligence they're creating risks human extinction." AI had its "official debut" as the biggest issue in American politics, former New York Assemblymember and RAISE Act author Alex Bores told Axios. "AI is reaching into every part of our society and economy and it's now crystal clear it's impacting every part of our politics, too." By the numbers : The anti-tech sentiment extended far beyond those states. Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals designed to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns , according to Ballotpedia. Ohio hosted the largest share of those ballot fights, and some votes are still forthcoming, including in Arkansas and North Dakota. Yes, but: In California, a measure that would've enacted a 5% wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets appeared headed for defeat early Wednesday morning. Proposition 40 faced a well-funded opposition from the state's tech luminaries, as well as prominent Democrats like Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra. The intrigue: Leaning into AI skepticism proved to be a winning strategy for Democrats in swing districts. Democratic challengers successfully weaponized AI policy , ousting Republicans in Ohio, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Democratic groups had poured ads into these districts attacking GOP incumbents for a 2025 vote that would've neutered state AI legislation. AI safety advocates won or were poised to win races on Tuesday that will expand their coalition in the new Congress, including Colorado's Manny Rutinel and Minnesota's Matt Little. The bottom line : For years, tech execs have dictated the terms of a seemingly limitless expansion, but this election proves that the ballot box still reigns supreme.

events.title: Hakeem Jeffries gets the majority of his dreams
events.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set to preside over a commanding Democratic majority after his party swept districts President Trump carried by double digits. Why it matters: Democrats' landslide win will make it much, much easier for the likely next speaker to secure the gavel without a sweat and ignore the demands of his progressive wing. Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.), a leader of the center-left New Democrat Coalition, told Axios in an interview Tuesday night that Jeffries "now has the space to utilize his full talents as speaker." The size of Democrats' victory, Stanton said, "allows him to govern without worrying about being leveraged by anyone." Driving the news: Jeffries is on track to enjoy a majority of dozens of votes, with the New York Times projecting Democrats to win as many as 256 seats to Republicans' 178. Democrats flipped districts where the national parties didn't even spend money, likely unseating Republicans such as Reps. Lauren Boebert and Richard Hudson who were considered safe just months ago. It's a major partisan win for Democrats as a whole, but the party's centrist wing is also hailing the result as a much-needed strategic victory over the left. Zoom in: Progressives — particularly "The Bloc," a group made up of hard-charging leftists like Darializa Avila Chevalier and Adam Hamawy — had hoped to use a small majority to extract concessions from Jeffries. Many of them have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries as speaker and signaled they would use their votes as leverage force votes on progressive legislation such as Medicare-for-All, defunding ICE and cutting aid to Israel. But the left's strategy is "going to look different from what it would have been with a smaller margin," one incoming House progressive told Axios, noting that "leaders have more flexibility when they have big majorities." Progressives "can't really extract much now [with this] colossal majority," a progressive strategist acknowledged, adding that "we don't have to do this high stakes Jeffries fight." Between the lines: Stanton noted that most of the incoming Democrats who won in purple and red districts were endorsed by the New Dems. The center-left group is one of Jeffries' most reliable power bases in the caucus. "Every single New Dem incumbent, every single candidate that got our endorsement that's winning tonight — and there's a lot of them — I have full confidence they're going to vote for Hakeem Jeffries as speaker," Stanton said. Yes, but: Several progressives who spoke to Axios noted that many of the Democrats who won upset victories in deep-red districts on Tuesday ran more as rural and rust belt populists than traditional pro-Israel, pro-business centrists. As Axios reported in October , many Democrats who ran in Trump double-digit seats did so with a message that savaged their own party's leadership as much as the GOP's. An incoming member of the progressive "Bloc," asked if Democrats big margin would make it harder for the left to get their demands met, replied, "Yes, but only if leadership takes the wrong lessons from tonight." "Progressive, populist politics won overwhelmingly and came ridiculously close in places no one expected to see. This kind of margin comes with an expectation that we deliver bold changes," they added. The bottom line: Progressives are warning Jeffries that he will regret looking at Democrats' massive victory as a green light to govern in increments. "I think there's a clear mandate from voters on what sort of progressive economic agenda they want to see," said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats.

events.title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
events.summary: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.What firms need to do nowSo, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to:Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.How we are supporting firmsWe are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.You can find more information:NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptographyG7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sectorCMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

events.title: Blue tsunami breaks MAGA: 5 takeaways from a blowout midterm election
events.summary: President Trump's Republican Party suffered an electoral humiliation Tuesday night that stretched across the battleground map and into some of the deepest-red territory in America. Why it matters: The 2026 midterms will go down as one of the most sweeping repudiations of a sitting president in modern American history, on a scale reminiscent of the post-Watergate reckoning of 1974. The big picture: Two years after Trump's comeback appeared to herald a historic political realignment , voters delivered a devastating verdict on his second presidency. Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress, on course to gain as many as 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats — eclipsing their wildest pre-election expectations. The wave swept deep into Republican territory, from Texas and Georgia to both Carolinas, flipping hundreds of legislative seats and delivering Democratic trifectas in the unlikeliest of states. 5 takeaways 1. Texas turns blue: After decades of dashed hopes, Democrats finally conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office. Gina Hinojosa became the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and possibly Texas' House of Representatives, suggesting that the state's political future could be up for grabs after 32 years of GOP dominance. 2. Democrats storm Senate: What once looked like an impossibly difficult map for Democrats gave way to a historic rout, as Republicans watched their 53-seat majority crumble in states Trump carried by double digits. Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio , Iowa and North Carolina , and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998. In Maine, Democrats finally toppled five-term Sen. Susan Collins after many failed attempts, putting them on course for a 54-seat majority — with Alaska and even Mississippi offering a chance to make it 55 or 56. 3. MAGA coalition collapses: The multiracial, working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly Tuesday, raising serious questions about the long-term durability of his MAGA movement. AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 and 60% of Hispanic voters backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war. In heavily Hispanic Starr County, Texas, which Trump famously flipped in 2024, Talarico led by nearly 60 points — a staggering 75-point reversal from two years prior. 4. GOP House firewall crumbles: Democrats are on course for their largest House majority since 2009, potentially winning as many as 255 seats. Casualties spanned the entire GOP conference, from MAGA firebrands to battle-tested moderates . Even seats redrawn to shield Republicans from a blue wave fell to Democrats, turning Trump's redistricting offensive into a spectacular miscalculation. With control of the House secured, Democrats wasted little time signaling what comes next. Incoming Oversight chair Robert Garcia distilled the party's appetite for investigations into two words : "Lawyer up." 5. 2028's winners and losers: Tuesday's landslide elevated a new generation of Democratic contenders and cast a shadow over Vice President Vance's presidential ambitions. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff , whose race was called 15 minutes after polls closed, immediately vaulted into the top tier of Democratic prospects. Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic victory for governor removed a key obstacle for both Ossoff and Sen. Raphael Warnock: She could appoint a Democrat to fill their seat if either became president. Vance, Trump's presumed political heir, now faces the fallout from a deeply unpopular Iran war and the collapse of a once-in-a-generation coalition he hoped would carry him to the White House. The bottom line: For a decade, Trump has been the gravitational center of American politics. Tuesday's results suggest that era may finally be drawing to a close.

events.title: UAE non-oil firms sharply raised prices in October amid rising confidence
events.summary: UAE non-oil businesses sharply raised their selling prices in October as firms passed on an increase in operating costs to consumers, while confidence among companies also soared last month. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index eased slightly to 54.8 in October, compared to 55.3 in September . But it remained above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. Output prices were raised at the “sharpest rate” since the survey began in August 2009, the report said. Firms linked price rises to spiralling operating costs and efforts to protect margins. Costs for companies also rose by the fastest pace since June 2022, driven predominantly by the higher purchase prices, the report said. Firms reported paying more for a wide range of raw materials, as well as fuel, energy , freight, maintenance, storage and rent. “The unprecedented rise [in selling prices] reflected efforts to pass cost burdens on to customers, with firms feeling the impact of higher fuel prices and increased charges for critical materials,” said David Owen, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “The findings point to greater inflationary risks for the UAE economy in Q4, especially in the light of successive increases in petrol and diesel prices.” Overall, the PMI was indicative of a “solid improvement in overall business performance”, the report said. New order growth and output continued to rise strongly, with business confidence improving to the highest since January. Firms linked higher activity to sectors including construction, retail, tourism and manufacturing, although some noted restraints from regional conflict , competition and lower discretionary spending, according to the report. New orders rose at a sharper pace than in September, supported by new clients and repeat business. The overall level of new export work rose at the quickest rate in two years. However, employment levels fell fractionally in October, marking the third decline in the past five months. Some firms reduced headcounts to control costs, which offset hiring at others in response to rising sales, the report said. “Order book levels grew at a faster rate in October, but capacity remains limited – signalled by another sharp increase in outstanding business,” Mr Owen said. The UAE's economy has continued to grow this year driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The country's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last month. The non-oil sector's contribution to the GDP during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent, to 79.2 per cent, the FCSC said. “Looking ahead, non-oil firms are becoming more upbeat. Year-ahead expectations rose to their highest since January, underpinned by robust demand forecasts and hopes that improving regional conditions will lift sectors such as tourism,” said Mr Owen. October’s PMI survey points to “continued expansion” in the UAE's non-oil private sector, said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. “Demand remained firm … although the after-effects of the regional conflict continued to disrupt trade and raise costs,” he added. Dubai PMI at eight-month high Non-oil private sector business activity in Dubai also rose sharply, reaching an eight-month high in October. The Dubai PMI reached 54.6, up from 54.5 in September, signalling a “strong improvement” in business conditions, S&P said. The upturn was underscored by a sharp increase in new business volumes that was the joint-fastest since February. Businesses also raised their output levels, but made modest reductions to staffing. Similar to the UAE, Dubai non-oil firms also reported a record increase in selling prices in October, with companies mainly passing along rising input costs to customers. “Local firms were more confident about future activity in October, but cost considerations meant that stockpiling efforts were less pronounced than in September,” the report said.

events.title: ‘A true icon of the hair industry’: celebrity hairstylist John Frieda dies aged 75
events.summary: Businessman styled stars such as Twiggy, Madonna and Joanna Lumley and created popular hair care line Frizz Ease John Frieda, the celebrity hairstylist who launched his own bestselling hair product range, has died aged 75. In an Instagram post, his salon wrote: “It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully … surrounded by his family. “John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better. “His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us. We will continue to do him proud. Our thoughts are with John’s family and everyone who loved him. Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts.” The London-born businessman, whose father was a hairdresser and whose grandfather was a barber, styled celebrities ranging from Twiggy and Jackie Kennedy Onassis to Scarlett Johansson, Madonna , Nicole Kidman and Diana, Princess of Wales. He created the famous “Purdey” hairstyle – a statement bowl cut – for Joanna Lumley in 1976 for her role in The New Avengers TV series , and opened his first salon that same year, aged 25. He went on to launch the popular Frizz Ease hair care line and open salons around the world. He also styled for British Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar Frieda married his first wife, the Scottish singer known as Lulu, in 1977. They had one child, Jordan Frieda. Frieda moved to the United States in 1990 to focus on his growing hair care brand, and his relocation contributed to the end of the marriage. He met his second wife, Avery Agnelli, widow to an heir of the Fiat car company, in 2002 and they married in 2019. They had two children together, Jackson and Leyla, and Frieda was stepfather to her daughter, Asia Agnelli Lagrange. Agnelli Lagrange shared a series of photos of them together on Instagram, writing: “Sadly my J has passed away. Today we lost the best man to ever exist. I share this because I know he touched the lives of so many.” The cause of death has not been made public. Born Alan Howard Frieda in Kenton, Middlesex, he began his career at London’s House of Leonard salon and adopted the name John because another stylist at the salon was also named Alan. In the 1980s he worked with the American hair care executive Gail Federici to create his own product line, and he launched Frizz Ease in 1988 and his Sheer Blonde line in 1998. Among those paying tribute on social media was Jo Wood, the model, TV personality and the wife of the Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood. She said: “Oh No… that’s so sad. When I was 16 and John worked as an assistant at Leonards, he would do my hair. He was so great… we would go to the pub after… but I couldn’t drink. RIP John it was lovely to know you.” Cetera Lamb, the creative director of Frieda’s London salon, said: “The industry has lost a true legend, a real maverick in hairdressing. For 50 years, he led our wonderful salon, leaving behind an incredible legacy of passion, creativity, vision and outstanding hairdressing.” In 2002, Frieda sold his hair care company to the Japanese conglomerate Kao in a deal valued at $450m. He retained ownership of five salons: two in London, two in New York and one in Los Angeles.

events.title: Everything you need to know about last night in under 1,000 words
events.summary: It was a drubbing on a scale that neither side saw coming: Democrats pummeled Republicans across the battleground map and into some of the most MAGA-friendly terrain in the country. Why it matters: The results were an emphatic rejection of Donald Trump's second term in office — and set the stage for two years of corruption investigations and legislative frustration for the lame-duck president. Here's a rundown of what you need to know about last night's historic GOP beatdown. The size of the Dem majorities It was clear early in the night that Democrats would flip the Senate. Few predicted how big their majority would end up. Democrats will have at least 54 Senate seats, and another two — in Alaska and Mississippi — were too close to call early Wednesday. The New York Times projects Democrats will win 257 seats vs. 178 for Republicans — a 79-seat majority. Those numbers could change as more races are called, but in any scenario it will be an astounding majority. The big surprises 1. Texas turns blue: After decades of dashed hopes, Democrats conquered the nation's most coveted Republican stronghold — in a landslide so sweeping that even three-term Gov. Greg Abbott was driven from office. Gina Hinojosa will be the state's first Latina governor, while James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton to become the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. The Democratic onslaught extended across statewide offices and into the legislature, suggesting that the entire state's political future could be up for grabs after 32 years of GOP dominance. 2. More red-state romps: Democrats broke a 94-year losing streak in Kansas, ousted Republicans in Ohio , Iowa and North Carolina , and captured South Carolina for the first time since 1998. 3. House district reversals. Tennessee's 4th Congressional District race hadn't been called as of the wee hours Wednesday. But the returns were stunning regardless of the outcome. Trump carried the district two years ago by 24 points, and the Democratic candidate, Victoria Broderick, spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14. There was no record of her airing a single paid ad. Yet Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%. Other House race results were littered with similar red-to-blue 180s from two years ago. How the pollsters performed Democrats fretted that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — in some cases by a lot. The midterm polling was "worse than you think," Lakshya Jain, a data and polling expert, wrote last night. "The polls actually missed low on Democrats more than they whiffed on Republicans in 2016. In fact, the national environment is D+13, which is four points more Democratic than the national polling average." How did the GOP redistricting play work out? Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday. Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin. In Florida, Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, and in Texas they're set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they heavily redrew in their favor. The GOP also failed to dislodge Democrats in Ohio and Alabama who they drew into Republican-friendly districts. MAGA coalition collapse The multiracial , working-class coalition that powered Trump's 2024 comeback fractured spectacularly Tuesday, raising serious questions about the long-term durability of his MAGA movement. AP's nationwide voter survey found roughly 70% of voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates, amid widespread anger over the economy and the Iran war. Hispanic voters swing back Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028. The clearest examples of the Latino shift away from Trump came in Texas counties that Republicans had celebrated as evidence of their growing strength. In heavily Hispanic Starr County, Texas, which Trump famously flipped in 2024, Talarico led by nearly 60 points — a staggering 75-point reversal from two years prior. Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in Texas' Rio Grande Valley that Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close. The verdict on AI Voters sent a clear message on Tuesday about AI and data centers: less construction, more regulation. Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout, given the state was expected to host nearly half of new 2028 data center capacity. Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape. 2028's winners and losers Tuesday's landslide elevated a new generation of Democratic contenders and cast a shadow over Vice President JD Vance's presidential ambitions. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff , whose race was called 15 minutes after polls closed, immediately vaulted into the top tier of Democratic prospects. Keisha Lance Bottoms' historic victory for governor removed a key obstacle for both Ossoff and Sen. Raphael Warnock: She could appoint a Democrat to fill their seat if either became president. Vance, Trump's presumed political heir, now faces the fallout from a deeply unpopular Iran war and the collapse of a once-in-a-generation coalition. Maria Curi, Hans Nichols, Zachary Basu, Russell Contreras, Andrew Solender and Mike Zapler contributed.

events.title: Google to invest US$15 billion in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028
events.summary: Google plans to build new data centre campuses in the states of Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. Google will invest US$15 billion in Malaysia from 2027 to 2028 for data centres, clean energy, water security and worker training, said Alphabet unit Google. It will build new campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, adding to its Elmina Business Park site, and expects the work to lift GDP and create jobs. Google plans more than one gigawatt of clean energy, will pay for all power used, and will upskill 800,000 Malaysians over five years. KUALA LUMPUR – Google will invest US$15 billion ( S$19.17 billion ) in Malaysia from 2027 to 2028 with the spending going towards data centre campuses , clean energy, bolstering water security and upskilling workers, the unit of Alphabet said on Nov 4 . Google plans to build new campuses in the states of Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, in addition to its first campus at Elmina Business Park in Selangor , which is already operational. “This investment aligns with Malaysia’s development priorities, providing the foundational computing capacity to deliver the upside of innovation across the country while adding local power and water resources as our operations scale,” Alphabet and Google’s president and chief investment officer Ruth Porat said. The construction phase for the campuses is expected to contribute an annual average of US$1.1 billion to Malaysia’s GDP and support more than 37,000 local jobs per year, Google said. The facilities, once operational, are projected to sustain more than 9,000 local jobs per year, with wages averaging 45% above the national median. Google said it also plans to add more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to Malaysia’s national grid. “Google will also pay for 100% of the power its data centre campuses use and the direct infrastructure costs required to connect them to the grid, while complying with all applicable local regulations,” it said. On efficiency, Google said its Malaysian campuses will run at a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.12 to 1.14. Google also announced its plans for four new programmes aimed at upskilling 800,000 Malaysians over the next five years. REUTERS

events.title: Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits
events.summary: Schneider Electric sees no slowdown in its datacenter business, but says operators must be more open with communities about the power, water, and land their projects will consume. As a supplier of electrical infrastructure, cooling, and power distribution equipment, Schneider has a direct view of operators' spending plans – and a commercial interest in continued construction. Steven Carlini, vice president of innovation and datacenter, said Schneider's pipeline showed no slowdown. "And Schneider has a lot of agreements, supply chain agreements with the larger datacenter operators." Reports earlier this year suggested only half the capacity planned for 2026 is actually under construction in the US, and land being cleared for new bit barn projects has plateaued. Carlini nevertheless said US companies were building as fast as they could, contrasting that with planning bureaucracy and other obstacles in Europe. "But the one thing that I think is going to be the biggest change is the level of transparency from the operators when they're trying to secure permits and when they're requesting power," Carlini said. "The way the model traditionally worked in the US is the operators would negotiate with the local jurisdictions that were responsible for issuing the permits, and there would be non-disclosures involved, almost universally. So the residents where these datacenters were going to be built had no visibility into these projects until construction started." Opposition to datacenter construction has grown in the US. Campaign groups called for a moratorium on new facilities late last year, and New York state imposed a halt this summer. The sheer scale of the new builds has also alarmed many folk, with Meta's Hyperion facility, for example, planned to reach 5 GW of power capacity and cover an area equal to a significant chunk of Manhattan . A recent survey by think tank Pew Research Center found that Americans are increasingly wary of datacenters , with more than half saying they are bad for the environment, bad for household energy bills, and consume water resources for cooling. In response, companies building and operating compute sheds need to be more upfront about what effect their plans will have on the local area, Carlini said. "They're going to have to disclose where the power is going to come from, how they're going to get the power, their water usage, their carbon emissions, the efficiency of the datacenter, where it is going to be located physically, the noise levels of the facility, the water sources, which is a big one, and how much water they're going to use is another big one that operators have traditionally not been very forthright in publishing." In Virginia – the world's "datacenter capital" – an ex-water sustainability program manager at AWS is taking his former employer to court over claims it published false and misleading statements about water use in the state. Carlini expects permitting requirements to force greater disclosure, followed by reporting obligations once facilities are operating. "And then they're going to have to report it as part of regulations during operations as well, so it's not going to be a case of here's our prediction, and then you get the permit and you never have to report again," he said. Datacenter owners and operators must win hearts and minds as well, Carlini added, a point already recognized by some in the industry at an event last year. "From a public relations perspective, that's another area where the operators really need to focus, because in many cases they've taken the position that they're benefiting the community," he said. "Those days are gone, so the operators are going to have to, from a PR perspective, engage with the local residents more amicably." People using Facebook or Gmail doesn't mean they'll welcome a datacenter next door, Carlini told us. "So it's going to have to be more like 'Here's how we're going to help,'" he said. Operators would need to acknowledge residents' concerns and explain any benefits, such as tax breaks or lower costs. For AI facilities, Carlini expects more attention to token-processing performance and efficiency, rather than power capacity alone. "I think we're going to start to see more and more focus on tokens per watt, tokens per dollar, and even datacenters could be sized in tokens as a performance metric for the IT rather than just the power metric," he told us. "I think the industry has suffered in the past because datacenters have always just been sized in power consumption, and that gave little idea what it was producing and what value [it] was adding." For more on the economics of tokens in AI processing, readers can refer to our article on this topic from earlier this year. ®

events.title: Google extends voluntary buyout offers to employees in several countries
events.summary: Parent company Alphabet’s workforce has grown steadily in recent quarters, but it has sought to shift resources toward priority areas. Google has expanded voluntary buyout offers to employees in Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland to cut costs while spending heavily on AI. The company said the programme, first used in some US and UK divisions, is for staff who no longer feel aligned with Google’s pace or direction. In Switzerland, the offer covered multiple divisions but excluded DeepMind; staff got one month’s salary per year of service, up to 12 months, after earlier 2023 layoffs and protests. ZURICH – Alphabet’s Google has expanded employee buyout offers to several countries in 2026 as it looks to rein in rising costs amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence. The search engine company confirmed to Reuters that it began offering voluntary exit packages in June to some employees in Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland. Reuters could not determine how many employees have accepted the latest round of offers, which had not previously been reported. “In 2025, some of our teams introduced a voluntary exit programme with severance,” a Google spokesperson said in a statement. “This past summer, in June, we expanded this programme globally in a few countries to support our important work ahead.” The move comes amid mounting AI spending that has unnerved Wall Street and dented Alphabet’s stock price . Microsoft last week offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to contain costs. Alphabet’s workforce has grown steadily in recent quarters, but it has sought to shift resources towards priority areas. The latest buyouts follow voluntary exit programmes offered since last year to employees in some divisions in the US and Britain. Executives have described the programme as an option for employees who no longer feel aligned with the company’s pace or direction. In at least one case, the company followed its voluntary offers to a division with a round of layoffs. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi has repeatedly highlighted AI and cloud computing as key hiring priorities in quarterly earnings presentations. Employees in Google Cloud and AI unit DeepMind have been excluded from past buyout offers. The latest expansion appears to follow the same pattern. In Switzerland, where Google employs about 5,000 people and has a major engineering hub in Zurich, three people familiar with the matter said the programme covered multiple divisions but excluded DeepMind. Employees began leaving in August after Google offered voluntary exit packages in the country, the people said. Google announced the packages in mid-June and gave responses by mid-July to employees who applied, they said. Staff who accepted received one month’s salary for each year of service, up to a maximum of 12 months. One person said at least four employees in a team of about 50 had accepted the offer. Google laid off more than 200 employees in Switzerland in 2023, prompting staff protests and a walkout. REUTERS

events.title: Adnoc Gas signs agreement to supply natural gas to Northern Emirates
events.summary: Adnoc Gas is planning to supply natural gas to the Northern Emirates as part of an agreement with Etihad Water and Electricity for new power generation, it said on Wednesday. The move is aimed at exploring future natural gas supply arrangements for new power generation capacity across the Northern Emirates. The collaboration would open a new domestic market for Adnoc Gas’s growing gas volumes while providing a reliable fuel source for additional UAE power generation capacity, the Abu Dhabi company said in a statement. The agreement will support the country's growing electricity needs and expand the domestic market as new supply comes online, it added. “Adnoc Gas is investing to meet the UAE’s growing energy needs,” said chief executive Fatema Al Nuaimi. “By expanding our capacity and infrastructure, we can connect new gas supply with new customers, support future power generation and create sustainable long-term value for our shareholders.” Adnoc Gas, listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, aims to deliver one of the world's largest integrated gas growth programmes to unlock additional supply for domestic and international markets. The programme includes Rich Gas Development, which will expand processing capacity and increase the availability of natural gas for domestic customers, and the Estidama project, which will optimise and modernise Adnoc Gas's pipeline network, extending it from 3,200km to more than 3,500km. “Together, these investments are strengthening the infrastructure needed to move additional gas from Adnoc Gas's processing facilities to existing and future customers,” the company said on Wednesday. Adnoc Gas caters to 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs, and supplies to customers in more than 20 countries. The demand for gas is growing globally as economies look to cut emissions to limit global warming. Burning natural gas produces lower emissions compared to crude and coal. Development of new data centres for AI is also boosting demand. Shell's LNG Outlook 2026, released in June, projected global demand would reach nearly 700 million tonnes a year by 2050. This is an increase of about 65 per cent from 2025 levels, with about 180 million tonnes of new annual supply expected to enter the market by 2030. “Gas is going to continue to grow and demand is going to continue in the long term,” Ms Al Nuaimi told delegates at Adipec on Tuesday. This week, Adnoc Gas also announced the signing of a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG to France's TotalEnergies. Adnoc is also scaling up a new global LNG trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the commercial capabilities of Adnoc Trading .

events.title: 'Thick, orange water' safe to drink, woman told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasWater's aging pipes in question as 'thick, orange' water seen in Hobart homes Sandy Bay resident Emma Thornley says she was initially told by TasWater that the water was safe to drink. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) Residents in the Hobart suburb of Sandy Bay say thick, orange water spurted from their taps on Tuesday after a water main burst. One resident says TasWater told her the "thick and viscous" liquid was fine to drink. TasWater says it is investing in infrastructure upgrades. When Hobart resident Emma Thornley put a load of whites in her washing machine on Tuesday morning, she was not expecting it to come out covered in dark-orange stains. "I ran to my kitchen tap, and [the water] was very dark browny-orange," she said. Ms Thornley let the water run for a while, which cleared it, but a few hours later she filled up the kettle straight under the tap. "I didn't watch the water going into it, which in hindsight was a bit silly, and then realised that the water in my cup of tea was really gritty and had a really foul taste," she said. It persisted on and off throughout the day. An sms sent by TasWater advising residents of Sandy Bay and South Hobart of the possibility of discoloured water being discharged from taps. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) The culprit was a 60-year-old burst water main on Regent Street, Sandy Bay, near Ms Thornley's house. Water issues are not uncommon in her Hobart suburb. "I think I've had about eight text messages [from utility TasWater] to alert me that the water quality would be affected or it might be cloudy or discoloured while they were doing work, but we usually get those texts in advance or ASAP when there's an issue," she said. Ms Thornley tried to report Tuesday's issue over the phone but was told the water was fine to drink. She took a bottle of the orange liquid to show the TasWater crew on her street, who advised her not to drink it. A Sandy Bay resident captured some of the murky water in a jar. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) "I don't want to drink it and I'm pretty sure they wouldn't either." Pensioner fears delays for urgent medical scope as waitlist grows ASIC fines Mona owner David Walsh's company for late financial report Topic: Business, Economics and Finance NSW man in court over alleged ice seizure at Tasmanian beach car park Glen Christensen also had issues with his water on Tuesday, despite living about 2 kilometres from the emergency works. He said he was trying to run a bath for his two-year-old granddaughter, but the water that came out was dirty with sediment. "The first time I called [TasWater], I was told to run the tap closest to the meter, which is my outdoor tap," Mr Christensen said. The Sandy Bay resident took to social media about the TasWater response to her concerns. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) He followed the advice, but it did not help. "We ended up resorting to a shower, at least that way she wouldn't be sitting in it, and whilst the shower was running there was a significant drop in water pressure, after that the water came clear," he said. Another resident commenting on social media also reported bath water running "brownish" in the evening. TasWater said its crews responded to the burst water main at about 9.45am and had restored supply to the majority of affected properties by 11.30am, with all properties restored by 5.30pm. Australia's national drinking water guidelines state that water should be aesthetically pleasing and pleasant to drink. "Many customers equate aesthetics with the safety of drinking water, so every effort should be made to meet the aesthetic guideline values," it states. TasWater's head of communications and engagement, Liz Hafner, said it was not uncommon for sediment to settle in pipes after an outage, and that crews routinely flush pipes once water has been restored to clear it. Water pipe leaked for nine months next to Barbara's home It took nine months to identify a damaged pipe belonging to state water utility TasWater as the cause of a leak damaging Barbara Turner's Launceston home. Two years later, she can't get rid of the mould. "Our initial advice provided to the customer was that the water was safe to drink [which] reflected the information available at the time," she said. "Once we became aware from the customer of the level of discolouration, we updated our advice and carried out further flushing." Some affected customers received text messages from TasWater, and the utility said it provided live updates on its website throughout the service interruption.

events.summary: Cadillac are jointly owned by Mark Walter Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group , has held talks about buying a majority stake in the Cadillac Formula One team for more than £2bn as Mark Walter continues to sell off his sporting assets amid allegations of insurance fraud. Cadillac entered F1 this year as a joint venture between General Motors and Walter’s TWG Global, which sold its controlling interest in the NBA’s Los Angeles Lakers and a 13% stake in Chelsea this summer, and is also looking to sell Los Angeles Sparks, the WNBA team. Walter is under investigation by the US Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission over alleged fraud involving the management of funds at his insurance companies Delaware Life, Clear Spring, and EquiTrust. TWG has said “there has been no fraud”. How do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts? In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. The 66-year-old Walter is also the controlling owner of Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Dodgers and insists they will not be sold. A move by FSG to buy into Cadillac could have implications for its position at Liverpool , which is valued at £5.5bn after this summer’s partial sale, presenting it with the opportunity to make a huge profit after it paid £300m for the entire club in 2010. FSG has a history of investing in motor sport through its 50% stake in the Nascar team RFK Racing, with the source adding that it has been attracted to F1 by the sport’s remarkable growth over the last decade, particularly in the US. F1’s annual revenue has more than doubled to $4bn (£3bn) since it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017, and the value of its TV rights continues to increase. events.title: How Texas went Democratic
events.summary: Texas woke up red on Tuesday and went to bed blue. Why it matters: Just months ago, Democratic campaigns in the MAGA heartland appeared quixotic — obligatory more than realistic. Now those Democratic candidates have swept to power, led by two state representatives from liberal Austin — James Talarico , soon to be seated in the U.S. Senate, and Gina Hinojosa , who will take her place in the new year in the governor's mansion. Zoom in: The Democratic victories were comprehensive. State Rep. Vikki Goodwin (D-Austin) unseated three-term Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, per the Associated Press. Democrat Nathan Johnson, a state senator from Dallas, defeated Republican Mayes Middleton, state senator from Galveston, in the race for attorney general. What they're saying: "We shocked the world tonight. With a Texas chip on our shoulder, we showed the world that anything is possible tonight," Hinojosa said. "We just took back Texas," Talarico told his supporters. What happened: An unpopular president and high gas and grocery prices deep-sixed red-state GOP candidates across the country. But the Texas GOP was further hampered by an unpopular U.S. Senate candidate (even members of his own party impeached him) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. And Greg Abbott, who had served as governor since 2015, was unwilling to debate his gubernatorial opponent. Meanwhile, the Democrats were disciplined, with Talarico and Hinojosa staying on message about affordability even as their Republican opponents tried to make the race about social issues. Amid a crush of cameras and security personnel, Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico toast at an Austin Whataburger after their victories Tuesday night. Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images Follow the money: Republicans went down despite a rescue mission from Elon Musk, who gave north of $150 million in support of Paxton's campaign in a single quarter this year — and gave at least $5.5 million to Abbott's campaign this cycle. The big picture: The Democratic wins have huge implications for the 2028 presidential race. Democrats have proven, after years of flailing, that they could win statewide in Texas, potentially putting the Lone Star State and its 40 electoral votes in play. Political pundits will be wondering: Was this a one-off wave amid a terrible midterm climate for Texas Republicans — or a sign of foundational change? The bottom line: Fireworks were shooting off in Austin Tuesday night, and state agencies so long occupied by the GOP will now be run by Democrats, opening the way for wide policy changes in long-conservative Texas.

events.title: Crypto dips on Democrat midterm wins, Binance hacks dent optimism
events.summary: Sentiment has also been hurt by the US$6 billion hack of the Binance platform last week, the largest heist in history. Crypto prices fell after Democrats won both US midterm chambers, raising fears of slower deregulation and weaker support for industry-friendly laws. Bitcoin briefly hit a six-week low, while the wider market lost about US$300 billion in October and bitcoin is down around 41% from its October 2025 peak. A US$6 billion Binance hack and heavy customer withdrawals hurt trust, as experts warned of security risks and pressure on future crypto legislation. LONDON/HONG KONG – Cryptocurrencies briefly dipped on Nov 4 as Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and House in the US midterm elections, a potential blow to an industry that has pushed for faster deregulation for digital assets. The sector has spent more than US$300 million (S$383 million) backing crypto-friendly Democrats and Republicans in roughly equal measure during the current and previous election cycles, hoping to pass legislation US crypto companies say will put them on a solid legal footing and allow them to thrive. Bitcoin briefly touched a six-week low before recovering to trade roughly flat by 07.15 GMT (3.15pm Singapore time) at US$78,070. Ether traded at US$2,292, up just 1%. Bitcoin has fallen by around 41% since hitting record highs above US$122,000 in October 2025, bringing the value of the broader crypto market to around US$2.61 billion, according to CoinMarketCap. The market has lost some US$300 billion in value in October alone, as deepening concern about future returns from AI and the strain of rising borrowing costs pushed investors into less risky assets such as government bonds and safe-haven currencies. Sentiment has also been hurt by the US$6 billion hack of the Binance platform last week , the largest heist in history. On Nov 3 , Binance customers had withdrawn a net US$4.72 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened following the hack at the weekend. “The market may be re-evaluating the risk-reward profile of crypto assets. On one hand, the string of security incidents is forcing investors to re-examine the industry’s security infrastructure and custody risks,” Tim Sun, Senior Researcher at HashKey, said. “On the other hand, potential shifts in the US political landscape could stall the progress of structural crypto legislation and institutional framework development. All of these factors leave the crypto market facing strong headwinds,” he said. Trump, who vowed to make the United States the “crypto capital of the world” during his 2024 presidential campaign, has made his own forays into digital assets, with the launch of his “Trump” meme coin, plus his family’s World Liberty Financial crypto platform, among other ventures. The sector has seen sweeping reforms in the almost two years since Trump returned to office, including lighter enforcement, the creation of a strategic bitcoin reserve. Washington has also allowed for easier access to banking and exchange-traded products and passed a federal stablecoin law that could help these assets move into the mainstream payments and money transfer systems. REUTERS

events.title: US midterms: What investors can expect after Democrats shatter Republican strongholds
events.summary: The US Democratic Party picked up 53 Senate seats and 222 seats in the House of Representatives as at 3pm on Nov 4, Singapore time. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a major rebuke to President Donald Trump. They took 53 Senate seats and 222 House seats. Markets expect more policy gridlock, less chance of big tax or spending changes, and possible tariff fights. US futures fell, while Asian shares recovered after the result. Investors will watch Treasury yields, the Fed, the US dollar, oil and gold. DBS said Singapore Reits, developers and aviation stocks may gain from the Democratic win. SINGAPORE – The US Democratic Party took control of both houses of Congress in a dramatic win in the US midterm elections. Seen as a rebuke of President Donald Trump’s policies, a sea of blue has picked up 54 Senate seats and 220 seats in the House of Representatives as at 9pm on Nov 4, Singapore time. Voters sent a strong message about their unhappiness with the state of the US economy, the Iran war and inflation to kick Republicans out of even traditional “red” strongholds. The elections, held on Nov 3 , determine control of all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate, midway through Trump’s four-year presidential term. Its implications will be felt far beyond the US’ borders as it raises the prospect of opposing forces between the White House and Congress. What does this mean for global markets? Equities: The Democratic sweep could make it harder for Trump to push through major legislative changes, potentially limiting further fiscal stimulus. Analysts at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, said Trump would likely face significant legislative resistance and policy gridlock, although he could continue pursuing policies through executive orders. BMI also warned that a sharp slowdown in data centre construction and artificial intelligence investment could lead to a greater-than-expected decline in overall investment, weighing on the US economy. US equity futures fell as Democrats gained ground, with S&P 500 equity futures down about 1% at the time of BMI’s commentary. Technology stocks also faced pressure amid concerns over AI valuations and the prospect of tighter regulatory scrutiny. Congressional aides said that while a rollback of tariffs is expected, Trump will remain undeterred in his zeal for more tariff actions. In Asia, stocks started on Nov 4 down but retraced decisively after news of the Democrats’ win. Singapore’s Straits Times Index lost 76 points in the morning, but was down just 0.66 point at 5,268.63 at the close. Interest rates and bonds: The election outcome could influence US Treasury yields through expectations for fiscal spending, government borrowing and inflation. Greater constraints on government spending could ease concerns over additional borrowing, although political disputes over fiscal policy may also create uncertainty. BMI flagged the US debt ceiling negotiations in 2027 as a major risk, warning that talks could become contentious at a time when Treasury yields are already elevated and fiscal risks are mounting. DBS Group Research strategist Philip Wee noted on Nov 2 that the midterms, falling oil prices and the US employment report on Nov 6 could prompt investors to reassess the Federal Reserve’s tightening outlook. The market-implied probability of a December rate hike had fallen to 73.5% from a peak of 90.8% on Oct 19, he said. Currencies: The US dollar weakened as investors assessed the implications for fiscal spending and monetary policy. Wee noted that the week’s developments could extend the dollar index’s retracement from its mid-October peak. For Singapore investors holding US dollar-denominated assets, movements in the greenback against the Singapore dollar could affect investment returns when converted into local currency. C ommodities: Oil and gold prices are also worth watching, particularly against the backdrop of the Middle East conflict. Gold fell 0.5% to US$3,925.25 an ounce in New York trading on Nov 3 , as investors weighed the prospects of a diplomatic resolution to the conflict. The precious metal had already slumped nearly 7% in October, falling below US$4,000 an ounce. Lower oil prices have eased inflation concerns, although rising bond yields have weighed on gold, which does not pay interest. The midterm results could increase policy uncertainty, although this may not necessarily translate into higher gold prices. What does this mean for Singapore stocks? DBS Group Research believes that November presents an opportunity for investors to buy on market weakness, with Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITS), property developers and aviation-related companies among the potential beneficiaries of a Democratic win.

events.title: AMC’s A-List members now make up 20% of its U.S. attendance. Its $4 billion debt is the harder test
events.summary: Fletcher Williams saw six movies at AMC theaters last month. At full price, that would have run about $150. He paid $29.99. Williams, 25, is one of more than 1.1 million members of AMC Stubs A-List, the subscription tier that lets moviegoers reserve up to four films a week, including IMAX and Dolby Cinema, for a monthly fee of roughly $24 to $30 depending on the state. As audiences return to theaters in 2026, AMC Entertainment is counting on the program to turn occasional ticket buyers into regulars. The open question is whether that loyalty can do what a run of hit movies has not yet done: make AMC consistently profitable while it carries roughly $4 billion in debt. A record quarter after a long way back The rebound is real. AMC reported $1.60 billion in revenue for the second quarter of 2026, up 14.2% from a year earlier and the highest quarterly total in its 106-year history . Worldwide attendance rose 13.5% to 71.3 million. Admissions brought in $863.1 million, up 13.2%. Food and beverage sales rose 15.3% to $576.1 million. The industry helped: the $2.99 billion domestic box office was the strongest second quarter in seven years, with six films opening above $75 million. The hole was deep. AMC’s revenue fell 77% in 2020 , from $5.47 billion to $1.24 billion, as the pandemic shut theaters. As recently as early 2025, chairman and CEO Adam Aron said the industry’s January-to-March domestic box office was its weakest since 1996 , setting aside quarters hit by COVID. Records have not yet meant profits. AMC posted an $11.4 million net loss in the second quarter as interest and other charges absorbed much of the gain. For 2025, it lost $632 million on $4.85 billion in revenue, according to Fortune ’s company data . Why a flat fee changes the math For frequent moviegoers, the arithmetic is simple. A standard adult ticket at AMC typically runs $13 to $15 before premium formats like IMAX or 3D, so a movie a week can top $65 a month in tickets alone. Williams first signed up in college, when he lived 15 minutes from an AMC. For the number of films he sees, he said, “The membership basically pays for itself.” “$25 to $30 is roughly the equivalent of a single ticket for a new movie where I live. Paying that once a month for the ability to see up to 4 movies a week is incredibly worth it,” said Williams, who now lives in Los Angeles. Members could see as many as 17 films a month, but the typical member sees two or three, according to AMC . Even at that pace, most come out roughly even or ahead. “I used to watch them casually, but after getting into film in 2024, I decided to enroll. I usually see at least 2 movies a month, and since the membership pays for itself if you do that, I’ve stayed subscribed,” said Autumn Miller, 28, of New York City. She saw five movies last month. AMC launched A-List in 2018 , when  Fortune  tracked it as AMC’s answer to MoviePass . Membership has more than doubled over the past five years, and A-List members now account for about 20% of AMC’s U.S. attendance , Aron told analysts in July. “We’ve seen significant membership growth in recent years, as movies have returned in much greater numbers to theatres, and at the end of the second quarter of 2026, A-List had grown to more than 1.1 million members,” AMC spokesperson Ryan Noonan wrote in an email. “A-Listers remain among our most engaged moviegoers, regularly seeing a broad range of films at AMC. We think the continued growth of A-List speaks volumes about how much our members enjoy the program and the value they see in it.” Loyalty that shows up beyond the ticket For some members, the subscription has changed how they spend on entertainment, not just how often they go out. “I think it’s changed how I approach entertainment more than anything. Instead of treating a movie as an occasional expense, I can make it a regular activity, and I’m more inclined to spend my entertainment budget on experiences I genuinely enjoy. I still have streaming services at home, but going to the theater offers something different that I can’t fully replicate on my couch,” said Noah Osborne, 28, of Phoenix. “I’d say I probably spend a bit less on streaming services since I’m able to watch the movie in the theater. A-Listers also have great deals on concessions, so I’m able to save some money there too,” said Sophie Guaman, 28, of [New York City / New York state]. That concession spending matters to AMC, which earns heavily on food and drinks. Food and beverage revenue per patron hit records in both its U.S. and international businesses in the second quarter. Members also do some of AMC’s marketing. On TikTok, subscribers post under #amctheatres, showing off their trips through the A-List priority line near the concession counter. “The enthusiasm our members continue to show for the program has exceeded our expectations, especially in the way they talk about A-List, both online and with their family and friends,” Noonan wrote. The debt test for A-List In October, AMC completed a $3.97 billion refinancing that pushed almost all of its debt maturities to 2031 and 2033 and, the company said, lowered its cost of capital. The deal buys time. It does not shrink the roughly $4 billion AMC owes. That is the real test for A-List. A program that brings in a fifth of U.S. attendance can keep seats filled between blockbusters. Whether it can generate enough steady cash to help pay down debt is a different question. The next read comes with AMC’s third-quarter report, covering July through September: whether attendance held after a record spring, and whether a bigger, more loyal audience starts to show up on the bottom line. events.title: Beyond The Chip: How AI Is Reshaping Semiconductor Design And Manufacturing
events.summary: While AI is transforming nearly every industry, one of its most significant impacts is happening behind the scenes, inside the semiconductor factories responsible for building the chips that power today’s AI revolution. During a recent presentation at the Global Semiconductor Alliance (GSA) European Executive Forum, I discussed how the conversation around AI scale is evolving. For years, the semiconductor industry focused primarily on transistor scaling. Today, however, the biggest challenges facing AI designers extend far beyond the transistor. Power delivery, connectivity, advanced packaging, and supply chain resilience are emerging as the primary constraints on AI scaling. At Intel Foundry, we’re addressing these challenges on two fronts. First, we’re developing advanced process and packaging technologies that help customers build increasingly capable AI systems. Second, we’re using AI and machine learning (ML) throughout our technology development and manufacturing operations to improve quality, accelerate yield learning, and help customers bring products to market faster. Three forces shaping the future of semiconductor design Three major AI trends are shaping what modern silicon must deliver: Agentic AI introduces multistep reasoning workloads that are far less predictable than traditional computing. Autonomous agents place new demands on power delivery and high-performance connectivity, making efficient scaling increasingly important. Physical AI brings intelligence to edge devices and real-world systems. Scalable AI-enabled automation and modeling are essential for cost-effective, high-yield manufacturing. The foundry industry increasingly views both agentic AI and physical AI as significant long-term growth drivers. Sovereign AI initiatives are increasing demand for secure, resilient, and geographically diverse manufacturing and supply chains to support both business continuity and national security needs. By maintaining Intel Foundry’s production capabilities across North America, Europe, and Asia, customers gain flexibility in determining where their products are manufactured while improving supply chain resilience and security. Multi-dimensional scaling: The new path forward A decade ago, the semiconductor industry largely focused on the system-on-chip (SoC) model, where a single chip integrated as much functionality as possible. Today, innovation has shifted toward a system of chips, using chiplet architectures that combine multiple specialized dies, memory stacks, and accelerators into a single solution. This approach provides greater modularity, scalability, and faster innovation cycles while enabling the performance required for advanced AI workloads. At the same time, scaling is no longer simply a matter of shrinking transistors. The industry is increasingly focused on optimizing performance across the entire system, from compute and memory to packaging and interconnects. Advanced process technologies such as gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, including Intel 18A with RibbonFET GAA technology, provide improved electrostatic control and support scaling beyond traditional FinFET architectures. Power delivery also has been reimagined. Intel 18A uses PowerVia, our backside power delivery technology that routes power through the back of the wafer rather than sharing frontside interconnect layers with signal routing. By separating power and signal paths, PowerVia reduces resistance, voltage drop, and power delivery noise. Combined with high-density metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors, the architecture improves power integrity. PowerVia delivers up to a 10% increase in cell utilization¹ and a 4% improvement in ISO-power performance.² Connection to the transistor layer is enabled through innovative nano through-silicon vias (TSVs) that are approximately 500 times smaller than conventional TSVs. While backside power adds manufacturing complexity, Intel Foundry optimized the overall cost structure by maintaining 32 nm lower-metal pitches on the frontside, enabling direct-print patterning rather than more expensive multi-patterning approaches. This balanced architecture allows Intel 18A and Intel 18A-P to deliver improved performance-per-watt and more efficient power delivery for AI-era workloads while remaining cost competitive. Intel 18A with PowerVia can provide approximately 18% performance-per-watt improvement versus Intel 3.³ Now in risk production, Intel 18A-P is expected to deliver an additional 9% performance-per-watt improvement over Intel 18A⁴ (see the Intel 18A family technical brief for details). As systems become increasingly modular, chips must communicate efficiently with one another. This is where Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) plays a critical role. UCIe provides a standardized interconnect for high-bandwidth, low-latency communication between chiplets, simplifying integration and enabling more scalable heterogeneous systems. Advanced packaging serves as the glue that connects all these technologies together. A complete AI package may combine I/O dies, advanced logic silicon, HBM, 2.5D integration, and 3D integration. Intel Foundry supports these designs through technologies including Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T), Foveros, and Foveros Direct. EMIB-T incorporates power-transfer capabilities directly into the bridge structure, helping improve power delivery efficiency and reduce inductive power droop in multi-die AI systems. It can also reduce package material requirements by eliminating the need for a full silicon interposer in many applications. Foveros Direct uses hybrid bonding to enable 3D integration, allowing designers to stack leading-edge compute dies on optimized base dies. This approach helps customers balance performance, power efficiency, and total cost of ownership (TCO) by placing each function on the process technology best suited to its requirements. Using AI across the semiconductor manufacturing lifecycle While AI is creating new challenges for chip designers, it is also helping solve many of the challenges associated with manufacturing advanced semiconductors. At Intel Foundry, AI and ML are already deeply integrated into our manufacturing workflows, actively supporting how we develop and manufacture leading-edge process technologies (see Figure 1). One area where AI is delivering value is design technology co-optimization (DTCO). Advanced process nodes involve enormous design spaces with countless tradeoffs between power, performance, and area (PPA). AI helps engineers explore these possibilities more efficiently and identify optimal solutions. Fig. 1: Intel Foundry’s deployment of AI and ML efforts across the manufacturing flow. AI’s role extends beyond product design and into every stage of the manufacturing lifecycle, transforming how we identify and correct manufacturing issues. events.title: Choosing The Right Power Transistor: Why Application Fit Matters More Than Technology
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage. Selecting a power transistor has become less about identifying a universally superior technology and more about matching device behavior to the demands of the application. Silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs each offer meaningful advantages, but those advantages do not carry the same value across every converter, motor drive, or power stage. The decisive factors are the electrical and thermal realities of the design: bus voltage, current profile, switching frequency, allowable temperature rise, control strategy, commutation behavior, PCB parasitics, and system cost targets. The discussion begins with the switching and conduction mechanisms that shape the behavior of every power transistor, including crossover loss, inductive switching, parasitic capacitance, reverse conduction and charge-recovery behavior, and the practical distinction between hard-switched and soft-switched operation. These operating modes create different selection priorities: hard-switched stages are often strongly influenced by turn-on loss and commutation behavior, while soft-switched stages depend on the charge to be commutated, the available current, and the ability to maintain soft switching across the operating range. On that basis, it compares silicon MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC MOSFETs, and GaN HEMTs in terms that matter to designers working on real hardware: voltage range, current capability, switching performance, gate-drive implications, thermal behavior, and implementation sensitivity. The discussion then moves into application context, including PFC, resonant conversion, synchronous rectification, and motor-drive design decisions, where lower device loss alone does not guarantee the best overall result. Thermal margins, board design, control choices, and total system cost all influence whether a given device technology improves the converter in a meaningful way. The application examples also show when direct transistor substitution can address the dominant limitation and when a topology change or hybrid implementation offers a more effective path. The role of simulation is also considered, showing where modeling is useful for relative comparison and where hardware validation remains essential before a design decision is finalized. The result is a practical framework for choosing among silicon, IGBT, SiC, and GaN technologies based on application fit rather than technology fashion, enabling power-electronics designers to select the device, and where appropriate the topology, that best aligns with the converter’s actual operating conditions and design priorities. events.title: Blog Review: Nov. 4
events.summary: Cadence’s Mick Posner introduces a physical AI sub-project workstream to extend the OCP’s Foundation Chiplet System Architecture’s data center, cloud, and server-centric baseline with the specification requirements to satisfy real-time, safety-critical physical systems, while retaining everything FCSA already defines. Synopsys’ Charlie Matar considers how design focus is shifting from the server to the rack , with silicon behavior shaping rack-level power and cooling requirements, while rack constraints influence decisions inside chips and packages. Siemens’ Harry Foster warns that while verification complexity has been managed by dividing large problems into smaller pieces, new challenges are emerging as the number and diversity of interactions influencing correct SoC behavior grows. Arm’s Zenon (Zhilong) Xiu examines how quarter-tile and structured sparsity outer product instructions make the SME2 programming model better suited to small, dense, quantized, and sparse matrix workloads in modern AI software. Keysight’s Linas Dauksa digs into AI data center infrastructure, including key components, energy demands and power density challenges, the array of liquid cooling technologies available, and what differentiates hyperscale facilities. SEMI’s Sungho Yoon considers factors related to a forecasted increase in wafer shipments , including rising process material sales and a high number of new and upcoming production lines. Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Systems & Design newsletter : Technology editor Brian Bailey poses the age-old question for anyone involved in the verification of semiconductor systems: in the age of AI, who verifies the verifier ? Axiomise’s Vidya Chandran Darbari and Ashish Darbari dig into what biological reasoning can teach us about verifying silicon systems. Keysight’s Chris Mueth explains why applying the appropriate level of simulation and abstraction at each stage of the design process is needed for effective thermal analysis. Siemens EDA’s Emma-Jane Crozier explores how self-verifying agents validate their decisions and why physics-based engines are the authority on correctness. Arteris’ Leon Brown looks at which products may fall within the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s scope and what information may need to be provided to customers. Movellus’ Aakash Jani and Siemens’ Henrique Mendes and Robert Wilcox separate false failures caused by voltage droop from real structural defects. ChipAgents’ Zackary Glazewski demonstrates how to deal with difficult bugs while intelligently deciding what to investigate, what to rerun, and where to spend compute. Vinci’s Hardik Kabaria examines why physics-based analysis becomes more consequential as chips, packages, boards, and systems are designed together. Cadence’s Reela Samuel breaks down how to orchestrate multi-step engineering workflows to reduce repetitive effort and explore more design options. Synopsys’ Anand Thiruvengadam outlines how autonomous engineering agents pursue an objective requiring hundreds or thousands of reasoning steps while maintaining context, evaluating results, and adapting along the way. The post Blog Review: Nov. 4 appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .
