events.title: Neural Super Resolution
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices. As AI becomes an increasingly important part of the graphics pipeline, Neural Super Resolution (NSR) offers a new approach to generating higher-quality images without the cost of rendering every pixel natively. This white paper explores how Imagination’s NSR technology uses neural reconstruction to upscale lower-resolution frames into higher-resolution outputs, combining current-frame data, temporal history and learned inference to deliver high visual quality with reduced bandwidth, power and memory demands. Unlike approaches that rely on separate AI accelerators, NSR runs directly within the GPU, enabling graphics, compute and AI workloads to work together in a unified execution environment. Readers will learn the principles behind neural super resolution, the role of Converged Acceleration in modern GPU design, and how Imagination’s E-Series architecture integrates matrix acceleration and neural processing into the graphics pipeline. The paper also explains the importance of data locality, microtiling and Self-Compression in achieving efficient neural rendering, while examining the performance, bandwidth and energy benefits of GPU-native super resolution. For graphics architects, developers and SoC designers, it provides insight into how neural graphics can improve image quality and performance while simplifying deployment on power- and bandwidth-constrained devices. Fig.1: Projected Doom Eternal performance and bandwidth improvements using NSR. Projected estimates for Doom Eternal compare native 4K rendering with 1080p rendering reconstructed to 4K using NSR on an EXD-64-2048 MC1 GPU modelled at 1 GHz. These figures should be treated as workload- and configuration-specific projections. Source: Imagination. events.title: Democrats ride inflation wave back into power in Congress
events.summary: James Carville's mantra rings in my ears every election cycle: "It's the economy , stupid." The famed political strategist coined the phrase in 1992 but it's still relevant now, with the Democrats on track to retake both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, gaining powerful oversight roles over Donald Trump 's presidency. The result will probably have a profound impact on the data centre buildout and other sectors. As results trickled in late into the night in Washington - and during the morning rush hour in Abu Dhabi - it became clear that this week's vote was a referendum on Mr Trump's performance as well as Americans' pocketbooks. Early results from NBC News's exit poll showed nearly half of voters saw the midterms as a rebuke of the US President, with the economy again being a key frustration. Mr Trump made sweeping promises during the 2024 election, when Americans chose to send him back to the Oval Office. Those promises included slashing energy costs, reining in price pressures and a pledge to “make America affordable again”. By most metrics, the economy is on solid footing. US manufacturing activity picked up in October despite uncertainty over policies from the Beltway and rising prices from the Iran war. Layoffs fell to their lowest level in 18 months, while job openings surged. The nation's GDP accelerated at a 3.4 per cent clip in the third quarter. Consumer spending is resilient. The unemployment rate continues to hover around a historically low 4 per cent. However, Mr Trump ran into the same problem that drove Democrats out of power in 2024 : inflation. For Joe Biden, it was a post-Covid inflationary surge exacerbated by a round of stimulus cheques that drove headline inflation to 9.1 per cent in 2022. The portrayal stuck with Kamala Harris, the Democratic party's nominee for president after Mr Biden unexpectedly dropped out of the race. For Mr Trump, it is the war in Iran , and the greatest oil shock in history, that has driven up energy prices amid an AI buildout. Headline inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent annual pace in September, compared to the 3 per cent rate in January 2025. The Federal Reserve has reversed its rate-cutting cycle and raised interest rates by a quarter point in August. It could do so again in December. Yields on the 10 and 30-year Treasuries recently climbed to their highest levels since before the 2008 global financial crisis. And while the share of voters who said inflation had weighed on them is similar to 2024 levels, roughly two-thirds of voters said the President had made the economy worse. Separate exit polls from NBC said 44 per cent of voters said their financial situation was worse than two years ago, compared to 18 per cent who said it was better. About 38 per cent said it is “about the same”. Seventy-five per cent of voters said they were either “dissatisfied” or “angry” about the country today, compared to 18 per cent who said they were “satisfied” and 7 per cent who said they were “enthusiastic”. Recent moves by the President suggest he understands he needed to regain control of prices, chief among them a disputed deal that allows the sale of Russian diesel to US and global markets. Mr Trump made a final appeal to voters on Tuesday, telling Fox and Friends that “inflation was solved”. Despite the millions of dollars spent on campaign finance this season, no messaging was stronger than the sticker shock consumers faced while filling up their cars and grocery carts. Traders on Wall Street took notice, too. Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were all in the red, while investors rushed into bonds for safety. The dollar extended its losses. Mr Trump spent his first two years in office touting deregulation, the data centre roll-out and a range of business-friendly policies. Now comes the reckoning.

events.title: GOP's redistricting firewall pummeled by blue wave
events.summary: Republicans tried to save their House majority with a bold wave of mid-cycle redistricting. It failed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday. Why it matters: Republicans not only fell short of winning seats in several districts they redrew to favor their candidates, they put some GOP incumbents in danger of losing by spreading their support thin. Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.), who has mostly won landslide reelections since entering Congress in 2010, trailed his Democratic opponent by 200 votes, according to the Tennessee secretary of state's unofficial final results . Republican state legislators carved up his district in an effort to shore up neighboring Republicans, making his district nearly 20 percentage points less GOP-leaning. State of play: While Republicans succeeded in picking up a Democratic district in Tennessee to make up for that loss, they largely failed to pick up the seats they tried to make reliably Republican in other states. Florida: Republicans are set to go 0-for-4 in redistricted seats, failing to unseat Democratic Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz, or capture a new seat that Democrat Pia Dandiya won. Texas: Republicans are set to narrowly win just one of the five districts they redrew heavily in their favor, with Democrats easily hanging onto several Rio Grande Valley and San Antonio-area seats. Ohio: Democratic Reps. Greg Landsman and Marcy Kaptur held on despite Republicans drawing them into more hostile territory. Alabama: Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures is also set for a comfortable win in a district Republicans had planned to fall into their hands. Louisiana: The district of retiring Democrat Rep. Cleo Fields, which Republicans made significantly more GOP-leaning will go to a December runoff between Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment. One of the most stunning results of the night was Democrats' multiple apparent victories in North Carolina, where House candidates were boosted by Sen-elect Roy Cooper's strong performance at the top of the ballot. Democrats are on track to flip several seats that were rated as likely or even solidly Republican by Cook Political Report, likely unseating Republican Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore. They are also likely to unseat Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, is behind by about 100 votes. In all, the state's House delegation could go from a 10-4 Republican majority to a 9-5 Democratic one. Between the lines: The North Carolina result is the product of a brutal 2024 gerrymander in which GOP state legislators diluted most solidly Republican districts to draw out several House Democrats. They redistricted again last year, only to put Democratic Rep. Don Davis in more hostile territory. GOP Rep. Greg Murphy — whose district was packed with more Democratic voters to make Davis' seat redder — barely hung on Tuesday night. Former Democratic Rep. Kathy Manning, who was one of the Democrats drawn out in 2024, told Axios that Tuesday's result was "absolutely" a result of GOP redistricting backfiring. The bottom line: Republicans "tried to break the laws and go against these norms in your massive authoritarian power grab," DNC vice chair Shasti Conrad told Axios. "How did that turn out?"

events.title: WIPEOUT: GOP LOSES HOUSE AND SENATE
events.summary: Republicans lost deep-red Senate seats in South Carolina , Kansas and Texas as well as House seats nationwide, AP projects, giving Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. Why it matters: President Trump made himself the face of the GOP campaign for control. Now his party is losing all over the map, and he's distancing himself from the outcome. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Former President Obama wrote on X: "Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face." Zoom in : Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won election to U.S. Senate from Michigan, AP projects, adding to the Democrats' already rushing blue wave. In Texas, James Talarico secured a history U.S. Senate seat, defeating Trump-backed Republican opponent, Ken Paxton. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott conceded to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the Texas governor race. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton flipped the country's longest-held Republican Senate seat, ending a 94-year drought. In Maine, Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson in the Senate race. In Minnesota , Democrat Peggy Flanagan won election to U.S. Senate, AP projects. In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham will lose reelection to Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, AP projects. In Iowa, Democratic nominee Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson to flip the Senate seat vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, AP projects. Data: AP; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Zoom out: Former Gov. Sherrod Brown (D) defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio, AP projects. Earlier in the night, Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Trump's handpicked candidate, Michael Whatley in North Carolina while Democrat Jon Ossoff won reelection to U.S. Senate in Georgia, AP projects. In North Carolina's 11th House district, Jamie Ager flipped the seat for Democrats. The seat is held by retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards , who ended his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be censured. Between the lines: The results tonight were a clear national test of Trump's second presidency , following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington. "I am absolutely willing to accept those results," Trump said in an interview with The New York Times. "We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out." Yes, but: Trump wrote on Truth Social he plans to criticize the candidates that lost. He also posted an image of a red hat with the word, "VETO." Earlier in the night, Trump raged on social media about the results. He made Fox News the subject of his ire by critiquing Fox's political polling , calling it "a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" He also texted on-air guests to rage against Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist he called "DUMB AS A ROCK." This came hours after he criticized multiple Democrat candidates as voters went to the polls. The intrigue: Tuesday night's results created some historic moments beyond control for Washington and Trump's ire. Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate after besting former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire race. There will be three Black women serving in the U.S. Senate for the first time in history after Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton won the Senate race in Illinois. She will join Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who became the first two Black women to serve simultaneously in 2025. What we're hearing: Voters identified the cost of living and government corruption concern as the two top issues in this year's election, according to exit polls from AP . Cost of living skyrocketed thanks to the Iran war and the president's tariff policies. Trump himself was deemed corrupt and dangerous in a poll of registered voters prior to the election. The bottom line: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress will open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock.

events.title: El-Sayed becomes first Muslim U.S. senator
events.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race, the Associated Press projected. He will become the nation's first Muslim senator. Why it matters: El-Sayed's win shows how an unapologetically progressive candidate can win in a battleground state President Trump carried just two years ago. The two candidates competed for the seat vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, with Republicans hoping to flip a seat Democrats have held for decades. But the GOP failed in its endeavor — and already lost its Senate majority. The race took a stunning turn in its final days, when Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers . The move sparked furious backlash from Democrats and prompted several of Stevens' staffers, including her chief of staff, to resign. The big picture: El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, ran on a progressive platform centered on Medicare for All, taxing billionaires and reducing corporate influence in politics. His victory comes after a contentious Democratic primary and a bitter general election campaign that featured personal attacks over his background, medical credentials and Muslim faith. Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who narrowly lost a 2024 Senate bid, sought to portray El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan . El-Sayed cast Rogers as a Washington insider aligned with Trump. Trump himself escalated the attacks in the final stretch of the race, questioning El-Sayed's loyalty to the U.S. and making unsubstantiated allegations of extremist ties. El-Sayed rejected the accusations. Between the lines: El-Sayed's win offers progressives a powerful new argument in the Democratic Party's debate over how to win back voters. Zoom out: Both candidates put affordability at the center of their campaigns but offered sharply different solutions. El-Sayed called for universal health care, tackling medical debt and higher taxes on billionaire wealth. Rogers emphasized tax cuts, expanding domestic manufacturing and more transparent health care prices. He also campaigned on stronger border security and immigration enforcement. What's next: El-Sayed will arrive in Washington with an ambitious progressive agenda — but turning campaign promises into legislation will be a different challenge. His signature Medicare for All proposal faces steep political obstacles, even with Democrats winning control of the Senate. His victory also gives progressives a new national figure as Democrats begin looking toward the 2028 presidential election.

events.title: The 5 biggest shockers of Democrats' stunning night
events.summary: In red states and blue, Republicans suffered losses on a scale even Democrats would never have dared to dream about 24 hours ago. Why it matters: Democrats worried that polls showing a blue wave were overestimating the party's strength. It turned out polls underestimated the size of the Democratic romp — by a lot. The margins Democrats racked up in red states were stunning: Georgia: Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection by nearly 18 percentage points. North Carolina: Former Gov. Roy Cooper won his Senate race by roughly 19 points. Texas: State Rep. James Talarico cruised to victory by approximately 12 points. These weren't nail-biters in competitive states. They were landslides in states President Trump carried just two years ago. 1. The Texas trifecta Democrats won the Texas House, Senate and governor's mansion, giving the party unified control of state government for the first time since 1995. The sweep came alongside Talarico's double-digit victory in the U.S. Senate race. Texas, long the GOP's biggest electoral stronghold, delivered Democrats victories up and down the ballot. 2. North Carolina was a bloodbath The man in charge of steering House Republicans to victory — Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee — lost his own seat. He'll join the ranks of other defeated party leaders — Speaker Tom Foley in 1994 and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 — who spent so much time trying to build a majority that they failed to protect themselves. The carnage extended across the state. North Carolina's congressional delegation could shift from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to five Republicans and nine Democrats. 3. The ridiculously cheap wins Democrats are leading in districts that received little or no outside spending from the DCCC or House Majority PAC, the party's main House super PAC, according to AdImpact. In North Carolina's 6th, 9th and 13th districts, Missouri's 2nd and Tennessee's 4th, Democratic candidates are on track to win despite receiving little financial support from national Democratic groups. North Carolina's 6th: Democrat Cyril Jefferson didn't spend a dime on advertising, according to AdImpact. Tennessee's 4th: Democrat Victoria Broderick spent just $90,000 on her entire campaign as of Oct. 14, according to her FEC filing. AdImpact has no record of any paid TV advertising. 4. Hispanic voters swung back in South Texas Democrats are poised to control three congressional seats in the Rio Grande Valley that President Trump carried in 2024 — and the margins weren't even close. Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) was leading Republican Tano Tijerina, 66% to 30%. Democrat Bobby Pulido was leading Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, 62% to 38%. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) was leading Republican Eric Flores, 56% to 40%. The results were a dramatic reversal in a region where Republicans had made significant gains with Hispanic voters during the Trump era. 5. Democrats won deep in Trump country Democrats didn't just flip swing districts — they broke through in some of the reddest corners of the House map. In Tennessee's 4th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 24 points, Broderick was leading Rep. Scott DesJarlais by roughly 200 votes. Two years ago, Broderick received just 26.8% of the vote to DesJarlais' 70%. The bottom line: The wave didn't discriminate. It washed away good candidates and bad, senators, governors and seasoned Republicans alike.

events.title: Dubai Investments raises $529m from first IPO in UAE this year
events.summary: Dubai Investments has raised Dh1.9 billion ($529 million) from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding, in the UAE’s first initial public offering this year. The company set the final pricing at Dh1.12 per share, settling in the middle of the announced range of Dh1.10 to Dh1.15, DIP Holding said on Wednesday in a statement to the Dubai Financial Market where its shares are traded. Dubai Investments offered 1.74 billion shares in its unit, to investors, which implies a market capitalisation of Dh9.7 billion at listing on the DFM. “The pricing reflects a conscious decision by Dubai Investments to offer new shareholders of DIP Holding an attractive entry point, with a good dividend yield and to support long-term value creation for all shareholders,” the company said in the bourse filing. The Dh1.12 a share price also implies a dividend yield of about 7.5 per cent, based on the expected annualised dividend of Dh725 million for 2027 financial year, the company added. The subscription period for the IPO, which began on October 27, concluded on November 3. The IPO attracted strong demand from local, regional and international investors, “witnessing multiple times coverage across the previously announced price range”, the company said without giving the total size of the order book. The final allocation of shares to individual subscribers, and eligible Dubai Investments employees and shareholders, is expected on November 10. Any refunds are set to commence on the same date, the company said. Shares of DIP Holding are expected to be listed on the DFM on November 11. Breaking the lull The transaction breaks the lull in the UAE IPO market, which had been a hotbed for public floats before disruption caused by the regional conflict, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of listings over the past few years. The IPO market in the broader Middle East slowed last year, amid the volatility in oil prices and geopolitical unrest. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The Iran war , which has severely disrupted economic momentum in region, has further dented investor sentiment, forcing companies to hold plans for tapping the equities markets to raise capital. DIP Holding, which operates the mixed-used master development Dubai Investments Park, said the success of the public offering signals “confidence in the country’s capital markets”. Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to primary 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate.

events.title: Our house purchase is at risk from a frozen Revolut account
events.summary: Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’ My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted. We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records. At one point Revolut also restricted my personal account, so we effectively had no access to any money. We keep being given deadlines for the restrictions to be lifted which are missed, and call centre staff, when we can get through, have little ability to find out what’s happening, or make anything happen. XWF , Oxfordshire Banks have legal powers, under anti-money-laundering regulations, to freeze accounts if a sudden windfall, overseas payment or unusual activity raises concerns. They are not required to warn customers or explain if they suspect foul play, although customers can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe a bank acted unfairly. There’s no suggestion foul play was suspected in your wife’s case and things progressed swiftly after I got involved. Accounts were reinstated, nearly three weeks after being suspended, and your wife was offered £175 as a goodwill gesture. Revolut says regulatory constraints prevented it explaining. “We’re sorry our review process took longer than usual, and our communication didn’t reach its usual standards, particularly given the inconvenience during an important life moment,” it says. events.title: Latinos' rejection of GOP boosts Dems in Texas upsets
events.summary: Latino voters helped Democrats break Republicans' decades-long grip on Texas and reclaim both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, casting doubt on President Trump's historic 2024 gains with the fast-growing electorate. Why it matters: Republicans bet Trump's Latino breakthrough two years ago would create a lasting GOP realignment in Texas and beyond. Tuesday's results exposed how quickly those gains could unravel — and raised new questions about Republicans' coalition heading into 2028. Early results show Hispanic voters' shift aided Democrats in capturing a Senate seat and the governorship in Texas for the first time in a generation. Tuesday's results — particularly in South Texas border counties — reflected some of the anger among Hispanics over high prices and the Trump administration's immigration enforcement. "This is what happens when you mess with the Latino community. We are sending a clear message," said Hector Sanchez Barba, president and CEO of the voting group Mi Familia Vota. By the numbers: Early NBC News exit poll results showed Latino voters moving away from Republicans. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification grew from 10 points in 2024, according to NBC's polling. Some 43% of Latino voters identified as Democrats, up from 39% in 2024. Republican identification slipped from 29% to 27%. In the early NBC exit poll, 75% of voters nationally described the economy as struggling, while 65% said Trump's policies had made economic conditions worse. State of play: Democrats reclaimed the House and Senate while ending Republicans' statewide winning streak in Texas dating to 1994. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton , winning a Senate seat Democrats last captured in 1988. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott , becoming Texas' first elected Latina governor. Early returns also suggested Latino voters helped Democrats win crucial House contests in Colorado and Georgia. Comedian Cristela Alonzo attends an election night watch party for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa at Assembly Hall in Austin, Texas. Photo: Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images What they're saying: "You know how Tim Russert would always say 'Florida, Florida, Florida?' For the last two cycles, I kept saying Texas, Texas, Texas. That's how I feel right now," Voto Latino CEO Maria Teresa Kumar told Axios. Kumar said the Democrats' historic Texas wins changes 2028 and will transform how presidential candidates talk to Latino voters and see Texas as purple. "There was this notion that we're a sleeping giant. Now, we're jumping up and down and waving our fist above the head," Janet Murguía, president and CEO of the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS told Axios. Zoom in: The clearest tests of the Latino shift came in Texas counties that Republicans had celebrated as evidence of their growing strength. Cameron County, which includes Brownsville and South Padre Island: Talarico led by 38 points in early, unofficial returns. Trump won by 6 points there in 2024. Hidalgo County, another majority-Latino border county: Talarico led by 47 points. Trump won it two years ago by 3 points. Webb County, home to Laredo: Talarico led by 49 points; it was Trump +2 in 2024. Context: Trump's 2024 success shattered longstanding assumptions about Latino voters. A Pew Research Center analysis found Trump won 48% of Latino voters in 2024, compared with 36% in 2020. An August Axios-reported poll of 17 competitive House districts foreshadowed the reversal, showing Democrats leading 58%–35% among Latino registered voters. Supporters react during a midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the Long Center in Austin, Texas. Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Image Reality check: A Democratic rebound doesn't mean Latino voters have returned to their old political loyalties. Democrats' 16-point advantage in Latino party identification remains far below their 33-point advantage in 2018, according to NBC. Republicans may have mistaken Trump's appeal for lasting GOP loyalty. Democrats risk confusing a backlash against Trump with renewed allegiance to their party. A September Axios analysis found 62% of Latino registered voters in 17 battleground districts trusted Democrats more to lower prices, compared with 36% who trusted Republicans. Economic frustration gave Democrats an opening without guaranteeing lasting support. The bottom line: Trump's Latino breakthrough reshaped politics in 2024. Two years later, those voters reminded both parties that winning their support once doesn't mean keeping it.

events.title: Bitcoin slides as Democratic sweep bets threaten crypto agenda
events.summary: Democrats, who have traditionally favoured tighter oversight of the crypto industry, had been expected to take control of the House of Representatives, a result that is now projected. Bitcoin fell to a seven-week low as early US election results pointed to a possible Democratic sweep of Congress, raising fears of a tougher crypto agenda and political gridlock. Democrats are projected to control the House and Senate, which could stall industry-backed bills like the Clarity Act and bring more scrutiny for digital-asset firms. Crypto markets are also under pressure from a US$6.3 billion Binance hack, weak retail demand, and heavy ETF outflows, while traders buy more downside protection. WASHINGTON – Bitcoin fell to a seven-week low as the prospect of a Democratic sweep of the US Congress began showing up in early US midterm election results, adding political uncertainty to a market already struggling with fragile investor appetite. The original cryptocurrency slid as much as 2.8% to US$75,630.57 in Asia trading on Nov 4 , its lowest level since Sept 17. It pared some losses to trade around US$76,600 as at 12.20pm in Singapore. The move followed declines in US stock futures and the dollar , while Treasuries gained, reflecting expectations that Democratic control of Congress could lead to gridlock in Washington. “Markets react to change, and a blue flip will likely introduce additional scepticism given the party’s historically choke point stance towards crypto,” said Daniel Reis-Faria, chief executive of ZeroStack. “I expect that uncertainty to be temporary.” Major cryptocurrencies began sliding as initial vote counts came in. They are also projected to take control of the US Senate. The digital asset industry has poured money into shaping the political landscape since US President Donald Trump ran for a second presidential term in 2024. Crypto companies contributed US$189 million (S$241.8 million) to political action committees in the 2026 midterm cycle through the first quarter – more than a third of election spending, according to the consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen. For investors, the immediate concern is that a Democratic takeover could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital asset firms. The broader macroeconomic implications are less clear. Political stalemate could limit further fiscal stimulus and weigh on speculative assets, though lower Treasury yields could eventually provide support by easing financial conditions. For now, Bitcoin trading offers limited utility as a gauge of broader market sentiment. Crypto has been grappling with the fallout from a US$6.3 billion hack of largest exchange Binance last week and diminished retail enthusiasm amid the artificial intelligence boom. Those pressures make it harder to separate the macro-driven market moves from industry-specific issues already weighing on digital assets. “Overall sentiment in crypto is near-term moderate fear and long-term uncertainty,” said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “Near-term fear because it is still tracking overall risk assets, and with the tech sell-off and potentially a restart to the war in the Middle East that is causing some downward pressure.” Democratic control of the Senate, in addition to the House, would put Congress at odds with Trump’s Republican White House. The Trump family’s financial gains from its crypto ventures became a contentious issue in 2026 , helping derail a regulatory Bill seen as critical to the industry. “With the Clarity Act already stalled in the Senate, a change in committee control would most likely mean renegotiation rather than a quick revival, and markets had largely priced that in,” said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. Bitcoin is down roughly 6% from a high on Oct 29 , before the Binance hack. More than US$1 billion flowed out of US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Oct 30 and Nov 2 . Options markets continued to show demand for downside protection across maturities, even as open interest remains tilted towards calls, or the right to buy Bitcoin, in several of the largest expiries. “As a Democratic sweep became more likely, clients shifted from buying upside calls to downside puts,” said Sean McNulty, a derivatives trader at market maker AQC Tech. “Attention is shifting back to interest rates and currencies, which is also driving Bitcoin’s decline today.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Swim and gym prices set to rise above inflation
events.summary: Bosses at Perdiswell Leisure Centre in Worcester want to increase its fees from January Published 4 November 2026, 06:13 GMT Inflation-busting price increases are on the way at a large Worcester leisure centre, with its operators blaming energy and staffing costs. The price of an adult swim at Perdiswell Leisure Centre could rise 6.8% – from £7.30 to £7.80 – if the new charges are approved. Fitness class fees would increase by 5.6% to £9.50, while the price of annual memberships would go up 4.9%. Bosses at Freedom Leisure, the site's operator, said staffing and energy bills were rising faster than income as Worcester City Council were asked to approve the new prices. A report on the price hikes, which outstrip the UK's 3.6% inflation rate, revealed energy costs had more than doubled in recent years, despite efforts to slash consumption. If councillors sign them off in a meeting at the end of November, the average fee at Perdiswell Leisure Centre would increase by 5.3% from January. Matt Wickham, from Freedom Leisure, said things are "tough" for the whole leisure industry Hiring the artificial pitch at Perdiswell, which can currently be done for £44 an hour, would cost 10% more, although the council said it would still be significantly cheaper than comparable pitches elsewhere in the city. Matt Wickham, Freedom Leisure's chief operating officer, explained the firm had seen "significant cost increases", with gas prices up by more than 50% over the second half of the year and minimum wages rising year-on-year. "It's really tough because we know people are feeling the pinch in different ways, but our priority is all about offering a value-for-money service to people from all walks of life," he said. He added the government should consider "immediate financial support" to help the leisure industry through the next 12 months and ongoing investment into leisure centre stock. If approved, the increases would also apply at St John's Sports Centre and Nunnery Wood Sports Complex, both of which are owned by Freedom Leisure. Gym-goers at Perdiswell had mixed views on the price increases – with some saying they were not surprised. Sue Guest said: "I've had two hip replacements so I come and do the aqua swim, it's very beneficial to me. "It would be a shame if they increase it, but then they (the operators) have their own expenses as well. "I think it's still reasonable value for money, actually." Colin English, a pensioner, said: "I use the gym quite a lot, I come at least four or five times a week. "They put the price up last year – if they do it again by these sorts of amounts I may have to reconsider because it's getting expensive." Another gym user called Vinny added: "It feels like everything is going up in price at the moment. "I'd never stop going though, this gym is important to me so I really don't mind." A final decision is expected to be made on 24 November, subject to discussions at two city council committees before then. events.title: Business-friendly Texas flips: Democrats end nearly 40-year drought, winning Senate seat and governor’s mansion
events.summary: It’s been nearly four decades since Texas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, and 36 years since one occupied the governor’s mansion. That all changed Tuesday night. While Democrats notched historic upsets nationwide — including in places like Kansas, which broke a 90-year streak — Texas carries outsized national weight given the recent corporate stampede to the state. SpaceX, Tesla, Chevron, and Caterpillar are among the corporate giants that relocated to Texas in search of lower taxes, light-touch regulation, and a business-friendly political climate. “In Texas, we’re welcome,” Chevron’s Andy Walz said after announcing a move from California. Last month, the parent company of the new Texas Stock Exchange raised $155 million in a third funding round meant to lure companies away from the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. Like Walz, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has cast Texas as a foil to California — a state Musk famously decried as the “state of overregulation, overlitigation, and overtaxation,” and whose billionaire wealth tax on the ballot Tuesday has alienated business leaders. Yet that corporate embrace has proved double-edged. Musk directed roughly $190 million of his $445 million midterm war chest into Texas, largely backing Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott. That deluge offered Democrat James Talarico an irresistible target down the stretch, allowing him to portray the race as Musk’s bid to buy a Senate seat. Abbott, a three-term incumbent, was also called out for being on Musk’s payroll. “Does Texas belong to the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live here?” said Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott to become the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990. “In less than one month, Elon Musk gave Greg Abbott $5 million to try and buy this election so that he can keep buying up Texans’ land, energy, and resources,” she added. Hinojosa, described as “a long shot” by the Texas Tribune and mostly ignored by Abbott for much of the year, also tapped into rising backlash over data center sprawl. She campaigned against what she termed a “Big Tech takeover of Texas land, resources, and schools.” — Shelly Banjo

events.title: Rogue UK energy bosses and brokers face crackdown on mis-selling
events.summary: Exclusive: Ofgem to be given powers to issue fines and rein in bonuses for executives who ‘reward themselves while customers suffer’ Energy bosses in the UK will have their bonuses curtailed when suppliers and brokers break the rules under a crackdown on mis-selling. Through the energy independence bill, which will be introduced on Wednesday, Ofgem will be given new powers to order compensation, impose fines and ban rogue operators that have pushed businesses and households into overpriced contracts. Companies with a business energy supply contract often use a broker to secure their deal, but – unlike the intermediaries who market mortgages or insurance deals – these energy middlemen are largely unregulated. The government said rogue brokers had been able to push small businesses into overpriced energy contracts while pocketing hidden commissions, leaving companies paying more than they should. These energy brokers and price comparison services will now be brought under Ofgem’s remit. The move is expected to save businesses more than £100m a year from hidden commissions and mis-selling. The watchdog will also be given powers to crack down on payments to bosses who have “rewarded themselves while customers suffer”. It follows public outrage over huge bonus payouts to executives despite investigations into the treatment of vulnerable customers . The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh , said: “People work hard for their money. They shouldn’t be ripped off by energy companies or forced to fight for fair treatment when things go wrong. “When energy bosses fail their customers, they shouldn’t be walking away with bumper bonuses while families and businesses pick up the bill.” The bill, which was announced in the king’s speech and is expected to set out more details on the government’s plans to transition to clean energy, comes as ministers face criticism over the green agenda. John Healey recently unveiled more than £3bn of cuts to the energy department’s budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending. The chancellor also said he would veto new offshore wind projects if they did not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government was moving away from the pro-renewables agenda. However, the government says it is still committed to its target of clean power by 2030. As part of the new bill, local authorities will be given stronger powers to tackle landlords who fail to meet energy efficiency standards, including fines of up to £30,000. Since 2020, it has been illegal to let properties with energy performance certificate ratings below E, unless the landlord can show that it is exempt. The government will also use the bill to introduce a moratorium on fracking by ending new licensing onshore in England. Fracking, which involves pumping liquid underground at high pressure to crack rock and release trapped oil or gas, is controversial because of its links to earthquakes and fears it could contaminate the water table. It was banned by the Conservative government in 2019. However, in 2022, Liz Truss used her brief tenure as prime minister to overturn the ban, prompting widespread anger. The minister for climate transition, Katie White, said the government was “putting communities first and protecting them from the risks of earthquakes and unsafe drilling”. The moratorium will not include lower-volume fracking operations or “proppant squeeze”, which the fracking industry says is not a form of fracking. However, Tony Bosworth, an energy campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said this was an attempt to “creep in through the back door under a different name”. The government said the low-volume activities were not under the scope of the ban and it was not aware of evidence that they posed the same risks as high-volume fracking. Prof Stuart Haszeldine of the University of Edinburgh has said that earthquakes caused by lower-volume fracking can be as large and unpredictable as those caused by high-volume fracking.

events.title: Why pharma firms are going to Earth’s orbit in search of new cancer drugs
events.summary: A space capsule 300 miles above us is growing the tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug in microgravity R oughly 300 miles above our heads, three washing machine-sized capsules are orbiting the Earth. Inside one of them, tiny crystals of a potential cancer drug are being grown in the weightlessness of space. The others are testing heat protection materials and navigation systems for when the capsules plunge back through Earth’s atmosphere at hypersonic speeds. Together, they represent a small but significant step towards what some hope will become a lucrative new industry: manufacturing drugs and other materials in space. The spacecraft belong to California-based Varda Space Industries. On 1 October, it launched two onboard the same rocket, followed by the third on 20 October. With a record three spacecraft now simultaneously in orbit for the first time, the company is edging closer to its ambition of operating a fleet of orbiting pharmaceutical factories. “We’re the first company in human history to launch multiple commercial re-entry vehicles simultaneously, and as the frequency of launches increases, the once ‘crazy future’ of manufacturing products in space is becoming more and more certain,” said Will Bruey, Varda’s chief executive. There are several reasons for wanting to manufacture certain materials in space, one of the most important being microgravity. On Earth, gravity causes particles suspended in liquids to settle, while differences in density create currents. Both can interfere with the growth of crystals. “If you are able to remove those effects, you can make crystals grow in a much more ordered sort of way,” said Dr Meganne Christian, mission manager for in-space manufacturing at the UK-based Satellite Applications Catapult. For pharmaceutical companies, this could open up new ways of formulating medicines, as the size, shape and arrangement of drug crystals can affect how easily drugs dissolve, how stable they are and how they can be administered. In some cases, this could enable drugs that currently require intravenous infusions to be reformulated into more convenient injections. Other materials, such as the semiconductors used in everything from smartphones to electric vehicles, could also benefit from being manufactured in space, where microgravity and the absence of air could help produce purer crystals with fewer defects. “Personally, I would really love to try and make graphene in microgravity,” said Christian. “Theoretically, it is this incredible material, but in practice you get a whole lot of defects in the crystals. It’s a similar story for semiconductors. If you can reduce the number of defects, you can get a much higher-performing material.” Scientists have been experimenting with manufacturing in microgravity for decades, particularly aboard the International Space Station (ISS). But the ISS has predominantly served as a “test kitchen” for scientific ideas and is scheduled to be retired around 2030. “It wasn’t necessarily designed with manufacturing in mind,” said Dr Ryan Reeves, deputy chief scientist for the ISS National Laboratory. Several companies are developing commercial space stations to replace the ISS, while others are designing specialist laboratories and equipment for conducting experiments aboard them. Among them is the UK-based BioOrbit, which recently sent a microwave-sized laboratory to the ISS as a step towards the production of self-injected cancer drugs. However, for large-scale manufacturing and certain industrial processes, “you need to get humans out of the picture, because we’re dirty, we cause vibrations, and we require a whole higher level of safety,” said Christian. This is where Varda’s autonomous factories come in. Known as free-flyers, they hitch a ride into orbit aboard SpaceX rockets, carrying miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the experiments are complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft, plunges through the atmosphere and parachutes safely back to an uninhabited region of Earth. Varda is among the furthest advanced in demonstrating this approach, having already returned several capsules from orbit. It plans to launch another seven missions in 2027, and a further 10 in 2028. The ability to conduct experiments frequently is particularly important for drug development. “If scientists have to wait 10 years between experiments or even a year, that really doesn’t fit into the speed of modern drug development,” said Michael Reilly, Varda’s chief strategy officer. While Varda’s manufacturing ambitions are focused on pharmaceuticals, other companies are developing similar systems to produce different materials. For example, Cardiff-based Space Forge is exploring a hybrid approach, in which semiconductor crystals grown aboard spacecraft could be returned to Earth and used as templates for growing larger quantities, much like a sourdough starter.

Deputy chief designer Wang Xiang explained the plans last weekend at an event called the Seventh Manned Space Symposium. Chinese state media has posted video of Wang discussing plans to reach Luna by launching two Long March 10 rockets. One will carry a lander named “Lanyue” and the other will hoist a crew capsule called “Mengzhou.” The two craft will meet in orbit around the Moon, where two of the three Taikonauts aboard Mengzhou will transfer to Lanyue and descend to set boot on regolith. In the video, Wang said China plans near-Earth orbit test missions for both vehicles in coming years, followed by an uncrewed visit to the Moon. If all goes well, China hopes to attempt a crewed landing by 2030. The Seventh Manned Space Symposium marked the 70th anniversary of the founding of China's space program and was also pitched as a moment for articulation of the nation’s ambitions in space under its 15 th five-year-plan, Beijing’s blueprint for the years 2026 to 2030. China called off its last moonshot in August, when authorities decided the Chang’e 7 robotic ice hunting mission “ failed to meet launch criteria ” just one day before its planned launch. The orbit required to reach the South Lunar Pole for that mission isn’t always easily accessible, so China plans to try again next year. When China tries to get Chang’e 7, Lanyue, and Mengzhou flying, it will at least have some new standards to apply to their operations after the China Manned Space Engineering Office last week published seventeen of them. One of the standards defines the architecture for Ethernet and Wi-Fi networks on China’s space station and other orbiters. Another governs signage used in orbit, in the hope that a standard means Taikonauts won’t make mistakes. A couple outline procedures for extravehicular activities, and use of a robotic arm to assist Taikonauts on such missions. events.title: Massive blue wave hands Congress to Democrats
events.summary: The News Democrats seized the House and Senate by wider margins that even party leaders had hoped in a wave election that served as a referendum on President Donald Trump. Democratic House candidates took districts Trump won by double digits just two years ago. They flipped Senate seats nationwide, including in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Competitive races haven’t been called in Michigan and Alaska, where Democrats could run up the score further. Trump told The New York Times on Wednesday night that he “was absolutely willing” to accept the results of the election. Democrats racked up stunning victories across the South. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988. Democrat Gina Hinojosa toppled incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democrat to take the governor’s mansion since Ann Richards in 1990. Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina won a Senate seat in his state, pulling off what no Democrat has there in 18 years. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, winning the seat formerly held by Lindsey Graham. Sen. Jon Ossoff held onto his seat in Georgia. Democrats scored victories across the Midwest, too. Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, overcoming a 94-year drought for Democrats in the state. In Iowa, Josh Turek beat Rep. Ashley Hinson to fill retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst’s seat. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Chris Pappas held retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s seat for Democrats in New Hampshire. Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins conceded to her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson. Polls in Alaska remain open until 1 am EST. Republicans held onto a Senate seat in Florida. Trump, reportedly watching returns from the White House, criticized Fox News coverage before most polls had closed. In a social media post Trump said Republicans would have had a better night if he’d been on the ballot. Democratic surge Democrats won other gubernatorial races in red states. Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial race in Georgia, a first for a Democrat in 28 years — a positive sign for Ossoff if he decides to pursue a 2028 presidential bid, since she would appoint his successor. Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, endorsed by Trump, to become the next governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy aired a late attack ad against Acton featuring her estranged mother, who backed her husband when Acton accused him of rape as a child. Ossoff, who Republicans had hoped to unseat this year, easily blew past GOP rival Rep. Mike Collins to win re-election. Pappas prevailed over former GOP Sen. John Sununu in another race that Republicans had initially hoped to contest. In North Carolina, Cooper scored the party’s first pickup of the night. House Republicans are also faltering in Florida, where three seats drawn to elect Republicans have so far gone to Democrats — re-elections for Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor, plus a victory for Rep.-elect Pia Dandiya. The GOP initially redistricted to try to gain four new House seats. All three of the Florida districts that Democrats have won so far on Tuesday night backed Trump in 2024. Urged to embark on mid-decade redistricting by Trump, Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis has warned that his party was losing some of its advantages, driven by voter anger about the war in Iran. David’s view As the night got better and better for Democrats, I started to hear them ask: Had they built a new national majority? Had they banished MAGA for good?Then they reminded themselves: Thinking like that is what got Republicans into this mess. Two Trump victories, and a 2020 loss that kept most of his coalition intact, convinced many conservatives that they had built a new party system that combined working class voters of all races, the social conservatives who made their local parties run, and the business community that rejected Trump after Jan. 6 but came running back in 2024. Who could beat that? Well, now we know. The Trump coalition came apart on Tuesday, with the president decisively unable to put himself “on the ballot” and turn out his unlikely voters. Plenty of signs were there during early voting – especially in North Carolina, a killing field where Republicans lost House and state legislative seats that were gerrymandered to be impossible to lose. (On a map drawn to elect three Democrats, the party is likely to win nine seats.) Democrats didn’t pretend that they had solved all their party’s problems. But they did learn from Trump’s first term, and the way they miscalculated what a fluke he was. Instead of moving to the left, betting that a more excited base could overwhelm MAGA, they nominated candidates who were willing to break with left-wing orthodoxy – Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek adopting a more conservative position on gender, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico becoming a booster of the energy industry. Their base was so furious at Trump that it was relatively easy to turn out. Persuasion was harder, but they got there; Democrats won back northeast Ohio, eastern Iowa, Texas’s Rio Grande Valley, and even parts of Florida that seemed to be racing away from their party. And Republicans couldn’t change the electorate. Trump wasn’t on the ballot, obviously – but for the first time, voters did not credit Trump with good management of the economy or with keeping America out of wars. The snazziest GOP bumper sticker of the Biden years was “I’d take some mean tweets and cheap gas right now.” Without cheap gas, voters weren’t willing to put up with Trump’s AI memes, jokes about men’s asses, and obsession with building a triumphant arch in Arlington. Finally, Republicans had a failure of imagination. Any reporter who covered the 2016 election remembers the disbelief, even anger, from Democrats who were told that Trump could win the Midwest. It was impossible, until it happened. And Republicans who’d been told that Texas could flip in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 could not imagine James Talarico – the “God is nonbinary” guy? – breaking the curse. Talarico is on track to lead a Democratic sweep of Texas statewide offices, cutting down some of the most powerful politicians in the state’s history. Democrats held onto the suburban gains they made from 2016 to 2020, then won back many of the place that no Democrat had won since Barack Obama. They are less afraid of Trump than of any time since the week before the 2016 election.

events.title: Singapore equity funds draw record $2.2b as bank dividends bolster local market
events.summary: Singapore-focused equity funds attracted a record $2.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026, with inflows more than double the previous quarter’s level and almost five times the $450 million recorded a year earlier, data showed. Singapore equity funds saw record inflows of $2.2 billion in Q3 2026, as Morningstar said strong market performance and the EQDP revived interest in local shares. Capital Group said Singapore companies paid US$7.6 billion in dividends, up 2.5% year on year, with underlying growth at 9.6% and banks DBS and OCBC driving gains. Investors also moved money into allocation funds and out of bond funds, which saw $1.04 billion in net outflows as rising bond yields hurt fixed-income returns. SINGAPORE – Investors are putting more money into Singapore stocks and equity funds, coinciding with higher dividend payouts from companies listed here, according to the latest data showing record fund inflows and stronger underlying dividend growth in the third quarter. Singapore-focused equity funds attracted a record $2.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026, with inflows more than double the previous quarter’s level and almost five times the $450 million recorded a year earlier, according to findings released on Nov 4 by Morningstar, an investment research and financial services firm. Separately, investment management firm Capital Group’s latest Dividend Watch report, also released on Nov 4, found that Singapore companies in its study paid a total of US$7.6 billion (S$9.7 billion) in dividends during the quarter, up 2.5% from a year earlier. Underlying dividend growth for Singapore companies was stronger at 9.6%, ahead of the global average of 7.5%. This measure strips out special dividends, currency movements and changes in payment timing to give a clearer picture of recurring payouts. Singapore’s dividend growth was overwhelmingly driven by banks, particularly DBS and OCBC, Capital Group said. At DBS, record fee income, buoyant wealth management activity and growing customer activity helped offset weaker margins, allowing the bank to continue returning surplus capital to shareholders. Meanwhile, OCBC benefited from record non-interest income and strong wealth management and trading revenues, the report said. Both reports point to renewed demand for Singapore equities, alongside growth in the cash that companies are returning to shareholders. Morningstar attributed the growing popularity of Singapore equity funds to strong market performance and measures under the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) to revitalise the local stock market. Arvind Subramanian, senior analyst and research manager at Morningstar, noted that Singapore investors have traditionally looked abroad for their equity and fixed-income exposure, while the local market tended to attract attention mainly during risk-on periods. “The EQDP measures and strong market performance have put Singapore equities back in the spotlight, with Singapore-focused equity funds becoming increasingly popular among investors,” he said. Singapore equities have recorded positive flows in every quarter since the fourth quarter of 2024, when the EQDP was first announced, and the pace has picked up sharply in 2026 so far. LionGlobal Singapore Trust saw the highest inflows of around $1.05 billion, while Amova Singapore Dividend Equity Fund drew about $530 million. Amova Singapore STI ETF added another $280 million, according to Morningstar. Funds combining different asset classes also attracted more money, driven by the strong appetite for equities. Allocation funds, which typically invest across assets such as shares and bonds, drew $2.45 billion in the third quarter, their strongest quarterly inflows in the past few years. This followed $1.83 billion in the second quarter and $1.49 billion in the first. PIMCO GIS Balanced Income and Growth Fund attracted about $870 million, while Allianz Income and Growth drew roughly $530 million. Schroder ISF Multi-Asset Growth and Income and Schroder Asia More+ also recorded notable inflows. The stronger appetite for stocks came at the expense of bonds, as investors pulled more money out of funds that invest solely in bonds. During the quarter, withdrawals accelerated from fixed-income funds, which recorded $1.04 billion in net outflows, data showed. It is also the third consecutive quarter of outflows from fixed income, and a reversal from the $3.36 billion attracted in the corresponding period of 2025. The PIMCO GIS Income Fund, usually among the category’s leading fixed income asset gatherers, recorded a second consecutive quarter of withdrawals, with investors pulling out about $790 million. Rising bond yields have weighed on fixed-income fund returns , as higher interest rates on new bonds make existing bonds with lower payouts less attractive , pushing down their prices. However, higher yields also offer investors more attractive income opportunities.

events.title: GOP's red wall comes crashing down
events.summary: Senate Republicans' worst nightmare came true Tuesday night, as they watched red state after red state fall to a historic Democratic wave . Why it matters: It's hard to remember now, but Republicans started off the 2026 cycle thinking they could expand their majority. They ended the night with what one source called a "huge f**king thumping" — losing or trailing in every toss-up on the map. At the start of the cycle, top operatives saw a red wall of incumbents in Trump-friendly states, an invincible Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and a vulnerable Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, who provided a path to expanding a majority. By 9pm Tuesday night, top GOP sources were quietly accepting the reality of the return of Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). "Republicans are going to wake up in a different country tomorrow and we are going to have to start from square one to reinvent a party," one senior GOP Senate aide told Axios on Tuesday evening. Between the lines: For the first time since 1972, Republicans lost a Senate seat in the home state of the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The defeat of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) came despite Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) leading the NRSC. Republicans also lost in the home state of the next expected NRSC chair, Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Zoom in: North Carolina and Georgia were expected to be the premiere races of the cycle not too long ago. Both were called for Democrats before 8:30pm EST. That was just the beginning of the nightmare. In Texas, Elon Musk's more than $150 million infusion wasn't enough to save Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton after Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn in a nasty primary. In Ohio, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) campaign had a rocky start — and wasn't bailed out by President Trump's publicity campaign about his rear end. Alaska started looking shaky even before a second Dan Sullivan joined the ballot, and Iowa wasn't a given either. In Kansas, alarm bells started ringing over an unprepared Sen. Roger Marshall. In South Carolina, Sen. Lindsey Graham died, and before Republican leaders could blink, Trump crowned Graham's sister, Darline, who had no political experience. And in Maine, Republicans held out hope that Susan Collins could pull out another miracle. A hope that quickly faded as results began to roll in. What we're hearing: "Absolutely brutal night," another senior GOP aide told us. "But also predictable. Signs were there for months. Biggest fear is that the party lacks the introspection, takes away wrong lessons, and doubles down on the policies and behavior that got us into this mess in first place." "Sometimes there are environmental challenges that even the strongest, best-resourced candidate can't overcome. We're seeing those challenges play out in real time tonight," said a third senior GOP aide. Yet another top operative conspicuously shared charts of Trump's dismal approval ratings. The bottom line: Democrats won Senate seats on Tuesday night for the first time in Texas since 1988, in Kansas since 1932 and South Carolina since 1998.

events.title: Senate goes Democratic in a ‘generational wipeout’ of Trump’s party
events.summary: The News Democrats have secured control of the Senate, a shocking collapse for a Republican majority that started the midterms with what looked like an impregnable red wall of conservative states. There were almost no blemishes for Democrats and few bright spots for Republicans. The GOP lost seats it held in Maine, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and North Carolina; failed to flip seats in New Hampshire and Georgia; and is now bracing for further losses that could hamper its effort to retake the Senate in 2028, when the map gives both parties pickup opportunities. Other than North Carolina, the GOP-held losses are in states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024. Republicans could afford to lose up to three seats; they’re on track to lose all of their tossup races. Senate seats in Maine and Alaska are also both at risk of flipping. “This is a generational wipeout,” one senior Republican strategist told Semafor. “We are going to have a full-on GOP civil war.” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said his party had pulled off a “generational remake of the Senate map” by winning so many tough states. After touting Democrats’ candidate qualify, he said Americans had reduced the GOP’s red wall to a “pile of bricks.” “Republicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff. Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time, he implemented things that raised their costs on electricity, on healthcare, on goods,” Schumer told reporters at a midnight press conference. He said he heard Trump’s remarks saying he’d work with a Democratic Congress but vowed his party is “going to deliver for the people of America with or without the president.” Democrats started Tuesday night with two quick, decisive Senate victories — by Georgia incumbent Jon Ossoff and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — that fueled their drive deeper into red territory, to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. Moving Money Around The party’s top Senate super PAC pulled down several weeks’ worth of ads in those two Southern states in recent weeks, per information shared with Semafor, saving $22 million in North Carolina and $11 million in Georgia. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also scrapped some ad buys in both states down the stretch, decisions that paid off as the party won both seats early on Tuesday night. Democrats felt optimistic about taking the majority earlier in the night than some had expected after the shocking win in South Carolina. Their decision to pull cash out of Georgia and North Carolina helped top Democratic groups approve new Senate spending in states like Mississippi, South Carolina, and Kansas. It also helped the party shore up candidates in the battleground states of Michigan and Maine as Republicans’ deep-pocketed Senate Leadership Fund super PAC poured in astounding sums. “The strength of the Cooper and Ossoff campaigns allowed Senate Majority PAC to re-invest our initial investments into our expanded battleground map. That is a game-changer when Republicans poured money into races,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC. Senate Majority PAC spent heavily in Kansas on top of its spending in traditional battlegrounds, while the DSCC put in $500,000 in South Carolina’s Senate race late, according to a person familiar with the buy. That spending followed $500,000 in Mississippi previously reported by Semafor. That was only possible due to the strength of Ossoff and Cooper, who both raised gobs of money and put away their opponents weeks ago. Cooper raised more than $49 million through mid-October, and Ossoff raised more than $100 million. Cooper and Ossoff are both notching considerable, double-digit victories over their respective opponents, Rep. Mike Collins and Michael Whatley. Burgess’s view In Senate races, candidate quality matters. And it can affect all of the other candidates on a party’s slate. Ossoff and Cooper ran such boringly effective campaigns that it allowed Democratic leaders to concentrate their efforts elsewhere. Appointed Sens. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Jon Husted of Ohio proved weak against Annie Andrews and former Sen. Sherrod Brown. And Trump’s decision to back Ken Paxton in Texas blew up spectacularly for Republicans. Notable Republicans were preparing to move their focus away from Georgia and North Carolina as early as September, as we first reported .

events.title: ‘Buckle up’: A defiant White House pins blame elsewhere
events.summary: The News The White House began Tuesday night with cautious optimism. As Democrats started racking up victories, President Donald Trump’s advisers grew more candid — and defiant. Trump spent the weeks before the midterms traveling across the country, hosting 30 events across 20 states in just over a month as he urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” What resulted was a midterm repudiation of Republicans that, as election night wore on, some in the White House were unwilling to own. “President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official told Semafor, arguing that he “did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.” Trump himself echoed the sentiment in a Tuesday night social media post : “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The early results on Tuesday night made clear that Trump’s aggressive campaign push wasn’t enough to surmount public frustration with the Iran war and his tariffs’ effect on the cost of living. Democrats quickly flipped North Carolina, held onto New Hampshire and Georgia — and then flipped long-scarlet South Carolina. Trump officials and people close to the White House quickly acknowledged that a massive blue wave was coming. One Trump administration official emphasized how much the war has directly affected Americans. That conflict amplified voters’ frustration as gas prices climbed, and many in Trump’s base felt betrayed by a president who’d campaigned on launching no new wars. Another Trump ally went even further, describing the war as a “disaster” and lamenting that “the Republican party doesn’t understand the Trump coalition, even though it’s 10 years in.” Officials’ efforts to pin their stunning midterm setback on other GOP leaders suggest that the White House has no plans to seek conciliation with ascendant congressional Democratic majorities. “Regardless of how today plays out, President Trump’s resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger,” the White House official added. “Buckle up.” Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday that he would accept the results of the election. Preparing for the Worst In the past few weeks, some administration officials have begun looking to hire lawyers to preempt Democrat-led investigations — an early sign that they knew Tuesday night’s results might not go their way. To that point, some advisers indicated to Semafor that the results rolling in so far were not surprising to them. Trump has often pointed over the past months to historical data showing that the party holding total control of Washington tends to perform poorly in midterm elections. Even before polls across the country closed, the White House began circulating talking points highlighting Trump’s efforts on the trail. That underlying message — that the president did what he could to help — largely persisted inside the administration as the losses mounted. One adviser told Semafor that Trump’s thinking remains along those lines: that he did what he could. Several Trump allies also argued to Semafor that poor candidate quality was partly to blame for Republican defeats, though the president openly endorsed several of the candidates who fell short. Main Character Syndrome Trump certainly made himself a central figure in Tuesday’s election. Democrats looked to amplify his calls for voters to pretend he was on the ballot, believing that voters were so dissatisfied with the administration that a midterm referendum on Trump would reward them. Trump watched the election results roll in from the White House East Room alongside Cabinet members, senior staff, and political advisers, another White House official told Semafor. At times, he took to Truth Social to rage against Fox News’ coverage of the evening. Some staffers ordered in from the Cheesecake Factory, an apparent nod to the now-famous quip from former President Barack Obama about Trump’s decorating. Shelby’s view Tonight’s results are a warning sign for the Republican Party as it tries to look past Trump. And they’re likely to surface a question that some of his aides knew they’d inevitably face: whether the coalition that pushed Trump to power can be reconstituted, and what the party will stand for after Trump leaves office. Some Republicans I’ve texted with tonight are already confronting that question. In the weeks and months ahead, anyone in the GOP who’s eyeing a 2028 run will need to look at the midterm results and find ways to run with a different message than Trump — while not angering him or his base.

events.title: Trump turns his ire toward Fox News on election night
events.summary: President Trump lashed out at Fox News on election night, attacking the network's personalities, polling and coverage as voters awaited midterm election results. Why it matters: Trump, who has repeatedly dined with Fox News patriarch Rupert Murdoch and hired talent from the network, has come to expect favorable coverage. But Fox's editorial decisions this election cycle suggest it isn't always willing to oblige. The latest: Under the shadow of a burgeoning blue wave, Trump wrote minutes before midnight Tuesday that "FoxNews [sic] bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse." Driving the news: Trump began the night by criticizing Jessica Tarlov, a Fox co-host and Democratic strategist, saying he'd "go somewhere else" until she was off the air. He reportedly went so far as to text her co-host, Greg Gutfeld, to complain. His ire then turned toward Fox's political polling , claiming, "Every question is a hit job, and every answer is 'BULLSHIT!'" Around half an hour later, he posted that Fox's ratings were down "because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!" Trump pointed to a "new CNN Poll" as an alternative, touting data demonstrating his strength among MAGA Republicans. But the two CNN polling segments he posted earlier in the night were both well over a month old. State of play : Trump's rocky relationship with Fox News has been a source of tension this election season and in previous elections. Fox's coverage of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has fueled tensions for months, Axios' Alex Isenstadt recently reported . Republicans reportedly worried that Fox was undercutting efforts to brand El-Sayed as far outside the mainstream. In late October, Trump posted that Fox was "spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas." He added, "That's the only reason this Race is close, if it is indeed close." The White House and Fox did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Meanwhile, Trump's former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, now a Fox pundit, appeared on the network's election night coverage and said she had just spoken with the president. Reality check: Murdoch, while he is a conservative, has always been passionate about the news business. Fox News did, after all, spark Trumpworld's ire by calling Arizona early for former President Biden in 2020. Zoom in: Fox News' business imperative means focusing on long-term credibility over short-term access and ratings — which took a downward turn last month in the lead-up to the election. The ratings decline could suggest some Republican viewers tuned out as pre-election polls pointed to possible Democratic gains . But for Trump, who has tried to make it a referendum on his popularity, it's personal.
