( ABC News: Ethan White ) Police say retail stores are actively monitoring and reporting suspicious purchases of jerry can and fuel as firebombings continue across Melbourne. The latest business to be targeted is a luxury and sports car workshop in Springvale, in the city's south-east. Police have repeated their warnings to young offenders who are being recruited by organised crime rings for the attacks. Victorian retail stores are actively monitoring jerry can and fuel purchases and reporting suspicious transactions to investigators, police have revealed. The alliance comes amid a wave of arson attacks across Melbourne linked to the extortion of business owners by organised crime gangs. Overnight, a luxury and sports car workshop at Springvale in the city's south-east joined the long list of hospitality, retail and car dealerships to be targeted by offenders. Police said an alarm alerted the owner of Etuners Motorsports to a fire at his Aspen Circuit premises just before midnight. "He subsequently called a friend to assist," Detective Inspector in charge of the Arson and Explosives Squad, Chris Murray, said. "On arrival, the premise was fully engulfed ... I think it took around about an hour to suppress the fire." The workshop was substantially damaged. The fire caused substantial damage to Etuners Motorsport. ( ABC News: Ethan White ) Inspector Murray said police were looking for three people — a driver and two masked offenders wearing hoodies who lit the fire. He said there was a drive-by shooting at the same business last week. "It's a reputable, successful business and therefore organised crime, if they are involved, are looking to exploit that," he said. Inspector Murray said detectives would examine the business's recent client list to see if there were any possible links to the incidents. Fuel monitoring scheme 'paying dividends' Inspector Murray said police had made hundreds of arrests in recent months after numerous firebombings across the city. He said Victoria Police had recently met with representatives from the retail sector, forming an alliance in which stores would actively monitor the sale of jerry cans and fuel. Any suspicious purchases would be reported to detectives. "That's paying great dividends for us," he said. "[Police] have once again raised the stakes and we have increased both overt and covert patrols all around the state. "My message is, if you want to roll the dice, there's every chance you're going to get caught." Detective Inspector Chris Murray says Victoria Police has formed an alliance with the retail sector to detect suspicious purchases of jerry cans and petrol. ( ABC News ) Inspector Murray repeated his warning to young offenders to think carefully before agreeing to carry out an attack for a crime gang. "The stats are pretty dire at the moment — we've got two individuals currently on life support in the Alfred hospital, we've had 20 offenders with serious injuries as a result of the act of arson and we've had one death," he said. He also warned that young offenders were finding themselves in situations which they could not easily walk away from. "We see this time and time again. If they dip their toe in the water and take one of these jobs on, the reality of trying to then remove themselves and say, "I've had enough" is very, very difficult," he said. "We've had families threatened, we've had individuals threatened." events.title: Australian banks lift interest rates
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia's banks lift mortgage rates in wake of RBA's fifth cash rate hike this year Australia's banks have lifted rates across a range of variable home loan products, business and personal loans and savings accounts. ( AAP: Joel Carrett ) Australia's big four banks have all lifted their interest rates on mortgages and savings accounts. They are responding to the RBA's decision to hike the cash rate to 4.85 per cent. These rate rises will take effect from mid-November, Australia's lenders will apply higher interest rates to variable mortgages in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to hike the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent on Tuesday. RBA governor Michele Bullock announced the cash rate was lifted to tackle persistent inflation in the Australian economy. "It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer. Their spending can't grow very quickly because their incomes aren't growing very quickly," Ms Bullock said. Set by the RBA, the cash rate is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks. Put simply, it is how much it costs banks to borrow from each other. When the RBA lifts the cash rate, it becomes more expensive for lenders to borrow from one another. Macquarie Bank was the first to respond, telling customers it would raise interest rates across its variable-rate home loan products by 0.25 per cent within an hour of the RBA announcement, saying customers had until November 19 before the higher rate kicked in. The next day, the big four banks all announced they would lift interest rates on variable home loans by 0.25 per cent. "A 0.25 per cent per annum increase to variable home loan rates will increase monthly repayments by approximately $79 on a variable home loan of $500,000 for an owner occupier loan with principal and interest repayments," ANZ said in a statement. Westpac, NAB, ANZ and CBA will apply the new rate from November 13. Westpac's chief executive, consumer, Carolyn McCann said the majority of its customers were ahead in mortgage repayments. In statements, all of the banks said customers under financial strain should contact their bank as soon as possible. Those with money in the right savings accounts will enjoy earning more interest when banks lift their rates in the middle of the month. But as the ABC has revealed , banks have been slower to pass on rate rises to savers and often require customers to meet a number of conditions before they can "unlock" the highest rates on offer. Comparison site Canstar said if those conditions were not met, customers reverted to a base rate of around 0.10 per cent. Not using the right account, missing monthly minimum deposits or not meeting withdrawal conditions on the account could cause the rate to plummet to the base rate. events.title: Britain’s housing market unlikely to recover until 2028, says Savills
events.summary: House prices forecast to fall by 1.5% next year as Middle East war keeps mortgage rates higher for longer Britain’s sluggish housing market is not expected to recover until 2028 as higher mortgage rates linked to the war in the Middle East deter buyers and weigh on prices. The property firm Savills said average house prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027, as the prolonged conflict undermines buyers’ confidence and keeps mortgage rates higher for longer. Improving economic prospects and mortgage affordability are expected to support a recovery from 2028. Savills expects house prices to rise by 15.8% – or £56,500 on average – over the five years to 2031, with values starting to recover in the second half of 2028. Nationwide said last week that UK house prices had risen by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years. The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566, the lender said . The Bank of England is widely expected to increase interest rates from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, putting further pressure on mortgage rates, after UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September. More than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027. Emily Williams, the director of residential research at Savills, said: “The drawn-out conflict in the Middle East has pushed back the prospect of meaningful mortgage rate relief, which will weigh on buyer sentiment and affordability. “We expect this will suppress activity and put pressure on prices next year. But this is unlikely to trigger a sharper correction. “Most homeowners have already absorbed higher borrowing costs since late 2022, with relatively few still needing to refinance directly from rates below 2%, and the labour market remains resilient.” The strongest five-year house price growth in percentage terms is forecast across northern England, Wales and Scotland, supported by relative affordability and economic prospects, according to the prediction. Savills expects first-time buyers to lead the recovery from 2028, helped by deposit affordability and government initiatives, which include the Your First Home scheme . It expects house price growth to accelerate in the second half of 2028, reaching 3.5% for the year as a whole.

events.title: How wall-climbing robots could help Gulf energy producers recover from attacks
events.summary: US technology company Gecko Robotics is deploying a new generation of wall-climbing robots across Adnoc's energy facilities to detect structural weaknesses and assess damage, after the Iran war exposed vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure across the Gulf. The company, which unveiled its Raptor robot exclusively to The National at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, is also considering manufacturing the machines in the UAE as it expands its partnership with Adnoc , including a new agreement with Adnoc Onshore. "When you think about that as it relates to post-attacks, that's where you should be able to think about Gecko's ability to understand what sort of damage has occurred, so that it increases how quickly you can get assets back up and running," Jake Loosararian, the company's chief executive and co-founder, told The National . The robot, which uses sensors and sound waves to identify structural faults without taking facilities offline, is three to five times faster than its predecessor and can collect millions of data points during inspections. The company claims it is up to 50 times faster than competitors' robots. Energy under threat Since the beginning of the Iran war , energy infrastructure has been attacked across the region. Demand for the robotics firm's services has been high, with large contracts awarded for military applications. The company is also expanding its military business, signing a $300 million agreement with the US Navy last week for robotics applications. The military is using robotics and AI to improve the readiness and performance of critical assets, a concept that also applies to energy infrastructure during regional conflicts, Mr Loosararian said. The technology provides data on "what to fix, how to fix it", while helping extend equipment lifespans and maintenance cycles, he added. Meet Raptor Raptor, Gecko's new wall-climbing robot, scans the surface and captures millions of data points during its inspections. "Raptor allows for a 50 x reduction in the cost of data collection, while also increasing the fidelity by roughly the same order of magnitude," he said. The robot is said to save time and money for companies, which do not have to take facilities offline for assessment; the advanced monitoring technology uses sensors and sound waves for detection, which is fed back to the digital layer that maps the assets. The company is focused on safety and building "better tools" for people. "Robotics are essential to ensure that resilience and readiness is possible in a world where we don't have a lot of these skilled workforces. And by the way, we should be building technology that makes people safe. And that's exactly what these robots are doing," he said. Changing priorities Mr Loosararian said energy companies need to adopt the latest technologies if they want to lead the sector. "If you don't have a path that leads you towards a more AI-native, robotic-native way of running infrastructure, you are operating in the ancient past, and that ancient path will lead you to demise," he said. "The energy companies that are looking more and more like tech companies are going to be the ones that win the day." UAE manufacturing ambitions Gecko is considering manufacturing robots in the UAE as demand grows, allowing it to develop and test the technology closer to the energy facilities where it is deployed. The company already deploys tens of robots a day in the region. "There's an abundance of energy infrastructure in the UAE," Mr Loosararian said. Building technology close to operating facilities would help avoid "the death of a lab", where equipment developed in controlled environments fails to perform as expected in real-world conditions, he said. The UAE is also seeking to expand local robotics manufacturing as part of its industrial development strategy. "Robotics is feeding a lot of sectors today, and it's enhancing and expediting production. It's becoming a big demand, not just for the production part, but also in ease of doing business for the end users," Ibtisam Al Saadi, acting assistant undersecretary for the industrial development sector at the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, told The National . She said interest among young Emiratis in robotics programming and manufacturing was growing, alongside locally manufactured drones and 3D printing. Gecko's expansion also includes an agreement with Adnoc Onshore, expected to be announced on Wednesday, to deploy robotics and AI models for critical infrastructure.

events.title: House Republicans torch each other over "brutal" midterms losses
events.summary: SHREVEPORT, La. — The GOP's election-night defeat has unleashed a wave of finger-pointing inside the House Republican conference, with members questioning whether Speaker Mike Johnson or any of the other top deputies can survive next week's leadership elections. Why it matters: Johnson spent months insisting Republicans would defy the odds and keep the House. But after losing the majority, he cast the defeat as all but inevitable, an explanation unlikely to satisfy Republicans ready for a new leadership slate. One House Republican told Axios that every member of GOP leadership will face a challenger because of the election results. Another said the losses have created a major opening for Republicans looking to challenge the current leadership team. A third said they no longer see a path for Johnson to remain atop the conference. Driving the news: At Johnson's election-night watch party in his hometown of Shreveport, the mood grew increasingly somber as it became clear Democrats would secure the House majority. Johnson remained offstage until just before 11pm Eastern time, even after networks projected Democrats would win control of the chamber. In a soundtrack to the GOP's election-night defeat, "White on the Ground" by the Kruse Brothers played over the speakers to a subdued crowd just before Johnson took the stage. "It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle," Johnson told supporters Tuesday night. "It's very, very difficult to overcome, and it looks like history will be kept here tonight." Behind the scenes: House Republicans were already privately unloading on their leaders Tuesday night, with some arguing the scale of the party's losses demands a change at the top. "I think Iran, ICE, inflation, fuel prices, lack of focus on pocketbook issues all played a part of this," one member told Axios. Asked for a vibe check, one member simply texted Axios: "Brutal." The scale of the losses was underscored by the defeat of NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) — the man tasked with preserving the Republican majority who couldn't hold onto his own seat. Zoom in: Johnson spent months crisscrossing the country in a last-ditch effort to save Republicans' fragile majority, traveling to more than 40 congressional districts across 22 states. Johnson publicly insisted in October that he intended to remain the top House Republican even if his party lost the majority, but he has yet to formally declare any plans to run for minority leader. Trump praised Johnson in an interview with Politico on Tuesday, but stopped short of endorsing him for the job. "He's going to have to make that decision," Trump said of Johnson. What we're watching: House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Nov. 10, with candidates required to declare by Nov. 6. Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are also being floated as potential contenders.

events.title: Democrats poised to claim a House majority bigger than they’d hoped
events.summary: The News House Democratic leaders are preparing to welcome moderate members from across the country and a majority big enough to manage comfortably and contain a restive progressive wing. After years of seeing hardline Republicans torment Speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson by maximizing their leverage in a slim House majority, Democrats are poised to make large enough gains to insulate themselves against unruly blocs in their caucus — particularly on the left. It might still be days until the full size of the majority is known. But Democrats are pushing into redder territory; in a shocking development for the GOP, its House campaigns chief, Rep. Richard Hudson, was on track to lose his deep-red North Carolina seat as of late Tuesday night. Democrats were leading late Tuesday in several of the Texas seats that House Republicans redrew at President Donald Trump’s behest to be more favorable to their party. They were ahead, too, in all four of the Florida seats that Republicans redrew. And in Ohio, where Republicans attempted to draw out Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the veteran lawmaker was leading her race; other Republicans, like Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, were trailing in early returns. Democrats have dealt with jitters for months now that an incoming progressive left could vote against Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ speakership bid, but the cushion provided by a larger House majority could all but moot a rebellion from the left both in an internal caucus election and the full speaker vote. The mood was jubilant at Jeffries’ watch party in Washington, DC, on Tuesday night, with cheers for every flipped race as TV networks called the House for Democrats surprisingly early in the night. Jeffries and Democratic leaders had taken a personal interest in defending redistricted territory and in recruiting candidates to run in redder seats. “Today begins the great American Comeback. In the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea, people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said Tuesday night. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.” ‘How to Lead’ Centrist Democrats are already trumpeting their role in recapturing the House majority. “I am feeling really good. New Dems are showing how to lead,” said Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., who chairs the New Democrat Coalition. The majority of the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” candidates this cycle were backed by the centrist bloc, which put substantial resources behind its candidates, too. Democratic leaders still face huge questions about how they’ll run the House floor and counter Trump. They’ve talked up an early agenda centered around reversing cuts to Medicaid and restoring lapsed healthcare tax credits, but could face pressure from the progressive left to put up a more ambitious plan. The jockeying for influence is already beginning. Leading up to Tuesday evening, Democrats from across the ideological spectrum were preemptively laying claim to their roles in helping flip the House and their visions for what a Democratic majority might be capable of doing. Progressives like Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said they wanted to vote on legislation that they would dare the Senate to filibuster or Trump to veto. “This is a mandate to deliver big change. No complacency,” he said in a statement. But with the House majority likely padded by redder territory this cycle, Democrats will face fierce internal resistance to progressive policy ideas like Medicare for All. Most candidates from purple districts, with the exception of some backed by the Progressive Caucus, have shied away from such ambitious proposals. Fred Wellman, one of those candidates who took operatives off-guard by triumphing in a red district in Missouri, told Semafor he wanted “to work towards a Medicare for All system, but right now we need to stop the bleeding.” “A lot of people were doubting us, and all I have to say at this point is ‘I told you so, you should’ve listened,’” he quipped. Nicholas’s view For all of the drama over individual races this cycle, Republicans across the country couldn’t outrun the overall environment. With diesel and gas prices still spiking through Election Day, and Trump’s approval rating sagging, voters were ready to punish Republicans. Democrats are on track for a majority far bigger than the 10-seat margin they’d publicly predicted heading into Tuesday. Now comes the hard part. Most in the party put aside their ideological differences over the last few years in pursuit of recapturing the House, but Democratic leaders are going to face tough decisions about their legislative agenda, all set against the backdrop of the 2028 presidential election.

events.title: India’s EloElo nabs $80M from NBCUniversal to bet on the country’s rising microdrama market
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. More than 118 million users watch microdramas every month as the serialized format has taken off in India. EloElo’s Story TV is one of the top apps for microdramas, with over 33 million active users , according to analysts. Banking on that scale, the company has raised $80 million in Series C from Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. This round brings its total fundraising to $130 million, with a valuation of $500 million. As people spend more time on platforms hosting verticalized videos, serialized content has become popular in multiple geographies, including the U.S., China, and India, with Hollywood celebrities like Issa Rae , James Franco, and Kim Kardashian investing in and starring in the format . Given India’s massive internet population of more than a billion and the country’s appetite for entertainment content, it presents a big market opportunity, with analysts expecting the industry to cross $3 billion to $4 billion in annual revenue by 2030 . Last year, dedicated apps like Story TV, Kuku TV, and Quick TV were among the top downloaded video-streaming apps in the country. Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart exec Saurabh Pandey, the Story TV platform has taken off in the last few years with a catalog of over 5,000 titles in six languages. Pandey told TechCrunch that because of the snackable content format, users log 95 minutes on the app on average through multiple sessions in a day. “I fundamentally believe that the next billion users will probably not grow up on a diet of watching television; they will grow up on a diet of watching content on their phones, right? And this content has to be, and this entertainment, designed very differently. It’s not going to be appointment viewing. It’s going to be within certain slots throughout the day. And a lot of this was earlier solved for short clips, but serialized storytelling was never solved,” Pandey said about the microdrama format. He believes that there still will be a place for big-screen viewing with family or friends, but the majority of entertainment consumption would be done through mobile. All microdrama platforms compete against platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, where creators are posting content for free. Some of them are also creating a way for creators to post serialized content . Pandey thinks that producing quality content on the platform will entice users to choose Story TV over other free platforms. The company points to its partnerships, such as the one with Indian TV production company Balaji Telefilms , to produce content. The company offers different kinds of subscriptions ranging from monthly, quarterly, and yearly to unlock content. It also offers some free content supported by ads, which might not be as lucrative a medium to make money as subscriptions, according to reports . Monetization is a challenge in India, as users often stick around for free content, but few convert to paid users. A report from analyst firm Redseer indicates that more than 40 million people have paid for microdrama at least once, but only 15 million to 17 million users pay for it on a monthly basis. A separate survey by Ormax Media suggested that 72% of people haven’t ever paid while consuming microdrama . All microdrama platforms want to have enough supply to engage different audiences and want to involve AI to solve that. Some platforms, like Google-backed Kuku, want to improve workflows and create more content , and some platforms like Dashverse’s ShortFree want to use video AI models to create serialized clips . At the moment, Story TV falls into the first camp with its Dolphin AI platform. Started as an internal tool to improve video creation, the company is now planning to make the tool widely available. It can act as an editor with templates and an array of models to create images, audio, and video, according to its website. EloElo’s vision is to have people use this tool for marketing campaigns and ads as well. Notably, while Indian platforms like Pocket and Kuku have built AI tools and given them to creators, it is likely to accelerate their content pipeline. But at InVideo, there hasn’t been a scaled effort to provide a good alternative to CapCut or Instagram Edits to creators from India. Pandey believes that human involvement is still paramount to producing good stories, and AI tools are still creative directors for steering. “My belief in involving AI is that AI is a really fast race car where AI is the engine, but you need an extremely capable Formula One driver to be on the steering wheel. That, for me, is the creative director or the showrunner. AI is supposed to work with them, augmenting their skill set. AI can help write stories, but so far the best stories I have loved have all had a very high human x AI element to it,” he said.

events.title: Josh Turek delivers flips control of Senate with Iowa upset
events.summary: Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson in a major upset Tuesday, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Iowa since 2008, the AP projected and sealing Democratic control of the chamber. Why it matters: Turek's victory delivers Democrats control of the Senate — and signals a political backlash against Republicans in a state Trump won comfortably just two years ago. The big picture: Turek's victory breaks the GOP's hold on both of Iowa's Senate seats for the first time since Democrat Tom Harkin left office in 2015, marking a major breakthrough for Democrats in a state that has shifted right. State of play: The Cook Political Report rated the race a toss-up after moving it left during the campaign as mounting frustration over rising costs, Trump's tariffs and the Iran war put Republicans on the defensive. Zoom in: Turek, a Council Bluffs state lawmaker and Paralympic medalist, built his campaign around affordability and appeals to working-class and independent voters. He criticized Trump's tariffs and other administration policies that he argued were hurting Iowa farmers and families. He also made government ethics and corruption a central theme, including support for a ban on congressional stock trading. Between the lines: Republicans had held both of Iowa's U.S. Senate seats since Harkin retired, while GOP candidates have increasingly dominated statewide races. The bottom line: Turek's win offers Democrats a potential roadmap for competing in increasingly Republican states — and raises questions about the GOP's political strength heading into 2028.

events.title: David Jones on brink of collapse and behind on rent to Westfield
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones on brink of collapse and behind on rent for Westfield stores David Jones has not paid rent since September for its Westfield stores. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) Major Australian retailer David Jones's days could be numbered, as shopping centre Westfield confirms the department store chain has not paid rent since September and is in breach of its contracts. A decision on the future of David Jones could be made within the next 24 hours. The ABC understands the three-person board of the 188-year-old retailer will need to meet imminently to decide whether to put David Jones into administration. Scentre Group, the owner of Westfield, issued a stock market update, revealing its financial exposure to the embattled department store. David Jones has a network of 43 stores in Australia and New Zealand. ( AAP: Dan Himbrechts ) It noted the chain occupied space at 17 Westfield locations and said David Jones had paid "all rent up to 30 September 2026". Scentre CEO Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since September and was "therefore in breach". Lifeline rejected, says Westfield owner Mr Rusanow today said the shopping centre group had offered a lifeline but was knocked back by the private equity owners of David Jones. "We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them," Mr Rusanow said. David Jones was acquired by Anchorage Capital Partners from South African group Woolworths Holdings in late 2022. Scentre's ASX filing noted that David Jones had provided $45 million in bank guarantees for its stores across the Westfield Australia and New Zealand portfolio, of which Scentre's share was about $30 million, equivalent to eight months' gross rent. David Jones's key lender has chipped in extra cash to the store to stock up ahead of Christmas. ( ABC News ) David Jones has a network of 43 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with flagship stores in Sydney and Melbourne CBDs, with about 50 million in-store visits a year and 5 million customers, according to its owners. MST Marquee senior research analyst Craig Woolford said the implications of a David Jones corporate collapse would be "far-reaching". "While never the 'right time', stakeholders will be looking to minimise the impact and maximise any potential recoveries. "Longer-term growth opportunities emerge for better-positioned retailers." David Jones facing 'alarming' speculation The major retailer is being forced to defend its viability amid speculation about department store closures and disgruntled suppliers. David Jones recently failed to file its financial accounts on time with the corporate regulator, ASIC, for a second year in a row. If the board agreed to put the retailer into voluntary administration, thousands of jobs could be made redundant. The news of the possible retail collapse comes a day after the Reserve Bank announced the fifth interest rate hike of 2026. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock expressed some sympathy for those on the wrong side of interest rate hikes at yesterday's press conference. "The fact that we've had this massive shock has meant that we're poorer and that's what people are feeling," she said. The ABC has contacted David Jones CEO Erica Berchtold directly for comment. events.title: Dow soars 1,500 points as Democrats sweep both chambers of Congress
events.summary: Live updates: Follow the latest news on US midterms US stocks rallied on Wednesday after Democrats romped to power in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, while President Donald Trump's acceptance of the midterm election results eased fears of political uncertainty on Wall Street. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed as high as 1,500 points before pulling back slightly as of 9.38pm GST. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were up 1.79 and 2.03 per cent, respectively. A Democratic sweep threatens to challenge cryptocurrency , financial firms, Big Tech and AI titans that have until now benefited from the Trump administration's deregulation agenda. Holding control of the Senate also provides Democrats with vast oversight power. “LAWYER UP,” Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California and the party's top policymaker on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, posted on social media. Big Tech shares were mixed. Nvidia was down 1.55 per cent. Tesla and SpaceX were down 2.48 and 2.87 per cent, respectively, while Meta was up 2.88 per cent and Microsoft gained 6.44 per cent. Google's parent company Alphabet was trading 4.20 per cent higher. Artificial intelligence was expected to be a particular point of focus after Democrats made inroads into Texas and Georgia, where some of the backlash against the AI buildout has been fiercest. Aliasgar Tambawala, chief investment officer at the Klay Group, said a Democratic sweep is unlikely to derail the AI buildout or the billions of dollars in capex spending to fund it. “Any legislation designed to materially restrict AI investment would still face President Trump's veto. He has been explicitly supportive of accelerating data centre construction, domestic technology investment, and reshoring manufacturing,” he said. Mr Trump told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the midterm election results, and was prepared to work with Democratic politicians. The US dollar fell against its group of 10 peers. Yields on the 10-year Treasury slid about 5 basis points to 4.89 per cent, with the yield on the 30-year Treasury sliding about 4 basis points to 4.128 per cent as investors expect Democrats to rein in government spending. “We see the result as mildly bearish for the greenback,” Matthew Ryan, head of market research at Ebury, wrote in a note. “A Democratic Congress is likely to rein in Trump’s fiscally expansionary agenda, easing deficit concerns and taking some of the heat out of the Treasury sell-off.” The price of Bitcoin rose 3.65 per cent to $80,162.16. Crypto corporations poured $206 million into the midterm elections, according to data compiled by Public Citizen. However, a $63 million push by crypto-backed political action groups to oppose a Democrat in Ohio's Senate race failed. Asian stocks In Asia, equity benchmarks slid, reversing earlier gains. MSCI's broadest ⁠index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan fell 0.5 per cent. South Korea's Kopsi slid 3.6 per cent, giving up its earlier gains of more than 3 per cent. Japan's Nikkei index fell 3.5 per cent, while the Hang Seng index in Hong Kong slipped 0.22 per cent. China’s Shanghai SE index also retreated by 0.21 per cent, while stocks in India dropped 0.13 per cent. European stocks rebounded, with the pan-European STOXX 600 index up 1.85 per cent and Germany's Dax gaining 2.23 per cent. Britain's FTSE 100 gained 1.59 per cent.

events.title: Emaar offers Dh15 a share for 100 per cent control of Emaar Development
events.summary: Dubai property developer Emaar Properties intends to make a voluntary cash offer to acquire up to 100 per cent of the shares in its listed unit Emaar Development that it does not already own. The biggest listed developer in the emirate is offering Dh15 ($4.08) per share to investors to take full control of its subsidiary. The proposed offer is subject to approval by Emaar Properties’ board, the company said in a filing on Wednesday to the Dubai Financial Market, where its shares are traded. The offer covers shares not already owned by Emaar Properties and its indirect wholly owned subsidiary, Emirates Property Holdings, according to the bourse filing. With the construction unit valued at more than Dh60 billion at current share price, the potential transaction could cost Emaar Properties as much as Dh12.6 billion, according to Bloomberg. Emaar Properties, the developer of the landmark Burj Khalifa in Dubai, currently owns just over 79 per cent of Emaar Development. Emaar had previously announced plans to increase its ownership of Emaar Development. In March 2022, its board approved a proposal to raise its stake in the subsidiary by up to three percentage points. Emaar raised Dh4.82 billion from the sale of a 20 per cent stake in its development business in November 2017, which at the time was the largest Dubai listing in three years. Emaar Development, which also trades on the DFM, is the property development arm of Emaar, specialising in residential communities and build-to-sell projects in Dubai. Its portfolio includes developments such as Dubai Hills Estate, Arabian Ranches, Emaar South and The Valley. The latest move comes as Dubai continues to navigate the economic fallout from the Iran war, which is now in its ninth month. The company’s ownership structure also shifted in May, when investment company Dubai Holding became the largest shareholder in Emaar Properties after acquiring a 22.27 per cent stake in the developer from the Investment Corporation of Dubai (ICD). One of the largest real estate developers in the Middle East, Emaar has a portfolio spanning residential, commercial, hospitality and retail assets across the Middle East and North Africa, Asia and Europe. Emaar, which has 90,000 units under production globally in 18 markets, is weathering the wave of geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds on the fundamental strength of its business. In September, Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar said that the property market in Dubai was set for a “nice balance” next year despite softening due to the Iran war, as the sector goes through a period of adjustment. In June, Emaar said it would unveil an “extraordinary” Dh200 billion megaproject in Dubai, set to house nearly 150,000 people. Emaar Properties reported a nearly 9 per cent annual increase in its second-quarter profit, as revenue rose during the period despite geopolitical uncertainty. Net profit attributable to owners of the company for the three months to the end of June climbed to Dh3.7 billion ($1 billion), while revenue for the three-month period rose 18 per cent to Dh11.5 billion. In the first half of 2026, net profit surged 22 per cent annually to Dh8.7 billion, as revenue rose 21 per cent to nearly Dh24 billion. Emaar Development also reported a sharp rise in second-quarter profit to Dh2.6 billion, up 43.5 per cent. Revenue for the period surged 32 per cent to Dh6.5 billion. First-half profit rose 48 per cent to Dh5.5 billion and revenue climbed 34 per cent to Dh13.3 billion. Its property sales during the period reached 22.4 billion.

events.title: Chinese stock investors stay on the sidelines even as state intervention gathers pace
events.summary: Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market. Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up its efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply. The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in the markets, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout from an AI stock rout in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

The house of Zen on Tuesday announced its Q3 2026 results, which saw it grow revenue 45 percent year-over-year to $13.4 billion. The company’s Data Center segment won $8.5 billion of revenue, up 97 percent year-over-year. Sales of silicon in AMD’s client and gaming segment slid eight percent to $3.7 billion, a worse fall than the five percent fall that helped to sink Intel’s share price . Intel, AMD’s great rival in the x86 market, offered revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion for its next quarter, which would represent almost no growth. AMD, by contrast, told investors it expects around $17 billion of revenue next quarter. CEO Lisa Su predicted even better days are ahead. “We think 2027 is going to be a very strong momentum year for both the CPU business as well as the data center AI business,” she said on the company’s earnings call. “We have said the overall company will grow greater than 80 percent, and for the data center CPU business, we will about double, and for the data center AI business, it will significantly more than double.” Su said AMD is confident its supply chain can meet that demand. “We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” she said. “We are also deepening our collaboration with our supply chain partners and investing alongside them to secure the long-term capacity our growth will require.” The CEO added that AMD has “strong confidence in our ability to sustain exceptional revenue growth for years to come, with earnings growing even faster.” If those predictions are correct, AMD will likely accelerate away from Intel to become the leading provider of x86 processors after years of challenging Chipzilla's lead. Intel would still have higher overall revenue, due to its foundry operations, but in terms of revenue earned from selling chips, AMD would become the market leader. AMD is arguably already the server CPU technology leader, and while it is second to Nvidia in the GPU market has trounced Intel. Even AMD's declining client and gaming revenue has an upside because it was the gaming part of the portfolio that created the problem. PC chip sales rose seven percent year-over-year to $2.9 billion. Su said strong sales of Ryzen mobile processors drove that growth. “Commercial is becoming a larger part of our client business as large enterprises adopt Ryzen PRO PCs across their employee base,” she said, pointing to strong adoption at the world’s largest banks, automotive companies, and healthcare concerns. Big corporate buyers are often a source of bigger profits and/or steadier revenue, so AMD looks to be taking the cream off the top of the PC market rather than scrounging for SMB and retail scraps. events.title: China Southern Airlines suspends direct Darwin to China route after one year
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts China Southern Airlines backs out of Darwin after one year in the region Direct flights from the Northern Territory to China with China Southern Airlines have been suspended. ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) China Southern Airlines will suspend its direct flights between Darwin and China. The direct route between Darwin and Guangzhou launched less than a year ago. The airline's final scheduled flight to Guangzhou will be on December 3. China Southern Airlines will suspend its direct Darwin to China flights after a year of operation, making it the latest in a suite of scrapped international routes out of Darwin. The Darwin to Guangzhou route launched in December last year and will cease at the end of its current season, with the final flight leaving Darwin on December 3. It was the only flight operating directly between China and the NT, and the farthest-reaching route out of the Territory. A spokesperson from the Airport Development Group (ADG), which operates Darwin International Airport, said the call was a commercial decision by China Southern. Direct flights from Darwin to Guangzhou were only introduced in December last year. ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) "Although ADG is disappointed by the airline's decision, decisions regarding individual routes and service schedules are commercial decisions made by airlines," they said. "Travellers from Darwin continue to have connectivity to China and other international destinations through established hubs including Singapore, Denpasar and Dili." The flight is the latest in a series of short-lived international routes out of Darwin. In 2025, Qantas launched a direct flight between Darwin and Singapore while AirAsia introduced services from Darwin to Bali and Kuala Lumpur. By June 2026, Qantas had reduced its Darwin to Singapore flights to cover the peak tourism season only, while AirAsia had pulled out of Darwin entirely. Darwin International Airport continues to connect passengers to Singapore, Denpasar and Dili. ( Facebook: Darwin International Airport ) The ADG spokesperson said it is exploring other international flight routes out of the Territory capital. "ADG continues to actively engage with airline carriers and other aviation partners about opportunities to strengthen Darwin's international connectivity," they said. Announced in August 2025, the Darwin to Guangzhou route was heralded as a boost to tourism which would deliver 52,000 seats between the two cities each year. In April this year, Tourism Minister Marie-Clare Boothby led a delegation of tourism operators to Guangzhou for talks with travel agents. "This mission was about showing that we are serious about growing our share of the Chinese traveller market," she said at the time. Marie-Clare Boothby said the Darwin to China route was about growing tourism in the NT. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "China — and particularly Guangzhou and the wider Guangdong province — offers the Territory a high-value and highly concentrated market." Northern Territory Chamber of Commerce CEO Glen Hingley, however, says the axing impacts more than just the tourism industry. Mr Hingley said stakeholders across the NT needed to collaborate, making flight routes in and out of Darwin viable for trade as well as tourism. "It's important that for these airlines when they make decisions to come here that they're not just looking at passengers, they're looking at the freight opportunities," he said. Glen Hingley says airline operators should be looking at freight opportunities as well as passengers. ( ABC News: Marcus Kennedy ) "We're the only destination that was flying a 737, the rest of Australia has wide-bodied aircraft, so they're able to make it work from a freight perspective." Mr Hingley said there was ample opportunity for the NT aviation industry and that overcoming the challenge of its small population required cooperation across sectors. "We've got to not operate in silos, whether that's different government agencies, different industry bodies, different industry sectors, and of course the airport," he said. "We're shouting at clouds if we're waiting for the federal government to intervene." events.title: Talarico flips Texas Senate seat in historic Democratic breakthrough
events.summary: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' closely watched U.S. Senate race, delivering a historic breakthrough for Democrats in a state Republicans have dominated for decades. Why it matters: Talarico's victory ends the nation's longest Democratic drought in statewide elections and flips a critical Senate seat as Democrats fight for control of the chamber. The Austin-area state representative becomes the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. His win also marks the first Democratic victory in a Texas statewide election since 1994, a stunning reversal in a state President Trump carried by nearly 14 points in 2024. What they're saying: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We just showed that a politics of division is no match for the politics of love," Talarico told thousands of supporters in Austin. "And we just sent a message to every billionaire mega donor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country — power belongs to the people." The big picture: The race became the nation's most expensive Senate battle after Texas Attorney General Paxton defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, with massive spending from both parties . Republican leaders had warned that Paxton's nomination could jeopardize the seat, and the party poured enormous resources into defending it. On the campaign trail: Talarico, a former public school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, built his campaign around affordability, public education and criticism of wealthy donors' influence over politics. Paxton, a three-term Texas attorney general and close ally of President Trump , emphasized immigration enforcement and conservative policies. Between the lines: Paxton's candidacy exposed divisions within the Texas GOP, with party leaders initially warning that nominating the attorney general could endanger a seat Republicans had held for decades. Paxton defeated Cornyn in the May Republican primary runoff after securing Trump's endorsement, setting up the costly general election battle. His campaign was also shadowed by years of legal and ethical controversies, including his 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House. The state Senate later acquitted him. The backdrop: Democrats have spent decades trying to turn Texas blue, with former Rep. Beto O'Rourke coming within roughly 220,000 votes of unseating Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018. Talarico's win marks a breakthrough for a party that has repeatedly fallen short in statewide contests, even as Texas' population and political landscape have changed. What's next: Talarico will take office in January.

events.title: ‘Not enough energy’ for the world due to geopolitical tensions, says Ducab chief
events.summary: The world needs to diversify its energy sources as geopolitical tensions put pressure on supplies and costs, the chief executive of UAE cable maker Ducab has said. Charles Edouard Mellagui warned that higher prices for raw materials could ultimately reach consumers’ bills. Speaking to The National at Adipec 2026 in Abu Dhabi this week, Mr Mellagui said oil and gas alone would not be enough to meet growing demand. “We have to prepare ourselves to add more energy [sources] because oil and gas are not enough,” he said. “We will need solar. We need wind. We need nuclear. We need battery storage.” He said geopolitical conflicts were putting the global energy system under strain, disrupting the movement of materials and equipment needed to maintain and expand supplies. “Given the geopolitical situation and crisis worldwide, there is not enough energy for the eight billion people in the world,” Mr Mellagui said. “That’s why we see the crisis going through the roof.” He added that geopolitical tensions “exacerbated” the problem and pushed countries to become sovereign in terms of energy. However, he believes the UAE was well prepared. For residents, the pressure could eventually be felt through costs, he said. “At first, they will see it in the bill because if you have raw material going up, of course, at the end of the day, the price will escalate.” Factories stayed open Despite disruption to international trade, Mr Mellagui said Ducab continued manufacturing cables used to carry electricity to homes, businesses and major infrastructure. He credited government support and the availability of ports, roads, lorries and trains for helping the company receive materials from overseas. “We have been able to bring raw materials from all over the world ... and we are able to produce the cable, and we did not close [our operations even] for a single day,” he said. He added that geopolitical tensions can make it difficult to bring the raw material to manufacture and to export, complicating the whole supply chain, while also highlighting the importance of producing locally. Ducab buys more than 40 per cent of its raw materials locally. Mr Mellagui said domestic suppliers had an important role in supporting production when importing became more difficult. “When you cannot import, or you import in a difficult situation, what matters is your ability as a country to produce locally,” he said. The company would still need international suppliers, he added. Local manufacturing was only one part of securing supplies. More equipment made in the UAE Mr Mellagui's comments followed Adnoc ’s announcement on Sunday about offering more than Dh60 billion ($16 billion) in local manufacturing opportunities through 2030. This includes electrical and automation systems, pumps, chemicals, piping and other equipment. Adnoc said producing more of these goods locally would shorten delivery times and reduce exposure to global supply disruptions. Mr Mellagui said demand from major businesses could help strengthen local manufacturers. Delivering power to growing communities New homes, industrial developments and AI data centres are adding to the need for electricity and the infrastructure that carries it. Mr Mellagui said several energy sources would be needed to meet demand. Ducab has supplied cables for major UAE projects including the Al Dhafra Solar Project, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park and Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant . Alongside expanding generation, the industry needed to reduce electricity waste, Mr Mellagui said. Ducab is developing cable designs intended to minimise those losses. He added that energy needs to be secure and available, but also affordable. Rising raw-material costs can push prices up further along the supply chain. AI ‘paying the bill back’ The growth of AI has increased attention on the electricity consumed by data centres. Mr Mellagui said the technology is now helping energy companies become more efficient. “AI is paying the bill back,” he said. “It has learnt, developed, consumed a lot of power, a lot of energy, and now, we are asking this AI to restitute to us what it has learnt.”

events.title: Journalist quizzed over 'nail in the coffin' remark at Jones trial
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Alan Jones trial hears journalist said police involvement would be 'nail in the coffin' for story Journalist Kate McClymont has given evidence for a second day. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) A journalist who broke stories on allegations against broadcaster Alan Jones has been quizzed in his trial for a second day over messages she sent to a complainant's mother. Kate McClymont wrote to a mother of one of the complainants that police involvement in the case would be "the nail in the coffin" for the story. Mr Jones denies indecently assaulting or sexually touching several young men who reported their allegations to the journalist and then later police. The journalist who broke stories alleging Alan Jones had indecently assaulted several men told the mother of one complainant that police involvement in her son's matter would be "the nail in the coffin" and she hoped "shit does hit the fan" for the radio host. NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Sydney Morning Herald chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont has been questioned about her stories on former 2GB host Alan Jones, who has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching in the NSW Local Court. Ms McClymont has been cross-examined for a second day, and has been asked about text messages she sent to the mother of one young man, Complainant A, who alleged he was 17 when Mr Jones kissed him without his consent. The Downing Centre Local Court trial heard Ms McClymont had already published her first story with allegations about Mr Jones when she came into contact with Complainant A's mother, who told the journalist that her son had made a statement to police in 2018, but asked that it was not investigated further at that time. In a snippet of a recorded phone call between Ms McClymont and the complainant's mother, Ms McClymont can be heard saying, "this would be an absolute nail in the coffin if the police were involved". Ms McClymont's messages have been the focus of Wednesday's evidence. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) "That's just brilliant, oh I am breathless," she tells the mother. Questioned about the intent of that comment, Ms McClymont said she did not mean "killing Mr Jones". "On the Friday, the police had said we have received no complaints about Alan Jones and we have not looked at him," she told the court. "The fact that someone has come forward and said we went to police and made a statement… as far as the story goes this is a significant event. "It is the nail in the coffin for the story." Alan Jones has pleaded not guilty to all charges. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) In March 2024, Ms McClymont texted the mother again, to let her know police were looking into other allegations against Mr Jones. "All I want to say is Alan Jones is the subject of a police investigation!!!!" Ms McClymont texted the woman. The court heard a later text said, "I hope the shit does hit the fan for him!" and finished with a smiley face and two 'poo' emojis. The defence has suggested previously that Ms McClymont did not like Mr Jones and was part of a media conspiracy along with broadcaster Ray Hadley and author Peter FitzSimons to bring down the former radio host, by unearthing false allegations against him. Hadley has given evidence in the criminal trial of his former 2GB stablemate. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The court also heard Ms McClymont was tipped off by a NSW Police media unit officer, on her private phone, about Mr Jones arrest in November 2024. Asked if the purpose of that was so that journalists and photographers could be there to capture the moment, Ms McClymont said that it was. The journalist said she declined to provide transcripts or recordings of her private conversations with confidential sources to police, because her sources had not given her clearance to do so. She did end up providing the interviews under court subpoena, the court heard.

events.title: Fake jobs and malicious code used by hackers in largest crypto-heist
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Binance investigation uncovers fake job plot involved in $9 billion crypto-heist Binance has investigated the hack on its assets. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) The crypto-exchange platform at the centre of a $9 billion cyber attack says hackers used job interviews and malicious code to steal the funds. The company says the hackers appeared to take their first steps towards the breach as early as June. It says 98 per cent of the affected assets have been recovered by drawing on its own funds. The world's largest crypto-exchange platform says attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal $US6.6 billion ($9 billion) in funds. The attack on Binance, believed to be the largest cyber attack in the cryptocurrency sector's history, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply. The FBI has attributed the four-hour attack on October 29 to North Korea-affiliated hackers. North Korea has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim "absurd rhetoric". Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack? Binance said the hackers began their plans as early as June. It said they first targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely known programming software Homebrew. Binance's cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company. After building trust with the subject through sharing social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process. The exercise contained malware that deployed "sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques", Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version. That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance's internal systems. Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers. Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack. According to Binance, 98 per cent of the affected assets have been replenished by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire. It said around one-third of the stolen assets had been frozen, meaning the attackers could not use them or convert them to another currency. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Salmon Tasmania is seeking an emergency permit to treat farmed fish with florfenicol to prevent a disease outbreak that caused mass mortalities last year. If approved, some fishing areas would be temporarily closed to prevent export bans being imposed by countries that have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild seafood. The lobster industry is opposed to the closure plan, with one outraged fisherman saying the salmon industry could face large-scale protests. Tensions have escalated between Tasmania's salmon industry and the wild seafood sector over plans to close some fishing areas when antibiotics are used in salmon pens. Salmon Tasmania has applied for an emergency permit to use florfenicol to treat farmed fish affected by a bacterial disease that caused mass mortalities in 2025 . A separate emergency permit issued late last year had to be revoked in March after traces of florfenicol were detected in wild seafood more than 10 kilometres away. The new permit application includes a plan to shut wild fisheries for up to six weeks if they are located within the same zone as salmon pens treated with antibiotics. The closures are designed to avoid trade bans being imposed by countries that have zero tolerance for antibiotics in rock lobster, abalone and other wild seafood. The Tasmanian Atlantic salmon farming industry has been hard hit by disease. ( Tassal ) Under the "Wild Fisheries Market Access Plan", Salmon Tasmania would also provide financial support to affected commercial fishers to ensure they were no worse off. Once implemented, Mr Way said he doubted the closures would be limited to six weeks in future years. "It's only four to six weeks now. What's next year, 12 weeks?" events.title: Alpha Dhabi expects hospitality to play key role in international portfolio
events.summary: Alpha Dhabi Holding is open to seeking more opportunities in the hospitality sector as part of its push to grow its international portfolio, a senior executive has said. The company, which is part of Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company (IHC), generated Dh7.7 billion ($2.1 billion) in revenue from its overseas portfolio companies in the first nine months of 2026, which is more than 13 per cent of its total revenue, it reported this week. “We will remain central to our investment approach alongside disciplined international expansion,” Alpha Dhabi Holding's chief investment and strategy officer Derek Nicholson told The National on Tuesday. “Our hospitality is an area where we can grow internationally … we look for opportunities that build on our capabilities and we're not here just to expand, for its own sake,” he said. Alpha Dhabi, which manages a portfolio of more than 250 public and private investments across 45 countries, has two hospitality units – National Corporation for Tourism and Hotels, and ADMO Lifestyle, the latter of which expanded in Egypt by acquiring the Nammos brand. The Egypt venture is a “model where we are the owners of the IP [intellectual property]”, Mr Nicholson said. He said this was an asset model to expand internationally and had given the group diversification “but we will continue to remain selective and focused on where we believe that we can generate long-term value”. Alpha Dhabi's net profit attributable to owners of the company for the nine months that ended on September 30 jumped nearly 41 per cent year-on-year to Dh7.78 billion, as revenue grew 6 per cent to about Dh58.3 billion. Last week, Alpha Dhabi Holding said it had signed an agreement to commit $1 billion for investments in artificial intelligence companies around the globe, investing through the Alpha Wave Global-managed fund Alpha Wave III. Mr Nicholson said Alpha Wave III was a “long-term investment theme” that also showed the “quality” of the companies New York-based Alpha Wave Global could source. Those companies include AI majors OpenAI and Anthropic, and Elon Musk's SpaceX. The venture fund will give Alpha Dhabi indirect exposure to the tech heavyweights. “When [Alpha Wave Global] approached us with Alpha Wave III, we decided that we wanted to continue our commitment to this sector,” Mr Nicholson said. “We see multi-trillion dollar investment over the next three to five years, and this is a theme where we think there are still opportunities to find best in class companies that are leaders in the sector.” In August, Alpha Dhabi , which was established in 2013, doubled its shareholding and capital commitment in its private credit joint venture with the UAE capital's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Company.

events.title: Stratton's win sets up Senate first for 3 Black women
events.summary: For the first time in history, three Black women will serve simultaneously in the U.S. Senate when Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton takes office in January. Why it matters: It took over 235 years for two Black women to serve in the U.S. Senate at the same time. Two years later, that number will grow to three. Driving the news: Stratton won election to the U.S. Senate on Tuesday, defeating Republican Don Tracy, per AP. She'll join Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), who were both elected in 2024 and became the first two Black women to serve simultaneously in 2025. The Stratton campaign did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. By the numbers: Stratton will become the sixth Black woman to serve in the U.S. Senate and the second from Illinois, where Carol Moseley Braun became the first Black woman ever elected to the chamber in 1992. Former Vice President Kamala Harris became the second Black woman elected to the Senate in 2016. Former Sen. Laphonza Butler became the third to serve when California Gov. Gavin Newsom appointed her in 2023, but she was never elected. The bottom line : Stratton and Sen. Tammy Duckworth will make Illinois the first state represented by two women of color in the Senate simultaneously. Go deeper: Juliana Stratton wins Illinois U.S. Senate race, making history

events.title: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump’s Republicans are routed in midterms
events.summary: Vote counting was under way in the US midterm elections, with Democrats snaring majorities in both houses of Congress for the rest of Trump’s second term. Oil prices rose as traders watched the Iran war, after Democrats won control of the US Congress in the midterms and investors weighed Trump’s next move. Brent and WTI gained 0.7% after earlier falls. Priyanka Sachdeva said Trump’s mixed signals cut trader confidence, but Strait of Hormuz risks still support prices. US strikes on Iran were described as limited. Crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels, far below forecasts, which analysts said was broadly supportive for oil. BEIJING – Oil prices rose on Nov 4 in a volatile session as investors awaited Washington’s next move in the war with Iran, after Democrat s captured control of US Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections. Brent futures rose 76 US cents, or 0. 7 %, to US$104. 36 a barrel at 3.30pm Singapore time . US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 63 US cents, or 0. 7 %, to US$96. 72 , reversing earlier declines. In the previous session, Brent settled at its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. “President Trump’s conflicting signals, with military strikes continuing alongside statements downplaying further escalation, have made it difficult for traders to build strong directional conviction,” said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova. “I believe some profit-taking and reduction in speculative long positions are justified, particularly after the sharp rally in October,” she said. “However, the underlying supply disruption risks around the Strait of Hormuz have not disappeared. An unexpected drawdown in US crude inventories is also offering some fundamental support,” Sachdeva added. The US had carried out “defensive” strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on Nov 3 . Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations. Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to end the US-Israeli war with Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US midterm elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Nov 3 that Iran and the US remain far from a deal to end their war . US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Nov 3 that the US had no immediate plans to strike Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said in the six-minute telephone interview. Meanwhile, crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended Oct 30, market sources said on Nov 4 , citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 barrels in crude inventories. Petrol stocks rose by 1.43 million barrels, while distillate inventories fell by 1.19 million barrels from a week earlier, the sources said. “Diesel inventories remain tight, while petrol stocks rose more than expected. The data are broadly supportive of oil prices,” Haitong Futures said in a note on Nov 4 . Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is due at 10.30am EST (11.30pm Singapore time) on Nov 4. REUTERS

events.title: Dollar dips with US midterm results in focus
events.summary: The yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. SHANGHAI/SINGAPORE – The dollar fell against most major currencies on Nov 4 ahead of results from US midterm elections, with investors bracing for a potentially strong Democratic showing. The first results in the US midterm elections began trickling in, with Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia in the first major race to be called. The question of whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from Donald Trump’s Republicans, though was likely still hours away from a definitive answer. The euro firmed 0.2% to US$1.1212, while the yen strengthened to 158.30 per US dollar in early trading. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of six currencies, edged down 0.2% to 101.7. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 4 basis points to 4.919%. “Given the Democrats are favoured right now, our expectation is that they will take control of both the House and the Senate,” said Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “If that pans out, the US dollar could sell off further from here, because a Democratic sweep would limit government spending over Trump’s term.” As of 7.30 pm ET (8.30am Singapore time), US media outlets had projected winners in a handful of House races after polls closed in 10 states, with voting still under way across much of the country. Kong said investors were also watching the risk of an escalation in the Middle East depending on the election outcome. “If the Republicans do lose control of the House and the Senate, what will the President do? He previously flagged that he will restart a bombing campaign in Iran after the election, so we are watching that very closely,” she said. “If he does ramp up the aggression in the conflict, then we could see oil prices jump sharply higher, and that will support the US dollar.” Oil prices were little changed at US$103.85 a barrel after easing about 1% on Nov 3 to the lowest in nearly four weeks. The market is weighing talks to end the wars in Iran and Ukraine against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. Sterling edged higher to US$1.3440, with traders eyeing the Bank of England’s policy announcement on Nov 5 . The central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee is expected to raise interest rates for the first time since August 2023. China’s offshore yuan last traded at 6.6673 per dollar, stabilising after suffering its biggest one-day drop since May 15 on Nov 3 , when the People’s Bank of China raised the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold in reserve in a move to slow the yuan’s rally. events.title: AMD sales forecast tops estimates on soaring AI chip demand
events.summary: Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3. AMD forecast fourth-quarter revenue of US$17 billion, above estimates, as strong AI chip demand and data centre sales stayed high. The result calmed worries about an AI bubble. AMD shares rose about 6% after the report, and the company’s value hit US$1 trillion in September. AMD’s data centre sales nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion, but PC and gaming sales fell 8%. Gross margin is set to narrow to about 55%. CALIFORNIA – Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), a key challenger to Nvidia in AI chips, gave a revenue forecast that exceeded analysts’ estimates, indicating that demand for data centre processors remains strong. Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion (S$21.7 billion), plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement on Nov 3 . That compares with an average analyst estimate of US$16.3 billion. The outlook provided fresh evidence that AI spending is sustainable, potentially helping soothe jittery investors. Under chief executive Lisa Su, AMD has become one of the most important suppliers of processors and computers that operate at the heart of AI facilities, underpinning a flood of new services. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our data centre portfolio,” chief financial officer Jean Hu said in the statement. AMD shares gained about 6% in late trading after the report was released. Even with recent turbulence, the stock has more than doubled in 2026 . The company’s valuation reached US$1 trillion in September, putting it in an elite group. The data centre growth has helped AMD offset a slump in the personal computer market , where rising memory chip costs have slowed production and depressed user demand . Intel, AMD’s top rival in that field, suffered its worst stock decline in decades after a downbeat earnings report last week. One possible weak spot for AMD: Its gross margin will narrow to about 55% in the fourth quarter. That measure – the percentage of sales after removing production costs – had been 56% in the previous period. AMD’s third-quarter sales rose 45% to US$13.4 billion. Profit climbed to US$2.09 a share, minus certain items. Analysts on average had predicted revenue of US$13.1 billion and earnings of US$1.97 a share. AMD continues to deliver record results and now boasts sales that are twice as big as they were two years ago. It has also been outperforming long-time nemesis Intel in the market for central processing units, or CPUs. But it is still well behind Nvidia in so-called AI accelerators, which are used to train and run artificial intelligence models. Sales at AMD’s data centre business nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion. Analysts had predicted a total of US$8.2 billion. PC and gaming-related sales shrank 8% to US$3.7 billion. Like other makers of components for PCs, AMD is suffering from a side effect of the data centre boom. AI servers require a massive amount of memory. That has cut into the supply of chips available for laptops and desktop machines – and forced prices up. AMD is debuting new product ranges in both the CPU and accelerator markets. The Santa Clara, California-based company is also taking on Nvidia more directly with its Helios server design. But Nvidia, the largest chipmaker and world’s most valuable company, has not been standing still. It is updating its own line-up at a fast pace and branching out into everything from software to networking to complete computers. BLOOMBERG
