events.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space. The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water. This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve. “Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2. Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground. Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station. “That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch. The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long. Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round. Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030. The company is also collaborating with satellite builders that are considering incorporating its PADS (printer-assisted deployment system) into their spacecraft to extend solar panels, antennas, or other components. events.title: Haley Stevens requests U.S. marshals' protection after death threats
events.summary: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens has requested U.S. marshals' protection after the Democrat told authorities she had received death threats for endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the swing state's hotly contested Senate race, two senior Trump administration officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Stevens' surprise decision Sunday to switch her endorsement to Rogers over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed was the biggest political story of the midterm campaign's final days. Stevens — who lost to El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary — was widely criticized by Democrats after siding with Rogers, and her top staff members resigned. "She has received death threats and reached out to the Marshals Service," one of the officials said. "There's a process to go through but she's a member of Congress and we expect her request will be fulfilled." Zoom in: Stevens' support for Israel and his criticism of the Jewish state was a major dividing line in their primary campaign. Stevens objected to El-Sayed's ties to controversial progressive streamer Hasan Piker and an ad by a PAC tied to Piker's uncle, Cenk Uygur, blaming Israel for rising grocery prices. El-Sayed disavowed the ad, but Stevens said she believed he hadn't done enough to address her concerns and didn't want her help on the campaign trail. The dispute came to a head when she was told she was no longer welcome at El-Sayed's campaign events. Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers after appearing with him at a church service on Sunday. Stevens could not be reached for comment Tuesday. The big picture: The political environment in Michigan has been volatile this weekend. On Monday, the New York Post reported a former El-Sayed staffer was one of several anti-Zionist activists federally indicted for allegedly terrorizing members of Michigan's Jewish community. On Sunday, a conservative Jewish activist was attacked by a progressive activist at a University of Michigan event where organizers were criticizing Islam. On Friday, U.S. officials announced the arrest of a Michigan man for allegedly threatening FBI director Kash Patel. Stevens recently clashed with an anti-Zionist activist whom she accused of trying to intimidate her over her support for Israel.

events.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
events.summary: The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month. The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders. The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP. The deal could have the following impact: Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment". Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July. Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his. At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing." Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way. "But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can. "And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration." Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news". "We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop." The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned. "It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said. "You just kind of give up because you're losing money." In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue. "The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added. Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU. Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards". Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix". "The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added. Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules. "Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk.

events.title: Calls for Qld to scrap 'ideologically driven' changes to industrial relation laws
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Proposed changes to Queensland's industrial relations laws 'ideologically driven', law firm says Deputy Prmier Jarrod Bleijie says the changes protect workers. ( ABC News: William Murray ) The Queensland government's proposed shake-up to industrial relations laws is an "ideologically driven" attempt to rehash the Campbell Newman era and should be abandoned, a law firm says. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie has introduced sweeping changes that he says "essentially mimicked" the federal Fair Work legislation introduced by Julia Gillard's government in 2009. However, law firm Maurice Blackburn has taken issue with this comparison in its submission to the committee examining the legislation. "Instead, they represent a cherry-picking of the restrictive provisions of federal law, while omitting the protective ones and going beyond our federal laws in key respects," its submission said. Maurice Blackburn has suggested the legislation be "abandoned" and that if this was not the committee's view, the would need to be "significant reconsideration" of the changes proposed. The legislation is in response to an independent review into industrial relations and the workers' compensation scheme , with the government accepting 104 of its recommendations. The wide-ranging changes include a "fit and proper" test for union officials, allowing workers to be represented by non-recognised union groups and allowing a ballot on a proposal after agreement from one union. Mr Bleijie said he believed the proposed changes were reasonable, balanced and ensured workers were protected. Queensland unions rallied against the government's proposed changes last month. ( ABC News: Curtis Rodda ) Under the legislation, Mr Bleijie would have the power to terminate protected industrial action in certain circumstances. The Queensland Council of Unions has spoken out against the proposed legislation since it was first mentioned in parliament last month, raising concerns it would restrict the ability for workers to exercise their rights and give the minister of the day "extraordinary power". Mr Bleijie said the minister's power to stop strikes would only be used in "very limited circumstances" when the safety or economy was at risk or such action was highly disruptive. Sweeping changes to Qld's industrial relation laws Protected industrial action could be terminated if it would threaten to endanger the life, personal safety, health or welfare or cause significant damage to the state's economy. The legislation also strengthens the test for claiming a psychological injury, requiring work to be the major contributing factor rather than a significant factor, after a substantial rise in claims in recent years. This move has been welcomed by Business Chamber Queensland however it noted this must not "create unnecessary barriers" for those with a genuine injury. The Queensland Law Society submitted the absence of a definition of "the major contributing factor" in the bill would cause "unnecessary complexity" when assessing a claim and lead to more disputes between workers and insurers. Public hearings will be held in Brisbane next week before the committee delivers its report on November 27. events.title: British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted
events.summary: Revolut says that in less than a year it's managed to slash its AI coding inference costs by roughly 90 percent by making self-hosted models its default instead of relying primarily on commercial services like Claude. Speaking at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month, David Abitbol, ops and infrastructure lead at the British fintech, described how it saw a 60 percent improvement in coding time and a 70 percent improvement in lead time following its rollout of AI coding tools to roughly 2,000 engineers. Revolut initially adopted GLM-5.1 before moving to GLM-5.3, which it now serves using 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Prior to its switch to GLM, Revolut had been experimenting with AI, deploying Gemini in early 2025 and Claude Code in early 2026. "We were highly skeptical about the cost of AI. We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI, and so when we launched it we launched it with strict budget limits," Abitbol said. Because of this, engineers only had access to a limited number of tokens, so the company began investigating self-hosting its own models. At $0.30 per million input/output tokens, self hosting GLM 5.1 cost about a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. And, as it turned out, when tokens are cheap, you stop worrying about how many they use or what they use them for. While Revolut did see improvements to coding speed, Abitbol noted the biggest bottleneck wasn't actually the code. Instead, he says the biggest gains came from letting the AI models deal with things like debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. "When you have unlimited tokens, you're free to do that," he said. "You no longer have to save your tokens for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task." Developed by Chinese open weights model dev Z.ai, GLM 5.1 isn't exactly a small model. At roughly 754 billion total parameters (40 billion activated for each token generated), the model requires roughly 380 GB of GPU memory just to hold the weights and another 6-26 GB per user to maintain context depending on precision. To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, equivalent in GPU count to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. But as Abitbol noted, the greatest performance gains didn't come from adding GPUs, but rather tuning the model's hyperparameters along with switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths. One key takeaway was that supporting a one-million-token context window doesn't necessarily make such a large window useful or efficient. "Long context is a scam. You really need to be mindful of that," Abitbol said. "Even though you can serve one million tokens, 256 [thousand] is really what you need." With these optimizations, Abitbol says that the company was able to achieve sub 3-second time to first token on context windows of around 256,000 tokens, and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second, both of which he notes are the sweet spot for the company's software engineers. "What you want to aim for is a sub-3 second time to first token. This is empirical evidence. As soon as you exceed 5 seconds, my Slack inbox starts to blow up," Abitbol said. "In terms of throughput, it doesn't really matter as much. We serve, in terms of interactivity, 200 tokens per second. People are fine [with that]. You don't need to go higher. The way people work has changed. We no longer look at the stream of thinking tokens. People run tasks in parallel and check in when the task is done." And if throughput is a concern, he notes engineers who sign in after 5 pm are getting closer to 800 tokens a second. However, it's worth noting that GLM hasn't replaced GPT or Claude entirely. The Chinese model is text only, so it isn't ideal for things like UI work. So instead, Revolut used a model router to direct vision queries to models like Gemini or GPT Luna while keeping code generation running on GLM. "Open source is now a priority at Revolut, and our economics are favorable. The billing is flat, we don't have any bill shock at the end of the month, and the frontier is the exception," Abitbol said. Having said that, Abitbol acknowledges that Chinese open weights models may be a concern for privacy and security reasons, but emphasizes that the major concern there is accessing them via APIs running out of China. When run on-prem or on regional cloud resources, there's really nothing to worry about. ®

events.title: That dream job offer might be from a North Korean hacker
events.summary: North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday. Why it matters : The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market , posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions. Driving the news : Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company. During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos. The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment. Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker. The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees. So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages. Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process. As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang. Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware. Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47. The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity. Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates , while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market. events.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop. Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months. This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware. That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto. Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft. The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems. These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters. By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.” But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention. While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise. A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack. The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident. The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history. Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph. events.title: Voting machine chaos hits key House battleground
events.summary: Voting machines across New York's Westchester County are rejecting paper ballots on Election Day , raising concerns about potential delays in one of the nation's most competitive House races. Why it matters: The contest between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley has emerged as a key battleground race in Democrats' push to gain control of the House. Catch up quick: The Westchester County Board of Elections said Tuesday it was aware of a problem preventing voting machines from accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. The Board of Elections said it is speaking with New York State officials and the Westchester County government "to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible." New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. The intrigue: Election officials initially blamed the thickness of paper ballots but later removed that explanation from their statement, per reports. The latest: On Tuesday afternoon, the New York State Board of Elections said the malfunction was linked to "an update to the county's election programming" released after initially testing Election Day equipment. Officials said the software update wasn't installed on all machines, leaving them unable to recognize and accept ballots. Officials are still working to restore the machines while voters continue casting emergency paper ballots, which will be counted once scanning resumes. What they're saying: Lawler said on social media officials were working with vendors to resolve the problem, while Conley reassured voters that their ballots would count. Lawler told reporters later Tuesday said both parties are working together to create a solution. "Do not leave the polling place without voting," he said, adding that all votes will be counted Tuesday night. He said "both parties will have representation" when votes are counted "so there be no question, that there be no conspiracy theory and that every vote is counted." Westchester County government wrote on its website: "Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted." What we're hearing: Voters in the county told Fox 5 NY that they had to fill out paper ballots instead of using the machines. Voters said their ballots were placed in a security box. Other voters shared discontent with the ballots issue on social media . Katie Miller , wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, claimed on X: "This is how the Left steals elections. Mike Lawler's competitive district and they are turning away voters." 💭 Thought bubble via Axios' Emily Peck : This is my district. Voting was orderly and not a problem at all this morning. Instead of putting my ballot in a scanner, I put it in an orange security bag. I also grabbed a piece of candy, and an "I Voted" sticker on my way out. Context: The county covers roughly 30% of New York's 17th District, which Lawler represents. Zoom out: The ballot-scanning problems come as technology vulnerabilities have been a key issue heading into the midterms, with researchers saying some vulnerabilities remain in plain sight. Officials in Broward County, Florida, reported a computer glitch that disrupted voting at polling locations early Tuesday, CNN reports. The malfunction reportedly caused systems designed to stop voters from receiving the wrong ballots to reject all ballots. Officials said the issue was resolved. What's next: Voters at affected polling locations were urged to remain in line and cast their ballots. Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about polling glitches in Broward County, Florida.

But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials. Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon. events.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
events.summary: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack . “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services. Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends. This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions . ®

events.title: Airbnb levy needed to 'turbocharge' community housing build, industry says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Community housing industry peak body proposes short-term rental levy to 'turbocharge' new builds CHIA NSW has made several funding proposals to guarantee funding for future community housing builds. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The peak body for the community housing industry has called for land tax changes and a new levy on short-stay rentals to raise $26 billion towards new community housing builds. The NSW social housing waiting list has grown to 72,000, which the Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) boss says is a record. NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson says the government is investing $6.6 billion into new social and affordable homes. A 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals, land tax reform and a rezoning windfall charge are among a suite of recommendations the NSW community housing sector is calling for to boost housing stock and address lengthy housing waiting lists. The Community Housing Industry Association NSW (CHIA) is pitching to the NSW government to adopt measures they say could raise $26 billion over the next 10 years and provide support for around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. Among the proposals analysed by the Labor-aligned McKell Institute is increasing NSW land tax rates from 1.6 per cent to 2 per cent and from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent for larger landholdings, while also adding a new 2.9 per cent rate for holdings above $50 million. The changes would still retain the $1.075 million tax-free threshold and the family home exemption and would bring in an estimated $25.9 billion over 10 years. The community housing industry body says the funding will support around 50,000 new social and affordable homes by 2050. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) CHIA NSW is also proposing a 7.5 per cent levy on short-stay rentals like Airbnb and Stayz, similar to the Victorian scheme that came into force last year. The levy is expected to raise $135 million annually. CHIA NSW CEO Luke Achterstraat said the proposals would help the 72,000 NSW households that remained on the social housing waiting list, which he said was an "all-time record". "Whilst we acknowledge the government's record $6.6 billion building homes for NSW package, we argue that funding should be turbocharged," Mr Achterstraat said. Mr Achterstraat stressed that the proposals were options rather than a full package of reforms. The peak body also suggested a windfall charge for land value increases after rezoning, which would raise $80 million a year. Mr Achterstraat said the revenue should be channelled into a long-term funding pool for community housing for future builds. "We need to move beyond funding cliffs and establish a long-term investment pipeline that gives community housing providers the certainty to keep building homes year after year,” Mr Achterstraat said. CHIA NSW will present the commissioned research at an event in the NSW parliament today. Labor government investing $6.6 billion Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the Labor government was investing $6.6 billion to deliver tens of thousands of social and affordable homes. "We're building 8,400 new public homes that will be owned by the people of NSW and remain part of the public housing system for generations," Ms Jackson said. Rose Jackson says the $6.6 billion is being invested to build tens of thousands of new homes. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "A long-term pipeline of social and affordable housing is essential to tackling the housing crisis. Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said the government was not using the $6.6 billion funding package fast enough and was 40 per cent behind on their National Housing Accord target of 377,000 new homes by 2029. "The social housing waitlist has increased from 55,000 to 72,000 under their watch. This is a massive failure." Mr Rath said the coalition planned to build 12,000 new homes to replace Long Bay Correctional Complex, 30 per cent of which would be social and affordable housing. NSW Greens housing spokesperson Jenny Leong said the government needed to look at rent controls to address the growing social housing waiting list. Her party has called for a rent freeze and then a 2 per cent annual cap on rent increases. Jenny Leong says a levy is a distraction from solutions such as bans and caps by local councils. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "We need investment in public housing, we need government support for genuinely affordable community housing, we need a crackdown on those seeking to profit from the housing crisis," Ms Leong said.

events.title: Multiple bankruptcies surround businessman at centre of T2D dispute
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businessman at centre of T2D dispute has been bankrupt four times Robert Cammarano (left) claims ownership of Career Boss Australia. ( ABC News: Eva Blandis ) The businessman claiming ownership of a company that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times. He was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over more than $2 million in "unreported and unexplained income" used to finance gambling losses. The lead contractors of the South Road project will appear before a parliamentary committee later this month. The businessman claiming ownership of a labour hire firm that won a now-cancelled contract on the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project has been bankrupt four times, including when the company won the public tender. Robert Mark Cammarano was also previously in a dispute with the tax office over whether more than $2 million used to fund gambling losses at Crown Casino was required to be declared as taxable income, the ABC can reveal. Mr Cammarano, 55, is suing in the Supreme Court, claiming beneficial ownership of all 100 shares in labour hire company Career Boss Australia, which in mid-2025 won a contract to supply workers to the Torrens to Darlington (T2D) project. The South Australian government said Mr Cammarano "wasn't a shareholder" when the contract was awarded. He was also not listed as a company director. Mr Cammarano alleges in his statement of claim that bikie Jamie Brown "coerced the transfer" of shares in the company by making "express threats of physical harm". Brown is yet to file a defence but has reportedly said he has "never threatened any shareholder and allegations to the contrary are simply false". Plans for the intersection of James Congdon Drive and South Road under the Torrens to Darlington project. ( Supplied: SA government ) Other respondents to the case have reportedly indicated they will dispute Mr Cammarano's ownership claims to the company. The Malinauskas government asked the T2D Alliance to suspend its contract with Career Boss Australia when Mr Cammarano's court action was reported in the media on October 18. On Monday, the T2D Alliance, led by contractor John Holland, cancelled the Career Boss contract entirely, although a court heard the labour hire company was still owed around $2 million for work performed . Mr Cammarano has been declared and discharged from bankruptcy on four separate occasions, according to Australian Financial Security Authority records. The declarations were made in 2000, 2007, 2016 and 2023. All four bankruptcies were by debtors petition, meaning Mr Cammarano applied to make himself bankrupt. He was not discharged from the latest bankruptcy until February 23, 2026, meaning he was a declared bankrupt when Career Boss Australia was awarded the T2D labour hire contract last year. The Torrens to Darlington project involves major road corridor works in Adelaide's west. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Mr Cammarano was not listed as a Career Boss director when the contract was awarded, according to ASIC records. Asked whether the state government should have known about the past bankruptcies before the contract was awarded, Mr Cammarano's lawyer, Scott Jelbert, told the ABC: "I don't think that they should have known." "He wasn't representing himself as the party they were contracting with," he said, adding that Mr Cammarano's interests were managed through a trust with his family "as the beneficiary". Mr Jelbert did, however, say that Mr Cammarano was not "hiding in the shadows" when Career Boss was preparing to tender for work on the South Road project. "I think they knew of him," Mr Jelbert said of the T2D Alliance's knowledge of Mr Cammarano, adding "he was a bankrupt and that happens". "He was up-front about his involvement with the company, for sure," he said. The project has a $15.4 billion price tag. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) The ABC contacted John Holland but the company declined to comment. Mr Jelbert said one of his client's bankruptcies came following a dispute with the Australian Tax Office over "unreported and unexplained income". Mr Cammarano declared a taxable income of $61,405 in 2017–18 and $61,789 in 2018–19, according to an Administrative Appeals Tribunal judgment. But the ATO amended the assessment based on records supplied by Crown Casino in Melbourne. "Funds used by [Mr Cammarano] to finance his gambling losses represented funds available to him in some form," the judgment said. Crown Casino supplied records to the ATO.

events.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform. “Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.” The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks, and office chairs. The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach. Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week , with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites. Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter. This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S. The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. events.title: Owners of banned NDIS company allegedly funded Ferrari and football club
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Owners of banned Perth NDIS company Adachi allegedly purchased Vic NDIS business Topic: Business and Industry Regulation Adrian Mtungwazi bought Daily Living Disability Services in 2024 with his wife Chiedza Mtungwazi. ( Supplied: LinkedIn ) The directors of a banned NDIS business in Perth have allegedly been able to buy another NDIS provider in regional Victoria. Both companies have gone into liquidation with significant debt, leaving regional clients without care and staff without jobs. The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission is investigating and no charges have been laid. The NDIS watchdog is investigating after the directors of a banned NDIS company that racked up a $6.8 million debt bought another NDIS business in Victoria's Latrobe Valley. Perth-based NDIS operator Adachi Disability Services was banned in February 2024. According to the liquidator's report, its directors allegedly used company funds to pay for a Ferrari, overseas property and fund a Zimbabwean football club called Adachi FC. The liquidator's report revealed that despite the ban placed on Adachi, its directors Adrian and Chiedza Mtungwazi were able to purchase Daily Living Disability Services (Daily Living) in Traralgon using Adachi funds. Daily Living collapsed overnight in March 2026, leaving its clients without care and owing its staff and the Australian Taxation Office an estimated $1.2 million. The closure has left NDIS advocates questioning how the directors were able to purchase the company despite the ban on Adachi, and calling for more checks and balances in the scheme. Peter Earnshaw took his son Liam to Daily Living Disability Services for five years. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) When Daily Living suddenly went into liquidation in March 2026, Gippsland families like Peter and Liam Earnshaw were completely blindsided. Mr Earnshaw's non-verbal autistic son Liam relied on Daily Living's services for five years, five days a week. "It gave him something to look forward to every day," Mr Earnshaw said. "He loved it, all of his friends were there." Clients were left without care and all staff lost their jobs overnight. As a single dad, Peter had to take two weeks off work to find alternative care for Liam, but finding another provider was difficult. "Being in a small town, it's hard to find a provider that's a good fit," he said. The former office of Daily Living Disability Services in Traralgon. ( ABC News: Lily Kristanto ) Mr Earnshaw said the directors should not have been able to buy another NDIS business if their original company was banned by the NDIS. He said the government should have noticed the "multiple red flags" when the directors allegedly bought another business. "There's no checks and balances," he said. "So what they do, they open up under a different company name. It's just too easy." Liam Earnshaw was devastated when Daily Living Disability Services closed down. ( ABC News: Tara Whitchurch ) A Ferrari, overseas property and a football club In his report, liquidator Andrew Yeo from Pitcher Partners, said Adrian Mtungwazi and his wife Chiedza took out "director loans" of $2.3 million. Mr Yeo alleged the couple used company money to buy assets that were "purely for the Directors personal use, including a Ferrari motor vehicle". The liquidator found Adachi company funds were sent to overseas bank accounts in South Africa, the Philippines, United Kingdom and Zimbabwe. Mr Yeo said his investigations indicated "Adrian may also have been providing funds to a Zimbabwe-based football club called 'Adachi FC'". The report stated in 2021 the NDIS watchdog, the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, was aware of alleged "regulatory issues" and alleged Adachi was "mismanaging client complaints". In February 2024, the NDIS watchdog placed a banning order on the company , which Mr Yeo said in the report was due to compliance issues. However in April 2024, the report revealed the directors used company funds to purchase an NDIS service provider in Traralgon, Victoria. When the Mtungwazis bought Daily Living Disability Services, Mr Yeo said they purposefully wanted to avoid being listed on ASIC records. Mr Yeo said the director of Daily Living was a former employee of Adachi and the Mtungwazis informed Mr Yeo that they held shares in the business for the Mtungwazis. "[The Mtungwazis] informed me that the purchase of the business was purposefully structured in a way that neither Chiedza or Adrian would be appointed as a director or shareholder on the ASIC records," Mr Yeo said.

events.title: IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts
events.summary: To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society ’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series. The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple , software company Tavant , and cybersecurity concern Zscaler . Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar . Technical discussions grounded in engineering Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work. Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples. The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations. Extending access through a virtual format The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel. For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization. Examining governed AI agents The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala , a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle. The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows. Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam , a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar. Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly. Building a continuing technical program Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations. Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems. Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community. Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

events.title: Binance hackers used fake job interview in US$6.3 billion attack
events.summary: The attack on Binance has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said hackers used a fake job interview and a tampered advert tool to reach engineers’ computers, then stole US$6.3 billion in crypto in a record attack. The breach began in June and grew through September and October, exposing wallet developers’ systems before the Oct 29 theft. Binance said it apologised and will repay users. The attack raised fresh fears over crypto security and North Korea-linked hacking. Binance is boosting AI detection and plans a security research fund with AI firms. PARIS/DETROIT – Hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two Binance software engineers before using a third’s computer to drain US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) worth of crypto in last week’s record heist, the exchange said on Nov 3. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off what could be the largest ever financial theft, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. Even as Binance scrambled to lock down its system and freeze withdrawals after detecting the attack late on Oct 29, the hackers were still making off with crypto from the exchange nearly four hours after the first theft, Binance said. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has blamed a North Korean hacking group, a claim North Korea has rejected. Binance has said it is repaying all customers whose funds were stolen. The attack has raised questions about how hackers breached the world’s largest crypto exchange after years of North Korea-linked attacks – which have grown in ambition and frequency – and renewed questions about the vulnerability of digital assets to cybercrime. Cybersecurity experts and government officials have for years warned about North Korean and other hackers using phoney job interviews to target employees at companies of interest, said Michael Barnhart, a researcher with cybersecurity firm DTEX. Fake job interviews are a well-known hacking technique. Binance said it had detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyberthreats in 2026. That shows Binance is “just getting barraged”, Barnhart said. Binance said in its report: “This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry.” Binance said the attack began in June when an employee on its wallet developer team downloaded a tool from the internet that hackers had tampered with. The exchange said it detected this afterwards, replaced the device and changed credentials, but the employee’s role and those of others on the wallet team were exposed. A source familiar with the incident said the tool’s malicious version had been placed in an advertisement, which meant it appeared higher in a search engine than the real version. Then in September, a second software engineer seeking a new job downloaded a “malicious code repository” onto the person’s computer after interviewing for what they thought was a legitimate role, including meeting virtually with the chief executive of a fictitious company, Binance’s report said. On Oct 20, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal artificial intelligence tool to gain control of the wallet developer’s system and that of a second wallet developer. Nine days later, the attacker used the second wallet developer’s computer, with stolen credentials from the first wallet developer, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack. A limited number of engineers at the company have direct access to wallets – which store or trade crypto – the source said. The attack unfolded quickly on Oct 29, removing 233.46 million XRP – a cryptocurrency – from five Binance hot, or internet-connected, wallets to an attacker-controlled address in just four minutes, before attackers withdrew other cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin, the exchange said in its report. Binance said it received an internal alert about large transfers and began investigating. It moved to suspend withdrawals, freeze affected tokens and remove unauthorised permissions, resulting in about US$2.85 billion of frozen assets, but suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorised asset movements. Attackers used 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account, while Binance said it was forced to build new procedures to revoke authorisations, slowing its response. The final unauthorised transfer was at 2356 GMT (7.56am the next day in Singapore), Binance said, nearly four hours after the attack began. Binance said as a result of the hack, it was increasing investment in AI-enabled detection and working on establishing a security research fund and targeted initiatives with leading AI companies. events.title: GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather
events.summary: The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather. As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then. The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications , alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience . The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents. High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges. However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site. Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively. Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage. The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure. The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change. Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders. The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators. Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities. When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions. And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators. These include avoiding prescriptive regulations and instead promoting outcome-based policies, encouraging dialog and consultation between governments, regulators, and operators, and developing resilience as a cross-sector responsibility. “Mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure,” says GSMA Foundation president and chief regulatory officer John Giusti. “Whether responding to extreme weather, power failures or other major disruptions, people, businesses and emergency services depend heavily on mobile networks,” he added. “Severe weather is already costing the industry billions of dollars, and those costs are set to rise substantially. Building resilience will require a coordinated effort amongst operators, governments and the wider ecosystem.” ®

events.title: States take steps to secure vote after federal pullback
events.summary: State officials have largely taken securing the 2026 midterm elections into their own hands after nearly two years of federal program and funding cuts during the second Trump administration. Why it matters: The reduction in federal support has come as AI tools threaten to make it easier for hackers to uncover software vulnerabilities, launch cyberattacks, and spread disinformation that undermines trust in election results. Reality check: Just because a security flaw exists doesn't mean hackers can exploit it to manipulate election results. Nearly all U.S. elections maintain paper records that can be used to verify electronic tallies. Threat level: Election officials are preparing for everything from cyberattacks and AI-generated disinformation to physical threats, logistical disruptions and legal challenges. The big picture: State election officials relied on homeland security agencies, fusion centers, police, National Guard units and private cybersecurity firms to prepare for the midterms, John Milhofer, a spokesperson for the National Association of Secretaries of State, told Axios. That group and the National Association of State Election Directors are helping states exchange threat intelligence and connect with federal agencies and private sector experts. Catch up quick: State resources have become more important after the Trump administration scaled back federal election security assistance. CISA cut election security personnel and services in 2025, while federal funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a key information-sharing network for election officials, ended that year. Election officials are receiving fewer election-specific threat briefings and less direct technical assistance, even after CISA outlined plans to restore some services in September. Zoom in: Michael Moore, chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office, told Axios that the state has been without a dedicated CISA cybersecurity adviser since March 2025. The Arizona Department of Homeland Security has helped fill the gap, providing security tools and monitoring services to smaller counties. On Election Day, Arizona is bringing together its state cybersecurity team, National Guard, the FBI and a representative from CISA's Region 9 office to coordinate responses to potential threats, Moore said. Moore's team has spent years conducting tabletop exercises covering cyberattacks, AI-generated impersonations of election officials, suspicious packages and other disruptions. Between the lines: Arizona is also getting threat intelligence from former CISA personnel who work in the space, election security nonprofits and officials in other states. Moore said his relationship with New Jersey's election security officials is particularly useful because his East Coast counterparts can warn him about threats hours before they might emerge in Arizona. What they're saying: A CISA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency will provide state and local government officials, including election officials and election vendors, "no-cost voluntary services" like vulnerability scanning and technical expertise, when they request it. "We are committed to supporting state and local elections officials to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy," the spokesperson added. Yes, but: Moore said he still wants CISA to return to its 2024 staffing levels — and then double them. "If we are literally experiencing a cyberattack from a nation-state, it shouldn't be Arizona versus that nation-state," Moore said. "We're the United States of America. It should be a unified response." David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, told reporters during a briefing Thursday that states have hired vendors and built their own networks to compensate for the federal retreat. "They might not be able to replace everything," Becker said. "They're not going to get the same bird's-eye national-level view of potential disinformation or potential cyber events." The bottom line: Election officials said they're prepared for disruptions, even if they can't prevent every attack. "The goal is prevent as much as we can, detect and recover," Moore said. "We're going to have some amount of disruption.... We're going to recover."

events.title: Improved asteroid deflection model runs faster, reveals more doomsday worries
events.summary: Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a method to make asteroid deflection modeling faster and more detailed. Their simulations also demonstrated just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate efforts to deflect a threatening space rock. Sandia researchers, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, were looking for a way to better model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid can change its trajectory, as explained in a recently published research paper . “Before, the calculations were so time-consuming, one could not do very many of them,” Moore told The Register . “So it was very difficult to explore different scenarios, different asteroids, or different mission concepts.” The complexity of those calculations forced earlier researchers to make compromises, often modeling asteroids as spheres or simplifying the physics involved. Perfectly spherical asteroids are rare, and their irregular shapes present an additional challenge for those keeping an eye on the skies to avert a potential asteroid apocalypse. To overcome the computational problem and enable better modeling of irregular asteroid shapes, Moore and his team combined two high-fidelity simulation codes already in use at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates the behavior of low-density gases. As Moore explained to us in an email, both codes are good at one particular part of asteroid impact modeling, but bad at the other. “ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” Moore told us. “This is a problem for asteroid deflection simulations, because as the gas expands around the asteroid, the calculation time goes up.” Earlier asteroid simulations using ALEGRA typically modeled asteroids as spheres to reduce calculation times. “SPARTA is more efficient at low gas densities,” Moore said. “The problem is, conversely, SPARTA gets more difficult to run at high gas densities. So the key here was using both codes.” In Moore’s model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA tackles the more dilute regions of an irregular shape. The result is two codes handling the parts of the problem they're best suited to solve, reducing the overall computational burden. The combined approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods, Moore said in a Sandia press release , while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection in irregularly shaped asteroids. Moore data, more problems The improved simulations reveal just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate attempts to calculate the outcome of a nuclear deflection. “We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.” Deflection simulations using detailed models of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu, and Itokawa – found that irradiating different sides of the same asteroid with X-rays from a nearby nuclear detonation could produce as much as a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences in deflection velocity depending on which side faced the blast. In other words, we need to be incredibly precise about where we detonate a nuclear device near an asteroid, or we risk giving it a much smaller shove than intended. With that in mind, the paper points out that we might know little about an incoming asteroid, and might not have enough time to get a good picture of it before attempting to deflect it and prevent life as we know it from ending in a planet-wide conflagration. We also can’t be quite sure an asteroid’s orientation will cooperate once our deflecto-bomb arrives. The team also pointed out that it’s tricky to get an accurate prediction without knowing the composition and internal structure of an asteroid. One small step for asteroid deflection, one giant heap of new things to worry about, in other words. But hey – at least we’re no longer limited to deflection models that treat asteroids as perfect spheres, even though the real threats are likely to be considerably lumpier. Let’s just hope we spot an asteroid threat from far enough away that we get a chance to study it first. ®

events.title: Keeping mortgage interest relief approved
events.summary: The States agreed to phase the tax relief out in 2015, but it was frozen between 2024 - 2026 A move to keep tax relief on interest paid on mortgage payments has been approved. Deputy Aidan Matthews, who brought the amendment to the Budget in Guernsey, said it was currently the "worst possible time" to consider phasing out the tax relief. It also meant that the phased withdrawal of the relief, which was agreed in 2015, would also stop, it was confirmed. The relief allows homeowners to apply for tax relief on any interest paid on the mortgage of their principle residence of up to £3,500 a year. Speaking against the move, Deputy Neil Inder said that, while the idea was right in isolation, if all amendments were approved, it would add "£20m to the budget". Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Alderney representative Alex Snowdon said the timing of the amendment was "important". He said: "There is a lot of Guernsey and Alderney people will be working two to three jobs that are really struggling to try and support the mortgage and their families. "I think this sends a strong message that we are trying to do a little bit to try and help people who are going through a very difficult time. "Some might say [these are] normal interest rates, but we've had money so cheap for so long that we are getting back to more difficult interest rates because house prices are going up so much people are borrowing so much more money." Deputy Jayne Ozanne said in the debate that she was "very split" on the amendment because it was an "unfair advantage" to homeowners over renters. "This will not solve the crisis of people leaving the island," she said. "They can not afford to save for a deposit for a mortgage because they are paying such high rents," she said. "Their monthly outgoings does not allow them to create the capital egg that they need to put a deposit down. This will not help that; it may help them once they've got a mortgage to decide to stay. "I'm wrestling because I feel there is an inequality here... the average rent in the island is over £2,000 per month while the average mortgage, I believe, is £1,000. "But two wrongs don't make a right. I recognise that families are feeling squeezed." Follow BBC Guernsey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . Send your story ideas to channel.islands@bbc.co.uk , external .
