events.title: Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station
events.summary: Britain's AI infrastructure boom could soon have an unlikely new home: Drax Power Station, where the operator of the country's largest biomass power plant has unveiled plans for a £20 billion datacenter development capable of consuming more than a gigawatt of power. Drax announced on Tuesday that it has teamed up with investment giant Brookfield and its UK-based AI infrastructure business Radiant to build the facility at its North Yorkshire site. The money would come through a joint venture between Brookfield and Qatar's Qai, although the £20 billion headline figure is more ambition than actual money on the table at this stage. The companies plan to start relatively small, at least by the standards of the AI industry's apparently bottomless appetite for electricity. The first phase would deliver up to 100MW of capacity by early 2028, backed by a proposed £2.5 billion investment. A second phase could add another 500MW between 2028 and 2031, with further expansion taking the site beyond 1GW after that. However, a few hurdles remain between today's announcement and a functioning AI megafactory. According to Drax's regulatory filing , the first phase still requires planning permission, regulatory and network approvals, commercial agreements, and final investment decisions. It also needs a tenant, which is a fairly important detail when you're proposing to spend billions on somewhere to house other people's computers. Drax reckons its existing infrastructure gives it an advantage over developers struggling to secure electricity connections. The 1,000-acre site already has access to 4GW of grid capacity, 2.6GW of active generation and cooling infrastructure, along with proximity to the UK's fiber network. The UK government estimated last week that all of Britain's existing data centers use around 2GW of electricity. Drax's proposed development alone could eventually need more than 1GW, although how much power it actually consumes will depend on how fully it's used. The first phase would draw electricity from the grid, but Drax wants to supply up to 500MW directly from its existing generating capacity under a long-term power purchase agreement, potentially allowing AI servers to run on electricity produced by burning imported wood pellets. That brings another complication. Drax signed a government-backed Contract for Difference agreement last year covering biomass generation between April 2027 and March 2031. The agreement allows the company to request permission to redirect up to 500MW of capacity towards a datacenter, but ministers and the Low Carbon Contracts Company would have to agree, taking into account consumer value, energy security, and sustainability. The announcement also arrives as enthusiasm for enormous AI server farms is proving rather less universal outside government and industry circles. Opposition to data center developments has been growing on both sides of the Atlantic, with communities raising concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, and the impact of industrial-scale facilities on their surroundings. A recent investigation found that businesses accounted for 84 percent of the stakeholders UK ministers met to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, while environmental groups secured precisely zero meetings. Drax and its partners are promising a community benefits fund and say public consultation will begin this month. Whether that will reassure residents concerned about another enormous consumer of electricity is a moot point. Drax CEO Will Gardiner said the project could "help secure the long-term future of the site and protect hundreds of jobs," while supporting Britain's ambitions to become a major player in AI. The government, unsurprisingly, is enthusiastic. Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds welcomed the proposed investment as an opportunity to create jobs and support Britain's reindustrialization. “Investments like this will help pave the way to a new age of British reindustrialization, creating good jobs in Yorkshire and delivering growth right across the country,” she said. Ministers may be enthusiastic, but Drax still has to find a customer, secure planning permission, and convince regulators before anyone starts plugging in servers. ®

events.title: Saudi Aramco reports profit surge on higher oil prices
events.summary: Saudi Aramco reported a 9% rise in profit and increased dividend payments, most of which go to the Saudi state, as a jump in crude prices more than made up for lower production. Profit rose to $31.2 billion in the third quarter, driven by a 35% increase in the average selling price of its oil, even as the company tackled repeated attacks on its facilities from Yemen’s Houthis and Iranian strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite Aramco’s ability to export oil at higher prices, its stock has lagged the global majors that mostly operate outside the Gulf. Although lower than prewar levels, Aramco reported higher oil production than the previous quarter as it embraced more risky ship-to-ship transfers to get crude out through Hormuz and boosted shipments through the Red Sea. Aramco is looking to maximize production through the end of the year, “utilizing all the routes that we have,” and sees buoyant demand lasting for several years, CEO Amin Nasser said on an earnings call. It could take two years to refill depleted global oil storage reserves even if the Iran war was resolved today, Nasser said. — Matthew Martin

events.title: At ADIPEC, war is the challenge and AI the opportunity
events.summary: Mohammed’s view Abu Dhabi’s annual energy exhibition is buzzing, tangible proof that the UAE has absorbed the blows of the Iran war and has its eye on the future. Most conversations I’ve had at ADIPEC, one of the biggest events on the global calendar, have focused on opportunities: oil above $100 a barrel, a new unconventional oil play being unlocked in the UAE, fusion, AI, and infrastructure upgrades. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke at the opening ceremony, a symbol of the close relationship between energy and technology. There’s plenty to be excited about in the industry that remains the Gulf’s economic lifeblood. But this ADIPEC isn’t like its predecessors, and it’s not just because of the war. The UAE’s decision to leave OPEC has changed the gathering’s makeup. This event previously brought together the group’s energy ministers, with major decisions made on the sidelines. This year, Saudi Aramco doesn’t even have a booth, a sign of increasingly fractured Gulf business relations. While the biggest Saudi, Kuwaiti, Omani, and Qatari companies stayed away, the rest of the world is here, with participants from more than 170 countries. Yet the absence of top executives from ExxonMobil and Chevron, as well as US government representation, has been noticed. Amos Hochstein, a former senior energy and national security adviser to President Joe Biden, was forceful in his critique : “I think they should be here,” he said of US officials. “The United States and UAE are close allies, you have to be here when it counts.” The war is transforming everything in the region, from trade flows to alliances, but the conflict itself may, in hindsight, seem temporary. The bigger shift will arguably come from AI, determining the future winners and losers. Hochstein said the UAE is a “critical partner for the US when it comes to AI buildout,” and Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and managing director and group chief executive of ADNOC, stressed the point by having Altman as the guest of honor. ADNOC agreed to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, part of a partnership with OpenAI and G42 to improve operations, strengthen resilience, and increase productivity. “From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI,” Al Jaber said. “And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” Notable Energy executives in Abu Dhabi are saying disruption is now a permanent feature of their business, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Reading the signs of war in the Gulf
events.summary: Separating signal from noise on whether the US-Iran war will escalate has been difficult for months, and now it’s a cacophony. Oil prices plunged on Monday on hopes of a deal with Tehran before jumping almost 2% Tuesday after the US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, reportedly in response to Iranian fire at an American plane . Yemen’s Houthis are still attacking Saudi Arabia and have advanced toward Aden, threatening to outflank Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and potentially extend Iran’s influence to Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf’s other maritime chokepoint. Then there’s diplomacy. US President Donald Trump told Axios he’s in “ no rush ” to resume strikes and repeated that Tehran wants a deal. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks are also returning to Abu Dhabi next week, with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner expected to attend, making an escalation during their visit seem less likely. The US midterm elections Tuesday are perhaps the noisiest indicator. Democratic control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in his last two years, potentially accelerating military plans before the new Congress takes office in January. But the president will still have considerable foreign policy powers. The final signal probably matters most: Where are the bombs and planes? Three US aircraft carrier strike groups are expected to arrive near Iran within two weeks , with the USS Theodore Roosevelt the last one to make its way from Japan. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Virgin Media O2 outlines plans to lay off thousands as revenue falls
events.summary: Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) wants to chop a third of its labor costs and is expected to lay off thousands of workers, giving staff more to think about than Christmas presents during the run up to year-end. Shrinking the workforce is one of a number of cost reduction measures designed to save the UK's second largest telecoms provider some £800 million by 2029. It currently employs 16,000 people and redundancies will "equate to roughly 30 percent of the company’s total people costs" over the next two years, VMO2 said on Tuesday. The majority of the redundancies will come from "non-customer facing roles," it claimed. The Register asked the telco to be more specific on the headcount cuts and the type of roles are at risk. A spokesperson refused to provide a number, saying those plans are being finalized and consultations are due to take place. Logically, if more senior head office positions are hit then fewer people will need to leave to meet the £300 million ($402 million) target figure. The Reg understands thousands of roles are at risk. Another lever management at VMO2 is pulling involves halting investment in any further fiber network upgrades beyond existing commitments. Instead, a low-cost upgrade will be deployed to its hybrid fiber-coaxial (HFC) network (i.e. cable customers) to bring 2 Gbps services to the majority of the network in 2027. Full fiber merger pledges VMO2 was formed in 2021 by the merger of broadband and TV biz Virgin Media and mobile operator O2. The pair pledged to spend £10 billion (c $13.4 billion) on beefing up 5G coverage and laying gigabit "full-fiber" fixed-line networks. Both Virgin Media and O2 talked up those connectivity commitments when justifying the case to combine their businesses, saying they needed greater economies of scale to compete with their rivals. However, business has not gone as planned, with revenue falling over several successive quarters. The latest figures for Q3 ended September 30 show total revenue down 5.7 percent year-on-year to £2.43 billion. The networks giant blamed consumer fixed market pressures, among other things. VM02 forecasts a revenue decline of 3 to 5 percent for the whole of 2026. In the consumer division, VMO2 talked of more clearly defining the role for each of its brands. O2 Business is planning to streamline the product portfolio. Tom Oughton, senior analyst at Megabuyte, said the changes were expected. "VMO2 has undergone a strategic review as it looks to address rising leverage, with today confirming a transformation program to ultimately bring c. £800 million ($1bn) in cost savings ahead of its first debt expiry in 2029. The routes to achieve this are the most obvious ones: reduce capex on full fiber and focus on HFC upgrade (lower cost, quick payback) and reduce operational costs by cutting headcount," Oughton said. "The obvious question is how a significant transformation will impact the business. VMO2 focuses on the benefits, but the business is declining 3-5 percent organically with 16-17k staff, so reducing headcount by 25 percent or more could stretch operations, worsen customer support, and cause broader disruption." Paolo Pescatore, founder and analyst at PP Foresight didn't mince his words either: "Virgin Media O2 is in serious trouble, with customer losses and declining service revenue and earnings exposing the scale of the challenge." "The business has lost its strategic direction, and continued customer departures suggest it is struggling to rebuild trust while rivals give people compelling reasons to switch. Cutting costs can buy time, but it cannot repair those relationships or compensate for weak execution," Pescatore added. "Management must show customers why they should join and stay; otherwise, it risks shrinking the business without fixing what is driving people away. Shareholders need to take a hard look at these businesses and make even tougher choices about their future." Noel McClean, deputy general secretary of Prospect union, said the job cuts " will be devastating for those directly affected and will of course have an impact on colleagues remaining in the business. "Industry conditions are tough but this level of cuts will drastically alter the way VMO2 works." ®

events.title: The US midterms decide who gets blamed for the economy that’s coming
events.summary: Liz’s view Today’s US midterm elections are a race to see who gets blamed for a host of economic problems coming down the pike. Democrats are favored to take the House, with control of the Senate still a toss-up. Whoever wins Congress inherits a stack of problems due to detonate over the next two years — just in time to crater 2028 ambitions — and few have obvious fixes. Inflation is running around 3.7%, rising in six of the past eight months, and the Fed has gone back to unpopular tightening. That a Trump-picked Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, is leaning hawkish into a midterm election underlines how stubborn the problem is. The labor market is no better. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September; July was revised into negative territory. Companies too uncertain about what’s ahead — and unsure of exactly how AI is muddying the employment picture — are neither hiring nor firing, leaving things in what Jerome Powell earlier this year called “ an uncomfortable kind of balance. ” Then there are the outside shocks. Reports that the White House is planning post-midterm strikes on Iran may push political fallout from an unpopular war outside the election window, but the economic weight of high gas and diesel prices lands on whoever’s nominally in charge come January. Those are the known unknowns. AI brings another set of unknown unknowns: A financial squeeze waiting to happen, as investment shows no signs of slowing down even as the returns on that investment appear even further out than we thought. A leaking AI bubble is likely to burst on the next Congress’s watch (as always, look to the jittery credit market , not the booming stock market, for signs of what’s to come). The second problem is political, and Congress has punted on it. Lawmakers left town in September with no movement on AI guardrails. Dozens of data-center moratoriums and AI referendums appear on the ballot today, with more than 20 in Ohio alone . Even some of President Donald Trump’s media allies concede that he owns the narrative on the economy no matter what happens on Capitol Hill. But a Democratic Congress would give the White House a foil it hasn’t had since the back half of Trump’s first term, and every stalled bill, shutdown, and soft jobs report could be pinned on the people holding the legislative pen — and subpoena power (more on that below in today’s newsletter). Either way, the winners tomorrow aren’t claiming a prize so much as signing for a package. Notable Who controls Congress will make little difference to the economy, analysts argue. “A lot of voters head to the polls Tuesday hoping for a fix for affordability,” The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator wrote. “ They are going to be disappointed .”

events.title: Corporate America prepares for post-midterm Democratic backlash
events.summary: The witness-prep business is about to take off for Washington law firms. As Democrats appear poised to take the gavel, at least in the hearing-happy House of Representatives, the task of helping corporate executives prepare for their turn in the chair — a DC practice known as “murder-boarding” — will be in high demand. Democrats have been plotting for months about how to go after corporations that have courted Trump’s approval, Semafor’s Nicholas Wu reported earlier this year, citing missives sent to companies over things like ballroom funds, antitrust suits, and business deals involving the Trump family and one-time “first buddy” Elon Musk. “Companies that made investments or commitments at the president’s urging should prepare for scrutiny,” said J. Peter Donald, a former spokesman for the FBI’s New York field office and assistant NYPD commissioner who now advises companies in tight spots. “Everything will be on the table. CEOs should be ready to explain their decisions under oath.” It’s a good time for companies to prepay any outstanding law firm bills and book some time on CEOs’ calendars for mock grilling. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal. Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice. Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave . —Amit Katwala Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.” But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks. So one month in, who’s on board? —James O’Donnell This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. events.title: Tech companies rummage for cash to fund the AI buildout
events.summary: Tech companies are turning over the couch cushions in their hunt for money to fund the AI buildout. Meta is prepping a big bond offering that includes its first-ever euro borrowing for up to $15 billion, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor, while Alphabet closed its second euro deal of the year. The tech giants that have run through US markets are now turning to other pools of capital. Alphabet this year issued its first-ever British sterling bond — a rare “ century bond ” that comes due in 2126 — along with deals that tapped Swiss and Japanese debt markets. For most companies, broadening lender bases is a test-the-pipes exercise to ensure that diverse funding is available if it’s needed. For hyperscalers today, it’s a globe-trotting bush-beating that’s crucial to funding the AI buildout that’s propping up their stock prices. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
events.summary: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg , Microsoft 365 , and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs , the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July. Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats. The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream. As reported last week , the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy. Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses. An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government. In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience. "For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report. "We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. "The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all." Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk. The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

events.title: Adipec: Welsh companies look to UAE for energy sector growth
events.summary: Welsh companies are looking to increase business with the UAE energy sector, with some already relying on the Middle East for more than half their sales. A Welsh delegation of more than 16 companies is attending Adipec in Abu Dhabi, representing fields such as electric energy, maritime vessels and industrial equipment. Holyhead Towing has operations in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar, and managing director Dylan Jones told The National the region now accounts for 70 to 75 per cent of its revenue. “We have eight vessels working here in support of the energy sector, predominantly oil and gas,” he said. “Also, infrastructure-type projects like land reclamation are quite big around Dubai and Abu Dhabi.” Attending Adipec is an ideal opportunity to meet customers in the one place, said Mr Jones. The Welsh government is supporting companies attending the exhibition through an export visit designed to help them meet customers and develop business overseas. Another Welsh firm, Tomoe Valve, exports about half its UK factory output to the Middle East, with the UAE accounting for its largest regional market. For the manufacturer, repeat visits to Abu Dhabi have helped build a market for products made in Wales. “The Middle East is obviously a large attraction for us,” the company's business development director Clive Johns told The National . “About 50 per cent of our capacity is exported to the Middle East from the UK factory.” Tomoe manufactures butterfly valves used to control the flow of liquid and gas through pipes. Its products were originally designed for the oil and gas industry, making the Middle East a natural market. The UAE now accounts for most of Tomoe Valve's regional business. Mr Johns said the Welsh government has always had some “very good” contacts in the Emirates, with the help of the British embassy. He now wants to develop work in Oman, Kuwait and Iraq. “Adipec is the place to do business in the Middle East, not just UAE,” Mr Johns said. The company entered the year with a strong order book, although projects have been taking longer to receive final investment approval amid regional uncertainty. “Stuff is still moving,” Mr Johns said. “But yeah, it [uncertainty] slowed things down.” As the UAE places increasing focus on localisation, the company is considering how domestic partners could take on assembly, testing and other work. Establishing its own factory would be expensive, Mr Johns said. However, he added they “definitely want to work with local Emirati companies”. For Clenergy EV, chief executive William David said growth in the region has created opportunities for charging infrastructure. “For us, the target market is any building that needs electric-vehicle charging infrastructure,” he said. Its priority at the exhibition is to find partners who understand domestic customers and can represent Clenergy. Mr David said Wales’s industrial history has continued to influence its energy businesses. “We were part of the Industrial Revolution. We had the coal mines transitioning to renewable power in Wales.” The company now intends to establish its business in the UAE's expanding transport and property market.

events.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026 some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014 there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.

events.title: Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans
events.summary: Apple says it sold more Macs in fiscal 2026 than in any previous year, but soaring memory prices are threatening to spoil the Cupertino-based gadget maker's record-breaking run. The warning came during Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO . "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts. Apple has already raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, including Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Those increases, along with existing inventories and cheaper components elsewhere, have softened the blow. Unfortunately for Apple, memory prices haven't finished climbing. "For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs," Ternus said, adding that Apple expects to pay more for memory beyond the end of the year. Mac buyers haven't been deterred so far. Apple pulled in $10.8 billion from Macs in the September quarter, up 24 percent year-on-year, following $10.35 billion in the June quarter, up nearly 29 percent year-on-year. The MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro accounted for much of the latest growth. "We have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time," Ternus said. Whether Apple can keep enough of them on shelves is another matter. COO Sabih Khan said the company had already experienced supply constraints across iPhone, Mac, and iPad during the September quarter, largely because of limited availability of advanced chipmaking capacity. Now memory is taking over as the chief headache. "For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected," Khan said. Apple isn't sitting idle. Ternus revealed that its manufacturing purchase obligations jumped by $33 billion between June and September as it bids to secure supplies, although he offered no indication of when the memory crunch might ease. Higher memory costs are also squeezing Apple's margins. CFO Kevan Parekh said gross margin fell by roughly one percentage point between the June and September quarters, excluding tariff effects, entirely because of memory costs. The damage would have been worse without existing inventory, cheaper non-memory components, and those price hikes. Apple expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to between 45 and 46 percent in December, primarily because of higher memory costs. Costs associated with rolling out Siri AI will also weigh on the figure. Parekh said Apple had "reluctantly" raised hardware prices, but supply constraints made it too early to assess how customers were responding. Meanwhile, Ternus is keen to sell customers on the Mac as an AI machine, particularly for running models locally. "Mac mini and Mac Studio in particular are pushing the boundaries of local private AI," he said, pointing to workloads that previously would have been difficult to run on desktop hardware. Apple has also refreshed its Mac lineup with M6-powered machines and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, giving customers more reasons to upgrade, provided there's enough memory to build the things. Not that the wider business is struggling. Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year-on-year, while iPhone revenue climbed 17 percent to $57.6 billion. Services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10 percent. Apple forecasts revenue growth of 7 to 10 percent in the December quarter despite the supply constraints. Even with memory prices running wild, it isn't expecting to go hungry. ®

events.title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
events.summary: Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga. Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme. That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year. But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit. The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case. Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice. "Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means." The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold. They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year Published 1 day ago Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced. With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost. Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait". "By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson. "Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them." The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks". But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer. Guidelines on whether to accept an offer The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers , external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders. It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed. The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes: Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty." But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered. "These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said. The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February. Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed".

Dist. 4 Projected winner Laura Gillen • D 1 hour ago Election 2026 live results: Trump defends Iran war after Vance blames it for GOP losses Saudi Aramco is reporting a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit, boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of a stake in a Malaysian company FRANKFURT, Germany -- Majority state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco on Tuesday reported a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit as earnings were boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of its stake in a Malaysian refining and petrochemical company. Net profit rose to $36.3 billion from $26.9 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Adjusted net profit, which leaves out the sale of a stake in PRefChem to Malaysian state oil company Petronas, rose 9% to $31.2 billion. The company also benefitted from high profit margins at its refineries turning crude into useable products such as diesel fuel. Saudi Aramco sold its oil for an average of $95.20 a barrel during the quarter, compared to $70.10 in the year-before quarter, the company said in a news release. Oil prices surged after the outbreak of the Iran war due to disruption of supply and uncertainty about the course of the conflict. events.title: Long-term demand for LNG will continue to rise, Adnoc Gas CEO says
events.summary: Demand for gas will continue to rise as the world requires more energy to power the development of artificial intelligence, the chief executive of Adnoc Gas has said. Severe disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has shut down about one fifth of the world’s monthly liquefied natural gas supply since the Middle East conflict started in February, adversely affecting some countries in Asia, Shell said in its latest LNG outlook. But Fatema Al Nuaimi told Adipec on Tuesday: “Gas is going to continue to grow and demand is going to continue in the long-term.” Ras Laffan in Qatar, the world's largest LNG refinery, was severely damaged by Iranian missile attacks. QatarEnergy declared long-term force majeure on contracts with buyers in China, South Korea, Italy and Belgium. However, global demand for LNG is projected to increase by around 65 per cent by 2050, to nearly 700 million tonnes a year, Shell said in its report. A key driver for growth comes with the rising development of new data centres to power AI technology. “We have these new demand hubs from AI … about 9.5 million tonnes of LNG required just for SpaceX,” Ms Al Nuaimi said. “We are an ambitious nation when it comes to building AI hubs to attract the biggest names in artificial intelligence and for this to be materialised, energy is required.” Abu Dhabi is investing heavily in AI infrastructure to support the growth of the technology. Among the projects is the 1-gigawatt Stargate UAE project being developed by Abu Dhabi-based AI company G42 in partnership with technology giants OpenAI, Oracle and Nvidia. It will lie within the 5GW UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. ⁠Ms Al Nuaimi called for flexibility and co-operation in ​managing gas contracts to adapt to changing market conditions. “Contracts are very rigid, written with terms and conditions, and no matter how you craft them, they are not fit for different circumstances that face us in the market. So it's important for us to be flexible and to work together eventually.” Adnoc Gas on Tuesday also announced the singing of a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global market. The agreement comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the commercial capabilities of Adnoc Trading . Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs as well as end customers in more than 20 countries.

events.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
events.summary: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found. Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report. The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic. "This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation. Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic . Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more. So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage". Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting. 'I was working 60 hours a week so I quiet quit' Published 31 August 2022 The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults. Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record. In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%. "Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added. This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found. Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade". Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs". "But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added. Are you quiet quitting? Tell us how and why. events.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
events.summary: Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period. The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000. The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance". Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres. Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September. It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen . Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold. As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo. Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible". Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October. Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before. iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn). Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn. Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn. However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively. Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes. Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan. Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products. Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages. Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular. Watch: Would you buy Apple's $2,000 foldable phone? Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple. Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood". Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%. Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business. While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive". However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading. events.title: Amid global uncertainty, top bankers back Hong Kong’s role as mainland China’s gateway
events.summary: Banking leaders say demand for diversification, yuan funding and cross-border capital flows is reinforcing the city’s appeal Global financial executives have voiced confidence in Hong Kong’s role as a bridge between mainland China and the rest of the world and as a safe haven helping businesses and investors navigate geopolitical tensions and shifting global capital flows. Speaking at the city’s annual Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit on Tuesday, banking leaders discussed how financial institutions were rethinking business and operational strategies in an increasingly uncertain environment, while highlighting Hong Kong’s position as an international financial hub that facilitated international capital flows and helped companies adapt to geopolitical realignments. Jean Lemierre, chairman of BNP Paribas, said European companies operating in Asia were increasingly seeking local funding and currency-hedging capabilities to manage volatility in regional markets.

events.title: How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath
events.summary: Early voting for the midterms in New York last month Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums . Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines . President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious. Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger? As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections. We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching . But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months. Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history. We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.” Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties , typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election. One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell , a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts . But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to. We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate. We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise. Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign. Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins , the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn , a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year. Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. events.title: Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge
events.summary: Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court. Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant. CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software. Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom. "It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register . CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware. As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor. Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers , keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover. Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase , for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives. CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand. Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe. "The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel ," he said . "Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about." We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed. "The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register . The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers. "We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger." The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared. "Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added. The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

events.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
events.summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .  Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.  A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).  Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.  The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.  A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.  During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.  There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.  Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.  Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.  It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.  “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior. Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. events.title: The US-China thaw may not outlive the Trump era
events.summary: Andy’s view The prospect of steep losses for Republicans in today’s midterms and the lame-duck presidency that ensues regardless raise a fundamental question about the outlook for a budding US-China détente. Can warming superpower ties outlive the Trump era? I wouldn’t count on it. It’s not that an election humiliation would crimp US President Donald Trump’s diplomatic style. On the contrary, there’s every expectation it would give him even greater incentive to build his legacy on the world stage. But the current thaw is so much an artifice of his own unabashed admiration for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. And a backlash is brewing. Trump boasts of a “great friendship” with the Chinese strongman — they’ve held two summits so far this year, with plans of another meeting in Shenzhen this month, and a fourth in Miami in December — speaks of a G2 to manage global affairs, and waves away strategic concerns that might strain the bromance. (Asked about reports that Chinese satellite imagery was used by Iran to kill US troops, Trump told reporters on Air Force One: “They basically do what we do.“) Yet US policy on China remains very much in play, and debates will surely heat up after the midterms as the race to succeed Trump gets under way across both parties. Although Republican hawks have largely fallen silent in Trump’s second term, within the Beltway a bipartisan tough-on-China consensus is intact. Foreign policy elites complain that Trump is ceding the Western Pacific to Beijing (Evan Feigenbaum of the Carnegie Endowment mocks the administration’s “ reverse pivot from Asia ” as the Pentagon diverts warships and marines to the Gulf.) Tech hawks accuse Trump of throwing away the US lead in AI by greenlighting exports of advanced Nvidia chips to China, or turning a blind eye to illicit transfers. The Taiwan lobby is outraged at his transactional approach to the island. Moreover, such criticisms are likely to intensify if an angry Trump, smarting from midterm defeats, focuses even more of his attention on deal-making with Xi. Ali Wyne, a US-China specialist at the International Crisis Group, sees bipartisan frustration at Trump’s China policy winding up like a coil, ever more tightly as he gives ground to Xi, and eventually unspooling “violently and unpredictably.” The next president, Wyne told me, will inherit a weaker hand vis-à-vis China and is likely to be “far more permissive of competitive and even confrontational actions.” Certainly, Trump’s successor — from either party — won’t have nearly the same latitude to manage China ties; one former American diplomat calls the president “ his own China desk officer .” (Of course, there’s always a chance that Trump himself will flip before he steps down, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed Xi for unleashing the pandemic on the world and wrecking his reelection chances.) The late Henry Kissinger, the architect of Nixon’s 1972 opening to China, observed that “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” In Trump’s ardent pursuit of Xi, critics suggest the US president forgot that lesson. Once Trump goes, a return to a colder, harder, more calculating is in the cards. Notable In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Thomas L. Friedman argues that as the world’s leading AI superpowers, with shared interests in safeguarding against AI’s risks, the US and China may be pushed toward “ mutually assured collaboration .”
