events.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers amid Michigan Democratic feud
events.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) made a stunning last-minute endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before Michigan's closely watched Senate election . Why it matters: Her endorsement gives Rogers a striking photo op as his party tries to peel away Black and Jewish voters in a tight race that could determine control of the Senate . Driving the news: Stevens appeared Sunday alongside Rogers at Detroit's Perfecting Church, where she praised his support for Black-owned businesses. Stevens later posted an endorsement on X. In a video, she said Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign. "And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said. Stevens' appearance with Rogers was arranged at the last minute after the two spoke Sunday morning, per a person familiar. She had previously planned to attend a Detroit church service with El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.). How it happened: The dispute escalated last week after Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, announced he would vote for Rogers. Stevens demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices and remove a campaign ad featuring Tucker Carlson. On Friday night, after El-Sayed's campaign said Stevens would not be welcome at his events, Rogers called Stevens and told her he would welcome her support, according to a person familiar with the conversations. The next day, El-Sayed explicitly rejected the outside ad's contents, prompting Stevens to publicly welcome his remarks. On Sunday morning, Stevens called Rogers back to say she would endorse him, the person said. She told Rogers she remained a Democrat and believed the party would still win a Senate majority. The intrigue: A video posted by Detroit journalist Sam Robinson showed Stevens entering the church and praising Rogers . Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), who helped organize the original planned appearance with El-Sayed, told CNN she asked Stevens not to attend because the dispute had become distracting. Stevens narrowly lost the August Democratic primary to El-Sayed but endorsed him afterward. The other side: A person close to El-Sayed argued Stevens' endorsement could actually help him by reinforcing his anti-establishment appeal. "It's good for Abdul," the person said, portraying Stevens as a symbol of the Democratic establishment, Congress and support for the Israeli government. The endorsement "shows Abdul is the candidate of change and for the people of Michigan," the person added . What she's saying: Stevens told Politico that El-Sayed had made clear she wasn't welcome in his campaign. " Abdul has run a magnificent campaign," she told Politico's Adam Wren. "He just was clear that I wasn't a part of it. I mean, I respect him. I wish him well. He very well could win. It's a close race. I mean, I'm voting for the other guy, and maybe some others are too." What he's saying: President Trump welcomed Stevens' endorsement in a Truth Social post Sunday afternoon, calling it "BIG" and praising her "bravery." Trump said Stevens has a huge following and "virtually unparalleled" respect among Michigan's Black and Jewish voters. "Haley said what few people are willing to say," Trump wrote, calling the endorsement an act of loyalty to Michigan. Trump said at an Iowa rally later Sunday: "I'd love her to join the Republican Party. Actually, I think that could happen maybe." Flashback: In August, Trump called Stevens a "Radical Left Socialist" during the primary vote count. What we're watching: Michigan voters choose between Rogers and El-Sayed on Tuesday, with Democrats facing a crucial test of whether they can reunite their coalition. events.title: Where Dems eyeing the White House are putting their midterm chips
events.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro 's chances of being a presidential contender in 2028 are riding on his winning reelection in a landslide Tuesday. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's future hinges on whether a fellow progressive can carry a swing state, for once. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has to show that his congressional redistricting gambit worked for Democrats — and he needs to beat back a state wealth tax proposal supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Driving the news: Democrats eyeing White House runs have spent the past year preparing to emerge from Tuesday's midterms with momentum, and an argument for a 2028 candidacy. They want Democrats to do well — but to each, some races are especially important. Some have focused their time and money on particular contests for ideological reasons, or a desire to show strength in their home states. Others have hedged their bets across the nation, so that Tuesday is unlikely to be a huge victory or a significant defeat. Here's how the top potential Democratic contenders for president have placed their bets in this week's elections — and what success or failure will look like for them. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez A great night: AOC has wagered just about everything on the Senate race in Michigan, where she's said that a win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would "break open the entire political calculus in America" and show that "anybody can win anywhere." She's weighing whether to run for president or the Senate, and much of her electability argument for a national campaign hinges on an El-Sayed victory. Progressives are desperate to establish that one of their own can carry a presidential battleground state. Ocasio-Cortez has contributed $1 million to help El-Sayed and stumped for him at several events. An El-Sayed victory "would prove to the country, and the world, that competent, courageous progressive populists can win in the most competitive swing states in America," said Bhavik Lathia, a left-wing strategist from Michigan. "The implications for 2028 would be enormous." AOC would get bonus points Tuesday if other progressives she's supporting — such as House candidate Randy Villegas in California and Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida — win their swing-seat races. Worst-case scenario: If El-Sayed loses, many progressives think AOC would be less likely to run for president. That's why she's widely viewed as having more on the line Tuesday than any other potential Democratic contender for president, followed by Shapiro. Josh Shapiro A great night: Shapiro needs to win so big Tuesday that it makes Democratic presidential primary voters see his technocratic "get shit done" brand of governing as the party's best bet to take down the GOP in 2028. Shapiro is less known nationally than many 2028 hopefuls, and that has been by choice. He's largely focused on Pennsylvania this year, even as would-be rivals for president crisscrossed the country. A blowout in America's biggest swing state could help him stand out. A good night for Shapiro would be defeating Republican Stacy Garrity by double digits and carrying three Democratic House candidates — Janelle Stelson, Bob Brooks and Paige Cognetti — across the finish line to defeat Republican incumbents. He'd have a great night if his coattails were so long that he pulled a fourth Democratic House hopeful, Bob Harvie, to victory — taking down GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who's known for surviving difficult electoral cycles. Shapiro would get extra credit if he helped Democrats win a trifecta in Harrisburg for the first time in decades by flipping control of the state Senate. Worst-case scenario: If only one or two Democrats in his state flip House seats or he wins by less than 10 points, Shapiro's setup for 2028 would fall short. Andy Beshear A great night: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who moonlights as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, put his chips this year on helping his party take control of a majority of the nation's governorships. Beshear would earn bragging rights if Democrats flip the two governors' seats needed to do that. He's eyeing the races in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. "I am laser-focused on these governors' races," he told us, arguing that the results will help determine what's possible in the 2028 presidential contest. "Rob Sand wins Iowa, Iowa's in play. When Amy Acton wins Ohio, Ohio's in play," Beshear said. Worst-case scenario: Beshear made enemies among some Latino Democrats this year when the DGA rebuffed calls to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor. If Hinojosa loses to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by a razor-thin margin or pulls an upset, Beshear's decision-making will come under heavy scrutiny — and he could have a problem with some Latino leaders in a 2028 campaign. Gavin Newsom A great night: Newsom won over many MS NOW moms and "resistance" liberals across the country when he responded to President Trump's push to create more GOP House seats in other states by fighting back with a successful voter proposition to do the same in California. His goal has been to gain five Democratic seats from the change to help Democrats take back the House. That's his bar to clear Tuesday. Some political insiders now think Democrats could gain 20 or more House seats across the country, so Newsom's contribution might not be as decisive as once thought. Newsom would score a political win if a proposed billionaire wealth tax on the ballot in his home state, which he opposes, fails. Worst-case scenario: If California voters approve the tax or Democrats flip fewer than five House seats there, it would diminish Newsom's California clout. Jon Ossoff A great night: A long-running knock against Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has been that he won his seat in 2021 by riding his fellow Peach State Sen. Raphael Warnock's coattails. Ossoff has the chance this year to prove he doesn't need Warnock, who isn't on the ticket. He's on his way to doing just that, with polls showing him comfortably leading GOP challenger Mike Collins. But to have a truly great night, Ossoff needs to show that he has enough sway in his state to help pull Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory. Worst-case scenario: If Bottoms were to lose, Democrats say, Ossoff would be even less likely to leave the Senate for a presidential run, since Georgia's governor has the power to make a temporary appointment if a senator steps down. Ossoff, for his part, has said he has "zero interest" in a 2028 bid. But Barack Obama made similar comments before jumping into the 2008 race. Kamala Harris A great night: Former Vice President Kamala Harris has rallied voters to fight back against GOP redistricting and a recent Supreme Court decision on the Voting Rights Act that threatens Black representation in Congress. events.title: AI trade falters after disappointing tech earnings
events.summary: Some investors are dialing back their expectations for US economic growth, as warning signs flashed red over the sustainability of the country’s breakneck AI buildout. The tech-heavy Nasdaq slid into correction territory on Friday as investors unwound their AI bets. Intel stock plunged 29%, the chipmaker’s biggest single-day selloff since the 1970s; concerns mounted over hyperscaler spending after disappointing Amazon and Google earnings; and S&P Global revised Meta’s outlook to “negative,” citing its high capex . Earnings misses are generating “ sober questions ” about the AI investments powering the economy, a strategist told Bloomberg. “You can’t find the growth slowdown in any of the economic data,” a portfolio manager told the Financial Times. “But… a reassessment of AI means a reassessment of growth expectations .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: North Korea blamed for crypto heist
events.summary: The FBI said that North Korea was responsible for stealing $6.3 billion from Binance last week in the largest-ever crypto heist , dealing a blow to the sector’s dream of becoming a mainstream asset. The incident follows other notable crypto thefts linked to Pyongyang, which devotes state resources to cultivating hackers, many of whom are China-based, to fuel an economic renaissance: North Korea’s economy expanded 3.7% in 2024 , the fastest rate in eight years, driving a construction boom that’s visible from space. AI threatens to supercharge North Korea’s cyber activities, an expert told the Financial Times: “AI has given hackers wings. The gates of hell have opened because North Korea has such a strong determination to carry out these attacks.” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
events.summary: US approval of the sale of 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine offers little immediate relief, analysts said, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that deliveries could take “a few years.” The $2.1 billion sale — funded through donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway — underscores Washington’s shift to relying on allies to cover the costs of Ukraine’s military assistance. As global interceptor stockpiles dwindle and Russian attacks intensify, Zelenskyy urged the US and Europe to provide interceptors “ now ” rather than wait for new production. But Washington’s own military priorities may constrain supplies: “Perhaps they intend to restart the war in Iran and don’t know how many Patriot missiles they’re going to need for themselves ,” a former American ambassador to NATO told Euronews. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: Wave of discontent sweeps Europe
events.summary: Gen Z-led protests in multiple German cities turned violent Saturday, with rioters looting stores and confronting police , as political and fiscal crises unleash a wave of discontent across Europe. France saw a third weekend of protests , which have also spread to Italy, Belgium, and Albania, driven by what a Belgian politician derided as the “TikTokization” of protests. The Élysée called a meeting last month with platforms to demand tighter moderation , as protesters of varying political outlooks took to the streets: “One crisis layers on top of the other,” the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations told the BBC, producing algorithmically sorted “tribes,” and “a sense of ‘ my crisis is more important than your crisis .’” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering stroke
events.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) had a stroke Saturday and is being treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital, his office said Sunday. The big picture: Murphy is one of the Senate's more visible Democrats and has been traveling the country campaigning ahead of Tuesday's midterms . Driving the news: Murphy, 53, began experiencing numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game Saturday, according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. He was taken to a hospital where doctors determined he had a stroke and transferred him to Johns Hopkins for monitoring. "The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said in a statement. What they're saying: President Trump told reporters Sunday afternoon that he had just learned of Murphy's hospitalization and would reach out to him "at the right time." Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who had a stroke during his 2022 Senate campaign, said in a statement he understands "all too well how much this impacts your life" and that his family is rooting for Murphy's recovery. What's next: The statement did not specify the severity of the stroke or when Murphy might be discharged. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments by President Trump and Sen. John Fetterman.
